Colorectal cancer is one of the most common malignancies worldwide, with approximately 1.8 million new cases diagnosed annually. A substantial proportion of patients with colorectal cancer will develop liver metastases, which are a major cause of morbidity and mortality. Surgical resection of colorectal liver metastases (CRLM) offers the potential for cure, but is often limited by the extent of liver involvement and the volume of the future remnant liver (FRL). The FRL is the portion of the liver that will remain after surgical resection, and its volume is a critical determinant of post-operative liver function. Patients with a small FRL are at increased risk of post-operative liver insufficiency, which can be fatal.

In an effort to increase the volume of the FRL and thereby expand the indications for surgical resection, various strategies have been developed. One such strategy is right portal vein embolisation (RPVE), which involves the selective occlusion of the right portal vein to induce atrophy of the right liver and hypertrophy of the left liver, including segments 2 and 3. RPVE has been shown to be a safe and effective means of increasing the volume of the FRL, thereby enabling surgical resection in patients who would otherwise be ineligible.

However, the optimal technique for RPVE remains unclear. Some studies have suggested that embolisation of segment 4, in addition to RPVE, may induce greater hypertrophy of the FRL. Segment 4 is a portion of the left liver that is often considered to be part of the FRL, but its embolisation may help to redirect portal blood flow to segments 2 and 3, potentially enhancing their hypertrophy. On the other hand, embolisation of segment 4 may also increase the risk of complications, such as liver insufficiency or bile duct injury.

Several studies have investigated the effects of RPVE with and without segment 4 embolisation on FRL hypertrophy, but the results have been inconsistent. Some studies have reported greater hypertrophy of the FRL with RPVE plus segment 4 embolisation, while others have found no significant difference. These conflicting results may be due to differences in patient populations, embolisation techniques, and methods of assessing liver volume and hypertrophy.

One of the major limitations of prior studies is the use of heterogeneous patient populations. Many studies have included patients with varying types of liver disease, including primary liver cancer, metastatic disease from other sites, and benign liver lesions. These differences in patient populations may confound the results, making it difficult to draw firm conclusions about the effects of RPVE with and without segment 4 embolisation.

Another limitation of prior studies is the use of hypertrophy metrics that are sensitive to baseline variables, such as liver function and body mass index. For example, some studies have used the kinetic growth rate (KGR) of the FRL as a measure of hypertrophy, but this metric can be influenced by factors such as underlying liver disease and portal vein pressure. Other studies have used the degree of hypertrophy (DH) of the FRL, which is a more direct measure of liver growth, but may still be affected by baseline variables such as liver volume and function.

In the present study, we aimed to investigate the effects of RPVE with and without segment 4 embolisation on FRL hypertrophy in a homogeneous population of patients with CRLM. We used a standardized approach to assessing liver volume and hypertrophy, and controlled for potential confounding variables such as prior chemotherapy and liver function. Our goal was to determine whether RPVE plus segment 4 embolisation results in greater hypertrophy of the FRL than RPVE alone, and to explore the potential implications of this finding for the management of patients with CRLM.

The management of CRLM is a complex and multidisciplinary process, involving surgeons, oncologists, radiologists, and other healthcare professionals. The decision to undertake surgical resection, and the choice of surgical technique, depend on a variety of factors, including the extent of liver involvement, the volume of the FRL, and the patient's underlying health status. RPVE, with or without segment 4 embolisation, is one of several strategies that may be used to increase the volume of the FRL and enable surgical resection. A better understanding of the effects of these strategies on FRL hypertrophy and patient outcomes is essential for optimizing the management of patients with CRLM.

In recent years, there has been increasing interest in the use of minimally invasive techniques, such as radiofrequency ablation and stereotactic body radiation therapy, for the treatment of CRLM. These techniques offer the potential for reduced morbidity and mortality, compared with traditional surgical resection, but may not be suitable for all patients. The use of RPVE, with or without segment 4 embolisation, may help to expand the indications for surgical resection, and to improve outcomes for patients with CRLM.

The present study is a retrospective cohort study, conducted at a single tertiary care center. We included consecutive patients who underwent RPVE or RPVE plus segment 4 embolisation for CRLM, between 2010 and 2015. Patients who had undergone prior major hepatic resection, or who had inadequate imaging data, were excluded from the study. We collected data on patient demographics, clinical characteristics, and outcomes, including liver volume and hypertrophy, and overall survival. Our goal was to determine whether RPVE plus segment 4 embolisation results in greater hypertrophy of the FRL than RPVE alone, and to explore the potential implications of this finding for the management of patients with CRLM.

This retrospective cohort study included consecutive patients who underwent right portal vein embolization (RPVE) or RPVE with additional embolization of segment 4 (RPVE + 4) for colorectal cancer liver metastases (CRLM) at a single tertiary referral center between 2010 and 2015. Patients were identified from a prospectively maintained database of all patients undergoing portal vein embolization (PVE) procedures. Inclusion criteria consisted of patients with CRLM who had not undergone prior major hepatic resection and had available imaging for volumetric analysis. Exclusion criteria included prior major hepatic resection, lack of available imaging, and insufficient clinical data.

Data were extracted from hospital electronic records, including patient demographics, clinical characteristics, and laboratory results. Information regarding prior chemotherapy, presence of metastases in the future remnant liver (FRL), and performance of subsegmental metastasectomy in the FRL was also collected. Chemotherapy regimens and number of cycles were recorded, as well as the timing of chemotherapy relative to PVE. The decision to undertake RPVE or RPVE + 4 was made by a multidisciplinary team, taking into account individual patient anatomy, tumor distribution, and planned surgical approach.

All patients underwent cross-sectional imaging, including computed tomography (CT) or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), before and after PVE. Imaging protocols consisted of standardized CT or MRI scans with contrast enhancement, allowing for accurate volumetric assessments of liver segments. Volumetric analysis of segments 2-3 was performed using specialized software, with measurements corrected for standardized liver volume. The degree of hypertrophy (DH) of segments 2-3 was calculated as the percentage increase in volume after PVE, relative to the pre-embolization volume.

PVE procedures were performed by experienced interventional radiologists using a standardized technique. Under conscious sedation and local anesthesia, a percutaneous transhepatic approach was used to access the right portal vein. Embolization was performed using a combination of coils, plugs, and particulate agents, with the goal of achieving complete occlusion of the right portal vein and, in the case of RPVE + 4, segment 4 portal vein branches. Technical success was defined as complete occlusion of the targeted portal vein branches, confirmed by post-procedure imaging.

The primary outcome measure was the degree of hypertrophy of segments 2-3, calculated as the percentage increase in volume after PVE. Secondary outcome measures included the kinetic growth rate (KGR) of the FRL, calculated as the percentage increase in volume per week, and the incidence of complications related to PVE. Patient survival was also evaluated, with follow-up data collected from hospital records and national cancer registries.

To minimize bias and ensure accurate volumetric assessments, a single experienced radiologist, blinded to patient outcomes, performed all volumetric analyses. Intra- and inter-observer variability was assessed using a subset of 20 patients, with excellent agreement observed between repeated measurements (intra-class correlation coefficient >0.9).

Statistical analysis was performed using dedicated software, with results expressed as mean ± standard deviation or median (interquartile range) as appropriate. Comparisons between RPVE and RPVE + 4 groups were made using Student's t-test or Mann-Whitney U test, as appropriate. Multivariate analysis was performed to identify potential confounding variables associated with the decision to undertake RPVE or RPVE + 4, including age, sex, presence of FRL metastases, and prior chemotherapy. A p-value <0.05 was considered statistically significant.

Ninety-nine patients underwent portal vein embolisation (PVE) for colorectal cancer liver metastases (CRLM) between 2010 and 2015, of whom 60 met the inclusion criteria. The primary reason for exclusion was prior major hepatic resection, which had been performed in 21 patients. A further 18 patients were excluded due to lack of available imaging. Thirty-eight patients underwent right portal vein embolisation (RPVE), and 22 underwent RPVE with additional embolisation of segment 4 (RPVE + 4). The decision to undertake RPVE or RPVE + 4 was made on a case-by-case basis, taking into account the individual patient's anatomy and the distribution of their liver metastases.

The baseline characteristics of the patients are shown in Table 1. The median age was 63 years (interquartile range 56-70), and 35 patients (58%) were male. Forty-five patients (75%) had undergone prior chemotherapy, with a median of 6 cycles (interquartile range 4-8). Eighteen patients (30%) had metastases in the future remnant liver (FRL), and 16 patients (27%) had undergone subsegmental metastasectomy in the FRL. The median carbohydrate antigen 19-9 (CA19-9) level was 35 kU/L (interquartile range 15-75).

Volumetric assessments of segments 2-3 were made on cross-sectional imaging before and after embolisation, using a standardized protocol. The median time to follow-up imaging after PVE was 35 days (interquartile range 30-49). The degree of hypertrophy (DH) of segments 2/3 was calculated as the percentage increase in volume, corrected for standardized liver volume. The results are shown in Table 2. The median DH of segments 2/3 was 9.5% (interquartile range 6.2-13.1%) in the RPVE group, and 12.1% (interquartile range 8.5-16.3%) in the RPVE + 4 group.

Comparison of the DH of segments 2/3 between the RPVE and RPVE + 4 groups showed a significant difference (p = 0.011). The mean DH of segments 2/3 was 7.7 ± 1.8% in the RPVE group, and 11.3 ± 2.6% in the RPVE + 4 group. This represents a 47% increase in DH in the RPVE + 4 group compared to the RPVE group. No significant difference was found in the kinetic growth rate (KGR) of segments 2/3 between the two groups (p = 0.23).

To assess for potential confounding variables, we examined the relationship between baseline characteristics and the decision to undertake RPVE or RPVE + 4. No significant association was found between the decision to undertake RPVE or RPVE + 4 and any of the baseline variables, including age, sex, prior chemotherapy, presence of metastases in the FRL, or CA19-9 level. This suggests that the decision to undertake RPVE or RPVE + 4 was not influenced by these factors, and that the observed difference in DH between the two groups is unlikely to be due to confounding.

We also examined the relationship between DH and clinical outcomes. The median overall survival was 2.4 years (interquartile range 1.8-3.5), and was not significantly different between the RPVE and RPVE + 4 groups (p = 0.56). The 1-year and 3-year survival rates were 83% and 44%, respectively, in the RPVE group, and 86% and 50%, respectively, in the RPVE + 4 group. No significant difference was found in the rate of postoperative complications or liver failure between the two groups.

In conclusion, the results of this study show that RPVE + 4 results in a significantly greater increase in DH of segments 2/3 compared to RPVE in patients with CRLM. This difference is unlikely to be due to confounding variables, and suggests that embolisation of segment 4 in addition to RPVE may be a useful strategy to induce greater hypertrophy of the FRL in patients undergoing major hepatic resection. However, the clinical significance of this finding is uncertain, as we did not find a significant difference in overall survival or clinical outcomes between the two groups. Further study is needed to fully understand the implications of this finding and to determine the optimal approach to PVE in patients with CRLM.

Mycotoxins, a class of naturally occurring compounds produced by various fungi, pose a significant threat to human and animal health due to their toxic, carcinogenic, and mutagenic properties [1]. These compounds can contaminate a wide range of food products, including grains, nuts, and spices, leading to significant economic losses and health risks [2]. The most common mycotoxins include aflatoxins, ochratoxin A, zearalenone, and trichothecenes, which are produced by fungi such as Aspergillus, Fusarium, and Penicillium [3]. The ingestion of mycotoxin-contaminated food can lead to a range of health problems, including liver and kidney damage, immunosuppression, and even cancer [4].

### Background and Context
The detoxification of mycotoxins is a critical step in preventing these adverse health effects. Various methods have been developed to detoxify mycotoxins, including physical, chemical, and biological approaches [5]. However, many of these methods have significant limitations, such as the loss of nutritional value, the formation of toxic byproducts, or the requirement for specialized equipment [6]. Enzymatic transformation, on the other hand, offers a promising alternative for the detoxification of mycotoxins. Enzymes are highly specific, efficient, and environmentally friendly biocatalysts that can convert mycotoxins into less toxic or non-toxic compounds [7]. The use of enzymes for mycotoxin detoxification has been extensively studied in recent years, and several enzymes have been identified as potential candidates for this purpose [8].

### Enzyme-Mediated Detoxification Mechanisms
The enzyme-mediated detoxification of mycotoxins involves a complex series of biochemical reactions, which are catalyzed by specific enzymes. These enzymes can be classified into several classes, including oxidoreductases, transferases, hydrolases, and lyases [9]. Each of these enzyme classes has a unique mechanism of action, which involves the binding of the mycotoxin to the enzyme's active site, followed by a series of chemical transformations that convert the mycotoxin into a less toxic compound [10]. For example, the enzyme lactonohydrolase has been shown to hydrolyze the lactone ring of aflatoxins, leading to the formation of less toxic compounds [11]. Similarly, the enzyme carboxypeptidase has been shown to cleave the peptide bond of ochratoxin A, leading to the formation of a less toxic compound [12].

### Molecular Modeling and Docking Studies
Molecular modeling and docking studies have been widely used to investigate the binding of mycotoxins to enzymes and to clarify the catalytic mechanisms involved [13]. These studies involve the use of computational models to predict the binding of mycotoxins to the active site of enzymes and to simulate the chemical transformations that occur during the detoxification process [14]. For example, molecular docking studies have been used to investigate the binding of aflatoxins to the enzyme lactonohydrolase, and to clarify the mechanism of lactone ring hydrolysis [15]. Similarly, molecular modeling studies have been used to investigate the binding of ochratoxin A to the enzyme carboxypeptidase, and to clarify the mechanism of peptide bond cleavage [16].

### Origins and Availability of Enzymes
The origins and availability of enzymes for mycotoxin detoxification are critical factors that determine their practical potential. Enzymes can be obtained from a wide range of sources, including plants, animals, fungi, and bacteria [17]. For example, the enzyme lactonohydrolase has been isolated from the bacterium Rhodopseudomonas palustris [18], while the enzyme carboxypeptidase has been isolated from the fungus Aspergillus niger [19]. The availability of these enzymes can be improved through recombinant DNA technology, which allows for the production of large quantities of enzymes in microorganisms such as Escherichia coli [20]. Additionally, the use of enzyme combinations, which involve the use of multiple enzymes with different specificities, can improve the efficiency and effectiveness of mycotoxin detoxification [21].

### Multifunctional Enzyme Combinations
The use of multifunctional enzyme combinations is a promising approach for the detoxification of mycotoxins. This approach involves the use of multiple enzymes with different specificities, which can act synergistically to convert mycotoxins into less toxic or non-toxic compounds [22]. For example, the combination of the enzymes lactonohydrolase and carboxypeptidase has been shown to be effective in detoxifying aflatoxins and ochratoxin A [23]. Similarly, the combination of the enzymes oxidoreductase and transferase has been shown to be effective in detoxifying zearalenone and trichothecenes [24]. The use of multifunctional enzyme combinations can improve the efficiency and effectiveness of mycotoxin detoxification, and can provide a promising solution for the prevention of mycotoxin-related health problems.

### Conclusion and Future Directions
In conclusion, enzymes offer a promising approach for the detoxification of mycotoxins. The use of enzymes with different specificities, such as lactonohydrolase and carboxypeptidase, can convert mycotoxins into less toxic or non-toxic compounds. Molecular modeling and docking studies can provide valuable insights into the binding of mycotoxins to enzymes and the catalytic mechanisms involved. The origins and availability of enzymes, as well as the use of multifunctional enzyme combinations, are critical factors that determine their practical potential. Future studies should focus on the development of efficient and cost-effective methods for the production and application of enzymes for mycotoxin detoxification, as well as the investigation of the potential health benefits of enzyme-mediated detoxification. Additionally, the development of novel enzymes with improved specificities and activities, such as through protein engineering and directed evolution, can provide new opportunities for the prevention of mycotoxin-related health problems [25].

The increasing demand for high-speed data transmission has driven the development of Optical Packet/Burst Switched (OPS/OBS) networks, which have emerged as a promising technology for future internet infrastructure. OPS/OBS networks offer several advantages over traditional circuit-switched networks, including improved bandwidth utilization, reduced latency, and increased scalability. However, the packet-switched nature of OPS/OBS networks also introduces new challenges, such as packet loss due to contentions and path failures, which can significantly impact the network's performance and reliability.

Packet loss in OPS/OBS networks can occur due to various reasons, including contention resolution, buffer overflow, and physical layer impairments. Contention resolution is a critical issue in OPS/OBS networks, where multiple packets may arrive at the same switching node simultaneously, competing for the same output port. In such cases, some packets may be dropped or delayed, resulting in packet loss. Additionally, physical layer impairments, such as signal attenuation, noise, and crosstalk, can also cause packet errors or loss during transmission. These packet losses can have significant impacts on the network's performance, including reduced throughput, increased delay, and decreased quality of service (QoS).

To mitigate packet loss and improve the reliability of OPS/OBS networks, various techniques have been proposed, including error correction coding, forward error correction (FEC), and path diversity. Error correction coding involves adding redundant information to the packets, which can be used to detect and correct errors during transmission. FEC is a specific type of error correction coding that adds redundant information to the packets, which can be used to correct errors without the need for retransmission. Path diversity involves transmitting packets over multiple disjoint paths, which can improve the reliability of the network by providing multiple routes for packet transmission.

While these techniques can improve the reliability of OPS/OBS networks, they also introduce additional overhead and complexity. For example, error correction coding and FEC require additional bandwidth and processing resources, which can increase the latency and reduce the throughput of the network. Path diversity, on the other hand, requires the establishment and maintenance of multiple disjoint paths, which can be complex and resource-intensive.

Recently, there has been a growing interest in exploiting the benefits of source coding and path diversity to provide efficient means for recovering from packet loss and improving the secrecy of OPS/OBS networks. Source coding involves encoding the packets at the source node using erasure codes, which can be used to recover the original packets in case of packet loss. Erasure codes are a type of error correction code that can recover the original data even if some of the coded packets are lost or corrupted during transmission. By combining source coding with path diversity, it is possible to provide a unified view of QoS in OPS/OBS networks, linking the interactions between survivability, performance, and secrecy.

Survivability, performance, and secrecy are three critical aspects of QoS in OPS/OBS networks. Survivability refers to the ability of the network to maintain its functionality even in the presence of failures or attacks. Performance refers to the ability of the network to provide high throughput, low latency, and reliable packet transmission. Secrecy, on the other hand, refers to the ability of the network to protect the confidentiality and integrity of the transmitted data. By exploiting the benefits of source coding and path diversity, it is possible to provide a unified view of these QoS aspects, enabling the design of more efficient and reliable OPS/OBS networks.

In this paper, we present the Coded Packet Transport (CPT) scheme, a novel transport mechanism for OPS/OBS networks that exploits the combined benefits of source coding and path diversity. The CPT scheme employs erasure coding at the OPS/OBS ingress node to form coded packets, which are transmitted on disjoint paths from the ingress node to an egress node in the network. The CPT scheme provides a unified view of QoS in OPS/OBS networks, linking the interactions between survivability, performance, and secrecy. We provide analytical models that illustrate how QoS aspects of CPT are affected by the number of disjoint paths, packet overhead, and processing delay. The CPT scheme offers several advantages over traditional transport mechanisms, including improved reliability, reduced latency, and increased secrecy. The CPT scheme is also flexible and scalable, making it suitable for a wide range of OPS/OBS network architectures and applications.

The rest of this paper is organized as follows. In the next section, we provide an overview of the CPT scheme, including its architecture and operation. We then present analytical models that illustrate the performance of the CPT scheme, including its reliability, latency, and secrecy. We also discuss the advantages and limitations of the CPT scheme, as well as its potential applications in OPS/OBS networks. Finally, we conclude the paper with a summary of the key findings and future research directions.

To evaluate the performance of the Coded Packet Transport (CPT) scheme, we developed a comprehensive methodology that incorporates analytical modeling, simulation, and experimental validation. Our approach involves several key steps, including network modeling, erasure coding, path selection, and performance analysis.

First, we modeled the Optical Packet/Burst Switched (OPS/OBS) network as a graph, where nodes represent optical switches and edges represent fiber links between them. Each link is characterized by its bandwidth, latency, and error probability. We assumed that the network is operated in a slotted mode, where time is divided into fixed-length slots, and each slot can accommodate a single packet. Packet arrivals at the ingress node are modeled as a Poisson process, and packet lengths are assumed to be exponentially distributed.

Next, we employed erasure coding at the OPS/OBS ingress node to generate coded packets. Specifically, we used a Reed-Solomon (RS) code, which is a type of non-binary erasure code that can correct errors and erasures. The RS code takes a block of k information packets and adds redundant packets to form a coded block of length n, such that any k packets from the coded block can be used to recover the original information. The number of redundant packets, n-k, determines the code's error-correcting capability.

To select disjoint paths from the ingress node to the egress node, we used a modified version of the Suurballe's algorithm, which is a well-known algorithm for finding two disjoint paths in a graph. The algorithm first finds the shortest path from the ingress node to the egress node, and then finds the next shortest path that is disjoint from the first path. We repeated this process until we found the desired number of disjoint paths.

Depression is a common mental illness that affects an estimated 300 million people worldwide, making it a significant public health concern [1]. The impact of depression on individuals, families, and societies is profound, with effects on physical health, social relationships, and economic productivity [2]. Despite its prevalence and burden, depression remains stigmatised in many communities, leading to barriers in seeking help and accessing care [3]. This stigma is not limited to the general public, as even healthcare professionals, including non-psychiatric physicians, may hold negative attitudes towards depression [4]. Such attitudes can affect the quality of care provided to depressed patients, making it essential to investigate and understand the attitudes of non-psychiatric physicians towards depression.

Non-psychiatric physicians, including primary care physicians, internists, and specialists in other medical fields, play a crucial role in the detection, diagnosis, and management of depression [5]. They are often the first point of contact for patients with depression, and their attitudes and beliefs can influence the care and treatment that patients receive [6]. However, non-psychiatric physicians may not always feel confident or competent in managing depression, which can lead to inadequate care and referral to specialist services [7]. Furthermore, the stigma associated with mental illness can be a significant barrier to care, with many patients preferring to consult non-psychiatric physicians for physical complaints rather than mental health concerns [8].

The stigma surrounding depression is a complex issue, influenced by cultural, social, and professional factors [9]. In many societies, including Saudi Arabia, mental illness is often viewed as a personal weakness or a sign of poor character, rather than a medical condition that requires treatment [10]. This stigma can be perpetuated by healthcare professionals, including non-psychiatric physicians, who may hold negative attitudes towards depression or view it as a less legitimate medical condition than physical illnesses [11]. Such attitudes can affect the care and treatment of depressed patients, leading to inadequate management and poor health outcomes [12].

The importance of understanding the attitudes of non-psychiatric physicians towards depression is highlighted by the significant role they play in the healthcare system [13]. In Saudi Arabia, non-psychiatric physicians are often the primary caregivers for patients with depression, and their attitudes and beliefs can influence the care and treatment that patients receive [14]. However, there is a lack of research on the attitudes of non-psychiatric physicians towards depression in Saudi Arabia, making it essential to investigate this issue [15]. This study aims to address this gap by exploring the attitudes of non-psychiatric physicians towards depression in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia.

The investigation of attitudes towards depression among non-psychiatric physicians is crucial for several reasons. Firstly, understanding the attitudes and beliefs of non-psychiatric physicians can help identify barriers to care and inform strategies to improve the management of depression [16]. Secondly, exploring the attitudes of non-psychiatric physicians can provide insights into the cultural and social factors that influence the stigma surrounding depression [17]. Finally, this study can inform the development of training programs and educational initiatives to improve the knowledge, skills, and attitudes of non-psychiatric physicians in managing depression [18].

The Revised Depression Attitude Questionnaire (R-DAQ) is a widely used instrument to assess attitudes towards depression among healthcare professionals [19]. The R-DAQ has been validated in several studies and has been shown to be a reliable and effective tool for measuring attitudes towards depression [20]. In this study, the R-DAQ will be used to survey non-psychiatric physicians in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, and explore their attitudes towards depression. The findings of this study will provide valuable insights into the attitudes of non-psychiatric physicians towards depression and inform strategies to improve the care and management of depressed patients in Saudi Arabia.

The context of this study is important to consider, as the cultural and social factors that influence attitudes towards depression can vary significantly between different countries and regions [21]. In Saudi Arabia, the cultural and social norms surrounding mental illness are complex and influenced by Islamic values and traditional practices [22]. The stigma associated with mental illness is significant, and many patients may prefer to seek care from non-psychiatric physicians rather than specialist mental health services [23]. Furthermore, the healthcare system in Saudi Arabia is undergoing significant changes, with an emphasis on improving the quality and accessibility of care [24]. This study will provide valuable insights into the attitudes of non-psychiatric physicians towards depression in this context and inform strategies to improve the care and management of depressed patients in Saudi Arabia.

In conclusion, the investigation of attitudes towards depression among non-psychiatric physicians is essential to improve the care and management of depressed patients. This study aims to explore the attitudes of non-psychiatric physicians towards depression in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, using the R-DAQ. The findings of this study will provide valuable insights into the attitudes and beliefs of non-psychiatric physicians and inform strategies to improve the care and management of depressed patients in Saudi Arabia. The study will also contribute to the existing literature on the stigma surrounding depression and the importance of addressing this issue in healthcare settings [25]. By exploring the attitudes of non-psychiatric physicians towards depression, this study will provide a foundation for developing training programs and educational initiatives to improve the knowledge, skills, and attitudes of non-psychiatric physicians in managing depression [26].

This study employed a cross-sectional design to investigate the attitudes of non-psychiatric physicians towards depression in four tertiary centres in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia. The study was conducted over a period of six months, from January to June 2022. The target population consisted of non-psychiatric physicians working in the four tertiary centres, which included King Khalid University Hospital, King Fahad Medical City, King Abdulaziz Medical City, and King Salman Hospital. A total of 380 non-psychiatric physicians participated in the study, representing a response rate of 75% [1].

The sampling frame consisted of all non-psychiatric physicians working in the four tertiary centres, including specialists and residents from various departments such as internal medicine, surgery, paediatrics, and obstetrics and gynaecology. The exclusion criteria included psychiatric physicians, physicians who had received specialized training in psychiatry, and those who had less than one year of experience in their current position [2]. The sample size was calculated using the formula for cross-sectional studies, with a margin of error of 5% and a confidence level of 95% [3].

Data collection was conducted using the Revised Depression Attitude Questionnaire (R-DAQ), a validated instrument that measures attitudes towards depression among healthcare professionals [4]. The R-DAQ consists of 20 items, each rated on a five-point Likert scale, ranging from strongly disagree to strongly agree. The questionnaire assesses four subscales: attitudes towards depression, confidence in dealing with depression, perceived stigma, and willingness to deal with depression [5]. The R-DAQ has been widely used in previous studies to assess attitudes towards depression among healthcare professionals, with reported Cronbach's alpha values ranging from 0.70 to 0.85 [6].

The study protocol was approved by the Institutional Review Board (IRB) of each participating hospital, and informed consent was obtained from all participants prior to data collection. The questionnaire was distributed to the participants in paper format, and completed questionnaires were collected by the research team. To ensure anonymity and confidentiality, participants were assured that their responses would not be linked to their personal identities [7].

Data analysis was performed using the Statistical Package for Social Sciences (SPSS) version 25. Descriptive statistics, including means and standard deviations, were calculated to summarize the demographic characteristics of the participants and their attitudes towards depression. Inferential statistics, including t-tests and analysis of variance (ANOVA), were used to compare the attitudes of non-psychiatric physicians towards depression across different demographic variables, such as age, gender, and department of practice [8]. The internal consistency of the R-DAQ was assessed using Cronbach's alpha, and the results showed a high level of reliability, with a Cronbach's alpha value of 0.82 [9].

To assess the validity of the R-DAQ, a pilot study was conducted with a sample of 20 non-psychiatric physicians, and the results showed a high level of face validity and content validity [10]. The pilot study also provided an opportunity to test the feasibility of the data collection process and to identify any potential issues with the questionnaire [11]. The results of the pilot study were used to refine the data collection process and to ensure that the questionnaire was clear and easy to understand.

The survey was completed by 380 non-psychiatric physicians, with a response rate of 95%. The majority of participants were males (73.2%), and the most common specialty was internal medicine (31.1%) [Table 1]. The mean age of participants was 35.4 years (SD = 6.2), and the mean number of years of experience was 8.5 (SD = 5.1). Most participants (85.5%) reported that they had received some training in psychiatry during their medical education, but only 21.1% reported feeling confident in diagnosing and treating depression [Table 2].

The Revised Depression Attitude Questionnaire (R-DAQ) was used to assess participants' attitudes towards depression. The R-DAQ consists of 22 items, each rated on a 5-point Likert scale, ranging from "strongly disagree" to "strongly agree". The mean total score on the R-DAQ was 63.2 (SD = 10.1), indicating a generally positive attitude towards depression [Table 3]. However, there was a significant variation in scores across different specialties, with obstetricians and gynecologists having the most positive attitudes (mean = 66.5, SD = 9.5) and surgeons having the least positive attitudes (mean = 59.2, SD = 10.5) [Table 4].

Factor analysis of the R-DAQ items revealed three underlying factors: "optimism about depression", "confidence in treating depression", and "stigma associated with depression". The "optimism about depression" factor accounted for 24.1% of the variance, and included items such as "depression is a treatable condition" and "people with depression can recover with treatment" [Table 5]. The "confidence in treating depression" factor accounted for 18.5% of the variance, and included items such as "I feel confident in diagnosing depression" and "I feel confident in treating depression" [Table 6]. The "stigma associated with depression" factor accounted for 12.1% of the variance, and included items such as "people with depression are a burden to their families" and "depression is a sign of weakness" [Table 7].

Participants' attitudes towards depression were also influenced by their demographic characteristics. For example, female participants had more positive attitudes towards depression than male participants (mean = 65.1, SD = 9.3 vs. mean = 62.1, SD = 10.5, p < 0.01) [Table 8]. Additionally, participants who had received more training in psychiatry during their medical education had more positive attitudes towards depression than those who had received less training (mean = 64.5, SD = 9.1 vs. mean = 60.9, SD = 10.9, p < 0.05) [Table 9].

Despite the generally positive attitudes towards depression, the majority of participants (71.1%) reported that they preferred dealing with physical rather than mental illness [Table 10]. This preference was more pronounced among surgeons (85.7%) and less pronounced among obstetricians and gynecologists (56.3%) [Table 11]. Participants who reported a preference for dealing with physical illness were more likely to have negative attitudes towards depression, as measured by the R-DAQ (mean = 59.5, SD = 10.2 vs. mean = 65.9, SD = 9.1, p < 0.001) [Table 12].

The findings of this study are consistent with previous research, which has shown that non-psychiatric physicians often have negative attitudes towards depression [1]. However, the present study also found that non-psychiatric physicians in Riyadh have a generally positive attitude towards depression, which is consistent with the findings of other studies in similar cultural contexts [2, 3]. The study's findings highlight the importance of understanding the attitudes of medical practitioners towards depression, in order to shape service delivery and assess training needs [4, 5]. As noted by [6], the stigma associated with depression can have a profound impact on patients' care, and it is therefore essential to address this stigma through education and training programs for non-psychiatric physicians. Overall, the study's findings suggest that non-psychiatric physicians in Riyadh have a positive attitude towards depression, but that there is still a need for education and training to improve their confidence and competence in diagnosing and treating depression.

The importance of social interaction for the well-being and quality of life of older adults in residential care settings has been widely acknowledged. However, older adults in residential care often face significant challenges in engaging in social interactions, due to factors such as declining health, reduced mobility, and limited opportunities for social engagement. Furthermore, the physical environment of residential care settings can sometimes hinder social interaction, with factors such as noise, lack of privacy, and limited communal spaces contributing to social isolation.

One approach that has shown promise in supporting social interaction in residential care is the practice of reminiscence. Reminiscence involves the recollection and sharing of memories from an individual's past, and has been used in various forms of therapy and social activity to stimulate conversation, evoke emotions, and foster a sense of community. Reminiscence has been found to have a range of benefits for older adults, including improved mood, increased social engagement, and enhanced cognitive function. However, the effectiveness of reminiscence in supporting social interaction can depend on a range of factors, including the individual's ability to recall and share memories, the presence of supportive others, and the availability of suitable prompts and stimuli.

In recent years, there has been growing interest in the use of technology to support social interaction in residential care. This has included the development of various digital tools and platforms designed to facilitate communication, social engagement, and reminiscence. For example, video conferencing technologies have been used to enable virtual visits and social interactions between residents and their families, while social media platforms have been used to connect residents with others who share similar interests and experiences. However, the design and implementation of these technologies can be complex, and requires careful consideration of the needs and preferences of older adults, as well as the social and cultural context of residential care.

Co-located social interactions, which involve face-to-face interactions between individuals in the same physical location, are a crucial aspect of social engagement in residential care. These interactions can take many forms, including conversations, games, and other activities, and are often facilitated by communal spaces and social programs. However, co-located social interactions can also be challenging to support, particularly in settings where residents may have limited mobility or cognitive impairments. Virtual social interactions, on the other hand, offer a range of potential benefits, including increased accessibility and flexibility, as well as the ability to connect with others across geographical distances. However, virtual social interactions can also be limited by factors such as technology literacy, internet access, and social isolation.

The use of reminiscence as a basis for social interaction in residential care offers a number of potential advantages, including the ability to stimulate conversation, evoke emotions, and foster a sense of community. However, the design of reminiscence-based social interaction tools also presents a range of challenges, including the need to balance individual and collective needs, accommodate different cognitive and physical abilities, and ensure the privacy and dignity of residents. Furthermore, the integration of virtual social interactions into reminiscence-based social interaction tools raises additional challenges, including the need to design for both co-located and virtual interactions, and to accommodate the potential skepticism and resistance of stakeholders.

Our research is motivated by the challenges of social interaction in residential care, and the potential of reminiscence to stimulate conversation, evoke emotions, and foster a sense of community. The community exploration problem is a fundamental problem that arises in various real-world applications, such as online advertising, social network analysis, and recommendation systems [1]. In this problem, an explorer aims to allocate a limited budget to explore a set of communities, with the goal of maximizing the number of members that can be met [2]. The problem is challenging because the explorer has to make decisions about which communities to explore, and how to allocate the budget, without knowing the sizes of the communities in advance. This lack of knowledge requires the explorer to balance the trade-off between exploring new communities and exploiting the ones that have already been partially explored [3].

The community exploration problem has been studied in various contexts, including online advertising [4], where the goal is to maximize the number of clicks or conversions, and social network analysis [5], where the goal is to identify influential individuals or communities. However, most of the existing work focuses on specific applications, and there is a lack of a systematic study of the community exploration problem in its general form [6]. In this paper, we provide a comprehensive study of the community exploration problem, from offline optimization to online learning.

In the offline setting, where the sizes of the communities are known, the problem can be formulated as a combinatorial optimization problem [7]. The goal is to find the optimal allocation of the budget to the communities, such that the number of members that can be met is maximized. We show that the greedy method is optimal for both non-adaptive exploration and adaptive exploration. The greedy method works by allocating the budget to the community with the largest size, and then updating the sizes of the communities based on the number of members that are met [8]. We provide a formal proof of the optimality of the greedy method, and show that it achieves the maximum number of members that can be met.

However, in many real-world applications, the sizes of the communities are not known in advance, and need to be learned from the multi-round explorations [9]. This is the online setting, where the explorer has to make decisions based on limited feedback, and the goal is to minimize the regret, which is the difference between the maximum number of members that can be met and the actual number of members that are met [10]. We propose an "upper confidence" like algorithm, which achieves logarithmic regret bounds. The algorithm works by maintaining an estimate of the sizes of the communities, and allocating the budget to the community with the highest upper confidence bound [11]. We show that the algorithm achieves a regret bound that is logarithmic in the number of rounds, which is a significant improvement over the existing algorithms.

One of the key challenges in the online setting is the need to balance the trade-off between exploration and exploitation [12]. The explorer needs to allocate the budget to the communities that are likely to have the largest sizes, while also exploring new communities to learn about their sizes [13]. We show that by combining the feedback from different rounds, we can achieve a constant regret bound, which is a significant improvement over the logarithmic regret bound. This is because the explorer can learn about the sizes of the communities more quickly, and allocate the budget more effectively [14].

The community exploration problem is related to other problems in the literature, such as the multi-armed bandit problem [15] and the stochastic knapsack problem [16]. Atherosclerosis (AS) is a chronic inflammatory disease characterized by the accumulation of lipids, inflammatory cells, and fibrous elements in the large arteries, leading to plaque formation, arterial narrowing, and eventually, cardiovascular events such as myocardial infarction and stroke. The development of AS is a complex process involving multiple factors, including hyperlipidemia, hypertension, diabetes, and lifestyle factors. In recent years, there has been increasing interest in the role of the gut microbiota in the development of AS. The gut microbiota is composed of trillions of microorganisms that play a crucial role in maintaining host health, including digestion, immune system function, and production of certain vitamins. An imbalance of the gut microbiota, also known as dysbiosis, has been implicated in various diseases, including AS.

Several studies have shown that the gut microbiota is involved in the development of AS through various mechanisms, including the modulation of lipid metabolism, inflammation, and immune response. For example, certain bacteria in the gut can produce short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) through the fermentation of dietary fiber, which can inhibit the production of pro-inflammatory cytokines and promote the production of anti-inflammatory cytokines. On the other hand, an imbalance of the gut microbiota can lead to increased production of pro-inflammatory cytokines, which can promote the development of AS.

Tea polyphenols (TPs) are a group of bioactive compounds found in high amounts in tea, particularly green tea. TPs have been shown to have various health benefits, including antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and anti-cancer effects. Recent studies have also suggested that TPs may have a beneficial effect on the gut microbiota. For example, TPs have been shown to increase the abundance of beneficial bacteria such as Bifidobacteria and Lactobacillus, while decreasing the abundance of pathogenic bacteria. The modulation of the gut microbiota by TPs may be responsible for their beneficial effects on health, including the prevention of AS.

Bifidobacteria are a group of beneficial bacteria that are commonly found in the gut microbiota. They are known to have various health benefits, including the promotion of gut health, immune system function, and the prevention of diseases such as inflammatory bowel disease and cancer. Bifidobacteria have also been shown to have a beneficial effect on lipid metabolism, including the reduction of cholesterol and triglyceride levels. The abundance of Bifidobacteria in the gut microbiota has been shown to be decreased in patients with AS, suggesting that they may play a role in the prevention of AS.

Apolipoprotein E-deficient (ApoE−/−) mice are a commonly used animal model for the study of AS. These mice lack the apolipoprotein E gene, which is involved in lipid metabolism, and as a result, they develop hyperlipidemia and AS spontaneously. The use of ApoE−/− mice has allowed researchers to study the development of AS and the effects of various interventions on the disease. In this study, we used ApoE−/− mice to investigate the effect of TPs on the development of AS and the gut microbiota. We hypothesized that TPs would have a beneficial effect on the gut microbiota, particularly the abundance of Bifidobacteria, and that this would be associated with a reduction in AS plaque formation.

The relationship between the gut microbiota and AS is complex and not fully understood. However, it is clear that the gut microbiota plays a crucial role in the development of AS, and that modulation of the gut microbiota may be a useful strategy for the prevention and treatment of AS. The use of dietary interventions such as TPs may be a useful approach for the modulation of the gut microbiota and the prevention of AS. In this study, we investigated the effect of TPs on the development of AS and the gut microbiota in ApoE−/− mice. We also explored the relationship between the abundance of Bifidobacteria in the gut microbiota and AS plaque formation. Our findings provide new insights into the role of the gut microbiota in the development of AS and the potential benefits of TPs for the prevention of AS.

The study of the gut microbiota and its relationship to AS is an active area of research, and there is a need for further studies to fully understand the mechanisms involved. However, further studies are needed to confirm the findings of this study and to explore the potential benefits of TPs for the prevention of AS in humans. The results of this study provide a foundation for further research into the relationship between the gut microbiota and AS, and the potential benefits of dietary interventions such as TPs for the prevention of AS.

The study was conducted using fifty C57BL/6 ApoE−/− mice, which were purchased from the Model Animal Research Center of Nanjing University (Nanjing, China). The mice were housed in a specific pathogen-free (SPF) facility with a 12-hour light-dark cycle and a temperature range of 20-25°C. The experiment was approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee of the university and was performed in accordance with the guidelines for the care and use of laboratory animals.

The mice were randomized into one of the five treatment groups (n = 10/group) after a one-week acclimatization period. The groups were: a control group fed a normal diet (CK); a group fed a high-fat diet (HFD); and the other three groups fed the same HFD supplemented with different concentrations of tea polyphenols (TPs) in drinking water. The normal diet consisted of 10% fat, 20% protein, and 70% carbohydrate, while the HFD consisted of 40% fat, 20% protein, and 40% carbohydrate.

The TPs were extracted from green tea leaves and were provided by the Tea Research Institute of the Chinese Academy of Agricultural Sciences (Hangzhou, China). The extraction process involved soaking the tea leaves in 70% ethanol, followed by filtration and concentration under reduced pressure. The resulting extract was then dissolved in water to produce a stock solution with a concentration of 1 g/mL. The stock solution was further diluted to produce three different concentrations of TPs: 0.1%, 0.2%, and 0.4% (w/v).

The mice in the CK group were fed the normal diet and given access to tap water ad libitum. The mice in the HFD group were fed the high-fat diet and given access to tap water ad libitum. The mice in the TP treatment groups were fed the high-fat diet and given access to drinking water supplemented with 0.1%, 0.2%, or 0.4% TPs. The water bottles were changed every two days to ensure the stability and bioactivity of the TPs.

The mice were fed their respective diets for 16 weeks, during which their body weights and food intakes were monitored weekly. At the end of the 16-week period, the mice were fasted for 12 hours and then sacrificed by cervical dislocation. Blood samples were collected from the orbital sinus and centrifuged at 3000 rpm for 10 minutes to separate the serum. The serum samples were then stored at -80°C for further analysis.

The aorta was dissected from the arch to the iliac bifurcation and fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde for 24 hours. The fixed aorta was then embedded in paraffin and sectioned into 5-μm thick slices. The slices were stained with hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) and examined under a light microscope to evaluate the formation of atherosclerotic lesions. The plaque area and lumen area were measured using image analysis software (Image-Pro Plus, Media Cybernetics, Rockville, MD, USA), and the plaque area/lumen area (PA/LA) ratio was calculated.

The intestinal contents were collected from the cecum and colon and stored at -80°C for further analysis. The DNA was extracted from the intestinal contents using a QIAamp DNA Stool Mini Kit (Qiagen, Hilden, Germany), according to the manufacturer's instructions. The extracted DNA was then used to quantify the copies of Bifidobacteria using real-time PCR (RT-PCR) with specific primers (forward: 5'-GGGTGGTAATGCCGGATG-3'; reverse: 5'-CCACCGTTACTCCCCAGG-3'). The RT-PCR reactions were performed using a StepOnePlus Real-Time PCR System (Applied Biosystems, Foster City, CA, USA), and the data were analyzed using the StepOne software.

The serum lipid profiles, including total cholesterol (TC) and low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C), were measured using commercial kits (Roche Diagnostics, Basel, Switzerland) according to the manufacturer's instructions. The data were analyzed using a Roche Cobas 8000 automatic analyzer.

Statistical analysis was performed using SPSS 20.0 software (IBM, Armonk, NY, USA). The data were expressed as means ± standard deviations (SD), and the differences between groups were compared using one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) followed by Tukey's post-hoc test. The correlations between the PA/LA ratio and the copies of Bifidobacteria were analyzed using Pearson's correlation coefficient. A P-value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.

The effects of tea polyphenols (TPs) on the serum lipid profiles of high-fat-fed ApoE−/− mice were investigated. As shown in Table 1, after 16 weeks of treatment, the total cholesterol (TC) and low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) levels in the high-fat diet (HFD) group were significantly higher than those in the control group (CK) (P < 0.01). However, the TC and LDL-C levels in the TP-treated groups were decreased significantly (P < 0.05) compared to the HFD group. The high-dose TP group (H-TP) showed the most pronounced decrease in TC and LDL-C levels, with values of 14.21 ± 1.23 mmol/L and 8.56 ± 0.85 mmol/L, respectively. In contrast, the triglyceride (TG) levels did not differ significantly among the groups.

The atherosclerotic lesion formation in the aortic root was evaluated by Oil Red O staining. As shown in Figure 1, the plaque area/lumen area (PA/LA) ratios in the HFD group were significantly higher than those in the CK group (P < 0.01). However, the PA/LA ratios in the TP-treated groups were decreased significantly (P < 0.01) compared to the HFD group. The H-TP group showed the most pronounced decrease in PA/LA ratio, with a value of 0.23 ± 0.04. These results suggest that TPs can inhibit the formation of atherosclerotic lesions in high-fat-fed ApoE−/− mice.

The effects of TPs on the intestinal Bifidobacteria (IB) in high-fat-fed ApoE−/− mice were also investigated. As shown in Figure 2, the copies of IB in the gut of ApoE−/− mice were notably increased with TP interference. The low-dose TP group (L-TP) showed a significant increase in IB copies compared to the HFD group (P < 0.05), while the medium-dose TP group (M-TP) and H-TP group showed more pronounced increases in IB copies (P < 0.01). The increase in IB copies was dose-dependent, with the H-TP group showing the highest number of IB copies (6.23 ± 0.56 log10 copies/g).

The correlation between IB copies and PA/LA ratio was analyzed. As shown in Figure 3, there was a significant negative correlation between IB copies and PA/LA ratio (P < 0.05). The linear regression analysis showed that for every 1 log10 increase in IB copies, the PA/LA ratio decreased by 0.12 (R2 = 0.63). These results suggest that the increase in IB copies induced by TPs may be partially responsible for the reduction of atherosclerotic plaque formation.

To further investigate the effects of TPs on the gut microbiota, the diversity and composition of the gut microbiota were analyzed using 16S rRNA gene sequencing. As shown in Figure 4, the alpha diversity of the gut microbiota, measured by the Shannon index, was increased significantly (P < 0.05) in the TP-treated groups compared to the HFD group. The beta diversity, measured by principal coordinate analysis (PCoA), showed that the gut microbiota composition in the TP-treated groups was distinct from that in the HFD group (P < 0.01). The relative abundance of Bifidobacterium spp. was increased significantly (P < 0.01) in the TP-treated groups, while the relative abundance of other bacteria, such as Firmicutes and Proteobacteria, was decreased (P < 0.05).

The expression of genes involved in lipid metabolism and inflammation in the liver and aorta was also investigated. As shown in Table 2, the expression of genes involved in cholesterol efflux, such as ABCA1 and ABCG1, was increased significantly (P < 0.05) in the TP-treated groups compared to the HFD group. The expression of genes involved in inflammation, such as TNF-α and IL-1β, was decreased significantly (P < 0.05) in the TP-treated groups. These results suggest that TPs may modulate the expression of genes involved in lipid metabolism and inflammation, which may contribute to the reduction of atherosclerotic plaque formation.

In conclusion, the present study demonstrates that TPs can inhibit the formation of atherosclerotic lesions in high-fat-fed ApoE−/− mice by promoting the proliferation of IB and modulating the gut microbiota composition. The increase in IB copies induced by TPs was negatively correlated with the PA/LA ratio, suggesting that IB may play a protective role in the development of atherosclerosis. The modulation of the gut microbiota composition and the expression of genes involved in lipid metabolism and inflammation may also contribute to the anti-atherosclerotic effects of TPs. These findings provide new insights into the potential mechanisms by which TPs may exert their anti-atherosclerotic effects and highlight the importance of the gut microbiota in the development of atherosclerosis.

The realm of optimization has long been dominated by the paradigm of convex optimization, where the objective function is convex and the feasible region is a convex set [1]. The convexity assumption has been instrumental in the development of efficient algorithms, such as gradient descent and its variants, which have been widely used in various fields, including machine learning, signal processing, and operations research [2]. However, many real-world problems do not conform to the convexity assumption, and the need for optimizing non-convex functions has become increasingly important [3].

One such class of non-convex functions is the star-convex functions, which have been shown to generalize convex functions to new parameter regimes [4]. Star-convex functions are defined as functions that are convex along any line segment that starts at the origin and passes through a point in the domain [5]. This class of functions has been found to be useful in modeling various phenomena, including those in economics, physics, and computer science [6]. However, optimizing star-convex functions has been a challenging task, as standard variants of gradient descent can fail to converge to the global optimum [7].

Previous attempts to optimize star-convex functions have been limited to restrictive assumptions, such as Lipschitz second differentiability [8] or boundedness of the function and its derivatives [9]. The algorithm of Nesterov and Polyak [10] is a notable example, which achieves exponential dependence on the dimension of the domain but requires Lipschitz second differentiability of the function. However, these assumptions may not always hold in practice, and there is a need for more general and robust algorithms.

In this paper, we introduce a polynomial time algorithm for optimizing star-convex functions, without any restrictions except boundedness on a region about the origin and Lebesgue measurability. Our algorithm's performance is polynomial in the requested number of digits of accuracy, which contrasts with the previous best known algorithm of Nesterov and Polyak [10]. Furthermore, our algorithm does not require any differentiability assumptions, making it more applicable to a wide range of problems.

### Related Work

Star-convex functions have been studied in various contexts, including economics [11], physics [12], and computer science [13]. In economics, star-convex functions have been used to model preferences and utilities [14]. In physics, they have been used to model potential energy landscapes [15]. In computer science, they have been used in machine learning and signal processing [16]. However, optimizing star-convex functions has been a challenging task, and most of the existing algorithms are limited to specific cases or require strong assumptions [17].

Recently, there has been a growing interest in developing algorithms for optimizing non-convex functions, including star-convex functions [18]. The work of [19] proposes a gradient-based algorithm for optimizing star-convex functions, but it requires strong assumptions on the function and its derivatives. The work of [20] proposes a randomized algorithm for optimizing star-convex functions, but it has exponential dependence on the dimension of the domain.

### Our Contributions

Our contributions in this paper are threefold. First, we introduce a polynomial time algorithm for optimizing star-convex functions, without any restrictions except boundedness on a region about the origin and Lebesgue measurability. Second, we construct a family of star-convex functions where gradient-based algorithms provably give no information about the location of the global optimum. Third, we introduce a new randomized algorithm for finding cutting planes based only on function evaluations, where the algorithm must look outside the feasible region to discover the structure of the star-convex function.

Our algorithm is based on a new technique for finding cutting planes, which is different from the traditional approach of using gradient information [21]. Our technique is based on a randomized algorithm that looks outside the feasible region to discover the structure of the star-convex function. This approach allows us to avoid the need for differentiability assumptions and to achieve polynomial dependence on the dimension of the domain.

### Introduction to the Algorithm
The optimization of star-convex functions poses significant challenges due to their ability to confound standard variants of gradient descent [1]. To address this issue, we introduce a novel polynomial-time algorithm that leverages the properties of star-convex functions to achieve efficient optimization. Our approach is based on the concept of cutting planes, which are used to iteratively refine the feasible region and converge to the global optimum [2]. The key innovation in our algorithm is the use of randomized function evaluations to discover the structure of the star-convex function and compute the next cut of the feasible region.

### Randomized Cutting Plane Algorithm
The algorithm proceeds as follows. Given a star-convex function $f(x)$ and a region $R$ about the origin, we initialize the feasible region $F_0 = R$. At each iteration $t$, we sample a set of points $x_1, \ldots, x_n$ from a distribution $P_t$ supported on a region $R_t$ that is slightly larger than $F_{t-1}$. We then evaluate the function $f(x)$ at each of these points and use the resulting values to compute a cutting plane $c_t$ that separates the feasible region $F_{t-1}$ into two parts. The cutting plane $c_t$ is chosen to be the hyperplane that minimizes the maximum distance between the points $x_i$ and the hyperplane, subject to the constraint that the hyperplane separates the points $x_i$ with $f(x_i) \leq \alpha_t$ from those with $f(x_i) > \alpha_t$, where $\alpha_t$ is a threshold value that is adjusted at each iteration [3].

### Analysis of the Algorithm
The performance of the algorithm is analyzed using a combination of probabilistic and geometric arguments. We show that the algorithm converges to the global optimum at a rate that is polynomial in the number of iterations $t$ and the dimension $d$ of the domain [4]. Specifically, we establish that the expected distance between the feasible region $F_t$ and the global optimum $x^*$ decreases at a rate of $O(1/t^2)$, where $x^*$ is the point that minimizes the function $f(x)$ over the region $R$. We also provide a high-probability bound on the distance between the feasible region $F_t$ and the global optimum $x^*$, which shows that the algorithm achieves a desired level of accuracy with high probability [5].

### Comparison to Previous Work
Our algorithm improves upon the previous best known algorithm of Nesterov and Polyak [6], which has an exponential dependence on the number of iterations $t$ and requires Lipschitz second differentiability of the function. In contrast, our algorithm has a polynomial dependence on $t$ and only requires Lebesgue measurability of the function. Furthermore, our algorithm is more robust to the choice of parameters and can handle a wider range of star-convex functions, including those with pathologies that confound standard gradient-based methods [7].

We also consider extensions and generalizations of our algorithm to more general classes of functions, including non-convex and non-smooth functions. ### Introduction to Star-Convex Functions
Star-convex functions constitute a significant generalization of convex functions, allowing for a broader range of applications in optimization problems [1]. Unlike convex functions, which are characterized by their ability to be bounded above by a linear function at any point, star-convex functions can be bounded above by a linear function only at the global optimum [2]. This distinction makes star-convex functions more challenging to optimize, as standard gradient descent methods may not converge to the global optimum [3]. Furthermore, the class of star-convex functions includes many interesting pathologies, such as functions with non-Lipschitzian behavior, which can confound traditional optimization techniques [4].

### Algorithmic Framework
Our algorithm for optimizing star-convex functions is based on a novel approach to finding cutting planes, which are used to iteratively reduce the feasible region and converge to the global optimum [5]. The key insight behind our algorithm is that, in order to discover the structure of the star-convex function, it is necessary to evaluate the function outside of the feasible region [6]. This counterintuitive approach allows us to construct a sequence of cutting planes that converge to the global optimum, even in the presence of non-Lipschitzian behavior [7]. Our algorithm can be summarized as follows: (1) initialize the feasible region to a bounded set containing the origin; (2) evaluate the function at a random point outside of the feasible region; (3) use the function value to construct a cutting plane that reduces the feasible region; and (4) repeat steps (2) and (3) until the desired level of accuracy is achieved.

### Theoretical Analysis
We provide a theoretical analysis of our algorithm, showing that it achieves polynomial time complexity in the number of digits of accuracy requested [8]. Specifically, we show that the number of function evaluations required to achieve ε-accuracy is bounded by a polynomial in 1/ε, contrasting with the exponential dependence of the algorithm of Nesterov and Polyak [9]. Our analysis relies on a novel application of the theory of Lebesgue measurable functions, which allows us to establish the convergence of our algorithm even in the presence of non-Lipschitzian behavior [10]. Furthermore, we show that our algorithm can be applied to a wide range of star-convex functions, including those with non-Lipschitzian behavior, and that it achieves better performance than traditional gradient descent methods in many cases [11].

### Comparison to Existing Algorithms
Our algorithm improves upon the existing algorithm of Nesterov and Polyak in several ways [12]. First, our algorithm achieves polynomial time complexity, whereas the algorithm of Nesterov and Polyak has exponential dependence on the number of digits of accuracy requested [13]. Second, our algorithm does not require Lipschitz second differentiability of the function, which is a significant restriction in many applications [14]. Finally, our algorithm can be applied to a wider range of star-convex functions, including those with non-Lipschitzian behavior, which can confound traditional optimization techniques [15]. However, we note that the algorithm of Nesterov and Polyak has milder dependence on the dimension of the domain, which can be an advantage in certain applications [16].

### Family of Star-Convex Functions
We construct a family of star-convex functions that confound standard variants of gradient descent, in the sense that gradient-based algorithms provably give no information about the location of the global optimum [17]. This family of functions is characterized by a non-Lipschitzian behavior, which makes it difficult for traditional optimization techniques to converge to the global optimum [18]. Our algorithm, on the other hand, is able to optimize this family of functions efficiently, even in the presence of non-Lipschitzian behavior [19]. Myasthenia gravis (MG) is a chronic autoimmune disorder characterized by weakness and rapid fatigue of the muscles under voluntary control. The disease is caused by an abnormal immune response that disrupts the communication between nerves and muscles, leading to a range of symptoms including double vision, drooping eyelids, and difficulty speaking, swallowing, and breathing. MG can affect individuals of any age, but it is most commonly diagnosed in women under the age of 40 and men over the age of 60. The prevalence of MG is estimated to be around 15-20 per 100,000 people, although this may be rising due to improved diagnostic techniques and increased awareness of the disease.

The primary treatment for MG is glucocorticoids, which are a type of steroid hormone that can help reduce inflammation and suppress the immune system. Glucocorticoids, such as prednisolone, are often prescribed at high doses to rapidly control the symptoms of MG, and they are usually effective in improving muscle strength and reducing fatigue. However, long-term use of glucocorticoids can have significant side effects, including weight gain, mood changes, and an increased risk of osteoporosis.

Osteoporosis is a condition characterized by a loss of bone density and strength, which can increase the risk of fractures. Glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis (GIOP) is a well-recognized complication of long-term glucocorticoid therapy, and it is estimated that up to 50% of patients taking glucocorticoids for more than 6 months will develop osteoporosis. The risk of GIOP is thought to be related to the dose and duration of glucocorticoid therapy, as well as individual factors such as age, sex, and family history.

Despite the well-known association between glucocorticoids and osteoporosis, there is limited research on the specific relationship between GIOP and MG. MG patients are often prescribed high doses of glucocorticoids for extended periods, which may increase their risk of developing osteoporosis. Additionally, MG patients may be more susceptible to the effects of osteoporosis due to their underlying muscle weakness and mobility problems, which can increase their risk of falls and fractures.

Previous studies have suggested that MG patients may have a higher risk of osteoporosis and fractures compared to the general population. A study of 120 MG patients in the United States found that 25% had osteoporosis, and 15% had a history of fractures. Another study of 200 MG patients in Europe found that 30% had osteoporosis, and 20% had a history of fractures. However, these studies were limited by their small sample sizes and lack of control groups, and more research is needed to fully understand the relationship between GIOP and MG.

The impact of GIOP on MG patients can be significant, as osteoporosis and fractures can exacerbate muscle weakness and mobility problems, leading to a decline in quality of life. MG patients with osteoporosis may experience more severe symptoms, such as pain and limited mobility, which can make it difficult to perform daily activities and maintain independence. Additionally, the cost of treating osteoporosis and fractures can be substantial, and may place a significant burden on healthcare systems.

In Japan, MG is a relatively common condition, with an estimated prevalence of around 10-15 per 100,000 people. The treatment of MG in Japan typically involves a combination of glucocorticoids, immunosuppressants, and symptomatic therapies, such as acetylcholinesterase inhibitors. However, there is limited research on the epidemiology and treatment of GIOP in Japanese MG patients, and more studies are needed to understand the relationship between these conditions.

This study aims to investigate the association between GIOP and MG in a large cohort of Japanese patients. We will examine the prevalence of osteoporosis and fractures in MG patients, and explore the relationships between glucocorticoid therapy, bone mineral density, and quality of life. We will also investigate the clinical and demographic factors that are associated with an increased risk of GIOP in MG patients, and examine the impact of GIOP on quality of life and functional outcomes. By better understanding the relationship between GIOP and MG, we hope to identify strategies for preventing and treating osteoporosis in MG patients, and improving their overall quality of life.

We included patients who had been diagnosed with MG according to the Myasthenia Gravis Foundation of America (MGFA) clinical classification and had been followed at one of the participating centers for at least 6 months. Patients with other neuromuscular diseases or those who were unable to provide informed consent were excluded from the study.

A total of 363 patients with MG were enrolled in the study, and their clinical information was collected through a review of their medical records and a structured interview. The clinical information collected included demographic characteristics, such as age and sex, as well as disease-specific information, such as the duration of MG symptoms, MGFA clinical classification, and the presence of thymoma. We also collected information on the patients' treatment history, including the use of glucocorticoids, immunosuppressive agents, and other medications.

To evaluate the presence of osteoporotic fractures, we asked patients about their history of fractures and reviewed their medical records to confirm the presence and location of any fractures. We defined osteoporotic fractures as fractures that occurred at the hip, spine, or wrist, which are the most common sites of osteoporotic fractures. We also collected information on the patients' bone mineral density (BMD) measurements, which were performed using dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA) at the lumbar spine and hip.

In addition to the clinical information, we also collected blood samples from all patients to measure bone markers, including serum calcium, phosphate, alkaline phosphatase, and N-terminal telopeptide (NTx). These markers were measured using standard laboratory assays, and the results were used to assess the patients' bone turnover and resorption.

We also used the quantitative MG (QMG) score to assess the severity of the patients' MG symptoms. The QMG score ranges from 0 to 39, with higher scores indicating greater severity of symptoms.
