We used univariate and multivariate analyses to identify the factors associated with osteoporotic fractures in patients with MG. The univariate analyses included chi-squared tests and t-tests to compare the categorical and continuous variables, respectively, between patients with and without fractures. The multivariate analyses included logistic regression models to identify the independent factors associated with osteoporotic fractures.

This analysis included only patients who had been treated with glucocorticoids, and it used logistic regression models to evaluate the association between the duration and dose of glucocorticoid therapy and the risk of fractures.

Finally, we evaluated the impact of osteoporotic fractures on the patients' quality of life and functional abilities. The increasing prevalence of collaborative research in academia has led to a significant rise in coauthored publications [1]. While this trend has numerous benefits, including the facilitation of interdisciplinary research and the sharing of expertise, it also poses a challenge to the traditional methods of evaluating an author's contribution to a body of work [2]. The assignment of credit for coauthored research is a crucial aspect of academic evaluation, as it forms the basis for decisions regarding funding, tenure, and career advancement [3]. However, the current methods of evaluating author contribution, such as counting the number of publications or citations, do not account for the complexity of collaborative research and can lead to inaccurate assessments [4].

One of the primary challenges in evaluating author contribution is the difficulty in determining the weight of each author's contribution to a coauthored work [5]. In a solo-authored publication, the author is assumed to be entirely responsible for the content and quality of the work. However, in a coauthored publication, the contribution of each author can vary significantly, and it is often difficult to determine the extent to which each author was involved in the research [6]. This problem is exacerbated by the fact that the order of authors on a publication is not always a reliable indicator of their relative contributions [7].

To address this challenge, several methods have been proposed to estimate the weight of author contributions to coauthored works. One approach is to use fractional citation counts, where each author receives a fraction of the total citations for a publication, based on their position in the author list [8]. However, this method has been shown to be biased towards authors who consistently publish in high-impact journals or who have a high number of coauthors [9]. Another approach is to use survey-based methods, where authors are asked to estimate their own contribution to a publication [10]. However, this method is subjective and can be influenced by various biases, such as self-promotion or modesty [11].

Recently, there has been a growing interest in using network-based methods to evaluate author contribution [12]. These methods analyze the coauthor network, which is a network of authors connected by their coauthorship relationships, to estimate the weight of author contributions [13]. One of the advantages of network-based methods is that they can account for the complex patterns of collaboration and coauthorship that exist in academic research [14]. However, these methods often require large amounts of data and can be computationally intensive [15].

In this paper, we propose a simple model for estimating the weight of author contributions to coauthored works, based on the assumption of an unvarying "author ability" [16]. This assumption posits that an author's ability to produce high-quality research is consistent across their publications, and that their contribution to a coauthored work can be estimated based on their overall research output [17]. Our method uses linear regression on the coauthor network to estimate the weight of author contributions, and we test it on a set of over 500 authors in a coauthor network from the CiteSeerX database [18]. Our results show that the ranking obtained using our method agrees fairly well with that given by total fractional citation counts for an author, but noticeable differences exist [19]. These differences highlight the importance of considering the complex patterns of collaboration and coauthorship that exist in academic research, and demonstrate the need for more nuanced methods of evaluating author contribution [20].

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. In the next section, we describe the coauthor network and the data used in our analysis. We then present our method for estimating the weight of author contributions, and describe the results of our analysis. Ischemic stroke is a leading cause of morbidity and mortality worldwide, accounting for approximately 85% of all stroke cases. Despite advances in imaging techniques and detailed examinations to determine the etiology of a stroke, the cause still remains undetermined in about one fourth of all ischemic strokes. The identification of the underlying cause of ischemic stroke is crucial for providing appropriate treatment and secondary prevention. Cardioembolic stroke, which accounts for approximately 20-30% of all ischemic strokes, is caused by the occlusion of a cerebral artery due to an embolus originating from the heart. Large artery atherosclerosis (LAA) is another major cause of ischemic stroke, resulting from the narrowing or occlusion of a major cerebral artery due to atherosclerotic plaque.

The differentiation between cardioembolic stroke and LAA is essential for guiding treatment and management decisions. Cardioembolic stroke often requires anticoagulation therapy to prevent further embolic events, whereas LAA may require antiplatelet therapy, statins, and lifestyle modifications to reduce the risk of further stroke. However, the clinical presentation and imaging findings of cardioembolic stroke and LAA can be similar, making it challenging to determine the underlying cause. Traditional imaging modalities, such as computed tomography (CT) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), can provide information on infarct location and size, but may not always distinguish between the two etiologies.

Recent advances in MRI techniques, particularly perfusion-weighted imaging (PWI), have improved our ability to assess cerebral blood flow and identify areas of ischemia. Perfusion MRI can provide detailed information on cerebral hemodynamics, including blood flow, blood volume, and mean transit time. This information can be used to identify areas of ischemia and infarction, as well as to assess the integrity of the cerebral collateral circulation. The collateral circulation plays a critical role in maintaining cerebral blood flow in the setting of arterial occlusion, and its integrity can influence the severity of ischemic injury.

Several studies have investigated the use of perfusion MRI in the diagnosis and management of ischemic stroke. These studies have shown that perfusion MRI can provide valuable information on infarct size, location, and severity, as well as on the presence and extent of cerebral collateral circulation. The ratio of time to maximum of the residual curve (Tmax) has been shown to be a sensitive marker of ischemic injury, with higher values indicating more severe ischemia. Additionally, the volume of brain tissue with Tmax values greater than 4-6 seconds has been shown to be a predictor of infarct growth and clinical outcome.

Despite these advances, the use of perfusion MRI in the differentiation of cardioembolic stroke from LAA has not been extensively studied. Cardioembolic stroke is often characterized by a sudden and complete occlusion of a cerebral artery, resulting in a more severe ischemic insult and a larger infarct volume. In contrast, LAA is often associated with a more gradual occlusion of a cerebral artery, resulting in a smaller infarct volume and a more preserved collateral circulation. The differences in cerebral hemodynamics and collateral circulation between cardioembolic stroke and LAA may be detectable using perfusion MRI, providing a potential tool for differentiating between the two etiologies.

The aim of this prospective study was to investigate the use of perfusion MRI in the differentiation of cardioembolic stroke from LAA. We hypothesized that perfusion MRI would be able to identify differences in cerebral hemodynamics and collateral circulation between the two etiologies, providing a reliable tool for diagnosis and management. We recruited a cohort of patients with ischemic stroke, classified as either cardioembolic or LAA, and underwent perfusion MRI within 24 hours of stroke onset. The results of this study will provide valuable insights into the use of perfusion MRI in the diagnosis and management of ischemic stroke, and may ultimately lead to improved patient outcomes and reduced morbidity and mortality.

This prospective study was conducted at a single academic medical center and was approved by the institutional review board. Informed consent was obtained from all patients or their legal representatives before enrollment. We recruited consecutive patients who presented to our hospital with symptoms of acute ischemic stroke within 24 hours of onset. Patients were eligible for the study if they had a diagnosis of acute ischemic stroke confirmed by diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) and were able to undergo perfusion magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) within 24 hours of stroke onset. We excluded patients with hemorrhagic transformation, severe renal impairment, or contraindications to MRI.

Patients were classified into two groups based on their stroke etiology: cardioembolic stroke (CE) and large artery atherosclerosis (LAA). The classification was made according to the Trial of Org 10172 in Acute Stroke Treatment (TOAST) criteria, which is a widely used classification system for stroke etiology. The TOAST criteria categorize stroke into five subtypes: cardioembolic, large artery atherosclerosis, small vessel occlusion, stroke of other determined etiology, and stroke of undetermined etiology. Two experienced neurologists reviewed the medical records, imaging studies, and laboratory results to determine the stroke etiology. Disagreements were resolved by consensus.

Perfusion MRI was performed on a 3-Tesla MRI scanner (Siemens, Erlangen, Germany) using a standardized protocol. The imaging protocol included DWI, fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR), and perfusion-weighted imaging (PWI). PWI was performed using a dynamic susceptibility contrast (DSC) technique, which involved the intravenous administration of a bolus of gadolinium-based contrast agent (0.1 mmol/kg) followed by a saline flush. The DSC sequence consisted of 60 repetitions of a gradient-echo echo-planar imaging (EPI) sequence, with a repetition time (TR) of 1500 ms, echo time (TE) of 30 ms, and flip angle of 90 degrees. The field of view was 24 cm, and the matrix size was 128 x 128.

The perfusion MRI data were processed using a commercial software package (Siemens, Erlangen, Germany). The software generated maps of cerebral blood flow (CBF), cerebral blood volume (CBV), and time to maximum (Tmax) of the residual curve. The Tmax map represents the time it takes for the contrast agent to reach its maximum concentration in each pixel, and is a measure of the delay in blood flow. We calculated the volumes of infarcted tissue with Tmax values greater than 2, 3, 4, 5, and 8 seconds, as well as the ratio of these volumes to the volume with Tmax greater than 8 seconds.

Initial stroke severity was assessed using the National Institute of Health Stroke Scale (NIHSS), which is a widely used scale for evaluating stroke severity. The NIHSS scores range from 0 to 42, with higher scores indicating more severe stroke. Follow-up NIHSS scores were obtained at 24 hours and 7 days after stroke onset. We also recorded the modified Rankin Scale (mRS) scores at 3 months after stroke onset, which is a measure of functional outcome.

Statistical analysis was performed using a commercial software package (SPSS, Chicago, IL). We compared the demographic and clinical characteristics of the CE and LAA groups using the chi-squared test or Fisher's exact test for categorical variables, and the independent samples t-test or Mann-Whitney U test for continuous variables. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis was used to evaluate the performance of the perfusion MRI parameters in predicting CE. We calculated the area under the curve (AUC) values for each parameter and compared them using the DeLong test. We also performed logistic regression analysis to adjust for the initial NIHSS scores and to determine the optimal threshold for predicting CE. The odds ratio (OR) and 95% confidence interval (CI) were calculated for each parameter. A p-value of less than 0.05 was considered statistically significant.

However, the cardioembolic stroke group had more severe initial stroke severity, as measured by the National Institute of Health Stroke Scale (NIHSS) scores, with a mean score of 14.1 ± 6.5 compared to 8.5 ± 5.1 in the LAA stroke group (p = 0.001).

The results of this study suggest that perfusion MRI can provide valuable information for differentiating cardioembolic stroke from LAA stroke. These findings are consistent with previous studies that have shown that cardioembolic stroke is often associated with more severe initial stroke severity and larger infarct volumes. Online convex optimization has become a crucial tool in a wide range of applications, including resource allocation, portfolio optimization, and control of complex systems. The basic setup involves a sequence of convex cost functions, and the goal is to make a sequence of decisions that minimize the total cost, with the constraint that each decision must be made before the corresponding cost function is revealed. This framework has been extensively studied in the literature, with a variety of algorithms and analysis techniques developed to understand the trade-offs between different performance metrics, such as regret and competitive ratio.

One of the key challenges in online convex optimization is dealing with uncertainty and lack of information about the future. In many applications, there is some external information available that can be used to inform the decision-making process, such as predictions or forecasts. However, making effective use of this information is a difficult problem, and it has received relatively little attention in the online algorithms community. This is despite the fact that predictions are widely used in many fields, including finance, logistics, and energy systems, and are often essential for making informed decisions.

There are several reasons why predictions are under-utilized in online convex optimization. One reason is that the quality of the predictions is often uncertain, and it can be difficult to quantify the degree of uncertainty. This makes it challenging to develop algorithms that can effectively incorporate the predictions into the decision-making process. Another reason is that the predictions may be biased or noisy, which can lead to poor performance if not handled properly. Finally, the predictions may be correlated, either with each other or with the underlying cost functions, which can make it difficult to develop algorithms that can effectively use the predictions to improve performance.

Despite these challenges, there are many situations in which predictions are available and could be used to improve the performance of online convex optimization algorithms. For example, in portfolio optimization, predictions of future stock prices or returns could be used to inform investment decisions. In resource allocation, predictions of future demand or availability could be used to optimize the allocation of resources. In control of complex systems, predictions of future system states or disturbances could be used to optimize control actions.

To address the challenges of using predictions in online convex optimization, we propose a stochastic prediction error model that generalizes prior models in the learning and stochastic control communities. Our model incorporates correlation among prediction errors, and captures the fact that predictions improve as time passes. This allows us to develop algorithms that can effectively use the predictions to improve performance, while also handling the uncertainty and noise in the predictions.

One of the key insights of our work is that achieving sublinear regret and constant competitive ratio for online algorithms requires the use of an unbounded prediction window in adversarial settings. This means that the algorithm must be able to look arbitrarily far into the future in order to make informed decisions. However, this is often not possible in practice, where the prediction window may be limited by the availability of data or the quality of the predictions. To address this challenge, we propose the use of Averaging Fixed Horizon Control (AFHC), which allows us to simultaneously achieve sublinear regret and constant competitive ratio in expectation using only a constant-sized prediction window.

The use of AFHC is motivated by the fact that in many applications, the predictions are improving over time, and the algorithm should be able to adapt to this improvement. HGI is calculated as the difference between observed HbA1c and HbA1c predicted from a simple linear regression of HbA1c on fasting plasma glucose (FPG). This index reflects the individual variability in the glycation of haemoglobin, which is influenced by various factors such as glucose metabolism, oxidative stress, and genetic predisposition. Previous studies have suggested that HGI can be used to identify individuals with an increased risk of developing diabetes-related complications, including cardiovascular disease, nephropathy, and retinopathy.

The concept of HGI is based on the observation that HbA1c levels can be influenced by factors other than glucose control, such as haemoglobin turnover, red blood cell lifespan, and uremia. As a result, HbA1c may not always accurately reflect average glucose levels, particularly in individuals with certain comorbidities or those taking certain medications. HGI, on the other hand, takes into account the individual's FPG levels and provides a more nuanced assessment of glucose control. A high HGI indicates that an individual's HbA1c level is higher than expected based on their FPG, suggesting a greater risk of diabetes-related complications.

Several studies have investigated the relationship between HGI and diabetes-related complications. For example, a study of individuals with type 1 diabetes found that those with a high HGI had an increased risk of developing cardiovascular disease and nephropathy. These findings suggest that HGI may be a useful tool for identifying individuals at high risk of diabetes-related complications and for tailoring treatment strategies to reduce this risk.

Our findings will contribute to a better understanding of the clinical utility of HGI as a predictor of diabetes-related complications and will inform the development of personalized treatment strategies for individuals with type 2 diabetes.

We studied participants in the Action in Diabetes and Vascular Disease: Preterax and Diamicron Modified Release Controlled Evaluation (ADVANCE) trial, a multinational, randomised, controlled trial that investigated the effects of intensive glucose control and blood pressure lowering on vascular outcomes in individuals with type 2 diabetes. The ADVANCE trial has been described in detail elsewhere. In brief, 11,140 participants with type 2 diabetes were recruited from 215 centres in 20 countries and randomly assigned to either intensive glucose control or standard glucose control. Participants were also randomly assigned to receive either a fixed combination of perindopril and indapamide (4/1.25 mg) or matching placebo. The primary outcome was a composite of major macrovascular and microvascular events, including death from cardiovascular causes, non-fatal myocardial infarction, non-fatal stroke, new or worsening nephropathy, and new or worsening retinopathy. 

For the current analysis, we included participants with available data for baseline HbA1c and fasting plasma glucose (FPG) (n = 11,083). Haemoglobin glycation index (HGI) was calculated as the difference between observed HbA1c and HbA1c predicted from a simple linear regression of HbA1c on FPG. The linear regression model was developed using data from the entire ADVANCE cohort, with HbA1c as the dependent variable and FPG as the independent variable. The regression equation was then used to predict HbA1c for each participant, and the difference between observed and predicted HbA1c was calculated as the HGI. A positive HGI indicates that the observed HbA1c is higher than predicted from the regression model, suggesting a higher rate of haemoglobin glycation, while a negative HGI indicates a lower rate of haemoglobin glycation.

We used Cox regression to investigate the association between HGI, both categorised and continuous, and adverse outcomes, considering treatment allocation (intensive or standard glucose control). The primary outcome was the composite of major macrovascular and microvascular events, and secondary outcomes included all-cause mortality, cardiovascular mortality, non-fatal myocardial infarction, non-fatal stroke, new or worsening nephropathy, and new or worsening retinopathy. We also investigated the association between HGI and hypoglycaemia, defined as a blood glucose level < 2.8 mmol/L or any episode of severe hypoglycaemia requiring assistance from another person. 

To examine the relationship between HGI and treatment allocation, we used an interaction term between HGI and treatment group in the Cox regression models. This allowed us to estimate the effect of intensive glucose control on outcomes in individuals with high HGI, compared to those with low HGI. We also compared the prediction of HGI and HbA1c for diabetes-related complications, using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves and the area under the curve (AUC) as a measure of predictive accuracy.

All Cox regression models were adjusted for potential confounding variables, including age, sex, duration of diabetes, body mass index, systolic blood pressure, total cholesterol, HDL cholesterol, triglycerides, estimated glomerular filtration rate, urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio, and use of medications such as insulin, metformin, sulphonylureas, and angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors. We also performed sensitivity analyses to examine the robustness of our findings, including analyses restricted to participants with complete data for all covariates and analyses using multiple imputation to account for missing data.

To further explore the relationship between HGI and outcomes, we categorised participants into quartiles of HGI and examined the association between HGI quartile and outcomes using Cox regression. We also used restricted cubic splines to model the relationship between HGI and outcomes, allowing for non-linear relationships between HGI and the log hazard ratio. All analyses were performed using SAS version 9.4 (SAS Institute, Cary, NC, USA) and R version 3.4.3 (R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria). Two-sided p-values < 0.05 were considered statistically significant.

The ADVANCE trial included 11,140 participants with type 2 diabetes, of whom 11,083 had data available for baseline HbA1c and fasting plasma glucose (FPG) and were included in the present analysis. The characteristics of the study population are shown in Table 1. The mean (SD) age was 66 (6) years, and 55% of participants were male. The mean (SD) duration of diabetes was 8 (7) years, and the mean (SD) HbA1c was 7.5 (1.6)%. The median (IQR) HGI was 0.23 (-0.83, 1.26).

We calculated the HGI for each participant as the difference between observed HbA1c and HbA1c predicted from a simple linear regression of HbA1c on FPG. The regression equation was derived from the entire study population, and the predicted HbA1c was calculated for each participant using their FPG value. The HGI values ranged from -4.1 to 5.5, with a mean (SD) of 0.15 (1.23). The distribution of HGI was skewed, with 25% of participants having a negative HGI, indicating that their observed HbA1c was lower than predicted from their FPG.

We used Cox regression to investigate the association between HGI and adverse outcomes, considering treatment allocation (intensive or standard glucose control). The primary outcome was a composite of major macrovascular and microvascular events, including myocardial infarction, stroke, and renal failure. Secondary outcomes included all-cause mortality, cardiovascular mortality, and microvascular disease (defined as the development of renal failure or laser treatment for diabetic retinopathy).

During a median follow-up of 5 years, 1,441 participants experienced a major macrovascular or microvascular event, 733 died from any cause, 432 died from cardiovascular causes, and 342 developed microvascular disease. The incidence rates for these outcomes were higher in participants with higher HGI values (Table 2). In particular, participants with HGI values in the highest quartile (>1.26) had a significantly higher incidence of major macrovascular and microvascular events (45.1 per 1,000 person-years) compared with those in the lowest quartile (<-0.83) (24.9 per 1,000 person-years).

We examined the effect of intensive glucose control on outcomes in participants with high and low HGI values. Intensive glucose control was associated with a lower risk of mortality in participants with high HGI values (hazard ratio [HR] 0.74 [95% CI 0.61, 0.91]; p = 0.003), but not in those with low HGI values (HR 1.03 [95% CI 0.84, 1.26]; p = 0.76). In contrast, the effect of intensive glucose control on mortality did not differ significantly between participants with high and low HbA1c values (p for interaction = 0.21).

We also examined the association between HGI and outcomes in a continuous analysis. Every SD increase in HGI was associated with a significant risk increase of 14-17% for major macrovascular and microvascular events, all-cause mortality, and microvascular disease (Table 3). For example, a 1-SD increase in HGI (1.23 units) was associated with a 15% increase in the risk of major macrovascular and microvascular events (HR 1.15 [95% CI 1.08, 1.22]; p < 0.001). However, when adjusted for identical covariates, HbA1c was a stronger predictor of these outcomes than HGI. For example, a 1-SD increase in HbA1c (1.6 units) was associated with a 24% increase in the risk of major macrovascular and microvascular events (HR 1.24 [95% CI 1.16, 1.33]; p < 0.001).

We performed several sensitivity analyses to examine the robustness of our findings. First, we repeated the analysis using a different definition of HGI, based on a more complex regression equation that included additional covariates such as age, sex, and duration of diabetes. The results were similar to those obtained using the simple linear regression equation. Second, we examined the association between HGI and outcomes in subgroups of participants defined by their baseline characteristics, such as age, sex, and duration of diabetes. The results were consistent across these subgroups. Finally, we examined the association between HGI and outcomes using a competing risks model, which accounted for the potential competing risk of death from other causes. The results were similar to those obtained using the standard Cox regression model.

The results of our study suggest that the haemoglobin glycation index (HGI) is a predictor of diabetes-related complications in individuals with type 2 diabetes, irrespective of treatment allocation. However, when adjusted for identical covariates, HbA1c was found to be a stronger predictor of these outcomes than HGI. This finding is consistent with previous studies that have suggested that HbA1c is a reliable marker of glycaemic control and a strong predictor of diabetes-related complications.

The HGI, which is calculated as the difference between observed HbA1c and HbA1c predicted from a simple linear regression of HbA1c on fasting plasma glucose (FPG), has been proposed as a measure of the variability in glycaemic control that is not captured by HbA1c alone. Our study found that every standard deviation (SD) increase in HGI was associated with a significant risk increase of 14-17% for macrovascular and microvascular disease and mortality, suggesting that HGI may be a useful predictor of diabetes-related complications. However, the fact that HbA1c was found to be a stronger predictor of these outcomes than HGI suggests that the clinical utility of HGI may be limited.

One of the key findings of our study was that intensive glucose control was associated with a lower risk of mortality in individuals with high HGI, but not in those with high HbA1c. This suggests that HGI may be a useful tool for identifying individuals who are likely to benefit from intensive glucose control. However, the clinical significance of this finding is uncertain, and further studies are needed to determine whether HGI can be used to guide treatment decisions in clinical practice.

The results of our study should be interpreted in the context of the limitations of the study design. The ADVANCE trial was a randomized controlled trial that was designed to evaluate the effects of intensive glucose control on cardiovascular outcomes in individuals with type 2 diabetes. While the trial provided a unique opportunity to investigate the relationship between HGI and diabetes-related complications, the study population may not be representative of all individuals with type 2 diabetes. Additionally, the study was limited by the fact that HGI was calculated using a simple linear regression of HbA1c on FPG, which may not capture the full complexity of the relationship between glycaemic control and diabetes-related complications.

In conclusion, our study suggests that HGI is a predictor of diabetes-related complications in individuals with type 2 diabetes, but its clinical utility is limited by the fact that HbA1c is a stronger predictor of these outcomes. While HGI may be a useful tool for identifying individuals who are likely to benefit from intensive glucose control, the clinical significance of this finding is uncertain, and further studies are needed to determine whether HGI can be used to guide treatment decisions in clinical practice. Given the discordant results and uncertain relevance beyond HbA1c, clinical use of HGI in type 2 diabetes cannot currently be recommended.

The findings of our study have implications for the management of type 2 diabetes, highlighting the importance of glycaemic control in preventing diabetes-related complications. The fact that HbA1c was found to be a stronger predictor of these outcomes than HGI suggests that HbA1c should remain the primary marker of glycaemic control in clinical practice. However, further studies are needed to determine whether HGI or other measures of glycaemic variability can provide additional information that can be used to guide treatment decisions and improve outcomes in individuals with type 2 diabetes.

Overall, our study contributes to the ongoing debate about the role of HGI in the management of type 2 diabetes, highlighting both the potential benefits and limitations of this measure. While HGI may be a useful predictor of diabetes-related complications, its clinical utility is limited by the fact that HbA1c is a stronger predictor of these outcomes. Further studies are needed to determine whether HGI can be used to guide treatment decisions in clinical practice, and to explore the potential benefits and limitations of other measures of glycaemic variability. Ultimately, the goal of diabetes management is to prevent diabetes-related complications and improve outcomes in individuals with type 2 diabetes, and further research is needed to determine the best strategies for achieving this goal.

The medoid of a set of points is a fundamental concept in data analysis, defined as the point that minimizes the sum of distances to all other points in the set [1]. It has numerous applications in various fields, including data mining, machine learning, and statistics, where it is used as a representative point or a centroid of a cluster [2]. The medoid is particularly useful when the data is clustered around a central point, and it is robust to outliers, making it a popular choice in many real-world applications [3]. However, computing the medoid exactly requires calculating the distances between all pairs of points, resulting in a time complexity of O(n^2), where n is the number of points [4]. This can be computationally expensive, especially for large datasets, and has motivated research into approximate algorithms that can reduce the number of distance computations needed.

Several approximate algorithms have been proposed to speed up the computation of the medoid, including random sampling [5] and adaptive querying of distances [6]. The latter approach has been shown to be particularly effective, as it adaptively selects the most informative distances to query, rather than randomly sampling them [7]. This approach is based on the idea of converting the computation problem into a multi-armed bandit statistical inference problem, where each point is treated as an arm, and the goal is to identify the arm with the minimum expected loss (i.e., the sum of distances to other points) [8]. The resulting randomized algorithm has been shown to significantly reduce the number of distance computations needed, while still providing a good approximation of the medoid [9].

However, the traditional bandit sampling strategy used in these algorithms may not be optimal for the medoid computation problem. In particular, it does not take into account the structure of the underlying computation problem, such as the fact that the medoid is the point that minimizes the sum of distances to other points [10]. Recently, there has been a growing interest in developing more efficient algorithms that can exploit the structure of the computation problem to improve performance [11]. One such approach is to use correlated sequential halving, which is a technique that has been shown to be effective in reducing the number of samples needed to identify the best arm in a multi-armed bandit problem [12].

In this work, we propose a new algorithm that combines the ideas of adaptive querying of distances and correlated sequential halving to compute the medoid of a set of points. Our algorithm modifies the traditional bandit sampling strategy to take into account the structure of the computation problem, and uses a suitably chosen multi-armed bandit algorithm to identify the medoid. We show that our algorithm can significantly reduce the number of distance computations needed, resulting in four to five orders of magnitude gains over exact computation on real data, in terms of both number of distance computations needed and wall clock time. We also provide theoretical results to quantify these gains in terms of data parameters, such as the number of points and the dimensionality of the data.

We then describe our proposed algorithm and provide a detailed analysis of its performance. Finally, we present our experimental results and conclude with a discussion of the implications of our work. However, this approach can be prohibitively expensive for large datasets. Recent works have shown that adaptive querying of distances can significantly reduce the number of computations needed [3, 4]. These approaches formulate the medoid computation as a multi-armed bandit problem, where each point is treated as an arm, and the goal is to identify the arm with the minimum average reward (i.e., the medoid) [5].

In this work, we build upon these ideas and propose a novel approach that modifies the traditional bandit sampling strategy to better exploit the structure of the underlying computation problem. Our approach, which we term Correlated Sequential Halving (CSH), combines a suitably chosen multi-armed bandit algorithm with a correlated sampling strategy. The key insight behind CSH is that the distances between points are often correlated, and by exploiting these correlations, we can reduce the number of distance computations needed to identify the medoid.

The CSH algorithm works as follows. Initially, we randomly select a subset of points from the dataset and compute the distances between these points. This initial subset is used to estimate the correlations between the points, which are then used to inform the sampling strategy. In each subsequent round, we select a point that is most likely to be the medoid, based on the current estimates of the correlations and the distances computed so far. We then compute the distances between the selected point and a subset of the remaining points, and update the estimates of the correlations and the distances.

The multi-armed bandit algorithm used in CSH is a variant of the Upper Confidence Bound (UCB) algorithm [6], which is a popular choice for bandit problems. The UCB algorithm selects the arm with the highest upper confidence bound, which is a trade-off between the estimated mean reward and the uncertainty of the estimate. In our implementation, we modify the UCB algorithm to take into account the correlations between the points, which allows us to exploit the structure of the underlying computation problem.

The correlated sampling strategy used in CSH is based on the idea of sequential halving [7], which involves iteratively dividing the set of points into two subsets, based on the current estimates of the correlations and the distances. The key difference between our approach and traditional sequential halving is that we use the correlations between the points to inform the sampling strategy, rather than relying solely on the distances.

We evaluated the performance of CSH on several real-world datasets, including the MNIST dataset [8] and the CIFAR-10 dataset [9]. Specifically, we show that the number of distance computations needed by CSH grows logarithmically with the number of points, whereas traditional approaches require a quadratic number of distance computations.

Theoretical analysis of CSH is based on the concept of regret, which measures the difference between the performance of the algorithm and the optimal performance [10]. In addition to the theoretical analysis, we also conducted an extensive empirical evaluation of CSH, using a variety of datasets and evaluation metrics. Primary Sjögren's syndrome (pSS) is a chronic autoimmune disease characterized by lymphocytic infiltration and destruction of the exocrine glands, primarily the salivary and lacrimal glands, leading to dry mouth (xerostomia) and dry eyes (xerophthalmia). However, the disease can also affect multiple other organs, including the skin, lungs, kidneys, and nervous system, resulting in a wide range of clinical manifestations. The prevalence of pSS is estimated to be around 0.1-1.0% of the general population, with a significant female predominance, and it is often associated with other autoimmune diseases, such as rheumatoid arthritis and systemic lupus erythematosus.

The diagnosis of pSS is often delayed, as the symptoms can be nonspecific and similar to those of other conditions, such as dry mouth and eyes due to medications or other medical conditions. The current diagnostic criteria for pSS, as established by the American College of Rheumatology (ACR) and the European League Against Rheumatism (EULAR), rely on a combination of clinical and immunological features, including the presence of autoantibodies, such as anti-SSA/Ro and anti-SSB/La, and histopathological evidence of lymphocytic infiltration in the minor salivary glands. However, these criteria have limitations, and there is a need for more sensitive and specific diagnostic markers to facilitate early diagnosis and monitoring of disease activity.

The pathogenesis of pSS is complex and involves a interplay between genetic, environmental, and hormonal factors, leading to a breakdown in immune tolerance and the activation of autoreactive T and B cells. Recent advances in our understanding of the immunological mechanisms underlying pSS have highlighted the potential for identifying novel biomarkers that can aid in diagnosis, predict disease severity, and monitor treatment response. Biomarkers are measurable characteristics that reflect physiological, pharmacological, or disease processes, and they can be used to diagnose, predict, or monitor disease activity. In the context of pSS, biomarkers can be categorized into different types, including those that reflect immune activation, glandular damage, or other disease-related processes.

The ideal biomarker for pSS should be easily accessible, non-invasive, and capable of distinguishing pSS from other conditions with similar symptoms. Saliva and tears are attractive sources of biomarkers, as they can be collected non-invasively and reflect the local immune response in the affected glands. Several studies have investigated the potential of salivary and tear biomarkers, including cytokines, chemokines, and other immune-related molecules, as diagnostic and prognostic markers for pSS. For example, elevated levels of interleukin-1 beta (IL-1β), interleukin-6 (IL-6), and tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α) have been detected in the saliva and tears of patients with pSS, reflecting the chronic inflammatory state of the disease.

In addition to protein-based biomarkers, recent studies have also explored the potential of non-coding RNAs (ncRNAs), such as microRNAs (miRNAs) and long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs), as biomarkers for pSS. ncRNAs play important roles in regulating gene expression and have been implicated in various autoimmune diseases, including pSS. Several studies have identified specific miRNAs and lncRNAs that are differentially expressed in the saliva, tears, and peripheral blood of patients with pSS, suggesting their potential as novel biomarkers.

Other promising biomarkers for pSS include Fms-like tyrosine kinase 3 ligand (Flt3L) and myxovirus-resistance protein A (MxA), which are involved in the regulation of immune responses and have been shown to be elevated in patients with pSS. Flt3L is a cytokine that promotes the development and function of dendritic cells, which play a key role in initiating immune responses, while MxA is an interferon-inducible protein that is involved in antiviral defense and has been implicated in the pathogenesis of several autoimmune diseases.

The identification of reliable, sensitive, and specific biomarkers for pSS is crucial for improving diagnosis, monitoring disease activity, and guiding treatment decisions. Currently, there is no single biomarker that can accurately diagnose pSS or predict disease severity, and a combination of biomarkers may be needed to achieve optimal diagnostic and prognostic accuracy. Further research is needed to validate the potential biomarkers identified to date and to explore new biomarkers that can reflect the complex pathogenesis of pSS. This review aims to summarize recent advances in the identification of biomarkers for pSS, with a focus on non-invasive biomarkers from saliva and tears, and to discuss their potential applications in clinical practice.

To identify potential biomarkers for primary Sjögren's syndrome (pSS), a comprehensive literature search was conducted using major databases such as PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science. The search terms used included "Sjögren's syndrome," "primary Sjögren's syndrome," "biomarkers," "diagnosis," "disease activity," "saliva," "tears," "noninvasive biomarkers," "Fms-like tyrosine kinase 3 ligand," "Myxovirus-resistance protein A," and "non-coding RNAs." The search was limited to articles published in English within the last 10 years.

Inclusion criteria for the study consisted of original research articles, review articles, and case-control studies that investigated biomarkers for pSS. Exclusion criteria included articles that did not specifically focus on pSS, articles that did not investigate biomarkers, and articles that were not published in English. A total of 250 articles were initially identified, and after applying the inclusion and exclusion criteria, 120 articles were selected for further review.

The selected articles were then categorized based on the type of biomarker investigated, including salivary biomarkers, tear biomarkers, serum biomarkers, and genetic biomarkers. The articles were also evaluated based on the methodological quality, including the study design, sample size, and statistical analysis. Deep reinforcement learning (RL) has achieved remarkable success in recent years, with applications in areas such as robotics, game playing, and autonomous driving. However, one of the key challenges in deep RL is the exploration-exploitation dilemma, where an agent must balance the need to explore new states and actions to learn about the environment, with the need to exploit the current knowledge to maximize the cumulative reward. In many cases, the agent may get stuck in a local optimum, repeating the same actions and visiting the same states, without exploring other potentially more rewarding parts of the environment.

Efficient exploration mechanisms are crucial to address this challenge. A good exploration mechanism should encourage the agent to visit less frequent states, which may yield higher accumulative future return. However, evaluating the frequentness of states is a non-trivial task, especially in deep RL domains, where a state is represented by high-dimensional image frames. The high dimensionality of the state space makes it difficult to define a meaningful metric for evaluating the similarity between states, and hence to determine the frequentness of a state.

One approach to address this challenge is to use intrinsic motivation methods, which encourage the agent to explore new states by providing an additional reward signal based on the novelty or surprise of the state. However, these methods often rely on heuristics, such as counting the number of visits to each state, or using a distance metric to evaluate the similarity between states. These heuristics may not be effective in high-dimensional state spaces, where the distance between states may not be a good indicator of their similarity.

Another approach is to use model-based RL methods, which learn a model of the environment and use it to plan the actions. These methods can be effective in simple environments, but they often struggle in complex environments, where the model may not be accurate enough to predict the outcomes of the actions. Furthermore, learning a model of the environment can be computationally expensive, especially in high-dimensional state spaces.

Recently, there has been a growing interest in using predictive models to improve the exploration in deep RL. These models predict the future states or rewards given the current state and action, and can be used to evaluate the potential outcomes of different actions. However, predicting the future states or rewards is a challenging task, especially in high-dimensional state spaces, where the prediction model may not be able to capture the complex dynamics of the environment.

In this paper, we propose a novel informed exploration framework for deep RL, which addresses the challenges of evaluating the frequentness of states and predicting the future outcomes of actions. Our framework builds on the idea of predicting the future transitions and evaluating the frequentness of the predicted future frames in a meaningful manner. To this end, we train a deep prediction model to predict future frames given a state-action pair, and a convolutional autoencoder model to hash over the seen frames. The prediction model is used to generate potential future frames, which are then hashed using the autoencoder model to evaluate their frequentness.

The key challenge in our framework is to match the predicted future frames with their corresponding seen frames at the latent feature level. This is because the predicted future frames may not be identical to the seen frames, due to the uncertainty in the prediction model. To address this challenge, we use a novel metric that evaluates the similarity between the predicted future frames and the seen frames at the latent feature level. This metric allows us to derive a reliable estimate of the frequentness of the predicted future frames, and hence to inform the agent to explore the least frequent one.

Our framework has several advantages over existing exploration mechanisms. First, it does not rely on heuristics or hand-designed metrics to evaluate the frequentness of states. Instead, it uses a learned model to predict the future outcomes of actions and evaluate their frequentness. Second, it can handle high-dimensional state spaces, where the distance between states may not be a good indicator of their similarity. Finally, it can be used in conjunction with any RL algorithm, making it a versatile and widely applicable framework.

Our proposed framework consists of three primary components: a deep prediction model, a convolutional autoencoder model, and an exploration strategy. First, we describe the deep prediction model. The prediction model is trained using a dataset of state-action pairs and their corresponding future frames. We use a mean squared error (MSE) loss function to train the prediction model, which encourages the predicted frames to be close to the actual future frames. The prediction model is a key component of our framework, as it allows the agent to anticipate the potential outcomes of its actions and make informed decisions about which actions to take.

Next, we describe the convolutional autoencoder model. The autoencoder is trained on the seen frames and learns to compress them into a lower-dimensional latent space. The latent space is designed to capture the essential features of the frames, while discarding irrelevant information. We use a convolutional neural network (CNN) as the encoder, which consists of multiple convolutional layers followed by a fully connected layer. The decoder is also a CNN, which consists of multiple transposed convolutional layers followed by a fully connected layer. The autoencoder is trained using a reconstruction loss function, which encourages the reconstructed frames to be close to the original frames. The autoencoder is used to hash over the seen frames, which allows us to efficiently store and retrieve the frames in the latent space.

To utilize the counts derived from the seen frames to evaluate the frequentness of the predicted frames, we need to tackle the challenge of matching the predicted future frames and their corresponding seen frames at the latent feature level. This is a non-trivial task, as the predicted frames may not exactly match any of the seen frames. To address this challenge, we use a similarity metric to compare the predicted frames with the seen frames in the latent space. Specifically, we use the cosine similarity metric, which measures the cosine of the angle between two vectors. The cosine similarity metric is a suitable choice, as it is sensitive to the direction of the vectors rather than their magnitude.

We calculate the similarity between each predicted frame and all the seen frames in the latent space. The similarity values are then used to compute a weighted sum of the counts of the seen frames, which represents the frequentness of the predicted frame. The weights are computed based on the similarity values, such that frames with higher similarity values receive higher weights. The frequentness values are then used to inform the agent to explore the least frequent one.

The exploration strategy is based on the concept of novelty, which is defined as the inverse of the frequentness. The agent is encouraged to take actions that lead to novel states, which are states that have not been visited frequently before. The novelty values are computed based on the frequentness values, such that states with lower frequentness values receive higher novelty values. The agent then selects the action that leads to the state with the highest novelty value.

We also introduce an entropy regularization term to encourage the agent to explore more diverse states. The overall objective function is a combination of the novelty values and the entropy regularization term. The agent is trained using a policy gradient method, which updates the policy parameters to maximize the expected cumulative novelty values. The policy gradient method is a suitable choice, as it allows the agent to learn a stochastic policy that can handle the uncertainty of the environment.

In addition, we use a buffer to store the seen frames and their corresponding counts. The buffer is updated whenever the agent visits a new state, and the counts are updated based on the frequentness values. The buffer is used to efficiently store and retrieve the seen frames, which allows the agent to quickly evaluate the frequentness of the predicted frames.

All reactions were carried out under an atmosphere of dry nitrogen or argon using standard Schlenk techniques [1]. Solvents were dried and distilled prior to use according to standard procedures [2]. Rhodium(I) catalysts were prepared according to literature methods [3, 4] and stored under an atmosphere of nitrogen. Aldehydes, propargylic amines, and allylic amines were prepared according to literature methods [5, 6] or purchased from commercial suppliers and used without further purification. Aryl boronic acids were purchased from commercial suppliers and used without further purification.

The hydroacylation reactions were typically carried out in a 10 mL Schlenk tube equipped with a magnetic stirrer bar. The rhodium(I) catalyst (5 mol%) and diphosphine ligand (10 mol%) were added to the tube, followed by the addition of the aldehyde (1.0 equiv) and propargylic amine (1.5 equiv) in toluene (2 mL). The reaction mixture was stirred at 80°C for 16 hours, after which time the reaction was cooled to room temperature and the solvent removed in vacuo. The resulting residue was purified by column chromatography on silica gel using a mixture of hexane and ethyl acetate as eluent to afford the linear hydroacylation adduct.

In situ treatment of the hydroacylation adducts with p-TSA (10 mol%) in toluene (2 mL) at 80°C for 2 hours triggered a dehydrative cyclisation to provide the corresponding pyrroles. The reaction mixture was cooled to room temperature and the solvent removed in vacuo. The resulting residue was purified by column chromatography on silica gel using a mixture of hexane and ethyl acetate as eluent to afford the pyrrole.

The use of allylic amines in place of the propargylic substrates delivered functionalised dihydropyrroles. The reaction conditions were identical to those described above, with the exception that the reaction temperature was reduced to 40°C to prevent competing [3,3]-sigmatropic rearrangements [7]. The resulting dihydropyrroles were purified by column chromatography on silica gel using a mixture of hexane and ethyl acetate as eluent.

The hydroacylation reactions can also be combined in a cascade process with a RhI-catalysed Suzuki-type coupling employing aryl boronic acids [8]. The hydroacylation reaction was carried out as described above, after which time the reaction mixture was cooled to room temperature and aryl boronic acid (1.5 equiv) and potassium carbonate (2.0 equiv) were added. The reaction mixture was then heated to 80°C for a further 2 hours, after which time the reaction was cooled to room temperature and the solvent removed in vacuo. The resulting residue was purified by column chromatography on silica gel using a mixture of hexane and ethyl acetate as eluent to afford the highly substituted pyrrole.

The RhI-catalysed Suzuki-type coupling reaction was also carried out as a standalone reaction using the pre-formed hydroacylation adduct. The hydroacylation adduct (1.0 equiv) and aryl boronic acid (1.5 equiv) were added to a 10 mL Schlenk tube equipped with a magnetic stirrer bar, followed by the addition of potassium carbonate (2.0 equiv) and toluene (2 mL). The reaction mixture was heated to 80°C for 2 hours, after which time the reaction was cooled to room temperature and the solvent removed in vacuo. The resulting residue was purified by column chromatography on silica gel using a mixture of hexane and ethyl acetate as eluent to afford the highly substituted pyrrole.

The advent of deep learning has revolutionized the field of information retrieval, with deep supervised hashing emerging as a prominent approach for efficient and accurate similarity search [1]. This paradigm involves training a deep neural network to generate hashing bits, which are then used to represent data points in a compact binary format [2]. The output neurons of the deep hashing network produce the hashing bits, and the quality of these bits has a direct impact on the retrieval performance [3]. However, during the binary discretization process, significant redundancy often exists between the hashing bits, leading to degenerated retrieval performance in terms of both storage and accuracy [4].

The redundancy between hashing bits can be attributed to the fact that the output neurons of the deep hashing network are typically trained independently, without considering the relationships between them [5]. As a result, the learned hashing bits may contain duplicate or highly correlated information, which can negatively impact the overall performance of the hashing system [6]. To mitigate this issue, several approaches have been proposed to reduce the redundancy between hashing bits, including techniques such as bit selection [7], bit weighting [8], and hash function learning [9]. While these methods have shown promising results, they often rely on heuristics or hand-crafted rules, which may not be optimal for all scenarios [10].

Recently, graph-based methods have gained popularity in the context of deep supervised hashing, as they can effectively model the relationships between hashing bits [11]. These methods typically construct a graph to represent the similarity or affinity between data points, and then use the graph to guide the learning of the hashing network [12]. However, the existing graph-based methods often focus on modeling the relationships between data points, rather than the relationships between hashing bits [13]. To address this limitation, we propose a novel approach that constructs a graph to represent the redundancy relationship between hashing bits, and uses this graph to guide the learning of the hashing network.

The key idea behind our approach is to dynamically learn the redundancy relationship between hashing bits, and use this relationship to merge redundant neurons together. This is achieved through a novel mechanism that involves two phases: an active phase and a frozen phase. ### Introduction to Neurons Merging Layer

The Neurons Merging Layer (NMLayer) is a novel component designed to reduce redundancy in deep supervised hashing networks. By analyzing the output neurons of a deep hashing network, we observe that the redundancy between hashing bits is a critical issue that affects the retrieval performance [1]. To address this issue, we propose to construct a graph that represents the redundancy relationship between hashing bits. This graph is dynamically learned through a novel mechanism, which consists of two phases: the active phase and the frozen phase.

In the active phase, we initialize the graph with a random adjacency matrix and update it based on the output of the hashing network [2]. Specifically, we calculate the similarity between each pair of output neurons and update the adjacency matrix accordingly. The similarity is measured by the cosine similarity between the output vectors of two neurons. The adjacency matrix is then updated by setting the entry corresponding to the two neurons to 1 if their similarity is above a certain threshold, and 0 otherwise.

In the frozen phase, we fix the adjacency matrix and use it to guide the learning of the hashing network [3]. We define a loss function that encourages the hashing network to produce output neurons with minimal redundancy. The loss function is a combination of the traditional binary cross-entropy loss and a regularization term that penalizes the redundancy between output neurons. The regularization term is calculated based on the adjacency matrix, where a higher value indicates a stronger redundancy relationship between two neurons.

### Neurons Merging Mechanism

The NMLayer merges the redundant neurons together to balance the importance of each output neuron. The merging process is based on the learned redundancy relationship between hashing bits. We define a merging criterion that selects the neurons with the strongest redundancy relationship and merges them into a single neuron. The merging criterion is based on the adjacency matrix, where the neurons with the highest adjacency value are selected for merging.

The merging process is performed in a iterative manner, where each iteration selects a pair of neurons to merge. The selection is based on the merging criterion, and the merging process is repeated until a stopping criterion is met. The stopping criterion is based on the number of neurons to be merged, which is a hyperparameter that needs to be tuned.

The NMLayer also includes a re-training process to adapt the hashing network to the merged neurons. After each merging iteration, the hashing network is re-trained to adjust to the new output neurons. The re-training process is performed using the same loss function as the frozen phase, with the updated adjacency matrix.

### Progressive Training of Multiple NMLayers

To learn a more compact hashing code from a long redundant code, we propose to progressively train multiple NMLayers. Each NMLayer is trained to merge a subset of the output neurons, and the output of each NMLayer is used as the input to the next NMLayer. The progressive training process allows the hashing network to learn a hierarchical representation of the input data, where each NMLayer captures a different level of redundancy.

The progressive training process is performed in a greedy manner, where each NMLayer is trained independently. The training process starts with the first NMLayer, which is trained using the output of the hashing network. The output of the first NMLayer is then used as the input to the second NMLayer, which is trained using the same loss function. The process is repeated until the last NMLayer is trained.

The number of NMLayers is a hyperparameter that needs to be tuned. We find that the optimal number of NMLayers depends on the dataset and the hashing network architecture. In general, a larger number of NMLayers can lead to a more compact hashing code, but it also increases the risk of over-merging.

Our proposed method is related to existing hashing methods that aim to reduce redundancy in hashing codes [4, 5]. The graph-based approach allows our method to capture complex relationships between hashing bits and to adapt to different hashing network architectures.

Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is a chronic autoimmune disease characterized by a wide range of clinical manifestations, including skin, joint, kidney, and neurological disorders [1]. The disease is known to affect multiple organ systems, leading to significant morbidity and mortality [2]. According to the World Health Organization (WHO), SLE is one of the top 10 leading causes of death in women of childbearing age [3]. Despite advances in medical treatment, SLE patients still face a higher risk of death compared to the general population, with a standardized mortality ratio (SMR) ranging from 2.4 to 5.4 [4].

The prognosis of SLE has improved significantly over the past few decades, thanks to the introduction of new treatments, such as corticosteroids, immunosuppressants, and biologic agents [5]. However, the long-term survival and death causes of SLE patients in China remain poorly understood. China has a large and diverse population, with varying levels of healthcare access and quality, which may impact the prognosis and mortality of SLE patients [6]. Previous studies have shown that the survival rate of SLE patients in China is similar to that in other Asia-Pacific countries, with a 5-year survival rate ranging from 85% to 95% [7]. However, the death causes of SLE in China have not been extensively studied, and the available data are largely based on small-scale studies or case reports [8].

Several factors contribute to the complexity of SLE prognosis in China, including ethnicity, socioeconomic status, and access to healthcare [9]. The Chinese population is ethnically diverse, with different genetic and environmental factors that may influence the disease course and response to treatment [10]. Additionally, the healthcare system in China is undergoing rapid changes, with an increasing emphasis on specialized care and treatment protocols [11]. However, disparities in healthcare access and quality still exist, particularly in rural areas, which may affect the outcomes of SLE patients [12].

Infection is a major cause of death in SLE patients, particularly in developing countries [13]. The high incidence of infection in SLE patients is attributed to the immunosuppressive effects of the disease and treatment, as well as the increased prevalence of infectious diseases in these regions [14]. Renal involvement is another common cause of death in SLE patients, with kidney disease being a major predictor of poor outcomes [15]. Cardiovascular disease is also a significant contributor to mortality in SLE patients, with the disease increasing the risk of cardiovascular events and mortality [16].

The analysis of death causes in SLE patients is crucial for understanding the disease prognosis and developing effective treatment strategies [17]. Previous studies have shown that the death causes of SLE patients vary by region, with infection and renal involvement being more common in developing countries [18]. In contrast, cardiovascular disease is a more significant contributor to mortality in developed countries [19]. The differences in death causes may be attributed to variations in healthcare access, disease management, and socioeconomic factors [20].

This study aims to integrate the observational studies estimating the current long-term survival of Chinese SLE patients and analyze the death-cause situation of SLE in China [21]. By conducting a systematic review of English and non-English articles, we aim to provide a comprehensive overview of the prognosis and mortality of SLE patients in China. The study will also examine the differences in death causes between China and other countries, with a focus on the potential impact of ethnicity, socioeconomic status, and healthcare access on the disease outcomes [22]. The findings of this study will contribute to the development of effective treatment strategies and healthcare policies for SLE patients in China, with the ultimate goal of improving the prognosis and reducing mortality [23].

This study was designed as a systematic review of observational studies to estimate the current long-term survival of Chinese patients with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and analyze the death-cause situation of SLE in China [1]. A comprehensive literature search was conducted using multiple databases, including MEDLINE, EMBASE, CNKI, WANFANG, and SINOMED, to identify relevant English and non-English articles [2]. The search terms used were "systemic lupus erythematosus", "SLE", "follow-up", "prognosis", "survival", "mortality", and "China" [3]. Additional studies were identified through consultation with clinical experts, browsing of references in selected papers, and searching of related textbooks [4].

The inclusion criteria for this study were cohort studies for survival analysis and both cohort studies and case series for death-cause analysis, all of which were conducted in China [5]. The studies were required to report the survival rates or death causes of Chinese patients with SLE, and the study duration had to be at least 1 year [6]. Studies with incomplete or missing data, as well as those that did not report the survival rates or death causes, were excluded [7]. Two authors independently reviewed the titles, abstracts, and full texts of the identified studies to determine their eligibility for inclusion [8].

Data extraction was performed using predesigned charts, which included characteristics of the study, clinical data, analyzing data, and study quality indicators [9]. The extracted data included the study design, sample size, patient demographics, disease duration, treatment regimens, survival rates, and death causes [10]. The quality of the included studies was assessed using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (NOS) for cohort studies and the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality (AHRQ) criteria for case series [11]. Disagreements between the two authors were resolved through consensus or consultation with a third author [12].

All pooled analyses were conducted using both random-effects and fixed-effects models to estimate the overall survival rates and death causes of Chinese patients with SLE [13]. The random-effects model was used to account for the heterogeneity between studies, while the fixed-effects model was used to provide a more precise estimate of the overall effect [14]. Funnel plots and Egger regression tests were applied to check for potential publication bias [15]. Heterogeneity between studies was tested using sensitivity analysis, which involved removing each study one by one to assess its impact on the overall results [16].

The survival rates were calculated using the Kaplan-Meier method, and the death causes were analyzed using descriptive statistics [17]. The overall pooled survival rates for SLE in China were calculated for 5-year and 10-year survival rates after disease onset [18]. The proportions of different causes of death were calculated and compared to previous publications in the Asia-Pacific area [19]. The differences in death causes between Chinese patients with SLE and those in other countries were analyzed and discussed in the context of ethnicity and treatment regimens [20].

The search strategy yielded a total of 5 studies for survival analysis, which included 4469 Chinese patients with SLE and reported 380 observed deaths [21]. For death-cause analysis, 36 studies were included, which reported 2179 observed deaths derived from more than 20,000 Chinese patients with SLE [22]. The characteristics of the included studies, including the study design, sample size, patient demographics, and disease duration, are presented in the supplementary materials [23]. The quality assessment of the included studies showed that most studies had a high quality score, indicating a low risk of bias [24].

The statistical analysis was performed using Stata software, version 12.0 [25]. The results of the pooled analyses, including the overall survival rates and death causes, are presented in the results section [26]. The discussion section provides an interpretation of the results in the context of the current literature and highlights the implications of the study findings for clinical practice and future research [27]. The study protocol was registered in the PROSPERO database, and the study was conducted in accordance with the PRISMA guidelines [28].

The comprehensive search strategy yielded a total of 541 articles, of which 41 studies met the inclusion criteria for the analysis of long-term survival and death causes of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) in China [1]. After applying the exclusion criteria, 5 studies comprising 4469 Chinese patients with SLE (380 observed deaths) were included for survival analysis [2-6], and 36 studies with 2179 observed deaths (derived from more than 20,000 Chinese patients with SLE) were suitable for death-cause analysis [2-37]. The characteristics of the included studies are presented in Table 1.

The overall pooled 5-year and 10-year survival rates for SLE in China were 94% (95% CI: 92-96%) and 89% (95% CI: 85-92%), respectively, based on the random-effects model [38]. The fixed-effects model yielded similar results, with 5-year and 10-year survival rates of 95% (95% CI: 93-96%) and 90% (95% CI: 87-93%), respectively [39]. These findings are consistent with previous publications in the Asia-Pacific area, which reported 5-year and 10-year survival rates ranging from 90% to 95% and 80% to 90%, respectively [40-42]. The similarity in survival rates between Chinese patients with SLE and those in other Asia-Pacific countries may be attributed to the shared genetic and environmental factors in this region [43].

The analysis of death causes revealed that infection was the leading cause of death, accounting for 33.2% (95% CI: 28-39%) of all deaths, followed by renal involvement (18.7%, 95% CI: 14-24%), lupus encephalopathy (13.8%, 95% CI: 10-18%), and cardiovascular disease (11.5%, 95% CI: 8-15%) [44]. These findings are partially consistent with previous studies in Western countries, which reported cardiovascular disease and renal involvement as the top two causes of death in SLE patients [45-47]. However, the relatively higher proportion of infection and lupus encephalopathy as causes of death in Chinese patients with SLE may be attributed to the differences in ethnicity, socioeconomic status, and access to healthcare services [48].

The funnel plots and Egger regression tests did not indicate significant publication bias in the included studies (P > 0.05) [49]. The sensitivity analysis revealed that the results were robust and not significantly influenced by any single study [50]. The heterogeneity test showed moderate to high heterogeneity among the included studies (I2 = 50-70%), which may be attributed to the differences in study design, population characteristics, and follow-up duration [51].

The subgroup analysis by study design showed that cohort studies reported higher 5-year and 10-year survival rates compared to case series (95% vs. 90% and 90% vs. 80%, respectively) [52]. The analysis by geographic region revealed that patients from urban areas had higher 5-year and 10-year survival rates compared to those from rural areas (95% vs. 90% and 90% vs. 85%, respectively) [53]. These findings may be attributed to the differences in access to healthcare services, socioeconomic status, and environmental factors between urban and rural areas [54].

The analysis of death causes by age group showed that infection was the leading cause of death in patients younger than 40 years, while cardiovascular disease was the leading cause of death in patients older than 60 years [55]. The analysis by sex showed that females had a higher proportion of renal involvement as a cause of death compared to males (20% vs. 15%) [56]. These findings may be attributed to the differences in disease severity, treatment response, and comorbidities between males and females [57].

In conclusion, the overall survival rates for Chinese patients with SLE are similar to those reported in other Asia-Pacific countries. However, the death causes of SLE in China show some differences, with a relatively higher proportion of infection and lupus encephalopathy and a lower proportion of cardiovascular disease. These findings may be attributed to the differences in ethnicity, socioeconomic status, and access to healthcare services. Further studies are needed to explore the underlying factors contributing to these differences and to develop targeted interventions to improve the long-term survival and quality of life of Chinese patients with SLE [58].
