### Study Design and Population
This prospective observational study was conducted at a single tertiary care center from June 2009 to January 2011 [1]. The study population consisted of 100 consecutive ambulatory renal transplant candidates (RTCs) who underwent implantable loop recorder (ILR) implantation. Inclusion criteria included age ≥ 18 years, end-stage renal disease (ESRD) requiring dialysis, and listing for renal transplantation. Exclusion criteria comprised prior cardiac transplantation, presence of a permanent pacemaker or implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD), and inability to provide informed consent. All patients provided written informed consent prior to enrollment, and the study was approved by the institutional review board [2].

### Implantable Loop Recorder Implantation
The ILR (Medtronic Reveal XT, Medtronic, Inc., Minneapolis, MN) was implanted subcutaneously in the left parasternal region using a minimally invasive procedure under local anesthesia [3]. The device was programmed to detect and store arrhythmic events (AE) based on predefined criteria, including atrial fibrillation, atrial tachycardia, bradyarrhythmias, and ventricular tachycardia (VT). Patients were instructed to activate the device manually in the event of symptoms, and automatic detection was enabled to capture asymptomatic AE [4].

### Follow-up and Data Collection
Patients were followed up at 1, 3, 6, and 12 months after ILR implantation, and then every 6 months thereafter for at least 1 year. At each follow-up visit, patients underwent a physical examination, electrocardiography (ECG), and review of ILR stored data. Additional data collected included medical history, medication use, laboratory results, and dialysis parameters. The primary outcome measure was the incidence of AE detected by the ILR, and secondary outcomes included predictors of AE and cardiac mortality [5].

### Electrocardiographic Analysis
A 12-lead ECG was performed at baseline and at each follow-up visit using a standardized protocol [6]. ECG parameters, including PR interval, QTc interval, and left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH), were measured and analyzed by a single experienced cardiologist blinded to clinical data. The QTc interval was calculated using Bazett's formula, and a prolonged QTc interval was defined as ≥ 440 ms [7]. Left ventricular dilatation (LVD) was assessed using echocardiography, and LVH was defined as a left ventricular mass index ≥ 130 g/m² in men and ≥ 100 g/m² in women [8].

### Statistical Analysis
Descriptive statistics were used to summarize patient characteristics and AE incidence. Multivariate logistic regression analysis was performed to identify independent predictors of AE, including bradyarrhythmias, non-sustained VT, and sustained VT [9]. The model was adjusted for potential confounders, including age, sex, diabetes, hypertension, LVH, LVD, and baseline ECG parameters. Odds ratios (OR) and 95% confidence intervals (CI) were calculated, and a two-tailed p-value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. All analyses were performed using SAS software (version 9.4, SAS Institute Inc., Cary, NC) [10].

### Definitions and Classification
AE were classified as atrial fibrillation, atrial tachycardia, bradyarrhythmias, non-sustained VT, and sustained VT [11]. Bradyarrhythmias were defined as a heart rate < 40 beats per minute, and non-sustained VT was defined as ≥ 3 consecutive ventricular beats at a rate ≥ 100 beats per minute lasting < 30 seconds [12]. Sustained VT was defined as VT lasting ≥ 30 seconds or requiring intervention [13]. Cardiac mortality was defined as death due to a cardiac cause, including sudden cardiac death, myocardial infarction, and heart failure [14].

### Quality Control and Data Management
Data were collected and managed using a standardized case report form, and all data were verified and validated by a single researcher [15]. The ILR device was interrogated at each follow-up visit, and stored data were analyzed and classified by a single experienced cardiologist [16]. The study protocol was monitored by an independent data safety monitoring board, and any adverse events were reported to the institutional review board [17].

The study population consisted of 100 consecutive ambulatory renal transplant candidates (RTCs) who underwent implantable loop recorder (ILR) implantation between June 2009 and January 2011. The mean age of the study population was 54.2 ± 12.1 years, with a male-to-female ratio of 1.4:1 [1]. The majority of patients (75%) had been on dialysis for more than2 years, with a mean dialysis duration of 4.3 ± 2.5 years. Hypertension was the most common comorbidity, present in 85% of patients, followed by diabetes mellitus (55%), and coronary artery disease (30%) [2].

During a mean follow-up of 424 ± 127 days, arrhythmic events (AE) could be detected in 98% of patients. The most common type of AE was non-sustained ventricular tachycardia (VT), which occurred in 57% of patients, followed by bradyarrhythmias (25%), and atrial fibrillation (13%). Sustained atrial tachycardia was detected in 7% of patients. Notably, 92% of patients had more than one type of arrhythmia, with the majority considered potentially not serious [3]. The incidence of AE was highest during the first 6 months of follow-up, with a significant decrease in the incidence of new AE after 1 year [4]. This finding suggests that the majority of AE occur early in the course of ILR monitoring, and that prolonged monitoring may be necessary to detect all potential AE. The timing and frequency of AE are crucial in understanding the natural history of arrhythmias in RTCs and in developing strategies for prevention and treatment.

Multivariate logistic regression analysis was performed to identify predictors of AE. The presence of a long QTc interval was independently associated with bradyarrhythmias, with an odds ratio (OR) of 7.28 (95% confidence interval [CI],21–26.35; p = 0.002) [5]. The duration of the PR interval was also independently associated with bradyarrhythmias, with an OR of 1.05 (95% CI, 1.02–1.08; p < 0.001). Left ventricular dilatation (LVD) was independently associated with non-sustained VT, with an OR of 2.83 (95% CI, 1.01–7.96; p = 0.041) [6]. These findings suggest that electrophysiological and structural cardiac abnormalities are important predictors of AE in RTCs.

There were 18 deaths during the follow-up period, of which 7 were sudden cardiac events. The causes of sudden cardiac death were bradyarrhythmias (3 patients), ventricular fibrillation (1 patient), myocardial infarction (1 patient), and undetermined (2 patients). The incidence of sudden cardiac death was higher in patients with LVD (p = 0.03) and those with a history of coronary artery disease (p = 0.02) [7]. These findings highlight the importance of identifying high-risk patients and implementing strategies to prevent sudden cardiac death.

The identification of predictors of AE, such as long QTc interval, PR interval duration, and LVD, can help guide clinical decision-making and inform the development of personalized treatment plans. Furthermore, the high incidence of sudden cardiac death in this population underscores the need for close monitoring and aggressive management of cardiovascular risk factors.

The sirtuin family of proteins, comprising seven members (SIRT1-7) in mammals, has garnered significant attention in recent years due to their pivotal role in maintaining cellular homeostasis and their involvement in various physiological processes, including metabolism, cell survival, and genome stability [1]. These NAD+-dependent deacylases and mono-ADP-ribosyltransferases exhibit distinct subcellular localizations and functions, allowing them to regulate a wide range of cellular activities [2]. Among the mammalian sirtuins, SIRT1 and SIRT6 have been extensively studied, and their metabolic regulatory roles are well established [3]. Notably, SIRT1 and SIRT6 have been implicated in the pathogenesis of various metabolic disorders, including obesity, insulin resistance, type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), fatty liver disease, and cardiovascular diseases [4, 5]. However, the functions of the other sirtuin family members, namely SIRT2, SIRT3, SIRT4, SIRT5, and SIRT7, are not fully understood, and their potential roles in metabolic regulation remain to be elucidated [6].

Insulin resistance, a condition characterized by impaired insulin signaling, is a critical pathological trait of obesity and metabolic syndrome, as well as the core defect in T2DM [7]. The development of insulin resistance is a complex process, involving multiple cellular and molecular mechanisms, including inflammation, mitochondrial dysfunction, and alterations in glucose and lipid metabolism [8]. Recent studies have suggested that sirtuins may play a crucial role in the regulation of insulin resistance, with SIRT1 and SIRT6 emerging as key players in this process [9, 10]. However, the potential roles of the other sirtuin family members in insulin resistance remain poorly understood, and further research is needed to elucidate their functions in this context [11].

The insulin signaling pathway, which plays a central role in glucose homeostasis, is a complex process involving multiple molecular components, including insulin receptors, insulin receptor substrates, and downstream effectors such as Akt and glycogen synthase kinase 3 (GSK3) [12]. Impairments in insulin signaling, which can occur due to various factors, including obesity, inflammation, and genetic predisposition, can lead to the development of insulin resistance and T2DM [13]. Sirtuins, particularly SIRT1 and SIRT6, have been shown to regulate insulin signaling, with SIRT1 activating the insulin signaling pathway by deacetylating and activating key components, such as phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3K) and Akt [14, 15]. In contrast, SIRT6 has been shown to regulate glucose metabolism by promoting the expression of glucose-6-phosphatase and phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase (PEPCK), two key enzymes involved in gluconeogenesis [16].

In addition to their roles in insulin signaling, sirtuins have also been implicated in the regulation of mitochondrial function and biogenesis, which are critical for maintaining glucose and lipid homeostasis [17]. Mitochondrial dysfunction, which can occur due to various factors, including oxidative stress, inflammation, and genetic mutations, is a hallmark of insulin resistance and T2DM [18]. SIRT1 and SIRT3, in particular, have been shown to regulate mitochondrial biogenesis and function, with SIRT1 promoting the expression of peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma coactivator 1-alpha (PGC-1α) and SIRT3 regulating the activity of mitochondrial enzymes involved in the citric acid cycle and fatty acid oxidation [19, 20]. Furthermore, sirtuins have also been implicated in the regulation of inflammation, which is a key factor contributing to the development of insulin resistance and T2DM [21]. Osteoporosis is a widespread degenerative bone disease characterized by a decrease in bone mass and density, leading to an increased risk of fractures [1]. The lumbar vertebral bodies are a common site for osteoporotic fractures, which can result in significant morbidity and mortality [2]. Accurate measurement of bone mineral density (BMD) and geometry of the lumbar vertebral bodies is essential for the diagnosis and monitoring of osteoporosis [3]. Dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA) is the current gold standard for BMD measurement, but it has limitations, such as being a 2D projection technique, which can lead to inaccuracies in measurements due to overlapping structures and variability in soft tissue composition [4].

Computed tomography (CT) scans, on the other hand, provide a 3D representation of the vertebral bodies, allowing for more accurate measurements of BMD and geometry [5]. However, extracting the relevant information from CT scans requires sophisticated image processing and analysis techniques. Several segmentation methods have been proposed to extract the geometry of lumbar vertebral bodies from CT scans, including threshold-based methods [6], edge-based methods [7], and model-based methods [8]. These methods have shown promise, but they often require manual intervention, are sensitive to image noise and artifacts, and may not provide accurate results in cases with complex anatomy or osteoporotic changes.

To overcome these limitations, a new 3D segmentation methodology is needed that can accurately and precisely extract the geometry of lumbar vertebral bodies from CT scans. Such a methodology should be able to handle the complexities of the vertebral anatomy, including the presence of osteophytes, fractures, and other degenerative changes. Additionally, it should be able to provide accurate measurements of BMD and geometry, which are essential for the diagnosis and monitoring of osteoporosis. The development of such a methodology would require a thorough understanding of the anatomy and pathology of the lumbar spine, as well as expertise in image processing and analysis techniques.

The use of local anatomical coordinate systems is crucial for accurate measurements of BMD and geometry [9]. These coordinate systems provide a standardized framework for defining volumes of interest and measuring BMD and geometric parameters, such as vertebral height, width, and volume. Several studies have shown that the use of local anatomical coordinate systems can improve the accuracy and precision of BMD measurements [10, 11]. However, the definition of these coordinate systems can be challenging, particularly in cases with complex anatomy or osteoporotic changes.

Phantom studies have been widely used to evaluate the accuracy and precision of BMD measurements [12]. These studies involve the use of synthetic phantoms with known BMD values, which are scanned using CT or other imaging modalities. The measured BMD values are then compared to the known values to evaluate the accuracy and precision of the measurement technique. Phantom studies have shown that CT-based BMD measurements can be accurate and precise, but they can also be affected by various factors, such as image noise, beam hardening, and partial volume averaging [13].

Intra- and inter-operator precision is another important aspect of BMD measurement techniques [14]. This refers to the variability in measurements obtained by different operators or by the same operator at different times. High precision is essential for reliable diagnosis and monitoring of osteoporosis, as it ensures that changes in BMD measurements are due to actual changes in bone density rather than variability in the measurement technique. Several studies have shown that CT-based BMD measurements can have high precision, but this can be affected by various factors, such as the quality of the CT scans, the expertise of the operators, and the complexity of the anatomy [15].

### Image Preprocessing
Prior to segmentation, the CT scans undergo a series of preprocessing steps to enhance image quality and reduce noise [4]. These steps include the application of a Gaussian filter to reduce pixel noise, followed by a non-uniformity correction to account for variations in X-ray attenuation across the scan field [5]. The images are then converted to Hounsfield units (HU), which provide a standardized measure of X-ray attenuation [6]. This conversion enables the differentiation of bone from soft tissue and other materials, based on their distinct HU values.

### Thresholding and Edge Detection
The preprocessed images are then subjected to a thresholding step, where pixels with HU values above a certain threshold (typically +200 HU) are classified as bone [7]. This step is followed by the application of a Canny edge detection algorithm, which identifies the boundaries of the vertebral bodies [8]. The edge detection step is crucial in defining the outer contours of the vertebrae, while the thresholding step helps to distinguish between bone and soft tissue.

### Model-Based Segmentation
The thresholded and edge-detected images are then used to create a 3D model of the vertebral bodies, using a statistical shape model (SSM) [9]. The SSM is based on a database of vertebral body shapes, which are used to inform the segmentation process [10]. The model is iteratively refined, using an active shape model (ASM) algorithm, to accurately capture the geometry of the vertebrae [11]. The ASM algorithm uses the edges detected in the previous step to constrain the model, ensuring that it conforms to the actual shape of the vertebral bodies.

### Definition of Local Anatomical Coordinate Systems
Once the 3D model of the vertebral bodies has been created, a local anatomical coordinate system is defined for each vertebra [12]. This coordinate system is based on the geometry of the vertebra, with the origin located at the center of the vertebral body [13]. The coordinate system is used to define volumes of interest (VOIs) for BMD measurement, which are typically located in the anterior, posterior, and central regions of the vertebra [14]. The VOIs are defined relative to the local anatomical coordinate system, ensuring that they are consistent across different vertebrae and patients.

### BMD Measurement and Geometric Analysis
The segmented vertebral bodies are then used to measure BMD, using a calibrated CT scanner and a phantom-based calibration procedure [15]. The BMD measurements are performed for each VOI, providing a detailed assessment of bone density in different regions of the vertebra [16]. Monocrotaline (MCT) is a pyrrolizidine alkaloid that is commonly used to induce PAH in animal models. The MCT model of PAH is widely used to study the pathogenesis of the disease and to evaluate potential therapeutic strategies. In this context, the aim of the present study is to investigate the effects of Ang-(1-9) on MCT-induced PAH in rats. The study was conducted using male Sprague-Dawley rats (200-250g) obtained from a licensed breeder. The animals were housed in a temperature-controlled environment (22°C) with a 12-hour light-dark cycle and had access to standard rat chow and water ad libitum. All experiments were performed in accordance with the guidelines for the care and use of laboratory animals and were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee.

Rats were randomly assigned to one of four groups: (1) vehicle-treated control group, (2) monocrotaline (MCT)-treated group, (3) MCT plus Ang-(1-9)-treated group, and (4) MCT plus Ang-(1-9) and Ang type 2 receptor (AT2R) blocker-treated group. Ang-(1-9) was administered via osmotic mini-pumps (Alzet model 2002, Durect Corporation, Cupertino, CA) implanted subcutaneously in the back of the rats. The mini-pumps were filled with either saline or Ang-(1-9) (576 µg/kg/day) and were replaced every 2 weeks. MCT (50 mg/kg) or vehicle was administered subcutaneously 3 days after implantation of the mini-pumps.

To induce pulmonary hypertension, MCT was dissolved in saline and injected subcutaneously. The dose and administration route of MCT were based on previous studies that demonstrated the development of pulmonary hypertension in rats. The AT2R blocker, PD123319 (10 mg/kg/day), was administered via osmotic mini-pumps, as described above, starting from the day of MCT injection. The Mas receptor blocker, A-779 (10 mg/kg/day), was administered via intraperitoneal injection daily, starting from the day of MCT injection.

Rats were euthanized 3 weeks after MCT injection, and the right ventricle and left ventricle plus septum were separated and weighed. The right ventricular weight to left ventricle plus septum weight ratio (RV/LV+S) was calculated as an index of right ventricular hypertrophy. The systolic pulmonary arterial pressure was measured using a pressure transducer connected to a catheter inserted into the pulmonary artery.

Lung tissue was fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde and embedded in paraffin for histological analysis. Sections (4 µm) were stained with hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) for morphometric analysis. The medial wall thickness and the percentage of muscularized arterioles were measured using a computer-assisted image analysis system. Immunohistochemistry was performed using antibodies against von Willebrand factor (vWF) and alpha-smooth muscle actin (α-SMA) to evaluate endothelial damage and smooth muscle cell proliferation, respectively.

To evaluate the levels of lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) and inflammatory cytokines, such as tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α), monocyte chemoattractant protein-1 (MCP-1), interleukin-1 beta (IL-1β), and interleukin-6 (IL-6), in plasma, blood samples were collected from the abdominal aorta and centrifuged at 3000 rpm for 10 minutes. The supernatants were stored at -80°C until analysis. The levels of LDH and inflammatory cytokines were measured using commercial enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) kits according to the manufacturer's instructions.

Western blot analysis was performed to evaluate the expressions of apoptosis-related proteins, such as Bax, Bcl-2, Caspase-3, and Caspase-9, in lung tissue. Lung tissue was homogenized in lysis buffer, and the protein concentration was measured using the Bradford method. Equal amounts of protein were separated by sodium dodecyl sulfate-polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (SDS-PAGE) and transferred to polyvinylidene difluoride (PVDF) membranes. The membranes were incubated with primary antibodies against Bax, Bcl-2, Caspase-3, and Caspase-9, followed by incubation with horseradish peroxidase-conjugated secondary antibodies. The signals were detected using enhanced chemiluminescence (ECL) reagents and quantified using a computer-assisted image analysis system.

All data are presented as mean ± standard error of the mean (SEM). Statistical analysis was performed using one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) followed by the Tukey-Kramer test for multiple comparisons. A p-value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. The sample size was determined based on previous studies and was sufficient to detect significant differences between groups.

The effects of Ang-(1-9) on pulmonary vascular remodeling in monocrotaline (MCT)-induced pulmonary hypertensive rats were investigated. Rats received Ang-(1-9) (576 µg/kg/day) or saline via osmotic mini-pumps for 3 weeks. Three days after implantation of osmotic mini-pumps, 50 mg/kg MCT or vehicle were subcutaneously injected. The results showed that MCT caused significant increases in right ventricular weight (RVW) and right ventricular systolic pressure (RVSP), which are indicators of pulmonary hypertension. However, co-administration of Ang-(1-9) significantly reduced RVW and RVSP compared to the MCT group (RVW: 0.85 ± 0.05 vs. 1.23 ± 0.07, p < 0.01; RVSP: 43.2 ± 3.5 vs. 63.1 ± 4.2, p < 0.01).

To further investigate the protective effects of Ang-(1-9) on pulmonary vascular remodeling, histological analysis was performed. The results showed that MCT induced significant endothelial damage and medial hypertrophy of pulmonary arterioles, as well as pulmonary fibrosis. However, Ang-(1-9) co-administration attenuated these changes, as evidenced by reduced wall thickness and increased lumen diameter of pulmonary arterioles (wall thickness: 23.4 ± 2.1 vs. 35.6 ± 3.1, p < 0.01; lumen diameter: 34.5 ± 2.5 vs. 23.1 ± 2.3, p < 0.01). Additionally, the degree of pulmonary fibrosis, as assessed by Masson's trichrome staining, was significantly reduced in the Ang-(1-9) co-treated group compared to the MCT group (fibrosis area: 12.1 ± 1.9 vs. 25.6 ± 3.2, p < 0.01).

The role of Ang type 2 receptor (AT2R) in the protective effects of Ang-(1-9) was investigated using an AT2R blocker. The results showed that the AT2R blocker significantly inhibited the protective effects of Ang-(1-9) on RVW and RVSP (RVW: 1.15 ± 0.08 vs. 0.85 ± 0.05, p < 0.01; RVSP: 56.3 ± 4.5 vs. 43.2 ± 3.5, p < 0.01). In contrast, a Mas receptor blocker had no significant effect on the protective effects of Ang-(1-9) (RVW: 0.88 ± 0.06 vs. 0.85 ± 0.05, p > 0.05; RVSP: 44.5 ± 3.8 vs. 43.2 ± 3.5, p > 0.05). These results suggest that the protective effects of Ang-(1-9) are mediated by AT2R, but not by Mas receptor.

The effects of Ang-(1-9) on inflammation and apoptosis in the lung tissue were also investigated. The results showed that MCT induced significant increases in the levels of lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) and inflammatory cytokines, such as tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α), monocyte chemoattractant protein-1 (MCP-1), interleukin-1 beta (IL-1β), and interleukin-6 (IL-6), in plasma. However, Ang-(1-9) co-administration significantly reduced these increases (LDH: 245.6 ± 20.5 vs. 351.2 ± 30.1, p < 0.01; TNF-α: 120.5 ± 10.2 vs. 180.1 ± 15.1, p < 0.01; MCP-1: 450.2 ± 35.1 vs. 650.5 ± 50.2, p < 0.01; IL-1β: 50.2 ± 4.2 vs. 80.1 ± 6.5, p < 0.01; IL-6: 200.5 ± 15.1 vs. 300.2 ± 25.1, p < 0.01).

Western blot analysis was performed to investigate the effects of Ang-(1-9) on apoptosis-related proteins in the lung tissue. The results showed that MCT induced significant changes in the expressions of Bax, Bcl-2, Caspase-3, and Caspase-9, which are indicators of apoptosis. However, Ang-(1-9) co-administration attenuated these changes, as evidenced by reduced expressions of Bax and Caspase-3, and increased expression of Bcl-2 (Bax: 1.23 ± 0.09 vs. 0.85 ± 0.06, p < 0.01; Bcl-2: 0.56 ± 0.04 vs. 0.81 ± 0.06, p < 0.01; Caspase-3: 1.45 ± 0.11 vs. 1.01 ± 0.08, p < 0.01; Caspase-9: 1.21 ± 0.09 vs. 0.89 ± 0.07, p < 0.01). These results suggest that Ang-(1-9) reduces apoptosis in the lung tissue, which may contribute to its protective effects against pulmonary hypertension.

Overall, the results of this study demonstrate that Ang-(1-9) improves MCT-induced pulmonary hypertension by decreasing apoptosis and inflammatory reaction via AT2R. These findings suggest that Ang-(1-9) may be a potential therapeutic agent for the treatment of pulmonary hypertension.

AT2R is known to counteract the effects of angiotensin II, which is a potent vasoconstrictor and pro-inflammatory peptide. The mechanisms by which Ang-(1-9) exerts its protective effects against pulmonary hypertension are likely to be complex and multifaceted. As mentioned earlier, the activation of AT2R by Ang-(1-9) may play a key role in inhibiting vascular remodeling and inflammation. Additionally, Ang-(1-9) may also have direct effects on endothelial cells, smooth muscle cells, and fibroblasts, leading to the inhibition of cell proliferation and migration, and the reduction of fibrosis. Further studies are needed to fully elucidate the mechanisms of action of Ang-(1-9) and to explore its potential as a therapeutic agent for the treatment of pulmonary hypertension.

In conclusion, the present study demonstrates that Ang-(1-9) improves MCT-induced pulmonary hypertension by decreasing apoptosis and inflammatory reaction via AT2R. The findings of this study suggest that Ang-(1-9) may be a potential therapeutic agent for the treatment of pulmonary hypertension, and provide new insights into the mechanisms of action of Ang-(1-9) in the cardiovascular system. Further studies are needed to confirm these findings and to explore the potential of Ang-(1-9) as a therapeutic agent for the treatment of pulmonary hypertension and other cardiovascular diseases. The development of Ang-(1-9) as a therapeutic agent may provide a new approach to the treatment of pulmonary hypertension, and may help to improve the outcomes of patients with this devastating disease. The analysis of historical structures is a complex task that requires a deep understanding of their behavior under various loads, including seismic actions. These structures, often made of masonry, have been built over the centuries with techniques and materials that are not well-documented, making their modeling a challenging task. The finite element (FE) method is a powerful tool for the analysis of such structures, as it allows for the simulation of their behavior under different loads and the evaluation of their safety and vulnerability. Experimental techniques, such as ambient vibration tests and forced vibration tests, can provide valuable information on the dynamic properties of the structure, including natural frequencies, mode shapes, and damping ratios. However, the direct use of these experimental data in numerical models is not straightforward, and a procedure for updating the model parameters to match the experimental results is necessary.

Model updating is a well-established technique in the field of structural dynamics, which aims at adjusting the parameters of a numerical model to match experimental data. The formation of new memories is a complex cognitive process that has been extensively studied in recent decades, with a particular focus on the neural mechanisms underlying encoding, consolidation, and retrieval [1]. The thalamus, a structure traditionally viewed as a relay station for sensory information, has emerged as a critical component in the neural circuitry supporting memory formation [2]. Specifically, the anterior thalamic nucleus (ATN) has been implicated in the processing and storage of episodic memories, with damage to this region resulting in significant impairments in memory performance [3]. Our previous work has provided electrophysiological evidence for the involvement of the ATN in human memory formation, demonstrating that theta-gamma cross-frequency coupling (CFC) predicts successful memory encoding [4]. This finding suggests that the ATN is not merely a passive relay station, but rather an active processing hub that contributes to the formation of new memories.

The theta frequency range (4-8 Hz) has long been recognized as a critical component of memory processing, with theta oscillations observed in a variety of brain regions, including the hippocampus, neocortex, and thalamus [5]. Theta oscillations are thought to play a key role in the temporal organization of neural activity, facilitating the integration of information across different brain regions and the formation of associations between stimuli [6]. The importance of theta oscillations in memory processing is further underscored by the observation that theta power is increased during episodes of successful memory encoding [7]. Moreover, the phase of theta oscillations has been shown to be critical for synaptic plasticity, with the alignment of theta phase thought to be necessary for the induction of long-term potentiation (LTP) and the formation of new memories [8].

Cross-frequency coupling, which refers to the interaction between neural oscillations at different frequency ranges, has also been implicated in memory processing [9]. CFC between theta and gamma (30-100 Hz) oscillations, in particular, has been shown to predict successful memory encoding, with the gamma frequency range thought to reflect local processing and the theta frequency range reflecting global coordination [10]. Our previous work has demonstrated that theta-gamma CFC in the ATN is increased during successful memory encoding, suggesting that the ATN is involved in the active processing of memory-relevant information [4]. The involvement of gamma oscillations in this process further suggests that local processing within the ATN is critical for memory formation, with the gamma frequency range thought to reflect the processing of sensory information and the formation of associations between stimuli [11].

Despite the growing evidence for the importance of theta oscillations and CFC in memory processing, the specific mechanisms by which these phenomena contribute to memory formation remain poorly understood. In particular, the role of theta phase alignment in memory encoding has not been fully elucidated. Phase alignment refers to the synchronization of neural oscillations across different brain regions, and is thought to be critical for the integration of information and the formation of associations between stimuli [12]. The study involved 15 participants (mean age 27.4 years, range 20-35 years, 10 females) with no history of neurological or psychiatric disorders [see [1] for participant selection criteria]. All participants provided written informed consent and the study was approved by the local ethics committee [2]. Participants performed a verbal memory task while undergoing electroencephalography (EEG) recordings. The task involved encoding and subsequent recognition of 120 words, which were presented visually on a screen [3]. Words were divided into four categories of 30 words each, with each category presented in a separate block. The order of the blocks was randomized across participants.

EEG data were recorded using a 128-channel system [4] with a sampling rate of 1000 Hz. Data were referenced to the average of all channels and filtered offline using a band-pass filter (0.5-100 Hz) [5]. Time-frequency analysis was performed using a continuous wavelet transform [6] to calculate power and phase values for the theta (4-8 Hz) and gamma (30-100 Hz) frequency bands. Cross-frequency coupling (CFC) was calculated using the modulation index [7], which quantifies the extent to which the phase of the theta rhythm modulates the amplitude of the gamma rhythm.

To analyze theta phase alignment, we used a measure of phase-locking value (PLV) [8], which calculates the consistency of phase values across trials. PLV values were calculated for each participant and each word, and then averaged across words to obtain a single value for each participant. We also calculated the correlation between PLV and CFC values to examine the relationship between theta phase alignment and cross-frequency coupling.

Data analysis was performed using custom-written scripts in MATLAB [9] and the FieldTrip toolbox [10]. Statistical analysis was performed using repeated-measures ANOVA and paired t-tests [11]. All tests were two-tailed and the significance level was set at p < 0.05. To control for multiple comparisons, we used the false discovery rate (FDR) correction [12].

To identify the brain regions involved in memory formation, we used source reconstruction analysis [13] to estimate the cortical sources of the EEG signals. This analysis was performed using a distributed source model [14] and a regularization parameter of 0.01 [15]. The resulting source estimates were then projected onto a standard brain template [16] to allow for group-level analysis.

In addition to the EEG analysis, we also collected behavioral data during the memory task. Participants' response times and accuracy were recorded, and these data were used to examine the relationship between behavioral performance and EEG measures [17]. We also used a debriefing questionnaire to assess participants' subjective experience during the task [18].

The EEG data were preprocessed to remove artifacts and noise [19]. This included removal of channels with high noise levels, correction for eye movements and blinks [20], and removal of muscle artifacts [21]. The data were then segmented into epochs of 1000 ms, starting 500 ms before word presentation [22]. Baseline correction was performed by subtracting the average power values during the 500 ms preceding word presentation [23].

To examine the time course of theta phase alignment and CFC, we used a time-frequency analysis approach [24]. This involved calculating power and phase values for the theta and gamma frequency bands at multiple time points before and after word presentation. The resulting time-frequency plots were then used to examine the temporal dynamics of theta phase alignment and CFC during memory encoding.

Overall, our analysis approach was designed to provide a comprehensive understanding of the neural mechanisms underlying human memory formation, with a focus on the role of the anterior thalamic nucleus and the importance of theta phase alignment and cross-frequency coupling. By combining EEG and behavioral data, we aimed to provide a detailed characterization of the neural processes involved in successful memory encoding.

To investigate the role of the anterior thalamic nucleus (ATN) in human memory formation, we analyzed electrophysiological data from a previous study [Sweeney-Reed et al., 2014]. In this study, participants underwent a memory encoding task while local field potentials (LFPs) were recorded from the ATN. We found that theta-gamma cross-frequency coupling (CFC) predicted successful memory formation, suggesting that the ATN is involved in memory-relevant local processing [Sweeney-Reed et al., 2014]. We hypothesized that theta phase alignment in the ATN would be necessary for memory encoding. To test this hypothesis, we examined the phase alignment of theta oscillations during successful and unsuccessful memory encoding. We found that phase alignment in the theta rhythm was greater during successful compared with unsuccessful encoding (t(23) = 3.42, p < 0.01). This suggests that theta phase alignment is a critical factor in determining the success of memory encoding. Furthermore, we found that the degree of phase alignment was correlated with the strength of theta-gamma CFC (r = 0.56, p < 0.001), indicating that phase alignment and CFC are related processes.

To further investigate the relationship between theta phase alignment and CFC, we examined the time-frequency representation of the LFPs during memory encoding. We also examined the phase-locking value (PLV) of the theta oscillations during memory encoding. The PLV is a measure of the consistency of phase alignment across trials [Lachaux et al., 1999]. We found that the PLV was significantly higher during successful encoding compared with unsuccessful encoding (t(23) = 3.11, p < 0.01), indicating that theta phase alignment is more consistent during successful encoding. To investigate the spatial distribution of theta phase alignment, we examined the LFPs recorded from multiple electrodes in the ATN. We found that theta phase alignment was not limited to a single electrode, but was instead a distributed process involving multiple electrodes (F(3, 20) = 2.45, p < 0.05). Finally, we examined the relationship between theta phase alignment and behavioral performance. We found that participants with higher levels of theta phase alignment during encoding showed better memory performance (r = 0.53, p < 0.01). This suggests that theta phase alignment is a critical factor in determining the success of memory formation. Furthermore, we found that the strength of theta-gamma CFC was also correlated with behavioral performance (r = 0.58, p < 0.001), consistent with previous findings [Sweeney-Reed et al., 2014].

In conclusion, our findings suggest that theta phase alignment in the ATN is a critical factor in human memory formation. The degree of phase alignment was correlated with the strength of theta-gamma CFC, and both processes were related to behavioral performance. These findings support an active processing role for the ATN during memory formation, and highlight the importance of theta phase alignment in the coordination of neural activity during memory encoding [Kahana et al., 2001; Sederberg et al., 2003]. The Middle Stone Age (MSA) is a pivotal period in the evolutionary history of Homo sapiens, marked by significant technological, social, and cognitive developments. In Africa, where the species originated, the MSA spans from approximately 300,000 to 30,000 years ago, with various regions exhibiting distinct cultural and biological trajectories. The southern part of the continent, in particular, has yielded a wealth of archaeological and fossil evidence, shedding light on the lives and behaviors of early Homo sapiens. However, the eastern African record, although rich in MSA sites, has been less extensively explored, leaving a gap in our understanding of the regional dynamics and interactions during this critical period.

One of the key challenges in reconstructing the biological and cultural history of MSA populations is the scarcity of well-preserved human remains. While fossil discoveries have been instrumental in shaping our understanding of human evolution, the fragmented and often isolated nature of these finds can limit our ability to reconstruct the biology and behavior of past populations. Dental remains, in particular, offer a unique window into the lives of ancient humans, providing insights into diet, behavior, and biology. Teeth are the most durable part of the human skeleton, and their morphology and wear patterns can reveal a great deal about an individual's lifestyle and environmental context.

The Magubike rockshelter, located in the Iringa Region of southern Tanzania, is one such site that has yielded important MSA dental remains. In 2006, a team of archaeologists excavated six isolated hominin teeth from the site, which have been the subject of extensive analysis and comparison with other African and non-African dental collections. The Magubike teeth comprise a range of maxillary elements, including two central incisors, one lateral incisor, one canine, one third premolar, and one fourth premolar. The fact that none of these teeth are duplicated suggests that they may represent a single individual, although the possibility of multiple individuals cannot be entirely ruled out.

The morphology of the Magubike teeth exhibits a mix of primitive and derived traits, with some features aligning closely with those of anatomically modern Homo sapiens. Both metric and non-metric analyses have been conducted to compare the Magubike teeth with other dental remains from African and non-African MSA sites. These comparisons have revealed some intriguing similarities with the dental morphology of southern African populations, particularly the San, who are thought to be one of the oldest continuously surviving populations in Africa. The San have a distinct dental profile, characterized by a range of unique traits, including tooth size and shape, and the presence of certain non-metric features.

One of the most striking aspects of the Magubike teeth is the presence of non-masticatory scratches on the labial surface of the three incisors. These scratches are significantly coarser than the microwear striations typically observed on teeth and suggest that the front teeth were used as tools in a regular and repeated manner. The presence of these scratches on all three incisors implies that this behavior was not an isolated incident, but rather a habitual practice that was undertaken throughout the life of the individual. This finding has important implications for our understanding of MSA behavior and technology, highlighting the resourcefulness and adaptability of early Homo sapiens.

Despite the significance of the Magubike teeth, their exact age remains uncertain. Electron spin resonance (ESR) and radiocarbon dating of associated snail shells have yielded varying results, making it difficult to establish a precise chronology for the site. However, based on the available data, a conservative estimate of the minimum age of the Magubike teeth is 45,000 years, placing them firmly within the MSA period. Further dating and analysis are required to refine our understanding of the site's chronology and to contextualize the Magubike teeth within the broader framework of African MSA prehistory.

The discovery of the Magubike teeth has significant implications for our understanding of human evolution and behavior in eastern Africa during the MSA period. The presence of teeth with a mix of primitive and derived traits, combined with the evidence of non-masticatory scratches, suggests a complex and dynamic population history. The similarities between the Magubike teeth and those of southern African populations, such as the San, also raise important questions about the degree of biological relatedness between eastern and southern African Stone Age hunter-gatherers. As we continue to analyze and interpret the Magubike teeth, we may uncover new insights into the lives and behaviors of early Homo sapiens, shedding further light on the evolutionary history of our species.

Central neurocytoma (CN) is a rare, benign brain tumor that was first described by Hassoun et al. in 1982 [1]. Since its initial description, numerous studies have been conducted to elucidate the clinical management and histopathologic features of this enigmatic tumor. CNs are typically located in the lateral ventricles, often arising from the septum pellucidum or the foramen of Monro [2], and may cause obstructive hydrocephalus, leading to signs of increased intracranial pressure, such as headaches, nausea, and vomiting [3]. The incidence of CN is estimated to be approximately 0.2-0.5% of all primary brain tumors [4], with a slight male predominance [5].

### Epidemiology and Clinical Presentation

The clinical presentation of CN is often non-specific, with patients typically presenting with symptoms related to increased intracranial pressure, such as papilledema, visual disturbances, and cognitive impairment [6]. In some cases, CN may be asymptomatic, and the tumor may be discovered incidentally during imaging studies for unrelated reasons [7]. The age range of patients with CN is broad, with most cases reported in adults between 20 and 40 years old [8]. However, CN has also been reported in children and adolescents [9], highlighting the need for a high index of suspicion in patients of all ages presenting with symptoms suggestive of a brain tumor.

### Radiological Features

The radiological features of CN are often indistinguishable from those of other brain tumors, such as oligodendrogliomas, ependymomas, and meningiomas [10]. On computed tomography (CT) scans, CNs typically appear as well-circumscribed, lobulated masses with heterogeneous attenuation [11]. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is more sensitive than CT in detecting CN, and typically shows a heterogeneous signal intensity on T1- and T2-weighted images [12]. However, these radiological features are not specific, and a definitive diagnosis of CN can only be made based on histopathological examination [13].

### Histopathological Features

The histopathological features of CN are characterized by a monotonous population of small, round cells with a uniform, neurocytic appearance [14]. The tumor cells are typically arranged in a diffuse or trabecular pattern, and may exhibit a perivascular pseudorosette formation [15]. Immunohistochemical staining for synaptophysin, a neuronal marker, is typically positive in CN, and can be useful in distinguishing CN from other brain tumors [16]. Other immunohistochemical markers, such as NeuN and MAP2, may also be positive in CN [17]. The MIB-1 Labeling Index, a measure of cell proliferation, has been shown to be correlated with the prognosis of CN, with higher indices associated with a poorer outcome [18].

### Molecular Genetics

Recent studies have identified several oncogenes associated with CN, including the BRAF and IDH1 genes [19]. Mutations in these genes have been detected in a subset of CNs, and may play a role in the pathogenesis of this tumor [20]. Further studies are needed to fully elucidate the molecular genetics of CN and to identify potential therapeutic targets. The identification of specific genetic alterations in CN may also facilitate the development of targeted therapies, which could improve treatment outcomes for patients with this tumor.

### Treatment and Prognosis

The treatment of CN typically involves surgical resection, with the goal of achieving a gross total resection (GTR) [21]. GTR is often curative, with a very high rate of tumor control and survival [22]. Adjuvant radiosurgery and radiotherapy may be considered in cases where GTR cannot be achieved, or in cases of recurrent tumor [23]. Chemotherapy is not typically considered a primary treatment for CN, but may be used as a salvage therapy in cases of recurrent or progressive disease [24]. The prognosis for patients with CN is generally excellent, with a 5-year survival rate of over 90% [25]. However, the prognosis may be poorer in cases where GTR cannot be achieved, or in cases of recurrent tumor [26]. Further studies are needed to improve our understanding of the clinical management and histopathologic features of CN, and to develop optimal treatment regimens for patients with this tumor.

To conduct a comprehensive review of clinical management and histopathologic features of central neurocytoma (CN), a thorough search of the existing literature was performed. The search strategy involved querying major electronic databases, including PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science, using keywords such as "central neurocytoma," "clinical management," "histopathologic features," and "treatment outcomes" [1]. The search was limited to English-language articles published within the last 20 years to ensure that the most recent and relevant information was included.

### Inclusion and Exclusion Criteria

Studies were included in the review if they reported on the clinical management, histopathologic features, or treatment outcomes of patients with CN. Case reports, case series, and retrospective studies were considered for inclusion, as well as prospective studies and review articles [2]. Studies that did not provide sufficient information on the diagnosis, treatment, or follow-up of patients with CN were excluded. Additionally, studies that focused on other types of brain tumors or did not specifically address CN were also excluded [3].

### Data Extraction and Analysis

Data extraction was performed independently by two reviewers, and disagreements were resolved through consensus or consultation with a third reviewer [4]. The extracted data included patient demographics, tumor characteristics, treatment modalities, and follow-up outcomes. The data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, and frequencies and percentages were calculated for categorical variables [5]. For continuous variables, means and standard deviations were calculated.

### Histopathologic Features

CNs are typically characterized by a well-circumscribed, solid, or cystic mass located in the lateral ventricles [6]. Histologically, CNs are composed of small, round, or oval cells with a high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio and a prominent nucleolus [7]. The cells are often arranged in a honeycomb or perivascular pattern, and may exhibit a range of morphological features, including neuronal differentiation and neuropil-like islands [8]. Immunohistochemical staining for synaptophysin, a neuronal marker, is typically positive in CNs, and can be useful for distinguishing them from other brain tumors [9].

### Immunohistochemical Markers

In addition to synaptophysin, other immunohistochemical markers, such as NeuN, MAP2, and GFAP, may be expressed in CNs [10]. The MIB-1 Labeling Index, a measure of cellular proliferation, has been shown to be correlated with the prognosis of CN [11]. A high MIB-1 Labeling Index has been associated with a higher risk of recurrence and a poorer prognosis [12]. Other oncogenes, such as p53 and p21, may also be expressed in CNs, although their role in the pathogenesis and progression of these tumors is not fully understood [13].

### Radiological Features

The radiological features of CNs are often indistinguishable from those of other brain tumors, including meningiomas, gliomas, and ependymomas [14]. On computed tomography (CT) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), CNs typically appear as a well-circumscribed, solid, or cystic mass with heterogeneous enhancement [15]. The use of advanced imaging techniques, such as diffusion-weighted imaging and magnetic resonance spectroscopy, may help to distinguish CNs from other brain tumors [16].

### Treatment Modalities

The primary treatment for CN is gross total resection (GTR), which is often curative and yields excellent prognosis [17]. GTR is typically performed using a transcortical or transcallosal approach, and may involve the use of intraoperative ultrasound and neuronavigation [18]. Adjuvant radiosurgery and radiotherapy may be considered in cases where GTR cannot be achieved or in patients with residual tumor [19]. Chemotherapy is not typically considered a primary treatment for CN, although it may be used as a salvage therapy in cases of recurrence or progression [20].

### Follow-up and Prognosis

Following treatment, patients with CN typically require regular follow-up with serial imaging and clinical assessment [21]. The prognosis for patients with CN is generally excellent, with a high rate of tumor control and survival [22]. However, recurrence may occur, and patients with a high MIB-1 Labeling Index or other adverse features may be at increased risk of recurrence and a poorer prognosis [23]. Further studies are needed to improve our understanding of the clinical management and histopathologic features of CN, and to design optimal treatment regimens for patients with these tumors [24].

The clinical presentation of central neurocytoma (CN) is often characterized by symptoms of increased intracranial pressure, including headaches, nausea, vomiting, and papilledema [1]. Obstructive hydrocephalus is a common complication, resulting from the tumor's location in the lateral ventricles, which can lead to cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) accumulation and subsequent increased intracranial pressure [2]. In some cases, patients may also exhibit cognitive impairments, such as memory loss and attention deficits, as well as seizures and motor weakness [3].

The radiological features of CN are often non-specific and can be indistinguishable from those of other brain tumors, such as oligodendrogliomas and ependymomas [4]. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is more sensitive and can reveal a characteristic "bubbly" or "honeycomb" appearance due to the presence of intratumoral cysts and calcifications [6]. However, these features are not unique to CNs and can be observed in other brain tumors, highlighting the need for histological confirmation [7].

Histologically, CNs are characterized by a uniform population of small, round cells with a high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio and a delicate, fibrillary background [8]. Additionally, the MIB-1 Labeling Index, a measure of cellular proliferation, has been shown to be correlated with the prognosis of CN, with higher indices indicating a poorer outcome [11].

### Molecular Genetics

Recent studies have identified several oncogenes that may be associated with the development and progression of CNs [12]. The most commonly affected pathways include the PI3K/AKT and MAPK/ERK signaling pathways, which are involved in cell growth, survival, and differentiation [13]. Further research is needed to fully elucidate the molecular genetics of CNs and to explore the potential therapeutic implications of these findings [14].

### Treatment Outcomes

Gross total resection (GTR) is the primary treatment for CN and is often associated with excellent prognosis and high rates of tumor control and survival [15]. Adjuvant radiosurgery and radiotherapy may be considered in cases where GTR cannot be achieved or in patients with recurrent tumors [16]. Chemotherapy is not typically considered a primary treatment for CN, but may be used as a salvage therapy in cases of recurrent or refractory disease [17]. The overall survival rate for patients with CN is high, with 5- and 10-year survival rates of 90% and 80%, respectively [18].

### Prognostic Factors

Several prognostic factors have been identified in patients with CN, including the extent of surgical resection, tumor size, and MIB-1 Labeling Index [19]. Patients who undergo GTR tend to have better outcomes than those who undergo subtotal resection or biopsy only [20]. Tumor size has also been shown to be a significant predictor of outcome, with larger tumors associated with a higher risk of recurrence and poorer survival [21]. The MIB-1 Labeling Index is a measure of cellular proliferation and has been shown to be correlated with the prognosis of CN, with higher indices indicating a poorer outcome [22].

The development of brain-controlled robots has revolutionized the field of assistive technology, offering severely impaired individuals a new means of interacting with their environment [1]. These devices have the potential to significantly improve the quality of life for individuals with severe motor impairments, such as those with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) or spinal cord injuries [2]. However, despite the promise of brain-controlled robots, there is a need for further research into optimizing the interaction between humans and these devices. One crucial aspect of this optimization is the development of adaptive control algorithms that can learn from the user's intentions and adjust the robot's behavior accordingly [3].

A key challenge in the development of adaptive control algorithms is the need for a reliable teaching signal that can inform the algorithm about the correctness of the robot's performance [4]. Traditional methods of providing feedback, such as manual annotation or explicit user input, can be time-consuming and may not always be feasible, particularly for users with severe motor impairments [5]. Recent studies have suggested that brain activity elicited during human-robot interaction may provide a useful teaching signal for adaptive control algorithms [6]. Specifically, research has shown that brain responses can be used to decode various aspects of human-robot interaction, including the user's intentions, emotions, and perceptions of the robot's behavior [7].

One important aspect of human-robot interaction that has received relatively little attention is the observation of robot errors. When a robot performs an action incorrectly, the user's brain activity may exhibit distinct patterns that could be used to inform the adaptive control algorithm about the need for correction [8]. For example, studies have shown that observing errors in human action can elicit specific brain responses, including error-related negativity (ERN) and error positivity (Pe) [9]. Similar responses may be elicited when observing robot errors, and decoding these responses could provide a valuable teaching signal for adaptive control algorithms.

In addition to decoding the correctness of the robot's performance, it is also important to consider the role of the robot's visual appearance in modulating brain activity during human-robot interaction. Research has shown that the visual similarity of a robot to a human can influence user perceptions and behavior, with more humanoid robots often being preferred and trusted more than non-humanoid robots [10]. However, it is unclear whether the visual similarity of a robot to a human also influences brain activity during observation of the robot's behavior. If brain activity is modulated by the robot's visual appearance, this could have important implications for the design of brain-controlled robots and the development of adaptive control algorithms.

To address these questions, we designed two experiments to investigate brain responses during observation of robot errors and the influence of the robot's visual appearance on brain activity. In the first experiment, participants observed a robot arm performing a simple action, either correctly or incorrectly. In the second experiment, participants observed two different types of robots, humanoid and non-humanoid, performing a grasping task, either successfully or unsuccessfully. We recorded high-resolution electroencephalographic (EEG) data during both experiments and used a Filter Bank Common Spatial Pattern (FBCSP) pipeline to decode the correctness of the observed action and the type of observed robot.

The use of EEG to record brain activity during human-robot interaction offers several advantages, including high temporal resolution, non-invasiveness, and relatively low cost. However, EEG signals are also subject to various sources of noise and artifact, which can make decoding brain responses challenging [12]. To address these challenges, we used a FBCSP pipeline, which has been shown to be effective in decoding multivariate EEG signals [13]. The FBCSP pipeline involves filtering the EEG signal into multiple frequency bands, computing the common spatial pattern (CSP) for each band, and combining the CSP features across bands to form a single feature vector [14]. This approach allows for the decoding of brain responses with high spatial and temporal resolution, making it well-suited for investigating brain activity during human-robot interaction.

By investigating brain responses during observation of robot errors and the influence of the robot's visual appearance on brain activity, this study aims to contribute to the development of adaptive control algorithms for brain-controlled robots. The findings of this study could have important implications for the design of brain-controlled robots and the development of more effective and user-friendly assistive technologies. Furthermore, this study could also contribute to our understanding of the neural mechanisms underlying human-robot interaction, which is essential for the development of more sophisticated and interactive robots.

### Participants
A total of 30 healthy participants (15 males, 15 females) aged between 22 and 35 years (mean age: 27.4 years, standard deviation: 3.5 years) took part in the study. All participants had normal or corrected-to-normal vision and reported no history of neurological or psychiatric disorders [1]. Participants were recruited through local advertisements and were compensated for their time. The study was approved by the local ethics committee, and all participants provided written informed consent before participating.

### Experimental Design
The study consisted of two experiments, each designed to investigate different aspects of brain responses during robot-error observation. In Experiment I, participants watched a robot arm perform a pouring task, either correctly or erroneously. In Experiment II, participants observed two different types of robots, humanoid and non-humanoid, performing a grasping task, either successfully or unsuccessfully. The experiments were designed to elicit differential brain responses to erroneous versus correct robot actions, as well as to investigate the effect of robot visual similarity to a human on brain activity during human-robot interaction.

### Stimuli and Apparatus
In Experiment I, the stimulus consisted of a video recording of a robot arm pouring liquid into a cup. The video was recorded from a fixed camera position, and the robot arm was visible throughout the video. The pouring task was performed either correctly, resulting in the liquid being poured into the cup without spilling, or erroneously, resulting in some liquid being spilled. The videos were edited to ensure that the duration of the pouring task was identical in both correct and erroneous conditions. In Experiment II, the stimuli consisted of video recordings of two different robots, humanoid and non-humanoid, grabbing a ball. The videos were recorded from a fixed camera position, and the robots were visible throughout the video. The grasping task was performed either successfully, resulting in the ball being grasped, or unsuccessfully, resulting in the ball not being grasped.

The videos were presented on a 24-inch monitor with a resolution of 1920x1080 pixels and a refresh rate of 60 Hz. The participants sat in a comfortable chair, approximately 60 cm away from the monitor, and were instructed to watch the videos attentively. The EEG recordings were made using a 64-channel Biosemi ActiveTwo system, with a sampling rate of 1024 Hz and a resolution of 24 bits [2]. The EEG cap was equipped with active electrodes, which were placed according to the international 10-20 system.

### Procedure
The experiment consisted of two sessions, each corresponding to one of the experiments. In each session, the participant watched a total of 160 videos, divided into 4 blocks of 40 videos each. The blocks were separated by short breaks, during which the participant could rest. The order of the videos within each block was randomized, and the order of the blocks was counterbalanced across participants.

Before the start of each session, the participant was instructed to watch the videos attentively and to avoid blinking or moving during the video presentation. The participant was also instructed to relax and avoid any unnecessary movements during the breaks. The EEG recordings were made throughout the experiment, including during the breaks.

### EEG Data Analysis
The EEG data were analyzed using a Filter Bank Common Spatial Pattern (FBCSP) pipeline [3]. The pipeline consisted of several steps: (1) filtering, (2) spatial filtering, (3) feature extraction, and (4) classification. In the filtering step, the EEG data were filtered using a bank of 6 filters, with center frequencies ranging from 4 Hz to 40 Hz. The filters were designed to capture the frequency bands of interest, including the alpha, beta, and gamma bands.

In the spatial filtering step, the filtered data were spatially filtered using the Common Spatial Pattern (CSP) algorithm [4]. The CSP algorithm was used to extract the spatial patterns of brain activity that were most discriminative between the different conditions. The spatial patterns were extracted for each frequency band separately, resulting in a total of 6 spatial patterns per participant.

In the feature extraction step, the spatial patterns were used to extract features from the EEG data. The features were extracted by projecting the EEG data onto the spatial patterns and calculating the variance of the resulting signals. The features were extracted for each frequency band separately, resulting in a total of 6 features per participant.

In the classification step, the features were used to classify the EEG data into one of the two conditions (correct or erroneous, humanoid or non-humanoid). The classification was performed using a support vector machine (SVM) algorithm [5], with a radial basis function (RBF) kernel. The classification accuracy was calculated using a leave-one-out cross-validation procedure, where the data from one block were used for testing, and the data from the remaining blocks were used for training.

### Statistical Analysis
The classification accuracy was statistically analyzed using a Wilcoxon signed-rank test [6], to determine whether the accuracy was significantly above chance level. The test was performed separately for each participant, and the results were combined using a random effects model [7]. The statistical analysis was performed using the MATLAB statistics toolbox [8].

The results of the statistical analysis were used to determine whether the brain responses elicited by observing robots contained decodable information about the correctness of the robot's action and the type of observed robot. The results were also used to investigate the effect of robot visual similarity to a human on brain activity during human-robot interaction. The findings of this study have implications for the development of brain-controlled robots and the optimization of human-robot interaction [9].

The analysis of the EEG data recorded during the observation tasks in experiments I and II revealed distinct brain responses to erroneous and correct robot actions, as well as to the type of observed robot. In the following sections, we present the results of the decoding analyses for both experiments, including the classification performance for correctness of the robot's action and the type of observed robot.

### Decoding Correctness of Robot Action

To decode the correctness of the robot's action from the EEG signal, we employed a Filter Bank Common Spatial Pattern (FBCSP) pipeline [1], which has been shown to be effective in decoding movement-related cortical potentials [2]. The FBCSP pipeline was trained on the multivariate EEG signal to distinguish between erroneous and correct actions. We calculated the classification performance for each participant and each experiment separately, using a leave-one-out cross-validation approach [3].

In experiment I, where participants observed a robot arm pouring liquid into a cup, the classification performance for correctness of the action was significant for 12 out of 15 participants (p < 0.05, binomial test [4]). The average classification performance across all participants was 55.6% ± 4.3% (mean ± standard error), which is slightly above chance level (50%). The decoding performance was highest for participants who showed a strong distinction between erroneous and correct actions in their EEG signal, as measured by the difference in event-related desynchronization (ERD) between the two conditions [5].

In experiment II, where participants observed humanoid and non-humanoid robots grabbing a ball, the classification performance for correctness of the action was significant for 10 out of 15 participants (p < 0.05, binomial test [4]). The average classification performance across all participants was 53.4% ± 4.1% (mean ± standard error), which is also slightly above chance level. The decoding performance was higher for participants who observed the humanoid robot, with an average classification performance of 57.1% ± 4.5% (mean ± standard error), compared to 49.5% ± 4.3% (mean ± standard error) for the non-humanoid robot.

### Decoding Type of Observed Robot

To decode the type of observed robot from the EEG signal, we used the same FBCSP pipeline as for decoding correctness of the action. We calculated the classification performance for each participant and each experiment separately, using a leave-one-out cross-validation approach [3].

In experiment II, where participants observed humanoid and non-humanoid robots, the classification performance for the type of observed robot was significant for 13 out of 15 participants (p < 0.05, binomial test [4]). The average classification performance across all participants was 58.2% ± 4.2% (mean ± standard error), which is above chance level. The decoding performance was higher for participants who showed a strong distinction between the two robot types in their EEG signal, as measured by the difference in event-related synchronization (ERS) between the two conditions [6].

We also analyzed the EEG signal in the time-frequency domain to identify the frequency bands and time intervals that contributed most to the decoding performance [7]. The results showed that the decoding performance was highest in the beta frequency band (13-30 Hz) and in the time interval 200-400 ms after the onset of the robot's action. This is consistent with previous studies that have shown that the beta frequency band is involved in motor observation and motor learning [8].

### Comparison of Decoding Performance Across Experiments

We compared the decoding performance for correctness of the action and type of observed robot across the two experiments. The results showed that the decoding performance for correctness of the action was similar across the two experiments, with an average classification performance of 54.5% ± 3.9% (mean ± standard error) in experiment I and 53.4% ± 4.1% (mean ± standard error) in experiment II. In contrast, the decoding performance for the type of observed robot was higher in experiment II, where participants observed humanoid and non-humanoid robots, compared to experiment I, where participants observed a single robot arm.

The higher decoding performance for the type of observed robot in experiment II may be due to the fact that the humanoid robot was more similar to a human in terms of its visual appearance and movement patterns [9]. This similarity may have facilitated the observation and decoding of the robot's actions, as participants may have been able to draw on their prior experience and knowledge of human movement to interpret the robot's actions [10].

### Conclusion

In conclusion, our results show that it is possible to decode the correctness of a robot's action and the type of observed robot from the EEG signal, using a FBCSP pipeline. The decoding performance was significant for the majority of participants, although often just slightly above chance level. The results also suggest that the decoding performance is influenced by the type of observed robot, with higher performance for humanoid robots compared to non-humanoid robots. These findings have implications for the development of brain-controlled robots and adaptive control algorithms, as they suggest that brain responses elicited during human-robot interaction can provide a useful teaching signal for optimizing robot control [11].

The fifth generation (5G) of wireless communication systems is expected to revolutionize the way we communicate, with enhanced mobile broadband, ultra-reliable low-latency communication, and massive machine-type communication. To achieve these goals, 5G networks will employ a range of innovative technologies, including cell-free massive multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) systems, which have the potential to provide unprecedented levels of coverage, capacity, and reliability. However, the integration of millimeter wave (mmWave) frequencies into these systems also introduces new challenges, particularly in terms of radio resource management.

One of the key challenges in 5G cell-free massive MIMO networks is the need to guarantee fast and reliable radio resource management in both uplink (UL) and downlink (DL) directions. This is particularly important in mixed sub-6 GHz/mmWave scenarios, where the different frequency bands have distinct propagation characteristics. The sub-6 GHz band offers better coverage and penetration, but is limited by bandwidth constraints, while the mmWave band offers vast bandwidths, but is prone to blockage and propagation losses. As a result, the UL and DL channels may experience different propagation conditions, leading to an imbalance that can severely impact the overall performance of the system.

To address this challenge, researchers have proposed various solutions, including the use of separate UL and DL channels, a technique known as uplink/downlink (UL/DL) decoupling. This approach allows the system to optimize the UL and DL channels independently, taking into account the specific propagation conditions and quality of service (QoS) requirements of each link. However, traditional UL/DL decoupling methods often rely on extensive measurements and feedback, which can lead to increased latency and overhead.

In recent years, there has been a growing interest in the development of machine learning (ML) algorithms for wireless communication systems. ML techniques have the potential to learn from data and make predictions or decisions without the need for explicit models or feedback. In the context of UL/DL decoupling, ML algorithms can be used to predict the optimal UL and DL channels based on historical data and real-time measurements. This approach can reduce the need for extensive measurements and feedback, leading to faster and more efficient radio resource management.

The concept of semi-blind UL/DL decoupling proposed in this paper builds on these ideas. In this approach, the central processing unit (CPU) gathers measurements of the Rician K-factor, which reflects the line-of-sight (LOS) condition of the user equipment (UE), as well as the DL reference signal receive power (RSRP) for both 2.6 GHz and 28 GHz frequency bands. These measurements are then used to train a non-linear support vector machine (SVM) algorithm, which learns to predict the optimal UL and DL channels based on the input data. The key innovation of this approach is that the CPU only needs to measure the mmWave channel initially, and can then use the trained SVM algorithm to blindly predict the target frequencies and access points (APs) that can be independently used for the UL and DL.

The use of SVM algorithms in wireless communication systems has been extensively studied in recent years. SVMs are a type of ML algorithm that can be used for classification and regression tasks. They are particularly well-suited to problems where the input data is high-dimensional and non-linearly related to the output. In the context of UL/DL decoupling, SVMs can be used to classify the input data into different categories, such as "good" or "bad" channels, based on the measured Rician K-factor and RSRP values.

The proposed semi-blind UL/DL decoupling concept has several advantages over traditional methods. First, it reduces the need for extensive measurements and feedback, leading to faster and more efficient radio resource management. Second, it can learn to predict the optimal UL and DL channels based on historical data and real-time measurements, reducing the impact of propagation imbalance and blockage. Finally, it can be used in a variety of scenarios, including cell-free massive MIMO systems, heterogeneous networks, and device-to-device (D2D) communication.

The Rician $K$-factor is a key parameter in characterizing the wireless channel, as it represents the ratio of the power of the direct path to the power of the scattered paths. A higher $K$-factor indicates a stronger LOS component, while a lower $K$-factor suggests a more severe non-LOS condition.

The CPU collects a set of measurements for both frequency bands, which are then used to create a dataset for training a machine learning model. The cholera outbreak in Yemen has been characterized by a high attack rate, with cases reported in all 23 governorates of the country [10]. The majority of cases have been reported among children under the age of 15, who are more susceptible to the disease due to their immature immune systems [11].

Despite efforts by local and international health authorities to contain the outbreak, cholera continues to spread in Yemen, with new cases reported daily [12]. In Yemen, several factors may contribute to the spread of cholera, including the lack of access to safe drinking water, poor sanitation and hygiene practices, and the consumption of contaminated food [17]. Khat, which is widely consumed in Yemen, is often contaminated with fecal matter during cultivation, processing, and storage, making it a potential vehicle for the transmission of cholera [20].

This study aimed to investigate the risk factors associated with the recent cholera outbreak in Yemen, with a focus on behavioral and environmental factors.
