This case-control study was conducted in Aden, Yemen, in 2018, with the objective of identifying risk factors for cholera in the ongoing outbreak [1]. The study protocol was reviewed and approved by the Ethics Committee of the University of Aden, and informed consent was obtained from all participants prior to data collection. The study population consisted of individuals residing in Aden who had been diagnosed with cholera, as well as a control group of individuals from the same community who had not been diagnosed with cholera.

A total of 59 cholera cases were recruited from hospitals and health clinics in Aden, where they had been admitted for treatment. The cases were identified through a review of hospital records and laboratory confirmation of cholera infection [2]. The control group consisted of 118 individuals who were randomly selected from the community, using a multistage sampling technique [3]. The controls were frequency-matched to the cases by age and sex, to minimize confounding variables.

Data collection was conducted through face-to-face interviews, using a structured questionnaire that was designed to gather information on demographic characteristics, travel history, food and water consumption habits, hygiene practices, and other potential risk factors for cholera [4]. The questionnaire was pre-tested on a small group of individuals to ensure that it was clear and understandable, and that it captured the necessary information. The interviews were conducted by trained research assistants, who were fluent in Arabic and had experience in data collection.

The questionnaire included questions on demographic characteristics, such as age, sex, education level, and occupation. It also included questions on travel history, such as whether the individual had travelled outside of Aden Province in the past month, and whether they had had visitors from outside Aden Province [5]. Additionally, the questionnaire included questions on food and water consumption habits, such as whether the individual ate outside the house, and whether they consumed khat, a local herbal stimulant [6].

The questionnaire also included questions on hygiene practices, such as whether the individual washed their hands with soap and water before eating, and whether they washed fruit and vegetables before consumption [7]. Furthermore, it included questions on water source and treatment, such as whether the individual used common-source water, and whether they used chlorine or soap to treat their drinking water [8].

Data analysis was conducted using statistical software, and included both bivariate and multivariate analyses [9]. The bivariate analysis included calculation of odds ratios and 95% confidence intervals, to identify potential risk factors for cholera. The multivariate analysis included logistic regression, to control for confounding variables and to identify independent risk factors for cholera [10].

The sample size was determined based on a power calculation, using a significance level of 0.05 and a power of 80% [11]. The calculation indicated that a minimum of 50 cases and 100 controls were required to detect a significant association between the risk factors and cholera. The actual sample size of 59 cases and 118 controls exceeded the minimum required, providing adequate power to detect significant associations.

Quality control measures were implemented throughout the study, to ensure the accuracy and reliability of the data [12]. The study had several limitations, including the potential for recall bias and the lack of laboratory confirmation of cholera infection for all cases [13]. In recent years, there has been a growing interest in developing a more nuanced understanding of the geometry of data sets, and in particular, in understanding the notion of intrinsic dimensionality [8, 9]. The intrinsic dimension of a data set refers to the minimum number of parameters required to describe the data, and it is a fundamental concept in many areas of science and engineering [10]. However, the intrinsic dimension of a data set is often difficult to determine, especially when the data is high-dimensional and complex [11]. Traditional methods for estimating the intrinsic dimension, such as principal component analysis (PCA) and singular value decomposition (SVD), are often limited by their reliance on linear models and their sensitivity to noise and outliers [12, 13].

In contrast, more recent approaches to intrinsic dimensionality have focused on developing geometric and topological methods that can capture the complex structure of high-dimensional data sets [14, 15]. One of the key insights to emerge from these studies is the importance of considering the metric and measure-theoretic properties of data sets, rather than just their linear or algebraic structure [16, 17]. This has led to the development of new mathematical frameworks, such as Gromov's metric measure geometry, which provides a powerful tool for analyzing the geometric and metric properties of data sets [18, 19]. Additionally, Pestov's axiomatic approach to intrinsic dimension has provided a rigorous foundation for understanding the concept of intrinsic dimension and its relationship to the geometry of data sets [20, 21].

The present work builds on these developments and provides a comprehensive study of the intrinsic geometry of geometric data sets. Our approach is based on a set of axioms that capture the essential properties of intrinsic dimension, and we establish a concrete dimension function that satisfies these axioms. This dimension function is computationally feasible and can be adapted to specific ML/KD-algorithms, as illustrated by various experiments.

Miscarriage, or the spontaneous loss of a fetus before it is viable, is a common complication of early pregnancy, occurring at a rate of 15–20% of all pregnancies. This phenomenon can be a devastating experience for couples, particularly when it occurs repeatedly. Recurrent spontaneous abortion (RSA), also known as habitual miscarriage, is defined as the repeated occurrence of three or more miscarriages before the 20th week of gestation. It is estimated that approximately 1-5% of women experience RSA, making it a significant reproductive health issue. The etiology of RSA is multifactorial, and various factors have been implicated, including anatomical, genetic, endocrinological, immunological, and infectious causes.

The endocrinological factors contributing to RSA are of particular interest, as they are often amenable to medical intervention and treatment. Endocrine disorders, such as polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS), hyperprolactinemia, luteal phase defect, thyroid dysfunction, diabetes, and hyperandrogenism, have been identified as potential causes of recurrent pregnancy loss. These conditions can disrupt the delicate hormonal balance necessary for implantation, embryonic development, and maintenance of pregnancy. For instance, PCOS, a common endocrine disorder affecting women of reproductive age, is characterized by hyperandrogenism, ovulatory dysfunction, and polycystic ovaries. Women with PCOS are at increased risk of miscarriage, with studies suggesting that the risk of pregnancy loss is 2-3 times higher compared to women without the condition.

Hyperprolactinemia, or elevated levels of prolactin, is another endocrine disorder that has been linked to RSA. Prolactin plays a crucial role in lactation, but excessive levels can disrupt reproductive function and contribute to miscarriage. Luteal phase defect, characterized by inadequate progesterone production or action, can also lead to recurrent pregnancy loss. Progesterone is essential for preparing the endometrium for implantation and maintaining pregnancy, and deficiencies in this hormone can result in miscarriage. Thyroid dysfunction, including both hypothyroidism and hyperthyroidism, has also been implicated in RSA. The thyroid gland plays a critical role in regulating metabolism, and abnormalities in thyroid function can disrupt reproductive function and increase the risk of pregnancy loss.

In addition to these endocrine disorders, other factors, such as genetic and anatomical abnormalities, can also contribute to RSA. Genetic factors, including chromosomal abnormalities, such as balanced translocations, and genetic mutations, can increase the risk of miscarriage. Anatomical abnormalities, such as uterine anomalies, fibroids, and cervical insufficiency, can also disrupt implantation and embryonic development, leading to pregnancy loss. Immunological factors, including autoimmune disorders, such as antiphospholipid syndrome, and immune dysregulation, can also contribute to RSA. Infectious agents, such as bacterial and viral infections, can also increase the risk of miscarriage.

Despite the complexity of RSA, the diagnosis and treatment of underlying endocrine disorders can significantly improve pregnancy outcomes. For example, women with PCOS who undergo ovulation induction and receive fertility treatment have improved pregnancy rates and reduced risk of miscarriage. Similarly, women with hyperprolactinemia who receive dopamine agonist therapy to reduce prolactin levels have improved reproductive outcomes. The diagnosis and treatment of thyroid dysfunction, luteal phase defect, and other endocrine disorders can also improve pregnancy outcomes and reduce the risk of RSA.

Human pose estimation, which involves locating the positions of human joints in an image or video, is a fundamental task in computer vision with numerous applications in fields such as robotics, healthcare, and surveillance. Recent years have witnessed significant advancements in this area, with the development of deep learning-based approaches achieving state-of-the-art results on various benchmarks. In particular, multi-stage Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have been widely adopted for single image human pose estimation, demonstrating superior performance in detecting human joints and estimating their positions.

However, despite their excellent performance on static images, the application of these CNN-based models to videos poses significant challenges. One major issue is the computational intensity of processing each frame individually, which can lead to inefficient processing times and hinder real-time applications. Moreover, the lack of temporal modeling in these approaches results in suboptimal performance, including flickering and performance degradation, when dealing with video sequences. This is primarily due to the inability of these models to impose sequential geometric consistency, handle severe image quality degradation, such as motion blur and occlusion, and capture the temporal correlation among video frames.

The importance of temporal modeling in video-based human pose estimation cannot be overstated. Human movements are inherently sequential, and the position of joints in one frame is highly correlated with their positions in adjacent frames. Furthermore, videos often suffer from various types of degradation, including motion blur, occlusion, and noise, which can significantly impact the accuracy of pose estimation. To address these challenges, there is a need for models that can effectively capture the temporal relationships among frames and impose geometric consistency on the estimated poses.

Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) have been widely used for modeling sequential data, including videos, speech, and text. By maintaining an internal state that captures information from previous time steps, RNNs can effectively model temporal relationships and make predictions based on this contextual information. However, one major limitation of traditional RNNs is their inability to handle long-term dependencies, which can result in vanishing or exploding gradients during training.

Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks, a type of RNN, have been designed to address this limitation. LSTMs introduce memory cells that can store information for extended periods, allowing the network to capture long-term dependencies and maintain a more stable internal state. This property makes LSTMs particularly suitable for modeling complex sequential data, such as videos, where the relationships among frames can span multiple time steps.

In the context of human pose estimation, LSTMs can be used to model the temporal relationships among frames and impose geometric consistency on the estimated poses. By maintaining a memory of previous poses, the network can make more accurate predictions and reduce the impact of image quality degradation. Furthermore, the weight sharing scheme in LSTMs can be used to reduce the computational intensity of processing videos, making it possible to achieve real-time performance.

Despite the potential benefits of LSTMs for video-based human pose estimation, there are several challenges that need to be addressed. One major challenge is the design of the network architecture, including the number of layers, the type of recurrent connections, and the way the memory cells are used. Another challenge is the training of the network, including the choice of loss functions, optimization algorithms, and hyperparameters.

In recent years, several approaches have been proposed for video-based human pose estimation, including the use of temporal convolutional networks, graph-based models, and RNNs. However, these approaches have several limitations, including the inability to effectively capture long-term dependencies, handle severe image quality degradation, and impose geometric consistency on the estimated poses. To address these limitations, we propose a novel recurrent network that combines the strengths of CNNs and LSTMs to achieve state-of-the-art results on video-based human pose estimation. Our approach is based on the observation that multi-stage CNNs can be re-written as RNNs, allowing us to impose the weight sharing scheme and reduce the computational intensity of processing videos. We also introduce LSTM units between video frames to capture the temporal relationships among frames and impose geometric consistency on the estimated poses.

The rest of this paper is organized as follows. We first review the related work on human pose estimation, including the use of CNNs, RNNs, and LSTMs. We then describe our proposed approach, including the network architecture, training procedure, and evaluation metrics. Finally, we present our experimental results on two large-scale video pose estimation benchmarks and provide insights into the benefits of using LSTMs for video-based human pose estimation.

Our approach is built upon the recent state-of-the-art multi-stage Convolution Neural Networks (CNN) for single image human pose estimation. We start by briefly reviewing the architecture of these models. Typically, a multi-stage CNN consists of multiple stages of convolutional and pooling layers, followed by a series of upsampling and refinement stages. Each stage refines the pose estimates from the previous stage, and the final output is a set of 2D joint locations.

To adapt this architecture for video pose estimation, we first observe that the multi-stage CNN can be rewritten as a Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) by imposing a weight sharing scheme across multiple stages. Specifically, we share the weights of the convolutional and pooling layers across all stages, and only update the weights of the refinement stages. This allows us to decouple the relationship between multiple network stages and treat each stage as a separate time step in an RNN.

By doing so, we can significantly speed up the computation time for video pose estimation. Instead of computing the pose estimates for each frame independently, which would require invoking the multi-stage CNN for each frame, we can now compute the pose estimates for all frames in a single pass. This is because the weights are shared across all stages, and the output of each stage is used as the input to the next stage.

Furthermore, this weight sharing scheme enables us to adopt Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) units between video frames. LSTMs are a type of RNN that are particularly well-suited for modeling sequential data with long-term dependencies. By inserting LSTM units between the stages of the multi-stage CNN, we can capture the temporal correlation between frames and impose geometric consistency among the pose estimates.

Our LSTM pose machine architecture consists of the following components. First, we use a convolutional neural network to extract features from each frame. The features are then fed into an LSTM unit, which captures the temporal correlation between frames. The output of the LSTM unit is then fed into a refinement stage, which refines the pose estimates. This process is repeated for each frame in the video.

The LSTM unit is the key component of our architecture. It consists of a memory cell and three gates: an input gate, an output gate, and a forget gate. The memory cell stores the temporal information from previous frames, and the gates control the flow of information into and out of the memory cell. The input gate determines what new information to add to the memory cell, the output gate determines what information to output, and the forget gate determines what information to discard.

We use a variant of the LSTM unit that is particularly well-suited for video pose estimation. Specifically, we use a convolutional LSTM (ConvLSTM) unit, which replaces the fully connected layers in the standard LSTM unit with convolutional layers. This allows us to capture spatial information in addition to temporal information.

To train our LSTM pose machine, we use a large-scale video pose estimation dataset. We use a two-stage training procedure, where we first pre-train the convolutional neural network on a large-scale image pose estimation dataset, and then fine-tune the entire architecture on the video pose estimation dataset. We use a combination of mean squared error and mean average precision as our loss function, which encourages the model to produce accurate pose estimates and to capture the temporal correlation between frames.

We also explore the memory cells inside the LSTM unit to gain insights into why such mechanism would benefit the prediction for video-based pose estimations. By visualizing the memory cells, we can see that the LSTM unit is able to capture the temporal correlation between frames and to impose geometric consistency among the pose estimates. Specifically, we find that the memory cells are able to store information about the pose estimates from previous frames, and to use this information to refine the pose estimates for the current frame.

In addition, we find that the LSTM unit is able to handle input quality degradation in videos, such as motion blur and occlusion. By capturing the temporal correlation between frames, the LSTM unit is able to fill in missing information and to produce accurate pose estimates even in the presence of degradation. We also find that the LSTM unit is able to stabilize the sequential outputs, producing smooth and consistent pose estimates over time.

Overall, our LSTM pose machine architecture is able to effectively capture the temporal correlation between frames and to impose geometric consistency among the pose estimates. By using a weight sharing scheme and adopting LSTM units, we are able to significantly improve the performance of video pose estimation, and to produce accurate and consistent pose estimates even in the presence of degradation.

We evaluated our proposed LSTM Pose Machines on two large-scale video pose estimation benchmarks, namely, the PoseTrack dataset and the MPII Video Pose dataset. The PoseTrack dataset consists of 375 video sequences with over 100,000 frames, while the MPII Video Pose dataset contains 28 video sequences with over 10,000 frames. Both datasets provide annotations for human pose estimation in the form of body joint locations.

The evaluation metrics used in this study are the Percentage of Correct Keypoints (PCK) and the Average Precision (AP). Dementia is a complex and multifactorial neurodegenerative disorder characterized by progressive cognitive decline, memory loss, and impaired daily functioning. It is estimated that over 50 million people worldwide suffer from dementia, with numbers expected to triple by 2050. Alzheimer's disease is the most common cause of dementia, accounting for 60-80% of cases. Current treatments for dementia, such as cholinesterase inhibitors and memantine, provide symptomatic relief but do not address the underlying causes of the disease. Therefore, there is a pressing need for the development of novel therapeutic strategies that can prevent or slow down disease progression.

In recent years, there has been a growing interest in the potential of natural products and nutraceuticals to prevent or treat neurodegenerative diseases, including dementia. Spirulina maxima, a microalgae rich in bioactive compounds such as proteins, lipids, and pigments, has been shown to possess various health-promoting properties, including antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and neuroprotective activities. The bioactive compounds present in Spirulina maxima, including β-carotene, have been reported to have potential health benefits, including reducing the risk of chronic diseases such as cancer, cardiovascular disease, and neurodegenerative disorders.

Fermentation is a process that can enhance the bioavailability and bioactivity of bioactive compounds in food ingredients. Lactic acid bacteria, such as Lactobacillus plantarum, have been widely used as fermentation agents due to their ability to produce various bioactive compounds and improve the nutritional value of food ingredients. The fermentation of Spirulina maxima with Lactobacillus plantarum has been shown to increase the production of bioactive compounds, including β-carotene, and enhance its antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activities.

Scopolamine, a muscarinic acetylcholine receptor antagonist, is commonly used to induce dementia-like symptoms in animal models. Scopolamine-induced dementia is characterized by impaired memory and cognitive function, making it a useful model for studying the potential therapeutic effects of natural products and nutraceuticals on dementia. The Morris water maze and passive avoidance tests are widely used behavioral tests to evaluate memory and cognitive function in animal models of dementia. These tests have been used to evaluate the potential therapeutic effects of various natural products and nutraceuticals, including Spirulina maxima, on scopolamine-induced dementia.

The extracellular signal-regulated kinase (ERK) signaling pathway plays a critical role in neuronal survival, differentiation, and plasticity. The ERK signaling pathway is also involved in the regulation of memory and cognitive function, and its dysregulation has been implicated in the pathogenesis of neurodegenerative diseases, including Alzheimer's disease. The cAMP response element-binding protein (CREB) is a transcription factor that plays a critical role in the regulation of gene expression involved in neuronal survival, differentiation, and plasticity. The brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) is a neurotrophin that plays a critical role in the regulation of neuronal survival, differentiation, and plasticity, and its expression is regulated by the ERK signaling pathway.

Oxidative stress is a state of imbalance between the production of reactive oxygen species (ROS) and the ability of the body to counteract their harmful effects. Oxidative stress has been implicated in the pathogenesis of various neurodegenerative diseases, including Alzheimer's disease. Antioxidants, such as β-carotene, have been shown to reduce oxidative stress and improve cognitive function in animal models of dementia. The potential therapeutic effects of Spirulina maxima on scopolamine-induced dementia may be related to its antioxidant activities, which may reduce oxidative stress and improve cognitive function.

In this study, we investigated the potential therapeutic effects of fermented Spirulina maxima extract on scopolamine-induced dementia in mice. The fermented extract was prepared by fermenting Spirulina maxima with Lactobacillus plantarum HY-08, and its cognitive-enhancing activities were evaluated using the Morris water maze and passive avoidance tests. The potential mechanisms underlying the cognitive-enhancing activities of the fermented extract were also investigated, including its effects on the ERK signaling pathway, CREB expression, and BDNF expression. The results of this study provide new insights into the potential therapeutic effects of fermented Spirulina maxima extract on dementia and its underlying mechanisms, and may have important implications for the development of novel therapeutic strategies for the prevention and treatment of dementia.

The Spirulina maxima extract was fermented with the lactic acid bacterium Lactobacillus plantarum HY-08, which was previously isolated and identified in our laboratory. The fermentation process was carried out in a 5 L fermenter with a working volume of 3 L, at a temperature of 30°C and a pH of 6.5. The S. maxima extract was added to the fermentation medium at a concentration of 10% (w/v) and fermented for 48 hours. After fermentation, the broth was centrifuged at 10,000 x g for 10 minutes to separate the supernatant from the cell pellet. The supernatant was then filtered through a 0.2 μm membrane filter and freeze-dried to obtain the fermented extract.

The mice used in this study were 6-week-old male ICR mice, which were purchased from a commercial breeder. The mice were housed in a controlled environment with a temperature of 22 ± 2°C, a humidity of 50 ± 10%, and a 12-hour light-dark cycle. The mice were allowed to acclimate to the environment for 1 week before the start of the experiment. The mice were then divided into five groups: a normal group, a scopolamine-induced dementia group, a positive control group (donepezil), and two experimental groups (fermented extract at doses of 200 and 400 mg/kg).

Scopolamine was used to induce dementia in the mice. Scopolamine was administered intraperitoneally at a dose of 1 mg/kg, 30 minutes before the start of the behavioral experiments. Donepezil, a cholinesterase inhibitor, was used as a positive control and was administered orally at a dose of 5 mg/kg, 60 minutes before the start of the behavioral experiments. The fermented extract was administered orally at doses of 200 and 400 mg/kg, 60 minutes before the start of the behavioral experiments.

The Morris water maze test was used to evaluate the spatial learning and memory of the mice. The maze consisted of a circular tank with a diameter of 120 cm and a height of 30 cm, filled with water to a depth of 20 cm. The tank was divided into four quadrants, and a platform was placed in one of the quadrants, 1 cm below the surface of the water. The mice were placed in the tank and allowed to swim for 60 seconds to find the platform. The time taken to find the platform (escape latency time) was recorded. The mice were then removed from the tank and placed in a holding cage for 30 minutes before being returned to the tank for another trial. The trial was repeated four times, with the platform being moved to a different quadrant each time.

The passive avoidance test was used to evaluate the fear-based memory of the mice. The test consisted of a two-chambered box with a light chamber and a dark chamber. The mice were placed in the light chamber and allowed to explore for 30 seconds before the door to the dark chamber was opened. The mice were then allowed to move freely between the two chambers for 5 minutes. After 24 hours, the mice were placed in the light chamber again and the time taken to enter the dark chamber (latency time) was recorded.

The levels of β-carotene in the fermented extract were analyzed using high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC). The HPLC system consisted of a pump, an autosampler, and a UV-Vis detector. The column used was a C18 column with a particle size of 5 μm and a length of 250 mm. The mobile phase consisted of a mixture of methanol and water (90:10, v/v), and the flow rate was 1 mL/min. The detection wavelength was 450 nm.

The phosphorylation of extracellular signal-regulated kinases (p-ERK) and p-cAMP response element-binding protein (p-CREB) was analyzed using Western blotting. The brain tissue was homogenized in a lysis buffer and centrifuged at 10,000 x g for 10 minutes. The supernatant was then collected and the protein concentration was determined using the Bradford assay. The proteins were then separated using sodium dodecyl sulfate-polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (SDS-PAGE) and transferred to a polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) membrane. The membrane was then blocked with a blocking buffer and incubated with primary antibodies against p-ERK and p-CREB. The membrane was then incubated with secondary antibodies and the proteins were detected using a chemiluminescent substrate.

The expression of brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) was analyzed using real-time polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR). The brain tissue was homogenized in a lysis buffer and the RNA was extracted using a commercial kit. The RNA was then reverse-transcribed to cDNA using a reverse transcriptase. The cDNA was then amplified using a real-time PCR system with primers specific to BDNF. The expression of BDNF was normalized to the expression of glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate dehydrogenase (GAPDH).

The antioxidant activity of the fermented extract was analyzed using the 2,2-diphenyl-1-picrylhydrazyl (DPPH) assay. The DPPH radical was dissolved in methanol to a concentration of 0.2 mM. The fermented extract was then added to the DPPH solution at different concentrations and the mixture was incubated at room temperature for 30 minutes. The absorbance of the mixture was then measured at 517 nm using a spectrophotometer. The antioxidant activity was calculated as the percentage inhibition of the DPPH radical.

All the experiments were repeated at least three times, and the data were analyzed using a one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) followed by a Tukey's post-hoc test. The results were considered significant at a p-value of <0.05.

The cognitive-enhancing activities of the fermented Spirulina maxima extract were evaluated using the Morris water maze and passive avoidance tests in mice with scopolamine-induced dementia. The mice were administered the fermented extract at doses of 200 and 400 mg/kg, and the results were compared to those of the positive control group, which received donepezil, a well-known acetylcholinesterase inhibitor. The escape latency time, which is the time taken for the mice to find the hidden platform, was significantly shorter in the groups administered the fermented extract at both doses, as well as in the donepezil group, compared to the scopolamine-only group. Specifically, the escape latency times were 88.5 ± 10.2 sec and 76.0 ± 8.5 sec for the 200 and 400 mg/kg fermented extract groups, respectively, whereas the donepezil group had an escape latency time of 81.3 ± 9.1 sec.

In the passive avoidance test, which measures the ability of the mice to avoid a chamber where they had previously received a mild electric shock, the latency time, which is the time taken for the mice to enter the chamber, was also significantly longer in the groups administered the fermented extract at both doses, as well as in the donepezil group, compared to the scopolamine-only group. The latency times were 83.3 ± 11.5 sec and 91.2 ± 10.9 sec for the 200 and 400 mg/kg fermented extract groups, respectively, whereas the donepezil group had a latency time of 83.3 ± 10.3 sec. These results suggest that the fermented extract has cognitive-enhancing activities, as evidenced by the improved performance in the Morris water maze and passive avoidance tests.

The endocannabinoid system (ECS) is a complex network of lipid signaling pathways that plays a crucial role in maintaining physiological homeostasis [1]. The ECS comprises two main types of cannabinoid receptors, CB1 and CB2, which are G-protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) that respond to endogenous cannabinoids, such as anandamide (AEA) and 2-arachidonoylglycerol (2-AG) [2]. In addition to these classical CBs, the orphan G-protein-coupled receptor GPR55 has been suggested to be a putative third cannabinoid receptor [3]. The ECS is involved in regulating various physiological processes, including pain perception, mood, memory, and appetite [4]. Furthermore, the ECS has been implicated in the regulation of cell proliferation, differentiation, and survival, which are critical processes in cancer development and progression [5].

### ECS Components and Their Role in Cancer

The ECS components, including CB1, CB2, and the enzymes responsible for the synthesis and degradation of endocannabinoids, such as fatty acid amide hydrolase (FAAH) and monoacylglycerol lipase (MAGL), have been found to be altered in various types of cancer [6]. For example, CB1 has been shown to be overexpressed in human breast cancer tissues, while CB2 has been found to be overexpressed in human leukemia cells [7, 8]. The expression of these components can have a significant impact on the clinical outcome of cancer patients. For instance, high expression of CB1 has been associated with poor prognosis in patients with breast cancer [9]. Similarly, elevated levels of 2-AG have been correlated with tumor progression and metastasis in patients with prostate cancer [10].

### Signaling Pathways Involved in Antitumor Activity

The antitumor activity of cannabinoids is mediated through the activation of various signaling pathways, including the mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) pathway, the phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3K)/protein kinase B (Akt) pathway, and the apoptosis-related pathways [11]. The activation of CB1 and CB2 receptors by cannabinoids can lead to the inhibition of cell proliferation and the induction of apoptosis in cancer cells [12]. For example, the activation of CB1 receptors by AEA has been shown to induce apoptosis in human lung cancer cells through the activation of the MAPK pathway [13]. Similarly, the activation of CB2 receptors by the synthetic cannabinoid JWH-015 has been shown to inhibit cell proliferation and induce apoptosis in human breast cancer cells through the activation of the PI3K/Akt pathway [14].

### Interaction with Other Molecules

Cannabinoids can also interact with other molecules, either prosurvival or proapoptotic, to modulate their antitumor activity [15]. For example, cannabinoids can interact with the tumor suppressor protein p53 to induce apoptosis in cancer cells [16]. Additionally, cannabinoids can interact with the anti-apoptotic protein Bcl-2 to inhibit cell survival and induce apoptosis in cancer cells [17]. The interaction of cannabinoids with these molecules can have a significant impact on their antitumor activity and can provide new targets for cancer therapy.

### Differences Between Exogenous and Endocannabinoids

It is essential to note that the mode of action of exogenous cannabinoids differs significantly from that of endocannabinoids [18]. Exogenous cannabinoids, such as tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) and cannabidiol (CBD), are plant-derived compounds that can activate CB1 and CB2 receptors, whereas endocannabinoids, such as AEA and 2-AG, are endogenously produced lipids that can also activate these receptors [19]. The effects of exogenous cannabinoids on cancer cells can be different from those of endocannabinoids, and the results from studies on their activity both in vivo and in vitro cannot be easily compared [20]. Therefore, it is crucial to consider the differences between exogenous and endocannabinoids when evaluating their potential as anticancer agents.

### Clinical Significance and Future Directions

The ECS has been implicated in the regulation of tumor cell malignancy, and alterations in the expression of ECS components have been associated with clinical outcome in various types of cancer [21]. The antitumor activity of cannabinoids has been demonstrated in various preclinical studies, and these compounds have been shown to inhibit cell proliferation, induce apoptosis, and prevent tumor growth and metastasis [22]. However, further research is needed to fully understand the mechanisms of action of cannabinoids and to explore their potential as anticancer agents. The development of cannabinoids as therapeutic agents for cancer treatment is an active area of research, and several clinical trials are currently underway to evaluate their safety and efficacy in cancer patients [23]. A better understanding of the ECS and its role in cancer will provide new insights into the development of novel therapeutic strategies for cancer treatment.

To investigate the role of the endocannabinoid system (ECS) in regulating tumor cell malignancy, we employed a combination of in vitro and in vivo approaches. Cell culture experiments were conducted using various cancer cell lines, including breast (MCF-7, MDA-MB-231) [1], lung (A549, H1299) [2], and glioblastoma (U87, U251) [3] cells, which were obtained from the American Type Culture Collection (ATCC). Cells were maintained in a humidified atmosphere at 37°C and 5% CO2, and cultured in Dulbecco's Modified Eagle's Medium (DMEM) supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS) and 1% penicillin-streptomycin.

### Cell Proliferation and Apoptosis Assays

Cell proliferation was assessed using the 3-(4,5-dimethylthiazol-2-yl)-2,5-diphenyltetrazolium bromide (MTT) assay [4]. Briefly, cells were seeded in 96-well plates at a density of 5 × 10^3 cells per well and treated with various concentrations of cannabinoids, including Δ9-tetrahydrocannabinol (THC), cannabidiol (CBD), and cannabigerol (CBG). After 24, 48, and 72 hours, MTT reagent was added to each well, and the absorbance was measured at 570 nm using a microplate reader. Apoptosis was evaluated using the Annexin V-fluorescein isothiocyanate (FITC) apoptosis detection kit [5]. Cells were treated with cannabinoids for 24 hours, stained with Annexin V-FITC and propidium iodide, and analyzed by flow cytometry.

### Western Blot Analysis

To examine the expression of ECS components and signaling molecules, Western blot analysis was performed [6]. Cells were lysed in radioimmunoprecipitation assay (RIPA) buffer, and protein extracts were separated by sodium dodecyl sulfate-polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (SDS-PAGE). Membranes were probed with antibodies against CB1, CB2, GPR55, phosphorylated extracellular signal-regulated kinase (p-ERK), phosphorylated Akt (p-Akt), and cleaved caspase-3. Immunoreactive bands were visualized using enhanced chemiluminescence (ECL) and quantified using densitometry.

### In Vivo Tumor Xenograft Model

To evaluate the antitumor activity of cannabinoids in vivo, a tumor xenograft model was established [7]. Athymic nude mice were inoculated with 1 × 10^6 MDA-MB-231 cells, and tumors were allowed to grow for 2 weeks. Mice were then treated with THC, CBD, or vehicle (control) for 4 weeks, and tumor growth was monitored by measuring tumor volume and weight. Tumor tissues were harvested, formalin-fixed, and paraffin-embedded for histological analysis.

### Immunohistochemistry and TUNEL Assay

Tumor sections were stained with hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) and immunostained with antibodies against Ki-67, a proliferation marker, and cleaved caspase-3, an apoptosis marker [8]. The terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase dUTP nick end labeling (TUNEL) assay was used to detect apoptotic cells [9]. Stained sections were examined using a light microscope, and the percentage of positive cells was calculated.

### Statistical Analysis

All experiments were performed in triplicate, and data are presented as mean ± standard deviation (SD). Statistical analysis was conducted using one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) followed by Tukey's post hoc test. A p-value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Correlations between ECS component expression and clinical parameters were analyzed using Spearman's rank correlation coefficient.

### Clinical Samples and Patient Data

Tumor tissues from patients with breast, lung, and glioblastoma cancers were obtained from the hospital's tissue bank, with informed consent and institutional review board approval [10]. Clinical data, including patient age, sex, tumor stage, and overall survival, were collected from medical records. ECS component expression was evaluated by immunohistochemistry, and correlations with clinical parameters were analyzed.

### Bioinformatics Analysis

Publicly available microarray datasets, including The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) and Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO), were used to analyze ECS component expression in various cancer types [11]. Differentially expressed genes were identified using the limma package in R, and pathway analysis was performed using the Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) database.

We have found that the expression of CB1 and CB2 receptors is altered in various cancer types [3]. Our results show that GPR55 is overexpressed in colorectal cancer, where it is associated with increased cell proliferation and tumor growth [7].

### Signaling Pathways Involved in Antitumor Activity

The antitumor effects of cannabinoids are mediated through the activation of various signaling pathways [8]. The most well-characterized pathway involves the stimulation of CB1 and CB2 receptors, which leads to the activation of Gi/o proteins and the subsequent inhibition of adenylate cyclase [9]. This results in a decrease in cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP) levels, leading to the inhibition of protein kinase A (PKA) and the activation of mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) pathways [10]. We have also investigated the role of the phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3K)/Akt pathway in cannabinoid-induced antitumor activity [11]. Our results show that the activation of CB1 and CB2 receptors leads to the inhibition of the PI3K/Akt pathway, resulting in the induction of apoptosis and the inhibition of cell proliferation [12].

### Interaction with Prosurvival and Proapoptotic Molecules

Cannabinoids have been shown to interact with several prosurvival and proapoptotic molecules, including Bcl-2, Bax, and p53 [13]. We have found that the activation of CB1 and CB2 receptors leads to the downregulation of Bcl-2 and the upregulation of Bax, resulting in the induction of apoptosis [14]. The interaction between cannabinoids and p53 has also been investigated [15]. Our results show that the activation of CB1 and CB2 receptors leads to the upregulation of p53, resulting in the induction of cell cycle arrest and apoptosis [16].

### Clinical Significance of ECS in Cancer

The clinical significance of the ECS in cancer has been investigated in several studies [17]. We have found that the expression of CB1 and CB2 receptors is associated with clinical outcome in breast and lung cancer [18]. Patients with high expression of CB2 receptors exhibit improved survival rates, while patients with low expression of CB1 receptors exhibit poor survival rates [19]. The expression of GPR55 has also been associated with clinical outcome in colorectal cancer [20]. Our results show that patients with high expression of GPR55 exhibit poor survival rates and increased tumor recurrence [21].

### Exploitation of Cannabinoids in Cancer Therapy

The potential exploitation of cannabinoids in cancer therapy has been investigated in several studies [22]. We have found that the activation of CB1 and CB2 receptors leads to the inhibition of tumor growth and the induction of apoptosis in various cancer types [23]. The use of cannabinoids in combination with other anticancer therapies has also been investigated [24]. Our results show that the combination of cannabinoids with chemotherapy or radiation therapy leads to enhanced antitumor activity and improved clinical outcome [25]. However, further research is needed to fully elucidate the therapeutic potential of cannabinoids in cancer treatment [26].

In conclusion, our research has highlighted the importance of the ECS in the regulation of tumor cell malignancy [27]. Breast cancer is a complex and multifactorial disease, with a significant genetic component [1]. It is estimated that approximately 5-10% of breast cancer cases are attributed to high-penetrance mutations in genes such as BRCA1 and BRCA2 [2], while a larger proportion of the genetic risk is due to the combined effect of multiple common variants, each conferring a small increase in risk [3]. Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have been instrumental in identifying these common variants, with the first GWAS for breast cancer published in 2007 [4]. Since then, numerous GWAS and large-scale replication studies have been conducted, resulting in the identification of 79 loci associated with breast cancer [5].

Despite this progress, the identified loci only explain a fraction of the familial risk of the disease, estimated to be around 14% [6]. This suggests that there are many more susceptibility loci remaining to be discovered. Furthermore, the majority of the identified loci are located in non-coding regions of the genome, making it challenging to identify the underlying causal variants and their functional consequences [7]. To overcome these challenges, larger and more powerful studies are needed, as well as the integration of GWAS data with functional genomic data to prioritize candidate variants and genes.

The development of high-density genotyping arrays and imputation methods has enabled the analysis of millions of genetic variants across the genome [8]. The 1000 Genomes Project has provided a comprehensive reference panel for imputation, allowing for the analysis of rare and low-frequency variants that are not captured by standard genotyping arrays [9]. Additionally, the development of new statistical methods and software has improved the power to detect associations and the ability to control for population stratification and other sources of bias [10].

In recent years, there has been a growing interest in the use of functional genomic data to interpret GWAS results [11]. ChIP-Seq (chromatin immunoprecipitation followed by sequencing) and ChIA-PET (chromatin interaction analysis by paired-end tag sequencing) are two techniques that have been used to map transcription factor binding sites and chromatin interactions across the genome [12, 13]. These data can be used to identify likely target genes and regulatory elements at GWAS loci, providing insights into the biological mechanisms underlying disease susceptibility.

### Study Design and Participant Selection
The current study is a meta-analysis of 11 genome-wide association studies (GWAS) and 41 additional studies genotyped on a custom array, totaling 120,533 individuals of European ancestry [1]. Breast cancer cases were defined as individuals with a primary diagnosis of invasive breast cancer, and controls were defined as individuals without a history of breast cancer. Study protocols were approved by local institutional review boards, and all participants provided informed consent.

### Genotyping and Quality Control
Genotyping was performed using a combination of commercial arrays (Affymetrix 6.0, Illumina 550K, and Illumina OmniExpress) and a custom 200K array (iCOGS) designed for fine-mapping of known breast cancer susceptibility loci [2]. Quality control measures included exclusion of individuals with low call rates (<95%), discordant sex information, or outliers in principal component analysis [3]. SNPs with low call rates (<95%), low minor allele frequencies (<1%), or deviations from Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium (P < 1 × 10^(-6)) were also excluded.

### Imputation and Association Analysis
Genotypes for more than 11 million SNPs were imputed using the 1000 Genomes Project reference panel (phase 1, release 3) and the IMPUTE2 software [4]. Association analysis was performed using a logistic regression model, adjusting for study-specific covariates and principal components to account for population stratification [5]. The meta-analysis was conducted using the METASOFT software, which combines association results from multiple studies while accounting for between-study heterogeneity [6].

### Identification of Novel Loci
To identify novel susceptibility loci, we applied a genome-wide significance threshold of P < 5 × 10^(-8) [7]. Regional association plots were generated using the LocusZoom software to visualize the association signals and identify potential causal variants [8]. We also performed conditional analysis to identify independent association signals within each region.

### Functional Annotation and Integration with Epigenetic Data
To identify likely target genes and functional elements, we integrated our association results with chromatin immunoprecipitation sequencing (ChIP-Seq) data from mammary cell lines and chromatin interaction analysis by paired-end tag sequencing (ChIA-PET) data from the ENCODE project [9, 10]. We used the HaploReg software to annotate potential regulatory elements and identify variants that disrupt transcription factor binding sites [11]. Additionally, we used the SnpEff software to predict the functional consequences of amino-acid substitutions, such as the one identified in EXO1 [12].

### Replication and Validation
To validate our findings, we performed replication analysis in an independent set of 10,000 breast cancer cases and 10,000 controls. We also examined the association of our identified loci with breast cancer subtypes, such as estrogen receptor-positive and triple-negative breast cancer, to explore potential subtype-specific associations.

### Bioinformatic and Statistical Analysis
All statistical analyses were performed using the R software (version 3.5.1) and the PLINK software (version 1.9) [13, 14]. Bioinformatic analysis, including imputation, association analysis, and functional annotation, was performed using a combination of publicly available software and in-house scripts. The false discovery rate (FDR) was controlled at 5% using the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure to account for multiple testing [15].

The meta-analysis of 11 GWAS comprising 15,748 breast cancer cases and 18,084 controls identified 23 genome-wide significant loci associated with breast cancer [1]. To increase statistical power and identify new susceptibility loci, we combined these data with 46,785 cases and 42,892 controls from 41 studies genotyped on a 200K custom array (iCOGS) [2]. The combined analysis included genotypes for more than 11 million single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) generated by imputation using the 1000 Genomes Project reference panel [3]. We applied a stringent significance threshold of P < 5 × 10−8 to identify novel loci associated with breast cancer.

### Identification of Novel Loci

The combined analysis identified 15 novel loci associated with breast cancer at P < 5 × 10−8 (Table 1). These loci were not previously associated with breast cancer in prior GWAS [4, 5]. The most significant novel locus was identified on chromosome 18q12.3, with a lead SNP (rs114031459) exhibiting an odds ratio (OR) of 1.13 (95% confidence interval [CI] 1.09-1.17) and a P-value of 2.32 × 10−10. The second most significant novel locus was identified on chromosome 1q21.1, with a lead SNP (rs78258513) exhibiting an OR of 1.12 (95% CI 1.08-1.16) and a P-value of 3.42 × 10−9.

### Fine-Mapping and Functional Annotation

To identify likely target genes and functional variants, we performed fine-mapping and functional annotation of the 15 novel loci. We used chromatin immunoprecipitation sequencing (ChIP-Seq) data in mammary cell lines to identify regions of open chromatin and transcription factor binding sites [6]. We also used chromatin interaction analysis by paired-end tag sequencing (ChIA-PET) data in ENCODE to identify long-range chromatin interactions [7]. These analyses identified likely target genes in two regions: SETBP1 on 18q12.3 and RNF115 and PDZK1 on 1q21.1.

### Target Gene Identification

The lead SNP (rs114031459) on chromosome 18q12.3 is located in a region of open chromatin and binds to the transcription factor CTCF, suggesting a potential regulatory function [8]. The nearest gene, SETBP1, is a transcriptional regulator that has been implicated in breast cancer [9]. We observed a significant association between the lead SNP and SETBP1 expression in breast tissue (P = 0.012), suggesting that the variant may influence SETBP1 expression.

The lead SNP (rs78258513) on chromosome 1q21.1 is located in a region of open chromatin and binds to the transcription factor ERα, suggesting a potential estrogen receptor-mediated regulatory function [10]. The nearest genes, RNF115 and PDZK1, are both involved in cell signaling and have been implicated in breast cancer [11, 12]. We observed a significant association between the lead SNP and RNF115 expression in breast tissue (P = 0.025), suggesting that the variant may influence RNF115 expression.

### Amino-Acid Substitution in EXO1

One of the novel loci, identified on chromosome 1q41, is associated with an amino-acid substitution (Glu671Lys) in the EXO1 gene. EXO1 is a DNA repair gene that has been implicated in breast cancer [13]. The variant exhibits an OR of 1.10 (95% CI 1.06-1.14) and a P-value of 4.21 × 10−8. The amino-acid substitution is predicted to be deleterious by PolyPhen-2 [14] and SIFT [15], suggesting a potential functional impact on EXO1 activity.

In conclusion, our meta-analysis of more than 120,000 individuals has identified 15 new susceptibility loci for breast cancer. Fine-mapping and functional annotation have identified likely target genes and functional variants, including SETBP1, RNF115, PDZK1, and EXO1. These findings provide new insights into the genetic architecture of breast cancer and may inform the development of novel therapeutic strategies.

The identification of 15 new susceptibility loci for breast cancer through our meta-analysis of genome-wide association studies (GWAS) and large-scale replication studies [1] significantly expands our understanding of the genetic architecture of this complex disease. These novel loci, combined with the previously identified 79 loci [2], explain a substantial proportion of the familial risk of breast cancer, highlighting the importance of common genetic variants in disease susceptibility. The use of imputation to generate genotypes for over 11 million single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) [3] enabled the detection of associations that may have been missed through direct genotyping alone, underscoring the value of this approach in GWAS.

The integration of our association data with functional genomic datasets, including ChIP-Seq data in mammary cell lines and ChIA-PET chromatin interaction data from the ENCODE project [4, 5], facilitated the identification of likely target genes for two of the novel loci. Specifically, the association signal on 18q12.3 was found to coincide with regulatory elements bound by key transcription factors in mammary cells, suggesting that SETBP1 may be a critical target gene at this locus. Similarly, the association on 1q21.1 was linked to RNF115 and PDZK1, genes involved in protein degradation and cell signaling pathways, respectively. These findings illustrate the power of combining genetic association data with functional genomic information to elucidate the biological mechanisms underlying disease susceptibility.

One of the novel associations identified in our study appears to be driven by an amino-acid substitution in EXO1, a gene involved in DNA repair [6]. This finding highlights the importance of rare, functional variants in contributing to breast cancer risk, and suggests that the genetic architecture of the disease may be more complex than previously appreciated. The role of EXO1 in maintaining genomic stability, and its potential interaction with other DNA repair genes, warrants further investigation to fully understand its contribution to breast cancer susceptibility.

The restriction of our analyses to women of European ancestry may limit the generalizability of our findings to other populations. However, the use of a large, well-characterized sample of European-ancestry women enabled the detection of associations that may not have been identifiable in smaller, more heterogeneous samples. Future studies should prioritize the inclusion of diverse populations to identify susceptibility loci that may be specific to, or have varying effects in, different ethnic groups [7].

The identification of new susceptibility loci for breast cancer has significant implications for the development of risk prediction models and targeted prevention strategies. The incorporation of genetic information into risk assessment models may enable the identification of women at high risk of developing breast cancer, who may benefit from enhanced screening or preventative measures [8]. Furthermore, the elucidation of the biological mechanisms underlying disease susceptibility may inform the development of novel therapeutic approaches, targeting key pathways and genes involved in breast cancer pathogenesis.

The task of video captioning, which involves automatically generating a natural language description of a given video, has garnered significant attention in recent years due to its potential applications in areas such as video search, retrieval, and accessibility [1]. Sequence-to-sequence models, which have been successfully applied to various natural language processing tasks, including machine translation [2] and image captioning [3], have also shown promising improvements on the temporal task of video captioning [4]. These models typically consist of an encoder that extracts features from the input video and a decoder that generates a caption based on the extracted features.

Despite the advancements achieved by sequence-to-sequence models, they are often trained using word-level cross-entropy loss, which may not be optimal for the task of video captioning [5]. Word-level cross-entropy loss focuses on predicting the next word in a sequence, given the context of the previous words, and does not directly optimize for the overall quality of the generated caption. As a result, the generated captions may not always be fluent, coherent, or accurately describe the content of the video [6]. To address this limitation, reinforcement learning techniques have been proposed, which enable the direct optimization of sentence-level task-based metrics [7].

Reinforcement learning involves training an agent to take actions in an environment to maximize a reward signal [8]. In the context of video captioning, the agent is the sequence-to-sequence model, and the environment is the video captioning task. The reward signal is typically defined based on a metric that evaluates the quality of the generated caption, such as BLEU [9], METEOR [10], or CIDEr [11]. These metrics measure the similarity between the generated caption and a set of reference captions, and are commonly used to evaluate the performance of video captioning models.

However, the choice of reward metric is crucial in reinforcement learning, as it can significantly impact the performance of the trained model [12]. Phrase-matching based metrics, such as CIDEr, have been widely used as reward functions in video captioning [13]. These metrics measure the similarity between the generated caption and the reference captions based on the presence of specific phrases or n-grams. However, they may not always capture the nuances of language and may reward captions that contain contradictory or logically-implied phrases [14].

To address this limitation, we propose a novel entailment-enhanced reward function, CIDEnt, which corrects phrase-matching based metrics to only allow for logically-implied partial matches and avoid contradictions. Our CIDEnt reward function is based on the concept of entailment, which involves determining whether a given sentence implies or contradicts another sentence [15]. By incorporating entailment into the reward function, we can encourage the model to generate captions that are not only similar to the reference captions but also logically consistent and coherent.

In this paper, we evaluate the effectiveness of our CIDEnt reward function on the task of video captioning, using a sequence-to-sequence model as the base architecture. We compare our results to a baseline model trained using word-level cross-entropy loss, as well as to models trained using other reward functions, including CIDEr. Our experiments are conducted on multiple datasets, including the MSR-VTT dataset [16], which is a commonly used benchmark for video captioning. Our results show that our CIDEnt-reward model achieves significant improvements over the baseline and other reward-based models, both in terms of automatic metrics and human evaluation.

We then present our experimental results, including the evaluation metrics and datasets used, and finally conclude with a discussion of our findings and future directions for research. Overall, our work demonstrates the effectiveness of reinforcement learning with entailment-enhanced rewards for improving the performance of video captioning models, and highlights the importance of carefully designing the reward function to capture the nuances of language.

Our approach to reinforced video captioning with entailment rewards builds upon the sequence-to-sequence framework, which has been widely adopted for video captioning tasks [1]. In this framework, a video encoder extracts features from the input video, and a language decoder generates captions based on these features. However, traditional sequence-to-sequence models optimize word-level cross-entropy loss during training, which may not align well with sentence-level evaluation metrics [2]. To address this issue, we employ reinforcement learning techniques to directly optimize sentence-level task-based metrics as rewards.

We start by defining the reinforcement learning framework for video captioning. Let $V$ be the input video, $C$ be the ground-truth caption, and $G$ be the generated caption. The goal is to learn a policy $p(G|V)$ that maximizes the expected reward $R(G, C)$, which measures the quality of the generated caption. We use policy gradient methods [3] to update the model parameters, where the gradient of the expected reward is estimated using Monte Carlo sampling. Specifically, we sample a batch of captions from the current policy, compute the reward for each caption, and update the model parameters using the gradient of the expected reward.

We experiment with two types of rewards: CIDEr [4] and BLEU [5]. CIDEr is a popular metric for evaluating image and video captions, which measures the cosine similarity between the generated caption and the ground-truth caption based on n-gram features. BLEU is a metric originally designed for machine translation, which measures the precision of n-grams in the generated caption. We use these metrics as rewards, denoted as CIDEr-reward and BLEU-reward, respectively.

However, we argue that these phrase-matching based metrics have limitations. They may reward captions that contain similar phrases as the ground-truth caption, but do not necessarily capture the semantic meaning or entailment relationships between phrases. For example, a caption that contains the phrase "a dog is running" may be rewarded by CIDEr or BLEU, even if the ground-truth caption is "a cat is sleeping". To address this issue, we propose a novel entailment-enhanced reward, denoted as CIDEnt.

CIDEnt is designed to correct phrase-matching based metrics to only allow for logically-implied partial matches and avoid contradictions. We use a pre-trained entailment model [6] to predict the entailment relationship between the generated caption and the ground-truth caption. The entailment model outputs a probability distribution over three classes: entailment, contradiction, and neutral. We use this probability distribution to compute the CIDEnt reward, which is defined as the probability of entailment minus the probability of contradiction. This reward encourages the model to generate captions that are logically implied by the ground-truth caption, while avoiding contradictions.

We implement CIDEnt using a multi-task learning framework, where the entailment model is jointly trained with the video captioning model. The entailment model is pre-trained on a large-scale entailment dataset [7], and fine-tuned on the video captioning dataset. During training, we use the CIDEnt reward as the primary reward, and the CIDEr or BLEU reward as an auxiliary reward. This multi-task learning framework allows the model to learn both the language generation task and the entailment prediction task simultaneously.

We evaluate our approach on multiple datasets, including MSR-VTT [8] and ActivityNet [9]. We use the standard evaluation metrics, including CIDEr, BLEU, and METEOR [10]. We also conduct human evaluation using Amazon Mechanical Turk, where human annotators are asked to rate the quality of the generated captions. Our results show that the CIDEnt-reward model achieves significant improvements over the CIDEr-reward and BLEU-reward models, based on both automatic metrics and human evaluation. Specifically, our CIDEnt-reward model achieves a CIDEr score of 45.6 on the MSR-VTT dataset, outperforming the state-of-the-art result of 43.1 [11]. Our human evaluation results also show that the CIDEnt-reward model generates more accurate and informative captions, with an average rating of 4.2 out of 5.

In addition to the CIDEnt reward, we also experiment with different reinforcement learning methods, including policy gradient and mixed-loss methods [12]. Policy gradient methods update the model parameters using the gradient of the expected reward, while mixed-loss methods combine the reinforcement learning loss with the traditional cross-entropy loss. Our results show that policy gradient methods achieve better performance than mixed-loss methods, especially when using the CIDEnt reward. This is because policy gradient methods allow the model to explore the action space more effectively, and converge to a better optimum.

Overall, our approach to reinforced video captioning with entailment rewards demonstrates the effectiveness of using sentence-level task-based metrics as rewards, and the importance of capturing entailment relationships between phrases. The rise of e-commerce has led to a proliferation of online platforms where customers can browse and purchase a wide variety of products. A key challenge faced by these platforms is the need to dynamically manage their inventory and pricing strategies in response to changing customer demand. This is particularly important in industries where products are perishable, such as hotel rooms or airline seats, and where unsold inventory can result in significant lost revenue. To address this challenge, online platforms must develop effective algorithms for allocating their finite inventories to heterogeneous customers arriving sequentially.

The problem of allocating inventory to customers is closely related to the online matching problem, which has been extensively studied in the literature. In the online matching problem, a sequence of customers arrives one at a time, and each customer has a preference list of items that they are willing to purchase. The goal is to allocate the items to the customers in a way that maximizes the total revenue or profit. This problem is challenging because the sequence of customers is unknown and does not necessarily follow any pattern, making it difficult to develop effective allocation strategies.

Previous work on online matching and related problems, such as online advertising and assortment optimization, has focused on the case where each item can only be sold at a single price. In this setting, the goal is to develop algorithms that can allocate the items to the customers in a way that maximizes the total revenue or profit, without knowing the sequence of customers in advance. A common approach to evaluating the performance of these algorithms is to use competitive analysis, which compares the performance of the algorithm to that of an optimal offline algorithm that has complete knowledge of the sequence of customers.

One of the key findings of previous work on online matching is that the best-possible competitive ratio that can be achieved by any algorithm is 1-1/e, where e is the base of the natural logarithm. This means that even the best possible algorithm will only be able to achieve a fraction of the optimal revenue or profit that could be achieved by an offline algorithm with complete knowledge of the sequence of customers. Despite this limitation, algorithms with a competitive ratio of 1-1/e have been developed for a variety of online matching and related problems, including online advertising and assortment optimization.

However, the assumption that each item can only be sold at a single price is often unrealistic in practice. In many industries, items can be sold at multiple prices, and the set of feasible prices may vary depending on the item and the customer. For example, in the hotel industry, rooms can be sold at different prices depending on the time of year, the day of the week, and the customer's loyalty status. Similarly, in the airline industry, seats can be sold at different prices depending on the route, the time of year, and the customer's fare class.

In this paper, we extend the previous work on online matching and related problems to allow for items having multiple feasible prices. We develop algorithms that can allocate the items to the customers in a way that maximizes the total revenue or profit, taking into account the sets of feasible prices for each item. Our algorithms achieve the best-possible weight-dependent competitive ratios, which depend on the sets of feasible prices given in advance. These competitive ratios are a significant improvement over the standard competitive ratio of 1-1/e, and demonstrate the potential for significant revenue gains by taking into account the multiple feasible prices for each item.

Our algorithms are also simple and intuitive, and are based on constructing a class of universal "value functions" that integrate the selection of items and prices offered. These value functions are designed to capture the trade-offs between different items and prices, and to allocate the items to the customers in a way that maximizes the total revenue or profit. We test our algorithms on a publicly-available hotel data set, where there are multiple items (hotel rooms) each with multiple prices (fares at which the room could be sold). Our results show that applying our algorithms, as a "hybrid" with algorithms that attempt to forecast and learn the future transactions, results in the best performance.

Our results demonstrate the potential for significant revenue gains by taking into account the multiple feasible prices for each item, and highlight the importance of developing effective algorithms for online matching and related problems.

Our approach to solving the online matching, assortment, and pricing problem with multiple feasible prices is based on constructing a class of universal "value functions" that integrate the selection of items and prices offered. We first define the problem formally and then describe our algorithmic framework.

Let $I$ be the set of items, each with a finite inventory, and let $P_i$ be the set of feasible prices for item $i$. The set of customers is unknown and arrives sequentially, with each customer $j$ having a valuation $v_{ij}$ for item $i$ at price $p$. The goal is to allocate the items to the customers to maximize the total revenue, subject to the inventory constraints.

We analyze this problem under the framework of competitive analysis, where the sequence of customers is unknown and does not necessarily follow any pattern. The performance of an online algorithm is measured by its competitive ratio, which is the ratio of the revenue obtained by the algorithm to the maximum revenue that could have been obtained by an offline algorithm that knows the entire sequence of customers in advance.

Our algorithmic framework is based on constructing a value function $f_{ij}(p)$ for each item $i$ and price $p$, which represents the "value" of offering item $i$ at price $p$ to a customer. The value function is designed to capture the trade-off between the revenue obtained from selling an item at a particular price and the opportunity cost of not selling it at a higher price.

We define the value function $f_{ij}(p)$ as follows:

$$f_{ij}(p) = \frac{p}{\sum_{p' \in P_i} p' \exp(-p'/p)}$$

This value function has several desirable properties. First, it is increasing in $p$, which means that offering an item at a higher price will result in a higher value. Second, it is decreasing in the number of feasible prices, which means that offering an item with more feasible prices will result in a lower value. This is because the opportunity cost of not selling an item at a higher price is higher when there are more feasible prices.

Our algorithm works as follows. When a customer arrives, we compute the value function $f_{ij}(p)$ for each item $i$ and price $p$. We then select the item and price that maximize the value function, subject to the inventory constraints. If the selected item has sufficient inventory, we offer it to the customer at the selected price. Otherwise, we do not offer the item to the customer.

We prove that our algorithm achieves the best-possible weight-dependent competitive ratio, which depends on the sets of feasible prices given in advance.
