Cryptococcosis is a life-threatening fungal disease caused by the Cryptococcus genus, which comprises two main species: Cryptococcus neoformans and Cryptococcus gattii [1]. While C. neoformans is primarily associated with immunocompromised individuals, C. gattii can infect both immunocompetent and immunocompromised hosts, leading to severe respiratory and neurological symptoms [2]. The species C. gattii is further divided into several molecular types, including VGI, VGII, VGIII, and VGIV, which exhibit distinct geographical distributions and varying degrees of virulence [3]. Serotype C C. gattii isolates, in particular, have been less extensively studied compared to serotype B isolates, which have been implicated in several outbreaks of cryptococcosis [4].

The pathogenicity of C. gattii is attributed to a combination of factors, including the production of a polysaccharide capsule, the ability to produce melanin, and the capacity to survive and replicate within host cells [5]. The capsule, composed primarily of glucuronoxylomannan (GXM), plays a crucial role in evading the host immune response by inhibiting phagocytosis and inducing anti-inflammatory responses [6]. The expression of capsule-associated genes, such as CAP10, CAP59, and CAP64, is tightly regulated and essential for capsule formation and maintenance [7]. Additionally, the production of melanin, a pigment that contributes to the fungus's ability to survive within the host, is a key virulence factor [8]. Chitin, a component of the fungal cell wall, is also important for the pathogenicity of C. gattii, as it can interact with host chitinases and modulate the immune response [9].

Molecular typing of C. gattii has revealed significant genetic diversity within the species, which is reflected in differences in virulence and clinical presentation [10]. The VGIII and VGIV molecular types, in particular, have been associated with distinct clinical outcomes and geographical distributions [11]. VGIII isolates are primarily found in the Americas, while VGIV isolates are more commonly isolated in Australia and Asia [12]. However, the pathogenic properties of serotype C C. gattii isolates, including those belonging to the VGIII and VGIV molecular types, remain poorly understood. Previous studies have focused primarily on serotype B isolates, which have been implicated in several outbreaks of cryptococcosis [13]. As a result, there is a need to investigate the pathogenic determinants of serotype C isolates to better understand their role in disease.

The murine model of cryptococcosis has been widely used to study the pathogenesis of C. gattii and to evaluate the efficacy of potential therapeutic agents [14]. This model allows for the assessment of fungal burden, host immune response, and clinical outcomes, providing valuable insights into the mechanisms of disease [15]. The use of intranasal infection, in particular, has been shown to mimic the natural route of infection and allows for the evaluation of early events in the infection process [16]. By utilizing this model, researchers can investigate the pathogenic properties of C. gattii isolates, including their ability to colonize the lungs, disseminate to the brain, and induce immune responses.

In recent years, several studies have investigated the genetic diversity of C. gattii, including the identification of genes involved in virulence and pathogenesis [17]. The development of molecular typing methods, such as multilocus sequence typing (MLST) and amplified fragment length polymorphism (AFLP), has enabled the classification of C. gattii isolates into distinct molecular types [18]. These studies have provided valuable insights into the population structure and evolution of C. gattii, highlighting the need for further research into the pathogenic properties of individual isolates. By examining the pathogenic determinants of serotype C C. gattii isolates, including those belonging to the VGIII and VGIV molecular types, researchers can gain a better understanding of the mechanisms underlying disease and develop more effective therapeutic strategies.

The present study aims to investigate the pathogenic properties of three serotype C C. gattii isolates, including two belonging to the VGIV molecular type (WM 779 and 106.97) and one belonging to the VGIII molecular type (ATCC 24066). By examining the capsule dimensions, expression of CAP genes, chitooligomer distribution, and induction of host chitinase activity, we sought to identify potential differences in pathogenicity between these isolates. Additionally, we evaluated the ability of each isolate to produce pigments, react with antibodies to GXM, and cause disease in a murine model of cryptococcosis. Our results provide new insights into the pathogenic diversity of serotype C C. gattii isolates and highlight the importance of considering molecular type and virulence factors in the development of therapeutic strategies.

### Strains and Culture Conditions
The three serotype C Cryptococcus gattii isolates used in this study were 106.97, ATCC 24066, and WM 779, which belong to the molecular types VGIV, VGIII, and VGIV, respectively [1]. Isolates were maintained on Sabouraud dextrose agar (SDA) at 25°C and subcultured every 2 weeks to ensure viability and prevent genetic drift [2]. For experimental purposes, cells were grown in Dulbecco's Modified Eagle's Medium (DMEM) at 37°C with 5% CO2, as previously described [3].

### Capsule Analysis
Capsule dimensions were determined using India ink staining and microscopy [4]. Briefly, cells were suspended in India ink and viewed under a light microscope at 400x magnification. The capsule size was measured as the difference between the outer edge of the capsule and the cell wall. A minimum of 100 cells were measured for each isolate, and the results were expressed as the mean ± standard deviation. The expression of CAP genes, which are involved in capsular polysaccharide synthesis, was analyzed by quantitative reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (qRT-PCR) using specific primers [5].

### Chitooligomer Distribution and Host Chitinase Activity
Chitooligomers were extracted from cells using a modified version of the protocol described by [6]. Briefly, cells were incubated with 1% chitinase in phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) for 2 hours at 37°C. The resulting chitooligomers were separated by size-exclusion chromatography and detected using a chitinase assay kit [7]. Host chitinase activity was induced in murine macrophages using a standardized protocol [8]. Macrophages were incubated with C. gattii cells for 24 hours, and chitinase activity was measured using a fluorometric assay [9].

### Pigment Production
Pigment production was analyzed using a modified version of the protocol described by [10]. Briefly, cells were grown on Niger seed agar for 7 days at 25°C, and the production of melanin and other pigments was assessed visually and by spectrophotometry [11]. The results were expressed as the mean ± standard deviation of three independent experiments.

### Antibody Reactivity
The reactivity of C. gattii cells with antibodies to glucuronoxylomannan (GXM) was analyzed using an enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) [12]. Briefly, cells were incubated with anti-GXM antibodies, and the resulting complexes were detected using a secondary antibody conjugated to horseradish peroxidase. The results were expressed as the mean ± standard deviation of three independent experiments.

### Murine Model of Cryptococcosis
A murine model of cryptococcosis was used to assess the pathogenicity of C. gattii isolates [13]. Briefly, mice were infected intranasally with 1 x 10^6 cells and monitored for lethality and pulmonary fungal burden over a period of 21 days. The fungal burden was determined by plating lung homogenates on SDA and counting the number of colony-forming units (CFU) [14]. The results were expressed as the mean ± standard deviation of three independent experiments.

### Statistical Analysis
Statistical analysis was performed using GraphPad Prism software [15]. Differences in capsule size, chitooligomer distribution, host chitinase activity, pigment production, and antibody reactivity were analyzed using one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) followed by Tukey's post-hoc test. Differences in lethality and pulmonary fungal burden were analyzed using the log-rank test and ANOVA, respectively. A p-value of <0.05 was considered statistically significant.

### Ethics Statement
All animal experiments were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC) and performed in accordance with the National Institutes of Health (NIH) guidelines for the care and use of laboratory animals [16]. The study was conducted in a Biosafety Level 2 (BSL-2) facility, and all personnel involved in the study followed standard operating procedures for handling infectious agents.

### Introduction to Results
The pathogenic diversity amongst serotype C VGIII and VGIV Cryptococcus gattii isolates was investigated through a comprehensive analysis of their virulence factors and ability to cause disease in a murine model. The study focused on three serotype C C. gattii isolates: 106.97, ATCC 24066, and WM 779, which belong to the molecular types VGIV and VGIII, respectively [1]. 

### Capsule Dimensions and Expression of CAP Genes
Capsule dimensions were measured using India ink staining and microscopy. The results showed that isolate ATCC 24066 (VGIII) had a significantly smaller capsule size compared to isolates WM 779 and 106.97 (both VGIV) [2]. The average capsule diameter for ATCC 24066 was 2.5 ± 0.5 μm, whereas for WM 779 and 106.97, it was 4.2 ± 0.7 μm and 4.5 ± 0.8 μm, respectively. These findings are consistent with previous studies, which have demonstrated that capsule size is an important virulence factor in Cryptococcus species [3]. 

The expression of CAP genes, which are responsible for capsule synthesis, was also investigated. Quantitative reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (qRT-PCR) analysis revealed that the CAP64 gene was upregulated in isolates WM 779 and 106.97 compared to ATCC 24066 [4]. This difference in CAP64 expression may contribute to the observed variations in capsule size amongst the isolates. 

### Chitooligomer Distribution and Induction of Host Chitinase Activity
Chitooligomers are known to play a role in the interaction between Cryptococcus species and their host [5]. The distribution of chitooligomers in the three isolates was analyzed using high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC). The results showed that isolates WM 779 and 106.97 had a higher concentration of chitooligomers compared to ATCC 24066. Furthermore, the induction of host chitinase activity was investigated using a murine macrophage cell line. The results showed that isolates WM 779 and 106.97 induced higher levels of chitinase activity compared to ATCC 24066 [6]. 

### Pigment Production and Reactivity with Antibodies to Glucuronoxylomannan
Pigment production is an important virulence factor in Cryptococcus species, and it has been shown to contribute to the pathogenesis of cryptococcosis [7]. The three isolates were analyzed for their ability to produce pigments, and the results showed that isolate WM 779 was more efficient than the other two isolates in producing melanin and other pigments. 

The reactivity of the three isolates with antibodies to glucuronoxylomannan (GXM) was also investigated. GXM is a major component of the Cryptococcus capsule and is recognized by the host immune system [8]. The results showed that the three isolates had distinct patterns of reactivity with antibodies to GXM, suggesting differences in their capsule composition and structure. 

### Pathogenicity in a Murine Model of Cryptococcosis
The pathogenicity of the three isolates was investigated using a murine model of cryptococcosis. Mice were infected intranasally with each of the isolates, and the course of infection was monitored. The results showed that isolates WM 779 and 106.97 (both VGIV) were more virulent than isolate ATCC 24066 (VGIII), as measured by lethality and pulmonary fungal burden [9]. Isolate WM 779 caused 80% mortality in infected mice, while isolate 106.97 caused 70% mortality. In contrast, isolate ATCC 24066 caused only 20% mortality. 

The pulmonary fungal burden was also measured, and the results showed that isolates WM 779 and 106.97 had higher fungal loads in the lungs compared to ATCC 24066. These findings suggest that the VGIV isolates are more virulent than the VGIII isolate in this model of infection. 

### Histopathological Analysis
Histopathological analysis of lung tissue from infected mice showed that isolates WM 779 and 106.97 caused more severe inflammation and tissue damage compared to ATCC 24066 [10]. The results also showed that isolate ATCC 24066 was unable to disseminate to the brain, whereas isolates WM 779 and 106.97 were able to cause brain infection in some mice.

In conclusion, the results of this study demonstrate a high diversity in the pathogenic potential of isolates of C. gattii belonging to the molecular types VGIII and VGIV. The differences in capsule dimensions, expression of CAP genes, chitooligomer distribution, and induction of host chitinase activity amongst the isolates may contribute to their distinct virulence profiles. The findings of this study have important implications for our understanding of the pathogenesis of cryptococcosis and the development of effective diagnostic and therapeutic strategies.

Sickle cell disease (SCD) is a genetic disorder that affects hemoglobin production, leading to the formation of abnormal red blood cells that can cause a range of health problems. It is the most common life-limiting genetic disease among African Americans, affecting more than 100,000 people in the United States. The disease is characterized by recurrent episodes of pain, increased risk of infections, and damage to various organs, including the lungs. Respiratory complications are a major cause of morbidity and mortality in patients with SCD, and asthma is a common comorbidity that can exacerbate the disease. However, the relationship between SCD and asthma is complex, and the diagnosis of asthma in patients with SCD can be challenging.

Asthma is a chronic inflammatory disease of the airways that is characterized by recurring episodes of wheezing, coughing, chest tightness, and shortness of breath. It is a common disease that affects people of all ages, but its prevalence and severity can vary depending on the population. In the general population, asthma is typically diagnosed based on a combination of clinical symptoms, pulmonary function tests, and response to treatment. However, in patients with SCD, the diagnosis of asthma can be more complicated. Wheezing, a common symptom of asthma, is also a frequent occurrence in patients with SCD, even in the absence of an asthma diagnosis. This has led to questions about the relationship between SCD and asthma, and whether wheezing in patients with SCD is a marker of asthma or a distinct entity.

The association between asthma and SCD has been recognized for several decades. Early studies reported a high prevalence of asthma in patients with SCD, and suggested that asthma may be a risk factor for acute chest syndrome (ACS), a life-threatening complication of SCD. ACS is characterized by a new pulmonary infiltrate on chest radiograph, often accompanied by fever, respiratory symptoms, and chest pain. It is a major cause of morbidity and mortality in patients with SCD, and is often precipitated by respiratory infections or asthma exacerbations. The relationship between asthma and ACS is complex, and it is not clear whether asthma is a cause or a consequence of ACS. However, it is clear that patients with SCD and asthma are at increased risk of developing ACS, and that asthma exacerbations can trigger ACS episodes.

In recent years, there has been growing interest in the relationship between wheezing and SCD. Wheezing is a common symptom in patients with SCD, and can occur in the absence of an asthma diagnosis. Several studies have reported that wheezing is a predictor of SCD severity, and that patients with SCD who wheeze are at increased risk of developing ACS and other complications. The mechanisms underlying wheezing in SCD are not fully understood, but it is thought to be related to the chronic inflammation and oxidative stress that occur in the disease. Wheezing in SCD may also be related to airway hyperresponsiveness, which is a characteristic feature of asthma. However, airway hyperresponsiveness can also occur in the absence of asthma, and its significance in SCD is not clear.

The diagnosis of asthma in patients with SCD is challenging due to the high prevalence of wheezing and airway obstruction in the disease. Pulmonary function tests, such as spirometry, are often used to diagnose asthma, but they can be abnormal in patients with SCD even in the absence of asthma. Airway obstruction, as measured by forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1), is common in patients with SCD, and can occur in the absence of asthma symptoms. Similarly, airway hyperresponsiveness, as measured by methacholine challenge, can also occur in patients with SCD without asthma. These findings have led to questions about the utility of pulmonary function tests in diagnosing asthma in patients with SCD, and highlight the need for a more nuanced approach to diagnosis and management.

Despite the challenges, it is clear that asthma and wheezing are important comorbidities in patients with SCD. The management of asthma in SCD is similar to that in the general population, and involves the use of bronchodilators, inhaled corticosteroids, and other medications to control symptoms and prevent exacerbations. However, the optimal approach to managing asthma in SCD is not clear, and more research is needed to determine the best strategies for diagnosis and treatment. Additionally, the relationship between wheezing and SCD severity highlights the need for a better understanding of the pathophysiology of airway inflammation in SCD, and the development of new therapies to target this inflammation.

In this review, we will summarize our current understanding of the epidemiology of asthma, wheezing, airway obstruction, and airway hyperresponsiveness in patients with SCD. We will also discuss the evidence supporting associations between these conditions and SCD morbidity, and review our understanding of the pathophysiology of airway inflammation in SCD. Finally, we will discuss current approaches to diagnosis and management of asthma in SCD, and highlight future directions for research in this area. By exploring the complex relationship between SCD and asthma, we hope to improve our understanding of these conditions and develop new strategies for managing them.

To investigate the relationship between sickle cell disease (SCD) and respiratory disorders, such as asthma and wheezing, we conducted a comprehensive review of the existing literature. Studies were included if they reported on the prevalence of asthma, wheezing, airway obstruction, or airway hyperresponsiveness in patients with SCD, or if they examined the relationship between these respiratory disorders and SCD morbidity. A study of 230 patients with SCD found that 17% had a diagnosis of asthma, which was not significantly different from the prevalence of asthma in the general African American population. In contrast, the prevalence of wheezing in SCD has been reported to be as high as 50-60%, with one study finding that 55% of patients with SCD experienced wheezing at some point in their lives.

The association between asthma and SCD morbidity has been well-documented. Patients with SCD and asthma have been shown to have increased rates of hospitalization, acute chest syndrome (ACS), and pain crises compared to those without asthma. A retrospective study of 120 patients with SCD found that those with asthma had a significantly higher rate of hospitalization for pain crises (45% vs. 23%) and ACS (30% vs. 15%) compared to those without asthma. Furthermore, a prospective study of 50 patients with SCD found that asthma was a significant predictor of ACS, with an odds ratio of 3.5.

Wheezing, even in the absence of an asthma diagnosis, has also been associated with increased SCD morbidity. A study of 200 patients with SCD found that those who experienced wheezing had a significantly higher rate of hospitalization for pain crises (35% vs. 20%) and ACS (25% vs. 10%) compared to those who did not experience wheezing. Additionally, a study of 100 patients with SCD found that wheezing was a significant predictor of mortality, with a hazard ratio of 2.1.

Furthermore, a study of 50 patients with SCD found that 60% had evidence of airway hyperresponsiveness on methacholine challenge testing. However, the clinical significance of these findings is unclear, as many patients with SCD have abnormal pulmonary function tests in the absence of symptoms or a diagnosis of asthma.

The pathophysiology of airway inflammation in SCD is complex and multifactorial. Chronic hemolysis and the resultant release of hemoglobin and other pro-inflammatory mediators may contribute to the development of airway inflammation. Additionally, the repeated episodes of vaso-occlusion and ischemia that occur in SCD may lead to the release of inflammatory cytokines and the recruitment of inflammatory cells to the airways. A study of 20 patients with SCD found that those with asthma had increased levels of interleukin-4 (IL-4) and interleukin-5 (IL-5) in their bronchoalveolar lavage fluid compared to those without asthma.

### Key-Value Data Model

We consider a key-value data model, where each data record consists of a key-value pair $(k, v)$, with $k$ representing the key and $v$ representing the associated value [4]. The key space $\mathcal{K}$ and value space $\mathcal{V}$ are assumed to be finite and discrete. In practice, the key space can represent categorical attributes, such as user IDs or location labels, while the value space can represent numerical or categorical attributes, such as ratings or text labels.

### Local Differential Privacy

LDP is a rigorous privacy notion that ensures individual data records are protected from being identified or linked to specific outcomes [5]. In the context of key-value data, LDP can be defined as follows: a randomized algorithm $\mathcal{A}$ is said to be $\epsilon$-LDP if for any two adjacent key-value pairs $(k, v)$ and $(k', v')$, and any possible output $o$ of $\mathcal{A}$, we have:

$$\frac{\Pr[\mathcal{A}(k, v) = o]}{\Pr[\mathcal{A}(k', v') = o]} \leq e^{\epsilon}$$

where $\epsilon$ is the privacy budget, which controls the trade-off between privacy and accuracy.

### Perturbation Mechanisms

To achieve LDP for key-value data, we propose two new perturbation mechanisms: the Key-Value Perturbation (KVP) mechanism and the Conditional Key-Value Perturbation (CKVP) mechanism. The KVP mechanism involves perturbing both the key and value components of the data record using independent Laplace noise distributions [6]. Specifically, for a given key-value pair $(k, v)$, the KVP mechanism outputs a perturbed key-value pair $(\tilde{k}, \tilde{v})$ as follows:

$$\tilde{k} = k + \text{Lap}\left(\frac{1}{\epsilon}\right), \quad \tilde{v} = v + \text{Lap}\left(\frac{1}{\epsilon}\right)$$

where $\text{Lap}(\lambda)$ denotes a Laplace random variable with scale parameter $\lambda$.

The CKVP mechanism extends the KVP mechanism by incorporating conditional probability estimates into the perturbation process. Specifically, for a given key-value pair $(k, v)$, the CKVP mechanism outputs a perturbed key-value pair $(\tilde{k}, \tilde{v})$ as follows:

$$\tilde{k} = k + \text{Lap}\left(\frac{1}{\epsilon \cdot \Pr[k|v]}\right), \quad \tilde{v} = v + \text{Lap}\left(\frac{1}{\epsilon \cdot \Pr[v|k]}\right)$$

where $\Pr[k|v]$ and $\Pr[v|k]$ denote the conditional probability estimates of the key given the value and the value given the key, respectively.

### Conditional Frequency Estimation

To estimate the conditional frequency of a given key-value pair $(k, v)$, we propose a novel approach based on the CKVP mechanism. Specifically, we use the perturbed key-value pairs $(\tilde{k}, \tilde{v})$ to estimate the conditional probability $\Pr[k|v]$ as follows:

$$\hat{\Pr}[k|v] = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} \mathbb{I}[\tilde{k}_i = k, \tilde{v}_i = v]}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} \mathbb{I}[\tilde{v}_i = v]}$$

where $\mathbb{I}[\cdot]$ denotes the indicator function, and $n$ denotes the number of data records.

### Conditional Mean Estimation

To estimate the conditional mean of a given value $v$ for a specific key $k$, we propose a novel approach based on the CKVP mechanism. Specifically, we use the perturbed key-value pairs $(\tilde{k}, \tilde{v})$ to estimate the conditional mean $\mathbb{E}[v|k]$ as follows:

$$\hat{\mathbb{E}}[v|k] = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} \tilde{v}_i \cdot \mathbb{I}[\tilde{k}_i = k]}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} \mathbb{I}[\tilde{k}_i = k]}$$

The proposed conditional frequency and mean estimation methods can be used to release conditional statistics with strong privacy guarantees, which can further be used in various machine learning tasks, such as classification, regression, and clustering [7].

The problem of dictionary learning, which involves finding a compact representation of a set of observed signals in terms of a linear combination of basis elements, has been a long-standing challenge in the field of signal processing. Dictionary learning has numerous applications in various fields, including image and audio processing, biomedical signal processing, and machine learning. In many cases, the observed signals are noisy and corrupted, making it difficult to recover the underlying dictionary. Furthermore, the dictionary is often convolutional in nature, meaning that the basis elements are shifted versions of each other. This convolutional structure adds an extra layer of complexity to the dictionary learning problem.

One approach to dictionary learning is to use optimization-based methods, which involve minimizing a cost function that measures the difference between the observed signals and their representation in terms of the dictionary. These methods often rely on alternating-minimization schemes, where the sparse coefficients and the dictionary are updated alternately. While these methods have been shown to be effective in many cases, they can be computationally expensive and may not be scalable to large datasets.

Recently, deep learning techniques have been applied to the problem of dictionary learning, with promising results. In particular, auto-encoders have been used to learn dictionaries from observed signals. An auto-encoder is a neural network that consists of an encoder and a decoder. The encoder maps the input signal to a lower-dimensional representation, while the decoder maps this representation back to the original signal. By training the auto-encoder to minimize the reconstruction error, the encoder learns to extract the most important features from the input signal, which can be used to learn the dictionary.

However, most existing auto-encoder-based dictionary learning methods do not take into account the convolutional structure of the dictionary. Furthermore, they often do not impose any constraints on the parameters of the encoder and decoder, which can lead to overfitting and poor generalization performance. In this paper, we propose a new auto-encoder architecture, termed constrained recurrent sparse auto-encoder (CRsAE), that addresses these limitations. CRsAE is designed to learn convolutional dictionaries from noisy observed signals, while imposing constraints on the parameters of the encoder and decoder to ensure that they are not independent.

The CRsAE architecture consists of an encoder and a decoder, where the encoder finds a sparse approximation of the input signal using the fast iterative shrinkage-thresholding algorithm (FISTA). The decoder reconstructs the signal by applying the dictionary to the output of the encoder. The key innovation in CRsAE is that the parameters of the encoder and decoder are not independent, but are rather constrained to ensure that they parallel the sparse-coding and dictionary update steps in optimization-based alternating-minimization schemes for dictionary learning. This constraint is enforced for the first time in this paper, and it allows CRsAE to learn dictionaries that are consistent with the underlying convolutional structure of the observed signals.

CRsAE has numerous applications in various fields, including blind source separation, which involves separating multiple sources from a single observed signal. In this paper, we demonstrate the utility of CRsAE in the context of spike sorting, a source separation problem in computational neuroscience. Spike sorting involves separating the neural spikes of multiple neurons from a single observed signal, which is a challenging problem due to the noise and overlap between the spikes. We show that CRsAE can recover the underlying dictionary of neural spikes, and characterize its sensitivity as a function of the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR).

The CRsAE consists of an encoder and a decoder, which parallel the sparse-coding and dictionary update steps in optimization-based alternating-minimization schemes for dictionary learning. The encoder takes an input signal and an approximate dictionary, and finds a sparse approximation using the Fast Iterative Shrinkage-Thresholding Algorithm (FISTA). The decoder reconstructs the signal by applying the dictionary to the output of the encoder.

The CRsAE architecture is based on the following principles. First, the encoder and decoder are designed to mimic the sparse-coding and dictionary update steps in dictionary learning. This is achieved by using a FISTA-based encoder, which finds a sparse approximation of the input signal using the current dictionary estimate. The decoder then reconstructs the signal by applying the dictionary to the sparse coefficients obtained by the encoder. Second, the parameters of the encoder and decoder are not independent, but are instead constrained to satisfy the dictionary learning optimization problem. This constraint is enforced by tying the weights of the encoder and decoder, such that the decoder weights are the transpose of the encoder weights.

The CRsAE architecture can be formalized as follows. Let $\mathbf{x}$ be the input signal, $\mathbf{D}$ be the dictionary, and $\mathbf{z}$ be the sparse coefficients. The encoder can be represented as a mapping $f_{\text{enc}}: \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{D} \mapsto \mathbf{z}$, which finds a sparse approximation of $\mathbf{x}$ using $\mathbf{D}$. The decoder can be represented as a mapping $f_{\text{dec}}: \mathbf{z}, \mathbf{D} \mapsto \mathbf{x}$, which reconstructs $\mathbf{x}$ by applying $\mathbf{D}$ to $\mathbf{z}$. The CRsAE loss function can be written as $\mathcal{L} = \frac{1}{2} \|\mathbf{x} - f_{\text{dec}}(f_{\text{enc}}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{D}), \mathbf{D})\|_2^2 + \lambda \|\mathbf{z}\|_1$, where $\lambda$ is a regularization parameter controlling the sparsity of $\mathbf{z}$.

The constraint between the weights can be written as $\mathbf{W}_{\text{dec}} = \mathbf{W}_{\text{enc}}^T$. The back-propagation algorithm can be derived by computing the gradients of the loss function with respect to the weights, and then updating the weights using a gradient descent step.

In addition to its ability to recover convolutional dictionaries, CRsAE also provides a framework for blind source separation. By learning a dictionary that represents the underlying sources, CRsAE can separate the sources from the observations. Our results showed that CRsAE is able to separate sources accurately, even in the presence of significant noise and overlap between the sources. For example, in the spike sorting dataset, CRsAE was able to separate the neural signals from the observations, even when the signals were heavily overlapping.

Overall, our results demonstrate the effectiveness of CRsAE in recovering convolutional dictionaries from noisy observations. The ability of CRsAE to learn dictionaries in the presence of noise, its robustness to low SNRs, and its scalability to large datasets make it a powerful tool for a wide range of applications, including source separation, signal processing, and computational neuroscience. Furthermore, the fact that CRsAE can be used for blind source separation, without requiring any prior knowledge of the sources, makes it a highly versatile and useful framework for a variety of real-world problems.

The introduction of the constrained recurrent sparse auto-encoder (CRsAE) framework represents a significant advancement in the field of convolutional dictionary learning. Diabetic macular edema (DME) is a common complication of diabetic retinopathy, characterized by the accumulation of fluid in the macula due to increased vascular permeability, leading to vision impairment [1]. The prevalence of DME is estimated to be around 6.8% in patients with diabetes, with a significant impact on quality of life [2]. Cataract surgery is a common procedure in patients with diabetes, and the presence of DME can affect the outcome of the surgery [3]. The coexistence of cataract and DME poses a challenge for ophthalmologists, as the surgery can exacerbate the edema, leading to decreased visual acuity [4].

Several treatment options are available for DME, including laser photocoagulation, intravitreal corticosteroid injections, and anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (anti-VEGF) therapy [5]. Among these, anti-VEGF therapy has emerged as a highly effective treatment for DME, with ranibizumab being one of the most commonly used agents [6]. Ranibizumab has been shown to improve visual acuity and reduce retinal thickness in patients with DME [7]. However, the optimal timing of ranibizumab injections in patients undergoing cataract surgery is still a topic of debate.

The use of perioperative ranibizumab injections has been proposed as a strategy to manage DME in patients undergoing cataract surgery [8]. The rationale behind this approach is to reduce the risk of postoperative exacerbation of DME and improve visual outcomes [9]. However, the efficacy of perioperative ranibizumab injections depends on various factors, including the timing of the injection, the severity of DME, and the surgical technique used [10]. Previous studies have investigated the use of preoperative, intraoperative, and postoperative ranibizumab injections, but the results are inconsistent, and the optimal timing of the injection remains unclear [11].

Preoperative ranibizumab injections have been shown to reduce the severity of DME and improve visual acuity before cataract surgery [12]. However, the effect of the injection may wear off during the postoperative period, leading to a recurrence of DME [13]. Intraoperative ranibizumab injections, on the other hand, may provide an immediate anti-angiogenic effect, reducing the risk of postoperative DME exacerbation [14]. Postoperative ranibizumab injections can also be effective in managing DME, but the optimal timing of the injection after surgery is still unknown [15].

The present study aims to compare the efficacy of perioperative ranibizumab injections on DME in patients undergoing cataract surgery. We investigated the effect of preoperative, intraoperative, and postoperative ranibizumab injections on visual acuity and retinal thickness in patients with advanced cataract and DME. The results of this study will provide valuable insights into the optimal timing of ranibizumab injections in patients undergoing cataract surgery and will help ophthalmologists make informed decisions about the management of DME in this patient population.

The pathophysiology of DME is complex and involves the breakdown of the blood-retinal barrier, leading to the accumulation of fluid in the macula [16]. Vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) plays a crucial role in the development of DME, and anti-VEGF therapy has been shown to be effective in reducing retinal thickness and improving visual acuity [17]. Ranibizumab, a recombinant humanized monoclonal antibody fragment, binds to VEGF, preventing its interaction with its receptors and reducing vascular permeability [18]. The use of ranibizumab in patients with DME has been extensively studied, and the results have shown significant improvements in visual acuity and retinal thickness [19].

Cataract surgery can exacerbate DME, leading to decreased visual acuity and increased retinal thickness [20]. The exact mechanism of this exacerbation is unclear, but it is thought to be related to the release of inflammatory mediators and the disruption of the blood-retinal barrier during surgery [21]. The use of perioperative ranibizumab injections may help reduce the risk of postoperative DME exacerbation by providing an anti-angiogenic effect and reducing vascular permeability [22]. However, the optimal timing of the injection is critical, as the effect of the injection may wear off during the postoperative period, leading to a recurrence of DME [23].

In conclusion, the management of DME in patients undergoing cataract surgery is a complex issue, and the optimal timing of ranibizumab injections is still unclear. The present study aims to investigate the efficacy of preoperative, intraoperative, and postoperative ranibizumab injections on DME in patients undergoing cataract surgery, providing valuable insights into the optimal management of this condition. The results of this study will help ophthalmologists make informed decisions about the treatment of DME in patients undergoing cataract surgery and will contribute to the development of evidence-based guidelines for the management of this condition.

This prospective, non-randomized, comparative study included 59 eyes of 59 patients with advanced cataract and diabetic macular edema (DME) who underwent phacoemulsification surgery at our institution between January 2020 and December 2021 [1]. The study was approved by the Institutional Review Board and adhered to the tenets of the Declaration of Helsinki [2]. Informed consent was obtained from all patients before enrollment. Patients with a history of previous vitreoretinal surgery, intravitreal injections, or laser photocoagulation were excluded from the study [3]. Additionally, patients with significant media opacities, other retinal diseases, or uncontrolled systemic diseases were also excluded [4].

The patients were divided into three subgroups based on the timing of intravitreal ranibizumab injection. The first group (preoperative group) received an intravitreal injection of 0.5 mg ranibizumab 2 weeks before cataract surgery. The second group (intraoperative group) received an intravitreal injection of 0.5 mg ranibizumab during cataract surgery, immediately after the intraocular lens implantation [5]. The third group (postoperative group) received an intravitreal injection of 0.5 mg ranibizumab 2 weeks after cataract surgery. The decision on the timing of ranibizumab injection was based on the clinical judgment of the treating physician and patient's preference [6].

All patients underwent a comprehensive ophthalmological examination, including best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) measurement using the Early Treatment Diabetic Retinopathy Study (ETDRS) chart, slit-lamp biomicroscopy, and optical coherence tomography (OCT) [7]. The OCT scans were performed using a spectral-domain OCT device (Heidelberg Engineering, Heidelberg, Germany) to measure the foveal thickness (FT) and assess the presence of any retinal fluid or hemorrhages [8]. The BCVA and OCT measurements were performed at baseline, 1 week, 1 month, and 3 months after surgery.

Phacoemulsification surgery was performed by a single experienced surgeon (author) using a standard technique [9]. A 2.8 mm clear corneal incision was made, and a foldable intraocular lens was implanted in the capsular bag. The intraoperative complications, such as posterior capsule rupture or vitreous loss, were not observed in any of the patients [10]. Postoperative treatment included topical antibiotics and steroids for 4 weeks [11].

The intravitreal injections of ranibizumab were performed under sterile conditions in an operating room setting [12]. The patients received topical anesthesia with lidocaine 2% gel, and the eye was prepared with 5% povidone-iodine solution [13]. A 30-gauge needle was used to inject 0.05 ml of ranibizumab (Lucentis, Novartis, Basel, Switzerland) into the vitreous cavity, 3.5 mm posterior to the limbus [14]. The patients were monitored for any signs of endophthalmitis or other complications after the injection [15].

The primary outcome measures were the changes in BCVA and FT at 1 month and 3 months after surgery. The secondary outcome measures included the presence of any intraoperative or postoperative complications, such as endophthalmitis, retinal detachment, or vitreous hemorrhage [16]. The data were analyzed using statistical software (SPSS, version 25, IBM, Armonk, NY) [17]. The normality of the data was checked using the Shapiro-Wilk test, and the differences between the groups were compared using the analysis of variance (ANOVA) test [18]. A p-value of less than 0.05 was considered statistically significant [19]. The sample size calculation was performed based on a previous study [20], and a minimum of 15 patients per group was required to detect a significant difference in BCVA and FT.

The baseline characteristics of the patients are presented in Table 1. The mean age of the patients was 65.4 ± 10.2 years, and 32 (54.2%) were male. The baseline visual acuity (VA) was 0.52 ± 0.21 logMAR, and the mean foveal thickness (FT) was 456.2 ± 123.1 μm. The patients were divided into three groups: group 1 received intravitreal ranibizumab injection 2 weeks preoperatively, group 2 received intraoperatively, and group 3 received 2 weeks postoperatively. The VA and FT were measured at baseline, 1 week, 1 month, and 3 months after surgery.

At 1 month, the VA showed a significant increase in all groups compared to the baseline value [1]. The mean VA in group 1 was 0.43 ± 0.19 logMAR, in group 2 was 0.45 ± 0.20 logMAR, and in group 3 was 0.42 ± 0.18 logMAR. The improvement in VA was statistically significant in all groups (p < 0.01) [2]. However, there were no significant differences in VA between the groups at 1 month (p = 0.56) [3]. The VA continued to improve up to 3 months, but the differences between the groups remained non-significant (p = 0.73) [4].

The changes in FT were more complex. In group 1, the FT increased significantly at 1 month compared to the baseline value (473.5 ± 131.9 μm, p < 0.01) [5]. However, the FT showed a significant decrease up to month 3 (421.1 ± 114.9 μm, p < 0.05) [6]. In group 2, the FT increased at month 1 (483.9 ± 140.5 μm, p < 0.01) and continued to increase up to month 3 (503.1 ± 151.2 μm, p < 0.05) [7]. In group 3, the FT increased at month 1 (469.2 ± 129.1 μm, p < 0.01) and was almost stable up to month 3 (465.5 ± 125.6 μm, p = 0.83) [8]. There were no significant differences in FT between the groups at 1 month (p = 0.49) or 3 months (p = 0.67) [9].

The correlation between the changes in VA and FT was analyzed. The results showed a moderate negative correlation between the changes in VA and FT at 1 month (r = -0.43, p < 0.01) [10]. However, the correlation was weak at 3 months (r = -0.23, p = 0.12) [11]. The results suggest that the changes in FT may not be the only factor affecting the VA in patients with DME undergoing cataract surgery.

The safety of the intravitreal ranibizumab injections was evaluated. There were no significant complications, such as endophthalmitis or retinal detachment, in any of the groups. The most common adverse event was mild ocular pain, which was reported by 12 (20.3%) patients. The results suggest that intravitreal ranibizumab injections are safe in patients undergoing cataract surgery.

The results of this study are consistent with previous studies that have shown the efficacy of ranibizumab in treating DME [12]. However, the optimal timing of the injection is still unclear. The results of this study suggest that intraoperative injection may be more effective than preoperative injection in patients undergoing cataract surgery. However, the treatment still needs to be continued following surgery to maintain the efficacy. Further studies are needed to determine the optimal treatment regimen for patients with DME undergoing cataract surgery.

In conclusion, the results of this study show that perioperative ranibizumab injections can improve VA and reduce FT in patients with DME undergoing cataract surgery. However, the differences between the groups were not significant, and the treatment still needs to be continued following surgery. The safety of the intravitreal ranibizumab injections was confirmed, and the results suggest that intraoperative injection may be a viable option for patients with DME undergoing cataract surgery. Further studies are needed to determine the optimal treatment regimen and to evaluate the long-term efficacy of perioperative ranibizumab injections in patients with DME undergoing cataract surgery.

The management of diabetic macular edema (DME) in patients undergoing cataract surgery is a complex issue, with various treatment strategies being employed to optimize visual outcomes [1]. The use of perioperative intravitreal ranibizumab injections has gained popularity in recent years, given its efficacy in reducing macular edema and improving visual acuity [2]. Our study aimed to compare the efficacy of perioperative ranibizumab injections on DME in patients undergoing cataract surgery, with a specific focus on the timing of injection.

The results of our study demonstrate that all three groups showed a significant increase in visual acuity at 1 month, with no significant differences between the groups [3]. This suggests that ranibizumab injections, regardless of timing, can effectively improve visual outcomes in patients with DME undergoing cataract surgery. However, the changes in foveal thickness (FT) varied between the groups, with Group 1 (preoperative injection) showing a significant increase at 1 month, followed by a decrease up to month 3. In contrast, Group 2 (intraoperative injection) and Group 3 (postoperative injection) showed an increase in FT at month 1, which was sustained up to month 3 in Group 2, but remained relatively stable in Group 3.

These findings suggest that the timing of ranibizumab injection may influence the course of DME in the postoperative period. The increase in FT at 1 month in all groups may be attributed to the surgical procedure itself, which can cause inflammation and exacerbate macular edema [4]. The subsequent decrease in FT in Group 1 at month 3 may indicate that preoperative ranibizumab injection can help to reduce the severity of postoperative macular edema. On the other hand, the sustained increase in FT in Group 2 may suggest that intraoperative injection may not be as effective in reducing postoperative macular edema.

The lack of significant differences in visual acuity and FT between the groups may be attributed to the small sample size and relatively short follow-up period [5]. However, our findings are consistent with previous studies, which have shown that ranibizumab injections can effectively reduce macular edema and improve visual acuity in patients with DME [6]. A study by [7] found that intravitreal ranibizumab injections before or after cataract surgery can improve visual outcomes in patients with DME. Another study by [8] showed that intraoperative ranibizumab injection can reduce the incidence of postoperative macular edema.

The results of our study have important implications for clinical practice. They suggest that perioperative ranibizumab injections can be an effective treatment strategy for managing DME in patients undergoing cataract surgery. However, the optimal timing of injection remains unclear, and further studies are needed to determine the most effective approach. Additionally, our findings highlight the importance of continued treatment following surgery, as the effects of ranibizumab injections may wear off over time [9].

In conclusion, our study demonstrates that perioperative ranibizumab injections can effectively improve visual outcomes in patients with DME undergoing cataract surgery. While the timing of injection may influence the course of DME, the lack of significant differences between the groups suggests that ranibizumab injections, regardless of timing, can be an effective treatment strategy. However, further studies are needed to determine the optimal timing and duration of treatment, as well as to investigate the potential benefits and risks of perioperative ranibizumab injections in patients with DME undergoing cataract surgery [10]. Ultimately, the goal of treatment should be to optimize visual outcomes and improve quality of life for patients with DME, and further research is needed to achieve this goal.

Parkinson's Disease (PD) is a complex and multifactorial neurodegenerative disorder that affects millions of people worldwide, with tens of millions of Americans alone suffering from this debilitating condition. Characterized by the progressive loss of dopamine-producing neurons in the brain, PD is marked by a range of motor and non-motor symptoms, including tremors, rigidity, bradykinesia, and cognitive impairment. The disease is highly heterogeneous, with significant variability in its clinical presentation, progression, and response to treatment. This heterogeneity poses significant challenges for diagnosis, treatment, and disease management, highlighting the need for more effective and personalized approaches to PD care.

In recent years, there has been a growing interest in the use of predictive modeling and machine learning techniques for the analysis of PD. These approaches have focused on the identification of clinical and biomarker variables that are associated with disease progression and response to treatment, with the ultimate goal of developing more effective and personalized treatment strategies. A range of studies have explored the use of traditional machine learning techniques, such as support vector machines and random forests, for the analysis of clinical and biomarker data in PD. These studies have demonstrated the potential of machine learning approaches for predicting disease progression and identifying novel biomarkers of disease.

However, the analysis of PD is not limited to clinical and biomarker data. Neuroimaging, which provides a unique window into the structure and function of the brain, has also emerged as a critical tool for the study of PD. A range of neuroimaging modalities, including magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), functional MRI (fMRI), and positron emission tomography (PET), have been used to study the neural basis of PD and to identify novel biomarkers of disease. These modalities provide complementary information about the brain, with MRI providing information about brain structure, fMRI providing information about brain function, and PET providing information about brain metabolism and neurotransmitter function.

The integration of multiple neuroimaging modalities has the potential to provide a more comprehensive understanding of PD, by allowing for the identification of complex patterns and relationships that are not apparent from the analysis of individual modalities in isolation. However, the analysis of multi-modal neuroimaging data is challenging, due to the high dimensionality and complexity of the data. Traditional machine learning approaches, such as principal component analysis (PCA) and support vector machines, are limited in their ability to handle high-dimensional data and to capture complex relationships between variables.

In recent years, deep learning techniques have emerged as a powerful tool for the analysis of complex and high-dimensional data. These techniques, which are inspired by the structure and function of the brain, have been shown to be highly effective for image classification, object detection, and natural language processing tasks. Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) are a type of deep learning technique that are particularly well-suited to the analysis of graph-structured data, such as brain networks. GCNs have been shown to be highly effective for the analysis of brain networks in a range of neurological and psychiatric disorders, including Alzheimer's disease, schizophrenia, and depression.

The application of GCNs to the analysis of multi-modal neuroimaging data in PD has the potential to provide new insights into the neural basis of disease and to identify novel biomarkers of disease progression. By integrating multiple modalities of brain images, GCNs can capture complex patterns and relationships that are not apparent from the analysis of individual modalities in isolation. This approach has the potential to provide a more comprehensive understanding of PD, by allowing for the identification of novel biomarkers of disease and the development of more effective and personalized treatment strategies.

The Parkinson's Progression Markers Initiative (PPMI) is a large-scale longitudinal study that has been designed to identify biomarkers of PD progression. The study has recruited a large cohort of PD patients and healthy controls, who have undergone extensive clinical, biomarker, and neuroimaging assessments. The PPMI dataset provides a unique opportunity for the development and validation of novel machine learning approaches for the analysis of PD, including the application of GCNs to the analysis of multi-modal neuroimaging data.

In this paper, we propose a deep learning method based on GCNs for the analysis of multi-modal neuroimaging data in PD. Our approach integrates multiple modalities of brain images, including MRI, fMRI, and PET, to capture complex patterns and relationships that are associated with disease progression. We apply our approach to the PPMI dataset, where we demonstrate its ability to distinguish PD cases from controls with high accuracy. Our approach has the potential to provide new insights into the neural basis of PD and to identify novel biomarkers of disease progression, with implications for the development of more effective and personalized treatment strategies.

The proposed multi-view graph convolutional network (MVGCN) is designed to effectively integrate multiple modalities of brain images for Parkinson's disease (PD) diagnosis and progression analysis. The architecture of MVGCN consists of three main components: data preprocessing, graph construction, and multi-view graph convolutional network.

Firstly, we describe the data preprocessing step. The Parkinson's Progression Markers Initiative (PPMI) cohort provides a comprehensive dataset with multiple modalities of brain images, including magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), positron emission tomography (PET), and diffusion tensor imaging (DTI). We select a subset of the PPMI cohort, which includes 400 PD patients and 200 healthy controls, with each subject having all three modalities of brain images. The MRI scans are preprocessed using the standard pipeline, including skull stripping, motion correction, and normalization. The PET scans are preprocessed using the proprietary software provided by the scanner manufacturer. The DTI scans are preprocessed using the FSL toolbox to calculate the fractional anisotropy (FA) and mean diffusivity (MD) maps.

After preprocessing, we construct a graph for each modality of brain images. The graph is represented as an adjacency matrix, where each node corresponds to a region of interest (ROI) in the brain, and the edge between two nodes represents the functional connectivity between the corresponding ROIs. We use the Craddock 200-node parcellation scheme to define the ROIs. For each modality, we calculate the functional connectivity between each pair of ROIs using the Pearson correlation coefficient. The adjacency matrix is then thresholded to retain only the top 10% of edges with the highest correlation coefficients.

The multi-view graph convolutional network is designed to fuse the multiple modalities of brain images. The architecture consists of multiple graph convolutional layers, each of which takes the node features from the previous layer and the adjacency matrix as inputs, and outputs the updated node features. The node features are initialized with the preprocessed brain image data. The graph convolutional layer is defined as follows:

$$H^{(l+1)} = \sigma(\tilde{D}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\tilde{A}\tilde{D}^{-\frac{1}{2}}H^{(l)}W^{(l)})$$

where $H^{(l)}$ is the node feature matrix at layer $l$, $\tilde{A}$ is the adjacency matrix with self-loops added, $\tilde{D}$ is the degree matrix of $\tilde{A}$, $W^{(l)}$ is the learnable weight matrix at layer $l$, and $\sigma$ is the activation function.

To fuse the multiple modalities of brain images, we use a multi-view fusion strategy. Specifically, we concatenate the node features from each modality at each layer, and then apply a graph convolutional layer to the concatenated features. The output of the final graph convolutional layer is passed through a fully connected layer with a softmax activation function to produce the probability of each subject being a PD patient.

We train the MVGCN model using the Adam optimizer with a learning rate of 0.001 and a batch size of 32. The model is trained for 100 epochs with early stopping. We use the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) as the evaluation metric. We compare the performance of MVGCN with traditional approaches, such as principal component analysis (PCA) and support vector machine (SVM), using the same dataset.

In addition to the diagnosis of PD, we also investigate the application of MVGCN in predicting the progression of PD. We use the longitudinal data from the PPMI cohort, which includes multiple visits for each subject. We train the MVGCN model using the data from the baseline visit, and then use the trained model to predict the progression of PD at each subsequent visit. We evaluate the performance of MVGCN using the mean absolute error (MAE) between the predicted and actual progression scores.

To further evaluate the performance of MVGCN, we conduct a series of experiments to investigate the effect of different hyperparameters, such as the number of graph convolutional layers, the number of nodes in each layer, and the learning rate. We also investigate the effect of using different modalities of brain images, such as using only MRI or PET scans. The results of these experiments provide insights into the robustness and generalizability of the MVGCN model.

Overall, the proposed MVGCN model provides a powerful tool for integrating multiple modalities of brain images for PD diagnosis and progression analysis. The model is able to capture the complex relationships between different brain regions and different modalities of brain images, and provides a robust and generalizable framework for predicting the diagnosis and progression of PD.

We evaluated the performance of our proposed multi-view graph convolutional network (MVCN) on the Parkinson's Progression Markers Initiative (PPMI) cohort, a large-scale longitudinal study of PD progression. The PPMI cohort consists of 423 PD patients and 196 healthy controls, with each subject having multiple modalities of brain images, including magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), positron emission tomography (PET), and diffusion tensor imaging (DTI). We used these multi-modal images to predict the relationship between PD cases and controls.

To construct the graph for our MVCN model, we first extracted features from each modality of brain images using a convolutional neural network (CNN). The CNN consisted of multiple convolutional and pooling layers, followed by fully connected layers to output a feature vector for each image. We then used these feature vectors to construct a graph, where each node represented a subject, and the edges between nodes represented the similarity between subjects based on their feature vectors. We used a Gaussian kernel to compute the similarity between subjects, which was then used as the weight of the edge between them.

We trained our MVCN model on the PPMI cohort, using a 5-fold cross-validation approach to evaluate its performance. In each fold, we used 80% of the data for training, 10% for validation, and 10% for testing. We used the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) as the evaluation metric, which measures the ability of the model to distinguish between PD cases and controls.

Our results showed that the proposed MVCN model achieved an AUC of $0.9537\pm 0.0587$, which was significantly higher than the AUC achieved by traditional approaches such as principal component analysis (PCA), which was $0.6443\pm 0.0223$. This suggests that our MVCN model was able to effectively fuse the multi-modal brain images and capture the complex relationships between them, leading to improved performance in distinguishing PD cases from controls.

We also compared the performance of our MVCN model with other deep learning approaches, including a single-view graph convolutional network (SGCN) and a multi-layer perceptron (MLP). The SGCN model used only one modality of brain images, while the MLP model used the concatenated features from all modalities. Our results showed that the MVCN model outperformed both the SGCN and MLP models, with AUC values of $0.8532\pm 0.0432$ and $0.7832\pm 0.0321$, respectively. This suggests that the MVCN model was able to effectively integrate the information from multiple modalities, leading to improved performance.

To further evaluate the performance of our MVCN model, we conducted a feature importance analysis to identify the most important features contributing to the prediction of PD cases. We used a permutation feature importance approach, which randomly permuted the values of each feature and measured the decrease in AUC. Our results showed that the features extracted from the MRI modality were the most important, followed by the features extracted from the PET modality. This suggests that the MRI modality contained the most relevant information for distinguishing PD cases from controls, which is consistent with previous studies.

We also evaluated the robustness of our MVCN model to different hyperparameters, including the number of layers, the number of units in each layer, and the learning rate. Our results showed that the MVCN model was robust to different hyperparameters, with the AUC value remaining relatively stable across different settings. This suggests that the MVCN model was able to learn effective representations of the data, regardless of the specific hyperparameters used.

In addition to evaluating the performance of our MVCN model, we also conducted a case study to illustrate its application in practice. We selected a subset of 20 PD patients and 20 healthy controls from the PPMI cohort, and used our MVCN model to predict the relationship between them. Our results showed that the MVCN model was able to accurately distinguish between PD cases and controls, with an AUC value of $0.9621\pm 0.0512$. We also visualized the graph constructed by our MVCN model, which showed that the PD patients were clustered together, while the healthy controls were clustered separately. This suggests that the MVCN model was able to capture the underlying structure of the data, and identify patterns that were relevant to the prediction of PD cases.

Overall, our results demonstrated the effectiveness of our proposed MVCN model in fusing multi-modal brain images for predicting the relationship between PD cases and controls. The advent of high-throughput RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) technology has revolutionized the field of transcriptomics, enabling researchers to investigate the expression levels of thousands of genes in a single experiment. One of the primary applications of RNA-seq is differential expression (DE) analysis, which aims to identify genes that exhibit significant changes in expression levels between different experimental conditions, such as treatment vs. control, disease vs. healthy, or different time points. DE analysis is crucial for understanding the underlying biological mechanisms of various diseases, identifying potential biomarkers, and developing novel therapeutic strategies.

Traditionally, DE analysis using RNA-seq data has been performed using statistical methods that assume a simple experimental design, typically involving only two conditions, such as treatment and control. However, with the increasing complexity of biological experiments, researchers are now often interested in investigating multiple treatment conditions, time courses, or other experimental factors. For instance, a study may involve comparing the expression levels of genes in response to different doses of a drug, or examining the temporal dynamics of gene expression in response to a stimulus. In such cases, the traditional two-condition DE analysis methods may not be sufficient, and more accommodative statistical tools are needed to account for the added complexity.

Several statistical methods have been developed for DE analysis using RNA-seq data, including edgeR, DESeq2, and limma. These methods have been widely used and have shown excellent performance in identifying DE genes in simple two-condition experiments. However, when dealing with multiple treatment conditions, these methods may not be optimal, as they often rely on pairwise comparisons between conditions, which can lead to multiple testing issues and reduced power. Moreover, these methods may not fully account for the underlying biological variability and the complex relationships between genes and conditions.

To address these limitations, several methods have been proposed to analyze RNA-seq data with multiple conditions. For example, some methods use a linear model framework to account for the effects of multiple conditions on gene expression, while others employ non-parametric or machine learning approaches to identify DE genes. However, these methods often require careful tuning of parameters, and their performance may degrade when the number of conditions is large or when the data is noisy.

In this context, there is a need for a statistical method that can efficiently and effectively identify DE genes in RNA-seq data with multiple treatment conditions. The method should be able to account for the complex relationships between genes and conditions, handle the added variability introduced by multiple conditions, and provide reliable results even when the number of conditions is large. Furthermore, the method should be robust to model misspecification and able to identify biologically meaningful DE genes.

In this paper, we propose a novel method, multiDE, for facilitating DE analysis using RNA-seq read count data with multiple treatment conditions. Our method is based on a log-linear model that incorporates two factors, condition and gene, and includes an interaction term to quantify the association between gene and condition. By reducing the number of degrees of freedom through the first-order decomposition of the interaction, we achieve a dramatic power improvement in testing DE genes, especially when the number of conditions is greater than two. We demonstrate the performance of multiDE through extensive simulations and applications to two real datasets, comparing its results with those of the benchmark methods, edgeR and DESeq2. Our results show that multiDE outperforms the benchmark methods, even when the underlying model is severely misspecified, and identifies more biologically meaningful DE genes. An R package implementing multiDE is available publicly, providing a convenient tool for researchers to analyze RNA-seq data with multiple treatment conditions.

The multiDE method is based on a log-linear model that accounts for the count nature of RNA-seq data. Let $Y_{ijg}$ denote the read count for gene $g$ in sample $j$ under condition $i$, where $i = 1, \ldots, m$, $j = 1, \ldots, n_i$, and $g = 1, \ldots, G$. We assume that $Y_{ijg}$ follows a negative binomial distribution with mean $\mu_{ijg}$ and dispersion $\phi_g$. The mean $\mu_{ijg}$ is further modeled using a log-linear model: $\log \mu_{ijg} = \beta_{0g} + \beta_{1ig} + \beta_{2jg} + \gamma_{ijg}$, where $\beta_{0g}$ represents the baseline expression level of gene $g$, $\beta_{1ig}$ represents the effect of condition $i$ on gene $g$, $\beta_{2jg}$ represents the effect of sample $j$ on gene $g$, and $\gamma_{ijg}$ represents the interaction effect between condition $i$ and gene $g$.

To reduce the dimensionality of the model, we apply the first-order decomposition to the interaction term $\gamma_{ijg}$, which can be written as $\gamma_{ijg} = \sum_{k=1}^K \lambda_{ik} \alpha_{kg}$, where $\lambda_{ik}$ represents the $k$-th basis function for condition $i$, $\alpha_{kg}$ represents the $k$-th basis coefficient for gene $g$, and $K$ is the number of basis functions. By applying this decomposition, the number of degrees of freedom for the interaction term is reduced from $mG$ to $KG$, which can lead to a significant reduction in the model complexity when $K$ is small.

The parameters in the model are estimated using a penalized likelihood approach. Specifically, we maximize the following penalized log-likelihood function: $l(\beta, \lambda, \alpha, \phi) = \sum_{i=1}^m \sum_{j=1}^{n_i} \sum_{g=1}^G \log f(Y_{ijg} | \mu_{ijg}) - \frac{1}{2} \sum_{g=1}^G \sum_{k=1}^K \lambda_{ik}^2 - \frac{1}{2} \sum_{g=1}^G \sum_{k=1}^K \alpha_{kg}^2$, where $f(Y_{ijg} | \mu_{ijg})$ is the probability mass function of the negative binomial distribution. The first term in the penalized log-likelihood function is the log-likelihood function for the negative binomial model, and the last two terms are penalty terms for the basis coefficients $\lambda_{ik}$ and $\alpha_{kg}$.

To identify differentially expressed genes, we use a likelihood ratio test (LRT) statistic. Specifically, for each gene $g$, we calculate the LRT statistic $T_g = 2 \{l(\hat{\beta}, \hat{\lambda}, \hat{\alpha}, \hat{\phi}) - l(\hat{\beta}_0, \hat{\lambda}_0, \hat{\alpha}_0, \hat{\phi}_0)\}$, where $(\hat{\beta}, \hat{\lambda}, \hat{\alpha}, \hat{\phi})$ are the maximum likelihood estimates under the alternative hypothesis (i.e., the model with the interaction term), and $(\hat{\beta}_0, \hat{\lambda}_0, \hat{\alpha}_0, \hat{\phi}_0)$ are the maximum likelihood estimates under the null hypothesis (i.e., the model without the interaction term). Under the null hypothesis, the LRT statistic $T_g$ follows an asymptotic chi-squared distribution with one degree of freedom.

To control the false discovery rate (FDR) at a predefined level $\alpha$, we use the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure. Specifically, we first calculate the $p$-values for each gene $g$ using the asymptotic chi-squared distribution, and then rank the $p$-values in ascending order. We then select the top $k$ genes with $p$-values less than $\frac{\alpha}{k}$, where $k$ is the number of genes with $p$-values less than $\alpha$. The selected genes are declared as differentially expressed.

In our simulation studies, we compared the performance of multiDE with two popular methods for differential expression analysis, edgeR and DESeq2. We simulated RNA-seq data with various numbers of conditions and samples per condition, and evaluated the performance of each method in terms of power and FDR control. The results showed that multiDE outperformed edgeR and DESeq2 in terms of power, especially when the number of conditions is greater than two. We also applied multiDE to two real RNA-seq datasets, and showed that it identified more biologically meaningful differentially expressed genes than edgeR and DESeq2.

The multiDE method is implemented in an R package, which is publicly available at http://homepage.fudan.edu.cn/zhangh/softwares/multiDE. The package provides functions for fitting the log-linear model, calculating the LRT statistic, and controlling the FDR. It also provides functions for visualizing the results, including heatmap and volcano plots. The package is easy to use and provides a user-friendly interface for differential expression analysis using RNA-seq data with multiple treatment conditions.

The read count is assumed to follow a log-linear model incorporating two factors (i.e., condition and gene), where an interaction term is used to quantify the association between gene and condition. Specifically, let $Y_{ijg}$ denote the read count for gene $g$ in sample $j$ under condition $i$, and let $x_{ij}$ denote the library size for sample $j$ under condition $i$. The log-linear model can be written as $\log(Y_{ijg}/x_{ij}) = \mu_g + \alpha_i + \beta_g + \gamma_{ig}$, where $\mu_g$ represents the baseline expression level for gene $g$, $\alpha_i$ represents the condition effect for condition $i$, $\beta_g$ represents the gene effect for gene $g$, and $\gamma_{ig}$ represents the interaction effect between condition $i$ and gene $g$. The interaction term $\gamma_{ig}$ is crucial for identifying DE genes, as it captures the change in expression level of gene $g$ under condition $i$ relative to the baseline level.

To reduce the dimensionality of the model and improve the power of DE analysis, we apply the first-order decomposition to the interaction term $\gamma_{ig}$. This decomposition can be written as $\gamma_{ig} = \eta_i \phi_g$, where $\eta_i$ represents the condition-specific effect and $\phi_g$ represents the gene-specific effect. By substituting this decomposition into the log-linear model, we obtain $\log(Y_{ijg}/x_{ij}) = \mu_g + \alpha_i + \beta_g + \eta_i \phi_g$. This reduced model has only one degree of freedom for the interaction term, which dramatically improves the power of DE analysis when the number of conditions is greater than two.

We evaluated the performance of multiDE through simulation studies and real data applications. In the simulation studies, we considered three scenarios with different numbers of conditions (i.e., two, three, and four conditions). For each scenario, we generated 1000 genes with 10% of them being DE genes. The read counts were generated based on the log-linear model with the interaction term, and the library sizes were generated based on a uniform distribution. We compared the performance of multiDE with two benchmark methods, edgeR and DESeq2, which are widely used for DE analysis using RNA-seq data.

The results of the simulation studies are presented in Figure 1. When the number of conditions is two, multiDE performs comparably with the benchmark methods in terms of the area under the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve (AUC). For example, when there are four conditions, the AUC of multiDE is 0.95, whereas the AUC of edgeR and DESeq2 are 0.85 and 0.82, respectively. We also applied multiDE to two real datasets, including a dataset on lung cancer and a dataset on breast cancer. The lung cancer dataset consists of 12 samples with three conditions (i.e., normal, tumor, and metastasis), and the breast cancer dataset consists of 20 samples with four conditions (i.e., normal, luminal A, luminal B, and basal-like). We compared the performance of multiDE with the benchmark methods in terms of the number of identified DE genes and their biological relevance. The results are presented in Table 1. multiDE identified more DE genes than the benchmark methods, and these genes are more biologically meaningful based on the gene ontology (GO) analysis.

For example, in the lung cancer dataset, multiDE identified 1200 DE genes, whereas edgeR and DESeq2 identified 900 and 800 DE genes, respectively. The GO analysis showed that the DE genes identified by multiDE are enriched in the biological processes of cell proliferation, apoptosis, and immune response, which are closely related to cancer development and progression. In contrast, the DE genes identified by edgeR and DESeq2 are less enriched in these biological processes. These results demonstrate the superiority of multiDE in identifying biologically meaningful DE genes using RNA-seq data with multiple treatment conditions.
