The experimental design and methodology used in this study are described in this section. The study consisted of two main parts: the data collection procedure and the data analysis procedure. In the data collection procedure, a triple-RSVP paradigm was designed and implemented to collect electroencephalography (EEG) data from participants. The data analysis procedure involved the use of two different P300 detection algorithms to classify the collected EEG data.

The triple-RSVP paradigm was designed to present three images simultaneously to participants, with a target image appearing three times in a random order. The images were presented on a computer screen, and participants were instructed to focus on the target image. The presentation duration of each image was 100 ms, and the inter-stimulus interval was 100 ms. The participants' EEG signals were recorded using a 64-channel EEG system, with a sampling rate of 1000 Hz. The EEG signals were filtered using a band-pass filter with a frequency range of 0.1-40 Hz to remove noise and artifacts.

A total of 20 participants, aged between 20 and 30 years, took part in the study. All participants had normal or corrected-to-normal vision and reported no history of neurological or psychiatric disorders. The participants were seated in a comfortable chair, approximately 1 meter away from the computer screen, and were instructed to minimize eye movements and blinks during the experiment. Each participant performed a total of 10 blocks, with each block consisting of 30 trials. In each trial, three images were presented simultaneously, and the participant's task was to detect the target image.

The EEG data collected during the experiment were analyzed using two different P300 detection algorithms: the support vector machine (SVM) algorithm and the random forest (RF) algorithm. Both algorithms were used to classify the EEG data into target and non-target categories. The SVM algorithm is a widely used machine learning algorithm that can be used for classification and regression tasks. The RF algorithm is an ensemble learning algorithm that combines multiple decision trees to improve classification accuracy.

The EEG data were preprocessed before being fed into the P300 detection algorithms. The preprocessing steps included artifact removal, noise reduction, and feature extraction. Artifact removal was performed using independent component analysis (ICA) to remove eye blinks and other artifacts from the EEG data. Noise reduction was performed using a wavelet denoising algorithm to remove high-frequency noise from the EEG data. Feature extraction was performed using a time-frequency analysis algorithm to extract relevant features from the EEG data.

The performance of the two P300 detection algorithms was evaluated using several metrics, including accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score. The accuracy metric measures the proportion of correctly classified trials, while the precision metric measures the proportion of true positives among all positive predictions. The recall metric measures the proportion of true positives among all actual positive instances, while the F1-score metric measures the harmonic mean of precision and recall.

To compare the performance of the triple-RSVP paradigm with the standard RSVP paradigm, a additional experiment was conducted using the standard RSVP paradigm. In the standard RSVP paradigm, a single image was presented at a time, and the participant's task was to detect the target image. The same participants and experimental setup were used in both experiments. The results of the two experiments were compared using a paired t-test to determine if there was a significant difference in performance between the two paradigms.

The multi-RSVP framework was also evaluated in terms of its universality and applicability. The framework was designed to be flexible and adaptable to different experimental conditions and participant populations. To demonstrate its universality, the framework was applied to different types of images, including objects, scenes, and faces. The results showed that the framework could be used with different types of images, and the performance was consistent across different image types.

Voltage-gated sodium channels are pivotal for the initiation and propagation of action potentials in excitable tissues, including neurons, muscle cells, and endocrine cells [1]. These channels are responsible for the rapid depolarization phase of the action potential, allowing for the transmission of electrical signals throughout the body [2]. The channels are composed of a pore-forming α-subunit and auxiliary β-subunits, which modulate the channel's biophysical properties and cellular localization [3]. The α-subunit is sufficient for channel function, and it is generally accepted that a single α-subunit forms a functional channel [4]. However, recent studies have suggested that sodium channel α-subunits may not function as solitary monomers, but rather interact with each other to form dimers [5].

The idea that sodium channels function as monomers is based on early biochemical and electrophysiological studies, which demonstrated that a single α-subunit is capable of forming a functional channel [6]. This concept has been widely accepted and has shaped our understanding of sodium channel structure and function [7]. However, several lines of evidence have emerged to challenge this traditional view. For example, studies have shown that sodium channel α-subunits can interact with each other through specific domains, suggesting a potential for dimerization [8]. Additionally, biochemical and biophysical analyses have revealed that sodium channels can exist as dimers or higher-order oligomers in native tissues [9].

The possibility that sodium channels function as dimers has significant implications for our understanding of channel assembly, structure, and function. Dimerization could provide a mechanism for cooperative gating, where the activity of one channel influences the activity of its dimeric partner [10]. This could allow for more complex and nuanced regulation of channel function, enabling the fine-tuning of electrical signaling in excitable tissues [11]. Furthermore, dimerization could also influence the biophysical properties of the channel, such as its voltage dependence, kinetics, and pharmacology [12].

Despite the growing evidence for sodium channel dimerization, the mechanisms underlying this process remain poorly understood. The regions of the α-subunit involved in dimerization, as well as the molecular interactions that mediate this process, are not well defined [13]. Additionally, the functional consequences of dimerization, including its effects on channel gating and biophysical properties, require further investigation [14]. The identification of proteins that interact with sodium channels and influence their dimerization and function could also provide important insights into the regulation of channel activity [15].

In recent years, several proteins have been identified that interact with sodium channels and modulate their function, including the 14-3-3 protein family [16]. The 14-3-3 proteins are a group of regulatory molecules that bind to specific phosphorylation sites on target proteins, influencing their activity, localization, and interactions [17]. These proteins have been implicated in the regulation of various ion channels, including potassium and calcium channels [18]. However, their role in regulating sodium channel function, particularly in the context of dimerization, is not well understood [19].

The conservation of sodium channel structure and function across different species is a notable feature of these channels [20]. Mammalian sodium channels, in particular, exhibit a high degree of sequence homology and functional similarity [21]. This conservation suggests that the mechanisms underlying sodium channel function, including dimerization, may also be conserved across species [22]. Investigating the conservation of sodium channel dimerization and its underlying mechanisms could provide important insights into the evolution of channel function and the development of channelopathies [23].

Channelopathies are a group of diseases caused by mutations in ion channel genes, including those encoding sodium channels [24]. These diseases can result in a range of neurological and muscular disorders, including epilepsy, arrhythmias, and myotonia [25]. Understanding the mechanisms underlying sodium channel function, including dimerization, could provide new opportunities for the development of therapeutic strategies to treat these diseases [26]. The identification of specific regions or proteins involved in sodium channel dimerization could lead to the development of targeted therapies, such as small molecules or biologics, that modulate channel function and alleviate disease symptoms [27].

In this study, we investigate the assembly, function, and gating of voltage-gated sodium channels, with a focus on the role of dimerization in channel function. We demonstrate that sodium channel α-subunits physically interact with each other and assemble, function, and gate as dimers. We identify the region involved in dimerization and show that 14-3-3 protein mediates the coupled gating of dimeric channels. Our findings have significant implications for our understanding of sodium channel structure and function, and highlight the importance of considering channel dimerization in the development of therapeutic strategies to treat sodium channelopathies.

To investigate the assembly and gating of voltage-gated sodium channels, we employed a combination of biochemical, biophysical, and molecular biology techniques. Initially, we expressed recombinant sodium channel α-subunits in HEK293 cells and used co-immunoprecipitation assays to examine potential interactions between these subunits [1]. Cells were transfected with cDNAs encoding Nav1.1, Nav1.2, Nav1.3, Nav1.4, Nav1.5, Nav1.6, Nav1.7, Nav1.8, and Nav1.9 α-subunits, and protein-protein interactions were assessed using specific antibodies against each subunit [2]. The nursing profession is built on a foundation of professional values that guide clinical decision-making and patient care [1]. These values, which include respect for patients' autonomy, dignity, and rights, as well as a commitment to providing safe and high-quality care, are essential for building trust and promoting positive health outcomes [2]. In recent years, there has been an increasing emphasis on the importance of professional values in nursing, driven in part by the growing complexity of healthcare systems and the need for nurses to navigate complex ethical dilemmas [3]. As a result, nurses are required to have a deep understanding of professional values and their application in clinical practice [4].

The importance of professional values in nursing has been recognized by numerous international organizations, including the International Council of Nurses (ICN) and the World Health Organization (WHO) [5]. These organizations have emphasized the need for nurses to be aware of and adhere to professional values, including respect for patients' rights, confidentiality, and dignity [6]. In addition, professional values have been shown to be associated with a range of positive outcomes, including improved patient satisfaction, better health outcomes, and increased job satisfaction among nurses [7]. Despite the importance of professional values, however, there is evidence to suggest that nurses may not always prioritize these values in their clinical practice [8]. This can be due to a range of factors, including lack of awareness, inadequate education and training, and workplace pressures [9].

In Iran, the nursing profession is rapidly evolving, with an increasing emphasis on the development of professional values and standards [10]. The Iranian Nursing Organization has developed a code of ethics that outlines the professional values and standards that nurses are expected to uphold [11]. However, there is limited research on the importance of professional values from the perspective of clinical nurses in Iran [12]. This study aims to address this gap by exploring the importance of professional values from the perspective of clinical nurses in hospitals affiliated with a medical university in Iran. The study used the Nursing Professional Values Scale-Revised (NPVS-R) to measure nurses' perceptions of professional values, including respect for patients' autonomy, confidentiality, and dignity [13].

The NPVS-R is a widely used instrument that has been validated in a range of international settings [14]. The scale consists of 26 items that measure nurses' perceptions of professional values, including respect for patients' autonomy, confidentiality, and dignity [15]. The scale has been shown to be reliable and valid, with high internal consistency and test-retest reliability [16]. In this study, the NPVS-R was used to measure nurses' perceptions of professional values and to identify areas where nurses may require additional education and training [17].

The study was conducted in four educational hospitals affiliated with Kerman University of Medical Sciences, Iran [18]. The hospitals provide a range of services, including medical, surgical, and pediatric care, and are staffed by a team of experienced nurses and healthcare professionals [19]. The study population consisted of clinical nurses working in the four hospitals, who were selected using a stratified random sampling method [20]. The sample size was calculated based on a power analysis, with a minimum of 250 nurses required to detect statistically significant differences [21].

The study findings have important implications for nursing education and practice in Iran [22]. The results suggest that nurses place a high value on respect for patients' autonomy, confidentiality, and dignity, which is consistent with international standards and guidelines [23]. However, the findings also suggest that nurses may require additional education and training on the importance of professional values, including respect for patients' rights and dignity [24]. This is consistent with previous research, which has highlighted the need for ongoing education and training to promote professional values and standards in nursing practice [25].

The study also highlights the importance of workplace culture and environment in promoting professional values and standards [26]. The findings suggest that nurses who work in hospitals with a strong emphasis on professional values and standards are more likely to prioritize these values in their clinical practice [27]. This is consistent with previous research, which has highlighted the importance of leadership and workplace culture in promoting professional values and standards in nursing practice [28]. Overall, the study findings suggest that professional values are essential for promoting high-quality care and positive health outcomes, and that nurses play a critical role in upholding these values in their clinical practice [29]. 

The relationship between nurses' demographic characteristics, such as age and work experience, and their perceptions of professional values is complex and multifaceted [30]. Previous research has suggested that older, more experienced nurses may place a higher value on professional values, including respect for patients' autonomy and dignity [31]. However, the findings of this study suggest that this relationship is not always straightforward, and that additional factors, such as participation in professional ethical training, may also play a role [32]. Further research is needed to fully explore the relationship between nurses' demographic characteristics and their perceptions of professional values [33].

In conclusion, professional values are essential for promoting high-quality care and positive health outcomes, and nurses play a critical role in upholding these values in their clinical practice [34]. The study findings highlight the importance of ongoing education and training to promote professional values and standards in nursing practice, as well as the need for a supportive workplace culture and environment [35]. Further research is needed to fully explore the importance of professional values in nursing practice, and to identify strategies for promoting these values in a range of clinical settings [36].

### Study Design and Setting
The present study employed a cross-sectional design to investigate the importance of professional values from clinical nurses' perspective in hospitals of a medical university in Iran [1]. The study was conducted in four educational hospitals affiliated with Kerman University of Medical Sciences, Iran, which is a major medical university in the country. These hospitals provide a wide range of medical services to patients and are also involved in education and research activities.

### Participants and Sampling
The study population consisted of clinical nurses working in the four educational hospitals. The inclusion criteria were: (1) being a registered nurse, (2) having at least one year of work experience, and (3) working in a clinical setting. The exclusion criteria were: (1) being a nurse manager or educator, and (2) having less than one year of work experience. A stratified random sampling method was used to select the participants [2]. The sampling frame was obtained from the hospitals' personnel departments, and the participants were selected randomly from each hospital. A total of 250 clinical nurses participated in the study.

### Data Collection Instrument
The data were collected using the Persian version of the Nursing Professional Values Scale-Revised (NPVS-R) [3]. The NPVS-R is a 26-item instrument that measures the importance of professional values from nurses' perspective. The scale consists of five subscales: (1) respect for persons, (2) beneficence, (3) non-maleficence, (4) autonomy, and (5) justice. The items are rated on a 5-point Likert scale, ranging from 1 (not important at all) to 5 (very important). The Persian version of the NPVS-R was translated and validated by [4], and it has been widely used in Iranian nursing research.

### Data Collection Procedure
The data were collected over a period of three months in 2016. The researchers visited each hospital and distributed the questionnaires to the participants. The participants were asked to complete the questionnaire anonymously and return it to the researcher. The questionnaires were collected, and the data were entered into a spreadsheet for analysis.

### Demographic Characteristics
The demographic characteristics of the participants, including age, sex, work experience, education level, and participation in professional ethical training, were collected using a demographic questionnaire. The questionnaire consisted of 10 items, and the participants were asked to provide information about their demographic characteristics.

### Data Analysis
The data were analyzed using descriptive and inferential statistics [5]. The mean and standard deviation of the NPVS-R scores were calculated to describe the importance of professional values from nurses' perspective. The frequencies and percentages of the demographic characteristics were calculated to describe the sample. The relationships between the NPVS-R scores and demographic characteristics were analyzed using Pearson's correlation coefficient and analysis of variance (ANOVA). The level of significance was set at 0.05.

### Validity and Reliability
The validity and reliability of the NPVS-R have been established in previous studies [3, 4]. The Cronbach's alpha coefficient of the NPVS-R was reported to be 0.92, indicating high internal consistency [3]. The content validity of the NPVS-R was established through a review of the literature and expert opinion [3]. The test-retest reliability of the NPVS-R was reported to be 0.85, indicating high stability [4].

### Ethical Considerations
The study was approved by the ethics committee of Kerman University of Medical Sciences. The participants were informed about the purpose and procedures of the study, and they provided written informed consent before participating in the study. The confidentiality and anonymity of the participants were ensured, and the data were stored securely.

### Limitations
The study had some limitations. The study was conducted in one medical university, and the results may not be generalizable to other settings. The study used a cross-sectional design, which provides a snapshot of the importance of professional values from nurses' perspective at one point in time. The study did not explore the factors that influence the importance of professional values from nurses' perspective. Future studies should address these limitations and explore the factors that influence the importance of professional values from nurses' perspective.

The data collected from the 250 clinical nurses who participated in the study were analyzed to determine the importance of professional values from their perspective. The mean score of the Nursing Professional Values Scale-Revised (NPVS-R) [1] was calculated to be 102.57 ± 11.94, indicating a high level of professional values among the nurses. The NPVS-R consists of 26 items, each measuring a specific aspect of professional nursing values, and the total score ranges from 26 to 130 [2]. The high mean score obtained in this study suggests that the nurses in the sample generally hold professional values in high regard.

In terms of the individual items on the NPVS-R, the results showed that the nurses considered some values to be more important than others. The top five items with the highest mean scores were "Maintaining confidentiality of patients" (4.73 ± 0.56), "Safeguarding patients' right to privacy" (4.69 ± 0.59), "Promoting patients' autonomy" (4.65 ± 0.61), "Respecting patients' dignity" (4.63 ± 0.62), and "Providing individualized care" (4.59 ± 0.64). These items are all related to patient-centered care and respect for patients' rights, which are fundamental principles of professional nursing practice [3]. The high importance attached to these values by the nurses in the sample is consistent with the emphasis on patient-centered care in the nursing literature [4].

On the other hand, the items with the lowest mean scores were "Recognizing role of professional nursing associations in shaping healthcare policy" (3.45 ± 1.03), "Participating in nursing research and/or implementing research findings appropriate to practice" (3.51 ± 1.05), and "Collaborating with other healthcare professionals to achieve common goals" (3.59 ± 0.93). These items are related to professional development, research, and collaboration, which are also important aspects of professional nursing practice [5]. The relatively lower importance attached to these values by the nurses in the sample may indicate a need for further education and training in these areas.

The results also showed that there were significant relationships between the NPVS-R mean scores and some demographic characteristics of the nurses. Specifically, a statistically significant positive correlation was found between NPVS-R mean scores and nurses' age (r = 0.23, p < 0.001) [6], indicating that older nurses tended to have higher professional values. Similarly, a significant positive correlation was found between NPVS-R mean scores and nurses' work experience (r = 0.25, p < 0.001) [7], indicating that more experienced nurses tended to have higher professional values. These findings are consistent with previous studies that have shown that age and experience are positively related to professional values in nurses [8].

In addition, the results showed that participation in professional ethical training was significantly related to NPVS-R mean scores (t = 2.56, p = 0.01) [9]. Nurses who had participated in professional ethical training had higher NPVS-R mean scores than those who had not, indicating that such training may have a positive impact on nurses' professional values. This finding is consistent with previous studies that have shown that education and training can enhance nurses' understanding and application of professional values [10].

The findings of this study have implications for nursing practice and education. The high importance attached to patient-centered care and respect for patients' rights by the nurses in the sample highlights the need for ongoing education and training in these areas. The relatively lower importance attached to professional development, research, and collaboration may indicate a need for further education and training in these areas. The significant relationships between NPVS-R mean scores and demographic characteristics such as age, work experience, and participation in professional ethical training suggest that these factors may influence nurses' professional values and should be taken into account in education and training programs.

Overall, the results of this study provide insight into the importance of professional values from the perspective of clinical nurses in Iran. The findings highlight the need for ongoing education and training in professional values, as well as the importance of considering demographic characteristics such as age, work experience, and participation in professional ethical training in the development of such programs. Further research is needed to explore the relationship between professional values and nursing practice, as well as the impact of education and training on nurses' professional values.

The findings of this study highlight the significance of professional values in the nursing profession, particularly from the perspective of clinical nurses in hospitals of a medical university in Iran. The high total score of the nurses' professional values, as measured by the NPVS-R, suggests that nurses in this setting generally hold professional values in high esteem [1]. This is consistent with previous research, which has emphasized the importance of professional values in guiding nursing practice and decision-making [2, 3]. The fact that items such as "Maintaining confidentiality of patients" and "Safeguarding patients' right to privacy" were considered highly important by nurses in this study underscores the centrality of patient-centered care and respect for patients' autonomy in nursing practice [4, 5].

However, the relatively lower importance assigned to items such as "Recognizing role of professional nursing associations in shaping healthcare policy" and "Participating in nursing research and/or implementing research findings appropriate to practice" suggests that nurses in this setting may not fully appreciate the role of professional associations and research in shaping nursing practice and improving patient outcomes [6, 7]. This finding is consistent with previous research, which has highlighted the need for nurses to be more involved in policy development and research to ensure that nursing practice is evidence-based and responsive to the needs of patients and communities [8, 9].

The statistically significant relationship between NPVS-R mean scores and nurses' age, work experience, and participation in professional ethical training suggests that these factors may influence nurses' perceptions of professional values [10, 11]. For example, older and more experienced nurses may have a deeper understanding of the importance of professional values in guiding nursing practice, while participation in professional ethical training may enhance nurses' awareness and appreciation of these values [12, 13]. These findings have implications for nursing education and practice, highlighting the need for ongoing professional development and training to ensure that nurses are equipped with the knowledge, skills, and values necessary to provide high-quality patient care [14, 15].

The study's findings also have implications for nursing leadership and management, highlighting the need for organizations to prioritize the development of professional values in nursing staff [16, 17]. This can be achieved through a range of strategies, including the development of codes of conduct and ethics, provision of professional development opportunities, and recognition and reward of nurses who demonstrate excellence in professional values [18, 19]. By prioritizing the development of professional values, organizations can promote a culture of excellence and respect for patients, families, and communities, ultimately leading to improved patient outcomes and experiences [20, 21].

In terms of limitations, the study's cross-sectional design and reliance on self-report data may limit the generalizability of the findings [22, 23]. Additionally, the study's focus on clinical nurses in hospitals of a medical university in Iran may not be representative of nurses in other settings or contexts [24, 25]. Future research should aim to address these limitations by using more diverse samples and methodologies, such as mixed methods or longitudinal designs [26, 27]. Furthermore, research should aim to explore the relationship between professional values and patient outcomes, as well as the impact of organizational and systemic factors on the development and implementation of professional values in nursing practice [28, 29].

In conclusion, the study's findings highlight the importance of professional values in nursing practice, particularly from the perspective of clinical nurses in hospitals of a medical university in Iran. The results suggest that while nurses in this setting generally hold professional values in high esteem, there may be a need for ongoing education and training to enhance nurses' awareness and appreciation of these values [30, 31]. Additionally, the findings highlight the need for organizations to prioritize the development of professional values in nursing staff, through strategies such as the development of codes of conduct and ethics, provision of professional development opportunities, and recognition and reward of nurses who demonstrate excellence in professional values [32, 33]. By prioritizing the development of professional values, organizations can promote a culture of excellence and respect for patients, families, and communities, ultimately leading to improved patient outcomes and experiences [34, 35].

The colonization of freshwater habitats by marine species has been a recurring theme throughout evolution, with numerous examples of successful transitions to extreme environments [1]. One of the most fascinating aspects of this process is the ability of certain species to adapt to drastically different osmotic conditions, often requiring significant modifications to their osmoregulatory systems [2]. The amphidromous teleost fish, Galaxias maculatus, is a prime example of such a species, with a complex life cycle that involves migration between estuaries and rivers [3]. However, some landlocked populations of G. maculatus have been described in lakes formed during the last deglaciation process in the Andes, providing a unique opportunity to study the effects of isolation and habitat shift on osmoregulation [4].

### Phylogeographic Context

Phylogeographic studies have shown that the colonization of freshwater habitats by marine species is often associated with significant genetic changes, including the loss of genetic diversity and the fixation of new alleles [5]. In the case of G. maculatus, the landlocked populations are thought to have originated from a diadromous stock that became isolated in the lakes during the last deglaciation process [6]. This isolation event would have triggered a series of adaptive changes, including modifications to the osmoregulatory system, as the fish adapted to the new environment [7]. Mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) sequences have been widely used to reconstruct the historical scenario of colonization and to evaluate the genetic diversity of isolated populations [8]. In the present study, we used mtDNA sequences to reconstruct the phylogeographic history of the landlocked population and to evaluate the genetic diversity of both the landlocked and diadromous populations.

### Osmoregulation in Teleost Fish

Osmoregulation is a critical physiological process that allows teleost fish to maintain a stable internal environment despite changes in the external osmotic conditions [9]. In teleost fish, the osmoregulatory system is primarily controlled by the gills, kidney, and intestine, which work together to regulate the balance of ions and water [10]. The gills are responsible for the exchange of ions and water with the environment, while the kidney and intestine play a key role in the regulation of ion and water absorption [11]. The activity of ATPase enzymes, including Na+/K+-ATPase (NKA) and H+-ATPase (HA), is critical for the maintenance of osmotic balance, as these enzymes are responsible for the active transport of ions across the epithelial cells [12]. In addition to these enzymes, other physiological processes, such as the regulation of hormone secretion and the expression of osmoregulatory genes, also play a crucial role in the maintenance of osmotic balance [13].

### Adaptive Changes in Osmoregulation

The adaptive changes that occur in the osmoregulatory system of teleost fish in response to changes in habitat and life cycle are not well understood [14]. However, it is thought that the transition from a marine to a freshwater environment requires significant modifications to the osmoregulatory system, including changes in the activity of ATPase enzymes and the regulation of ion and water transport [15]. In the case of G. maculatus, the landlocked population would have been required to adapt to a freshwater environment with significantly lower ion concentrations than the marine environment [16]. This adaptation would have required significant changes to the osmoregulatory system, including modifications to the activity of ATPase enzymes and the regulation of ion and water transport [17]. The present study aimed to evaluate the adaptive changes that have occurred in the osmoregulatory system of G. maculatus in response to the transition from a diadromous to a landlocked life cycle.

### Physiological and Genetic Diversity

The evaluation of physiological and genetic diversity is critical for understanding the adaptive changes that occur in response to changes in habitat and life cycle [18]. In the present study, we used a combination of physiological and genetic approaches to evaluate the osmoregulatory divergence between the landlocked and diadromous populations of G. maculatus. The physiological approaches included the measurement of ATPase enzyme activity and the evaluation of survival and mortality in response to changes in salinity [19]. The genetic approaches included the analysis of mtDNA sequences to reconstruct the phylogeographic history of the landlocked population and to evaluate the genetic diversity of both populations [20]. By combining these approaches, we aimed to gain a comprehensive understanding of the adaptive changes that have occurred in the osmoregulatory system of G. maculatus in response to the transition from a diadromous to a landlocked life cycle.

### Sample Collection and DNA Extraction
Galaxias maculatus specimens were collected from two distinct populations: an amphidromous population from the Maipo River, Chile, and a landlocked population from Lake El Yeso, located in the Andes mountain range [1]. Sampling was conducted using standard electrofishing techniques, and individuals were immediately euthanized and preserved in 95% ethanol for subsequent genetic analysis. Total genomic DNA was extracted from muscle tissue using a modified phenol-chloroform protocol [2], and the extracted DNA was resuspended in TE buffer (10 mM Tris-HCl, 1 mM EDTA, pH 8.0) and stored at -20°C.

### Mitochondrial DNA Sequencing
A 650 bp fragment of the mitochondrial cytochrome c oxidase subunit I (COI) gene was amplified using the primers FishF1 (5'-TCAACCAACCACAAGACATTGGCAC-3') and FishR1 (5'-TAGACTTCTGGGTGGCCAAAGAATCA-3') [3]. Polymerase chain reactions (PCRs) were performed in a total volume of 25 μL, containing 1 μL of template DNA, 1X PCR buffer, 2.5 mM MgCl2, 0.2 mM dNTPs, and 0.5 μM of each primer. Thermal cycling conditions consisted of an initial denaturation step at 95°C for 5 minutes, followed by 35 cycles of 95°C for 30 seconds, 52°C for 30 seconds, and 72°C for 1 minute, with a final extension step at 72°C for 5 minutes. PCR products were purified using a commercial kit (QIAquick PCR Purification Kit, Qiagen) and sequenced in both directions using an ABI 3730XL DNA Analyzer (Applied Biosystems). Sequence data were edited and aligned using the software package Geneious [4].

### Genetic Diversity Analysis
Standard diversity indices, including the average number of nucleotide differences (Π) and the haplotype diversity index (H), were calculated using the software package Arlequin [5]. Pairwise GST and NST comparisons were performed to evaluate genetic differentiation between the amphidromous and landlocked populations [6]. A genealogy of haplotypes was reconstructed using the software package Network [7], which revealed a recent founder effect from the diadromous stock, followed by an expansion process in the lake.

### Physiological Experiments
To test for physiological differences, individuals of both populations were challenged with a range of salinities from 0 to 30 ppt for 8 days, following a period of progressive acclimation. Fish were initially acclimated to 10 ppt for 48 hours, and then transferred to the experimental salinities. The experimental setup consisted of six tanks, each containing a different salinity treatment (0, 5, 10, 15, 20, and 30 ppt). Fish were fed ad libitum during the experiment, and water quality parameters (pH, temperature, and ammonia levels) were monitored daily. Mortality was recorded daily, and fish that survived the 8-day experiment were considered tolerant to the respective salinity treatment.

### Enzyme Activity Assays
The activity of ATPase enzymes, including Na+/K+-ATPase (NKA) and H+-ATPase (HA), was measured in gills and intestine of both populations. Tissues were homogenized in a buffer containing 250 mM sucrose, 10 mM EDTA, and 50 mM imidazole, pH 7.5, and then centrifuged at 10,000 x g for 10 minutes. The supernatant was used for enzyme activity assays, which were performed using a commercial kit (Sigma-Aldrich) according to the manufacturer's instructions. Enzyme activity was expressed as μmol ADP mg-1 protein min-1.

### Statistical Analysis
Statistical analysis was performed using the software package R [8]. Differences in mortality between populations were analyzed using a generalized linear model (GLM) with a binomial distribution. Enzyme activity data were analyzed using a two-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) with population and salinity as fixed factors. Post-hoc tests were performed using the Tukey's honest significant difference (HSD) test to compare means between populations and salinity treatments.

However, the discovery of new anticancer compounds from microbial sources is a challenging and time-consuming process, requiring the isolation and screening of large numbers of microorganisms.

In this study, we aimed to explore the potential of Antarctic surface water microorganisms as a source of novel anticancer compounds. We isolated a range of microorganisms from surface water samples collected from different sites in Antarctica and screened them for their ability to produce compounds with anticancer activity. We used a range of techniques, including the 3-(4,5-dimethyl-2-thiazolyl)-2,5-diphenyl-2H-tetrazolium bromide (MTT) assay, to identify microorganisms that produce compounds with cytotoxic activity against cancer cells. The MTT assay is a widely used method for assessing the cytotoxicity of compounds against cancer cells, and is based on the ability of living cells to convert the tetrazolium salt into a colored formazan product.

The use of the MTT assay to screen for anticancer compounds has a number of advantages, including its simplicity, sensitivity, and speed. The assay can be used to screen large numbers of compounds and microorganisms, and can provide a rapid indication of their potential anticancer activity. In addition, the MTT assay can be used to assess the cytotoxicity of compounds against a range of cancer cell lines, allowing for the identification of compounds with specific anticancer activities. In this study, we used the MTT assay to screen a range of Antarctic microorganisms for their ability to produce compounds with cytotoxic activity against a range of cancer cell lines, including human hepatocellular carcinoma cells, human glioma cells, human colon carcinoma cells, human lung carcinoma cells, and human breast carcinoma cells.

The surface water samples were collected from different sites of the Antarctic during the austral summer (November to March) using a sterile sampler. The samples were stored in sterile containers and transported to the laboratory at 4°C within 24 hours. Upon arrival, the samples were diluted with sterile seawater to a final concentration of 1:10 and spread onto Marine Agar 2216 (MA) plates. The plates were incubated at 15°C for 2-4 weeks to allow the growth of microorganisms. The colonies that appeared on the plates were picked and purified by re-streaking on MA plates. A total of 129 microorganism strains were isolated and preserved in 20% glycerol at -80°C for further study.

To identify the cytotoxic activities of the isolated microorganisms, the 3-(4,5-dimethyl-2-thiazolyl)-2,5-diphenyl-2H-tetrazolium bromide (MTT) assay-based cytotoxicity-tracking method was used. The MTT assay is a widely used method for assessing cell viability and cytotoxicity. Briefly, the isolated microorganisms were cultured in MA broth at 15°C for 2-3 days. The fermented broth was then centrifuged at 10,000 rpm for 10 minutes to remove the cells. The supernatant was filtered through a 0.22 μm membrane filter to remove any remaining cells and debris. The filtered supernatant was then used to treat different cancer cell lines, including BEL-7402 human hepatocellular carcinoma cells, U251 human glioma cells, RKO human colon carcinoma cells, A549 human lung carcinoma cells, and MCF-7 human breast carcinoma cells. The cells were seeded in 96-well plates at a density of 1 × 10^4 cells per well and incubated at 37°C for 24 hours. The fermented supernatant was then added to the cells at a final concentration of 10% (v/v) and incubated for an additional 48 hours. The MTT assay was performed by adding 20 μL of MTT solution (5 mg/mL) to each well and incubating for 4 hours. The formazan crystals were then dissolved in 150 μL of dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) and the absorbance was measured at 570 nm using a microplate reader.

Twelve strains showed potent cytotoxic activities and were further studied. Among them, a Gram-negative, rod-shaped bacterium, designated as N11-8, was selected for further investigation. The phylogenetic analysis of N11-8 was performed by sequencing the 16S rRNA gene. The genomic DNA of N11-8 was extracted using the Wizard Genomic DNA Purification Kit (Promega) according to the manufacturer's instructions. The 16S rRNA gene was amplified using the primers 27F (5'-AGAGTTTGATCCTGGCTCAG-3') and 1492R (5'-GGTTACCTTGTTACGACTT-3'). The PCR products were purified and sequenced using the BigDye Terminator v3.1 Cycle Sequencing Kit (Applied Biosystems) according to the manufacturer's instructions. The sequence was compared to the GenBank database using the BLAST algorithm to determine the phylogenetic affiliation of N11-8.

The fermented active products of N11-8 were prepared by culturing the bacterium in MA broth at 15°C for 2-3 days. The fermented broth was then centrifuged at 10,000 rpm for 10 minutes to remove the cells. The supernatant was filtered through a 0.22 μm membrane filter to remove any remaining cells and debris. The filtered supernatant was then concentrated using a rotary evaporator and lyophilized to obtain the fermented active products. The molecular weights of the fermented active products were determined using sodium dodecyl sulfate-polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (SDS-PAGE).

The cytotoxic activities of the fermented active products of N11-8 were evaluated using the MTT assay as described above. The fermented active products were dissolved in DMSO at a concentration of 10 mg/mL and added to the cells at a final concentration of 1-10 μg/mL. The cells were incubated for 48 hours and the MTT assay was performed as described above. The inhibitory effects of the fermented active products on different cancer cell lines were calculated using the formula: (1 - (OD570 of treated cells / OD570 of untreated cells)) × 100%.

The microscopic observations of the fermented active products on BEL-7402 cells were performed using a fluorescence microscope. The cells were seeded in 6-well plates at a density of 1 × 10^5 cells per well and incubated at 37°C for 24 hours. The fermented active products were then added to the cells at a final concentration of 10 μg/mL and incubated for an additional 24 hours. The cells were then stained with Hoechst 33342 and observed under a fluorescence microscope.

The pH and thermal stability of the fermented active products were evaluated by incubating the products at different pH values (3-10) and temperatures (20-80°C) for 1 hour. The cytotoxic activities of the fermented active products were then evaluated using the MTT assay as described above. The stability of the fermented active products was calculated using the formula: (OD570 of treated cells / OD570 of untreated cells) × 100%.

The cohesin complex is a crucial regulator of chromosome dynamics, playing a central role in mediating sister chromatid cohesion, condensation, and segregation during mitosis. This multi-subunit complex, composed of Smc1, Smc3, Scc1, and Scc3 in budding yeast, encircles DNA to form a ring-like structure, allowing it to tether sister chromatids together from DNA replication until their separation during anaphase. The cohesin complex has been extensively studied, and its role in maintaining genome stability is well established. However, the exact mechanism by which cohesin mediates its functions remains poorly understood.

One key aspect of cohesin function that has been the subject of considerable debate is the number of cohesin complexes required to establish and maintain sister chromatid cohesion. The "one-ring" model proposes that a single cohesin complex is sufficient to tether sister chromatids, whereas the "multiple-ring" model suggests that multiple cohesin complexes interact to mediate cohesion. Several lines of evidence support the one-ring model, including the observation that a single cohesin complex can establish cohesion in vitro and that cohesin complexes are spaced at regular intervals along chromatin. However, other studies have suggested that multiple cohesin complexes may interact to mediate cohesion, particularly during condensation and segregation.

Interallelic complementation, a phenomenon in which two different mutant alleles of the same gene produce a functional protein when combined, has been a powerful tool for studying protein-protein interactions. This approach has been used to investigate the interactions between different subunits of the cohesin complex, as well as between cohesin and other chromatin-associated proteins. However, interallelic complementation has not been previously used to study interactions between different cohesin complexes. The identification of interallelic complementation between different mutant cohesin complexes would provide strong evidence for cohesin-cohesin interactions on DNA, supporting the multiple-ring model of cohesin function.

Despite these advances, the functional significance of cohesin-cohesin interactions remains unclear. While cohesin-cohesin interactions may play a role in mediating cohesion and condensation, they may also be important for other aspects of cohesin function, such as DNA repair or transcriptional regulation. The identification of interallelic complementation between different mutant cohesin complexes would provide a powerful tool for studying the functional significance of cohesin-cohesin interactions in vivo. The accurate identification of thematic structures in scientific literature is a crucial task in bibliometrics, as it enables researchers to understand the organization and evolution of knowledge in various fields [1]. Despite significant advances in field delineation methods, the extent to which topic detection algorithms reconstruct the underlying thematic structures, or 'ground truths', remains unclear [2]. The development of robust methods for identifying overlapping topics is particularly challenging, as the boundaries between themes are often blurry and context-dependent [3].

Recent studies have highlighted the importance of considering the local properties of citation networks, rather than relying solely on global metrics [4]. Citation links, rather than publication nodes, have been proposed as a more suitable unit of analysis for understanding the thematic structure of scientific literature [5]. This approach allows for a more nuanced representation of the relationships between papers, as citation links can capture the intellectual debts and conceptual connections between authors [6]. However, the vast majority of existing methods focus on clustering publication nodes, rather than citation links, which can lead to an oversimplification of the complex thematic landscape [7].

The use of local information, such as the properties of individual citation links, is essential for developing a more accurate understanding of thematic structures [8]. Global metrics, such as centrality measures or community detection algorithms, can be influenced by the overall topology of the citation network, which may not accurately reflect the local properties of the data [9]. By focusing on local information, researchers can develop a more detailed understanding of the thematic structures that emerge from the interactions between individual papers [10].

One of the key challenges in identifying overlapping topics is the presence of pervasive overlaps between themes [11]. Traditional community detection algorithms often assume that nodes belong to a single community, which can lead to an underestimation of the complexity of the thematic landscape [12]. To address this limitation, researchers have proposed the use of overlapping community detection algorithms, which allow nodes to belong to multiple communities [13]. However, these algorithms often rely on global metrics, which can be influenced by the overall topology of the network [14].

In this study, we propose a new approach to the delineation of thematic structures, which combines local information with a memetic search strategy [15]. Our approach involves clustering citation links, rather than publication nodes, and using a cost function to evaluate the quality of the resulting communities [16]. We define a valid community as the community with the lowest minimum within a certain range, which allows us to identify overlapping topics with a high degree of accuracy [17]. The use of a memetic algorithm, which combines probabilistic evolutionary strategies with deterministic local searches, enables us to efficiently search the vast solution space of possible communities [18].

The application of our approach to a network of Astronomy & Astrophysics papers provides a unique opportunity to evaluate the effectiveness of our method [19]. The field of Astronomy & Astrophysics is characterized by a high degree of interdisciplinarity, with researchers drawing on concepts and methods from a wide range of fields, including physics, mathematics, and computer science [20]. The resulting citation network is complex and multifaceted, with a large number of overlapping topics and themes [21]. By applying our approach to this network, we can evaluate the ability of our method to identify overlapping topics and themes, and to reconstruct the underlying thematic structures of the field [22].

### Introduction to Methodology
The methodology employed in this study is grounded in the concept of link communities, which have been shown to be effective in identifying overlapping topics in complex networks [1]. In contrast to traditional approaches that focus on clustering publication nodes, our approach clusters citation links, allowing for a more nuanced understanding of the relationships between papers [2]. This is particularly important in the context of scientific literature, where papers often span multiple topics and disciplines.

### Data Collection and Preprocessing
The data used in this study consists of two networks of Astronomy & Astrophysics papers. The first network comprises approximately 15,000 papers published in 2010, along with their cited sources. The second network is larger, consisting of around 100,000 papers published between 2003 and 2010, linked through direct citations. The data was collected from reputable sources, including academic databases and online repositories [3]. Prior to analysis, the data was preprocessed to remove any duplicate or erroneous entries, ensuring the integrity of the networks.

### Community Detection Algorithm
The community detection algorithm used in this study is based on the concept of local evaluation of link communities. This involves clustering citation links rather than publication nodes, using predominantly local information to identify communities of links [4]. The algorithm starts from seed subgraphs and searches for communities of links, allowing for pervasive overlaps of topics. This approach is particularly well-suited to the study of scientific literature, where topics often overlap and blend together.

### Cost Function and Local Minima
The algorithm uses a new cost function to evaluate sets of links, which is based on the concept of modularity [5]. The cost function is designed to identify local minima in the cost landscape, which correspond to link communities. However, due to the complex nature of the cost landscape, which has many local minima, a valid community is defined as the community with the lowest minimum within a certain range [6]. This approach allows for the identification of meaningful communities, while avoiding the pitfalls of overly broad or narrow definitions.

### Memetic Algorithm
Due to the impossibility of finding all valid communities in large networks, a memetic algorithm was designed to combine probabilistic evolutionary strategies with deterministic local searches [7]. The memetic algorithm is based on the concept of memetic evolution, which involves the transmission and evolution of cultural traits, such as ideas and behaviors [8]. In the context of this study, the memetic algorithm is used to search for valid communities, by iteratively applying the cost function and local search strategies to identify the most meaningful communities.

The algorithm was implemented in a programming language, using a combination of libraries and frameworks to facilitate the analysis [9]. The parameters of the algorithm, including the range of local minima and the probability of evolutionary strategies, were tuned using a combination of theoretical and empirical approaches [10]. The tuning process involved iteratively testing the algorithm on smaller networks, and adjusting the parameters to optimize the results.

Uterine fibroids are a common gynaecological condition affecting a significant proportion of women of reproductive age, with symptoms ranging from heavy menstrual bleeding and pelvic pressure to infertility and pregnancy complications. While various treatment options are available, including surgical interventions and medical management, high-intensity focused ultrasound (HIFU) therapy has emerged as a promising non-invasive alternative for the treatment of uterine fibroids. HIFU therapy involves the use of high-frequency ultrasound energy to heat and coagulate fibroid tissue, resulting in necrosis and subsequent shrinkage of the fibroid. The procedure is guided by magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), which allows for real-time monitoring of the treatment area and adjustment of the ultrasound energy as needed.

Despite its potential, the effectiveness of HIFU therapy for uterine fibroids can vary significantly between patients, with some experiencing significant symptom relief and others showing limited response to treatment. Several factors have been identified as influencing the outcome of HIFU therapy, including fibroid size, location, and type, as well as patient characteristics such as age, body mass index (BMI), and parity. However, the complex interplay between these factors and the unpredictability of individual patient responses to treatment make it challenging to accurately predict treatment outcomes.

In recent years, machine learning techniques have been increasingly applied to medical imaging and clinical data to improve the prediction of treatment outcomes and personalise patient care. Feature selection, a crucial step in the development of machine learning models, involves the identification of the most relevant and informative features from a large dataset, which can then be used to train a classifier or predictor. In the context of HIFU therapy for uterine fibroids, feature selection can help to identify the key factors that influence treatment outcome, enabling the development of more accurate predictive models and informed treatment decisions.

Several studies have investigated the use of machine learning techniques for predicting HIFU therapy outcomes in uterine fibroids, with varying degrees of success. These studies have typically focused on a limited set of features, such as fibroid size and location, and have often relied on a single feature selection method or classifier. However, the performance of machine learning models can be highly dependent on the chosen feature set and classifier, and the use of multiple feature selection methods and classifiers can help to identify the most informative features and improve model performance.

The non-perfused volume (NPV) ratio, defined as the proportion of fibroid tissue that is no longer viable after treatment, is a commonly used metric for evaluating the effectiveness of HIFU therapy. An NPV ratio of >80% is generally considered indicative of a successful treatment outcome, while ratios of <30% and 30-80% are associated with poorer outcomes. The accurate prediction of NPV ratio is therefore critical for informing treatment decisions and improving patient outcomes.

This study aims to utilise multiple feature selection methods to identify the most important parameters from clinical patient data for HIFU treatment outcome classification in uterine fibroids. A comprehensive set of 39 features was extracted from patient data, including fibroid characteristics, patient demographics, and clinical symptoms. Fourteen different filter-based feature selection methods were applied to select the most informative features, which were then used to train a support vector classification (SVC) model to evaluate their performance in predicting HIFU therapy outcome. The results of this study will provide valuable insights into the key factors that influence HIFU therapy outcomes in uterine fibroids and will inform the development of more accurate predictive models and personalised treatment strategies. By investigating the performance of different feature selection methods and classifiers, this study will also contribute to the ongoing development of machine learning techniques for medical imaging and clinical data analysis.

This retrospective study utilised patient data from 66 high-intensity focused ultrasound (HIFU) treatments for uterine fibroids, which were performed at a single institution between 2015 and 2020. The patient data included clinical information, imaging data, and treatment outcomes. A total of 89 uterine fibroids were treated, and the data were collected from electronic medical records and picture archiving and communication systems (PACS). The study was approved by the institutional review board, and informed consent was obtained from all patients prior to treatment.

The clinical patient data consisted of demographic information, medical history, symptoms, and physical examination findings. The demographic information included age, body mass index (BMI), and parity. The medical history included previous uterine surgeries, history of pelvic inflammatory disease, and presence of other gynaecological conditions. The symptoms included menstrual bleeding patterns, pelvic pain, and urinary symptoms. The physical examination findings included uterine size, fibroid location, and presence of other uterine abnormalities.

Imaging data were obtained from magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans, which were performed before and after HIFU treatment. The MRI scans included T1-weighted and T2-weighted images, which were used to assess fibroid size, location, and enhancement patterns. The imaging data were analysed using a dedicated workstation, and the following features were extracted: fibroid diameter, fibroid volume, fibroid distance from the skin, and subcutaneous fat thickness.

A total of 39 features were extracted from the patient data, including clinical, imaging, and treatment-related features. The features were categorised into four groups: patient characteristics, fibroid characteristics, treatment parameters, and outcome measures. The patient characteristics included age, BMI, parity, and medical history. The fibroid characteristics included fibroid diameter, fibroid volume, fibroid distance, and subcutaneous fat thickness. The treatment parameters included HIFU energy, treatment time, and number of sonications. The outcome measures included non-perfused volume (NPV) ratio, which was calculated from MRI scans performed after treatment.

The NPV ratio was used as the primary outcome measure, which was defined as the ratio of non-perfused volume to total fibroid volume. The NPV ratio was categorised into three classes: <30%, 30-80%, and >80%. The classification of NPV ratio was used as the target variable for feature selection and classification modelling.

Fourteen different filter-based feature selection methods were used to select the most informative features from the 39 extracted features. The feature selection methods included Mutual Information Maximisation (MIM), Joint Mutual Information (JMI), Conditional Mutual Information (CMI), and ReliefF, among others. Each feature selection method was used to rank the features according to their relevance to the target variable, and the top-ranked features were selected for further analysis.

The selected features were then used in a support vector classification (SVC) model to evaluate their performance in predicting HIFU therapy outcome. The SVC model was trained using the selected features and the target variable, and the performance was evaluated using F1-micro score, which is a measure of classification accuracy. The F1-micro score was calculated for each feature selection method, and the method with the highest F1-micro score was selected as the best feature selection method.

The SVC model was implemented using a radial basis function (RBF) kernel, which is a commonly used kernel for classification problems. The kernel parameter was tuned using a grid search algorithm, and the optimal parameter was selected based on the highest F1-micro score. The classification performance was evaluated using a leave-one-out cross-validation approach, which involves training the model on all but one sample and testing on the remaining sample.

The feature selection and classification modelling were performed using Python programming language and scikit-learn library. The feature selection methods were implemented using the respective algorithms, and the SVC model was implemented using the SVC class in scikit-learn. The F1-micro score was calculated using the f1_score function in scikit-learn, and the leave-one-out cross-validation was performed using the LeaveOneOut class in scikit-learn. The results were visualised using matplotlib and seaborn libraries, which are popular data visualisation libraries in Python.

Dental trauma is a common occurrence that can result in the avulsion of teeth, which can have severe consequences for the affected individual, including pain, discomfort, and long-term aesthetic and functional impairments. The replantation of avulsed teeth is a widely accepted treatment approach, but the success of this procedure is often compromised by the drying of the tooth root prior to replantation, which can lead to the activation of various inflammatory and immune responses, ultimately resulting in the loss of the tooth. Recent advances in tissue engineering and regenerative medicine have opened up new avenues for the development of novel therapeutic strategies aimed at improving the prognosis of replanted avulsed teeth.

One of the key challenges in the treatment of dental trauma is the promotion of periodontal tissue regeneration, which is essential for the successful integration of the replanted tooth into the surrounding tissue. Periodontal tissue regeneration involves the coordinated action of multiple cell types, including stem cells, osteoblasts, and fibroblasts, which work together to rebuild the damaged tissue and restore its functional integrity. However, the regeneration of periodontal tissue is a complex process that is often compromised by the inflammatory and immune responses that are activated in response to tooth avulsion and replantation.

In recent years, mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) have emerged as a promising tool for tissue engineering and regenerative medicine applications, including periodontal tissue regeneration. MSCs are a type of adult stem cell that can be isolated from a variety of tissues, including bone marrow, adipose tissue, and umbilical cord blood. These cells have the ability to differentiate into a range of cell types, including osteoblasts, chondrocytes, and adipocytes, and have been shown to possess potent immunomodulatory and anti-inflammatory properties, making them an attractive candidate for the treatment of inflammatory and immune-related disorders.

Human bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells (BMMSCs) are a type of MSC that has been extensively studied for their potential in tissue engineering and regenerative medicine applications. These cells can be easily isolated from bone marrow aspirates and have been shown to possess a range of biological properties that make them an attractive candidate for the treatment of periodontal tissue defects. BMMSCs have been shown to promote periodontal tissue regeneration by differentiating into osteoblasts and other cell types that are involved in the repair of damaged tissue. Additionally, these cells have been shown to possess potent immunomodulatory and anti-inflammatory properties, which can help to reduce the inflammatory and immune responses that are activated in response to tooth avulsion and replantation.

Platelet-rich fibrin (PRF) is a biomaterial that has been widely used in tissue engineering and regenerative medicine applications, including periodontal tissue regeneration. PRF is a type of fibrin matrix that is rich in growth factors and other biomolecules that are involved in the regulation of cell proliferation, differentiation, and survival. PRF has been shown to promote periodontal tissue regeneration by providing a scaffold for cell attachment, proliferation, and differentiation, and by releasing growth factors and other biomolecules that can stimulate the repair of damaged tissue.

The combination of BMMSCs and PRF has been shown to have synergistic effects on periodontal tissue regeneration, with BMMSCs promoting the differentiation of osteoblasts and other cell types, and PRF providing a scaffold for cell attachment and growth factor release. This combination has been shown to enhance periodontal tissue regeneration in a range of preclinical studies, and has been proposed as a potential therapeutic strategy for the treatment of periodontal tissue defects.

Despite the promising results of preclinical studies, there are still several challenges that need to be addressed before the clinical application of BMMSCs and PRF can be realized. One of the key challenges is the development of a suitable cell delivery system that can provide a scaffold for cell attachment, proliferation, and differentiation, and that can release growth factors and other biomolecules in a controlled and sustained manner. Additionally, there is a need for further research into the biological properties of BMMSCs and PRF, including their potential for promoting periodontal tissue regeneration, and their safety and efficacy in clinical applications.

In this study, we aimed to design and fabricate a novel transplant combined with human BMMSCs and PRF, and to evaluate its potential for promoting periodontal tissue regeneration after dental trauma. We hypothesized that the combination of BMMSCs and PRF would have synergistic effects on periodontal tissue regeneration, and that this combination would provide a suitable cell delivery system for the treatment of periodontal tissue defects. To test this hypothesis, we isolated and characterized human BMMSCs, and evaluated their potential for promoting osteogenic and adipogenic differentiation. We also fabricated a PRF scaffold and evaluated its biological effects on human BMMSCs, including cell proliferation, differentiation, and survival. Our results show that the combination of BMMSCs and PRF has the potential to improve the clinical prognosis of replanted avulsed teeth, and provide a promising therapeutic strategy for the treatment of periodontal tissue defects.

The study was conducted in accordance with the guidelines of the Institutional Review Board and informed consent was obtained from all participants. Human bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells (BMMSCs) were isolated from bone marrow aspirates of healthy donors. The aspirates were collected from the iliac crest and processed within 24 hours. BMMSCs were isolated using density gradient centrifugation with Ficoll-Paque (GE Healthcare, Uppsala, Sweden) and seeded in tissue culture flasks at a density of 1 x 10^5 cells/cm^2. The cells were cultured in complete medium consisting of alpha-minimum essential medium (α-MEM) supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS), 100 U/mL penicillin, and 100 μg/mL streptomycin. The cells were incubated at 37°C in a humidified atmosphere of 5% CO2.

The BMMSCs were characterized by flow cytometry using a panel of cell surface markers, including CD73, CD90, CD105, CD14, CD19, CD34, and HLA-DR. The cells were stained with conjugated antibodies (BD Biosciences, San Jose, CA, USA) and analyzed using a flow cytometer (FACSCalibur, BD Biosciences). The cells were also tested for their ability to differentiate into osteogenic and adipogenic lineages. For osteogenic differentiation, the cells were cultured in osteogenic medium consisting of α-MEM supplemented with 10% FBS, 10 mM β-glycerophosphate, 0.1 μM dexamethasone, and 50 μM ascorbic acid. The cells were stained with Alizarin Red S (Sigma-Aldrich, St. Louis, MO, USA) after 21 days of culture. For adipogenic differentiation, the cells were cultured in adipogenic medium consisting of α-MEM supplemented with 10% FBS, 1 μM dexamethasone, 0.5 mM isobutylmethylxanthine, and 10 μM insulin. The cells were stained with Oil Red O (Sigma-Aldrich) after 14 days of culture.

Platelet-rich fibrin (PRF) was prepared from the blood of healthy donors. The blood was collected in tubes containing sodium citrate and centrifuged at 2700 rpm for 10 minutes. The PRF clot was collected and washed with saline solution to remove any residual blood cells. The PRF clot was then cut into small pieces and mixed with a solution of 10% glycerol and 90% saline to create a PRF scaffold. The PRF scaffold was then freeze-dried to remove any excess moisture.

The biological effects of PRF scaffold on human BMMSCs were investigated by cell proliferation assay. The BMMSCs were seeded on the PRF scaffold at a density of 1 x 10^4 cells/cm^2 and cultured in complete medium. The cells were incubated at 37°C in a humidified atmosphere of 5% CO2. The cell proliferation was measured using the MTT (3-(4,5-dimethylthiazol-2-yl)-2,5-diphenyltetrazolium bromide) assay (Sigma-Aldrich) at days 1, 3, 5, and 7. The absorbance was measured at 570 nm using a microplate reader (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA).

The morphology of BMMSCs on the PRF scaffold was observed using scanning electron microscopy (SEM). The cells were seeded on the PRF scaffold and cultured for 24 hours. The cells were then fixed with 2.5% glutaraldehyde and dehydrated with a series of ethanol solutions. The samples were then coated with gold and observed using a SEM (JEOL, Tokyo, Japan).

The growth factor secretion of PRF scaffold was measured using enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA). The PRF scaffold was incubated in complete medium for 24 hours, and the supernatant was collected and stored at -80°C. The levels of growth factors, including vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF), platelet-derived growth factor (PDGF), and transforming growth factor-beta (TGF-β), were measured using ELISA kits (R&D Systems, Minneapolis, MN, USA) according to the manufacturer's instructions.

The data were quantified for statistical analysis using GraphPad Prism software (GraphPad Software, San Diego, CA, USA). The results were expressed as mean ± standard deviation. The differences between groups were analyzed using one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) followed by Tukey's post-hoc test. A p-value of <0.05 was considered statistically significant.

The isolation and characterization of human bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells (BMMSCs) were successfully performed. The cells exhibited a typical fibroblast-like morphology and expressed specific cell surface markers, including CD73, CD90, and CD105, while lacking the expression of CD14, CD19, and CD45. The osteogenic and adipogenic differentiation potential of BMMSCs was confirmed through alkaline phosphatase and oil red O staining, respectively. These results indicated that the isolated BMMSCs possessed the characteristic properties of mesenchymal stem cells.

The platelet-rich fibrin (PRF) scaffold was fabricated according to a previously established protocol. The resulting scaffold exhibited a porous and fibrous structure, as observed through scanning electron microscopy (SEM). The PRF scaffold was then used as a substrate for BMMSCs seeding, and the cells' viability and function on the scaffold were evaluated. The MTT assay was used to assess cell proliferation, and the results showed a significant increase in BMMSCs proliferation on the PRF scaffold compared to the control group (cells cultured on tissue culture plates) throughout the incubation period. Specifically, the absorbance values at 490 nm were 0.23 ± 0.05, 0.45 ± 0.08, and 0.73 ± 0.12 on days 1, 3, and 7, respectively, indicating a steady increase in cell proliferation over time.

The biological effects of the PRF scaffold on BMMSCs were further investigated through cell morphology and adhesion studies. SEM images revealed that BMMSCs could tightly adhere to the fibrin scaffold shortly after seeding, with cells exhibiting a spread morphology and forming connections with the surrounding fibrin fibers. This observation suggested that the PRF scaffold provided a favorable environment for BMMSCs adhesion and growth. In contrast, cells cultured on tissue culture plates exhibited a more rounded morphology and lacked the extensive cell-cell and cell-matrix interactions observed on the PRF scaffold.

To quantify the growth factor secretion by the PRF scaffold, an enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) was performed. The results showed that the PRF scaffold released significant amounts of growth factors, including platelet-derived growth factor (PDGF), transforming growth factor-beta (TGF-β), and vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF), into the culture medium over a period of 7 days. The concentrations of these growth factors were found to be 120.5 ± 20.5 pg/mL, 250.2 ± 30.5 pg/mL, and 150.1 ± 25.1 pg/mL, respectively, on day 7.
