A combination of neuroanatomical techniques was used to investigate the central projections of sensory neurons from the antenna and the labial pit organ in the migratory armyworm Mythimna separata. Adult moths were obtained from a laboratory colony and maintained on a diet of sugar water and wheat bran at 25°C under a 16:8 light:dark photoperiod. Prior to dissection, moths were anesthetized by cooling them to 4°C for 30 minutes. The head and thorax were then dissected in physiological saline, and the antennae and labial palps were exposed.

To visualize the central projections of sensory neurons, backfilling techniques were employed. The antennal nerve or the labial nerve was cut, and a small crystal of tetramethylrhodamine dextran (TMR, Molecular Probes) or fluorescein dextran (FD, Molecular Probes) was applied to the cut end. The preparation was then incubated in physiological saline at 4°C for 24-48 hours to allow the dye to diffuse into the nerve and label the sensory neurons. After incubation, the head and thorax were fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde in phosphate buffer (pH 7.4) for 2 hours at room temperature.

Confocal microscopy was used to examine the labeled sensory neurons and their central projections. The fixed preparations were rinsed in phosphate buffer and then mounted in Vectashield (Vector Laboratories) on glass slides. Images were acquired using a Zeiss LSM 510 confocal microscope with a 20x or 40x objective lens. Z-stacks of optical sections were taken at 1-2 μm intervals, and the images were later reconstructed into three-dimensional models using Zeiss LSM Image Browser software.

To specifically stain the antennal sensory neurons, dye application was made to each of the three antennal segments (scape, pedicle, and flagellum). A small crystal of TMR or FD was applied to the cut end of the antennal segment, and the preparation was incubated as described above. This approach allowed us to determine the specific projections of sensory neurons from each antennal segment.

In addition to backfilling, immunocytochemistry was used to label specific neuropils and neurons in the central nervous system. The fixed preparations were incubated in primary antibodies against synaptic vesicle protein (SV2, Developmental Studies Hybridoma Bank) or glutamine synthetase (GS, Abcam) overnight at 4°C. The preparations were then rinsed in phosphate buffer and incubated in secondary antibodies conjugated to Alexa Fluor 488 or 647 (Molecular Probes) for 2 hours at room temperature. The labeled preparations were then mounted and examined using confocal microscopy as described above.

Three-dimensional reconstructions of the central nervous system were made using Amira software (Visage Imaging). The reconstructions were based on z-stacks of optical sections acquired using confocal microscopy. The neuropils and neurons were manually segmented and labeled, and the three-dimensional models were used to visualize the central projections of sensory neurons from the antenna and labial pit organ.

To quantify the projections of sensory neurons, the number of labeled axons and terminals was counted in each neuropil. The counts were made from z-stacks of optical sections, and the data were analyzed using GraphPad Prism software. Statistical analysis was performed using one-way ANOVA or t-test, and the results were considered significant at p < 0.05.

The nomenclature used to describe the neuropils and neurons in the central nervous system of Mythimna separata follows that established for other lepidopterans. The antennal lobe is divided into glomeruli, each receiving input from specific sensory neurons. The gnathal ganglion and prothoracic ganglion are part of the ventral nerve cord and contain neurons involved in feeding and locomotion. The antennal mechanosensory and motor center is a distinct neuropil that receives input from mechanosensory neurons and sends output to motor neurons. The specific staining experiments and three-dimensional reconstructions allowed us to determine the precise projections of sensory neurons from the antenna and labial pit organ to these neuropils.

The central projections of antennal and labial palp sensory neurons in the migratory armyworm Mythimna separata were investigated using a combination of neuroanatomical techniques, including backfills, confocal microscopy, and three-dimensional reconstructions. The labial sensory neurons were found to project via the ipsilateral labial nerve and terminate in three main areas of the central nervous system: the labial-palp pit organ glomerulus of each antennal lobe, the gnathal ganglion, and the prothoracic ganglion of the ventral nerve cord. These findings are consistent with previous studies and provide further evidence for the importance of the labial pit organ in insect sensory perception.

The antennal sensory axons were also found to project to multiple areas of the central nervous system. The ipsilateral antennal nerve targets mainly the antennal lobe, the antennal mechanosensory and motor center, and the prothoracic and mesothoracic ganglia. To further investigate the specific projections of antennal sensory neurons, dye application was used to stain each of the three antennal segments (flagellum, pedicle, and scape) separately. The results of these experiments indicate that the antennal lobe receives input from flagellar olfactory neurons exclusively. In contrast, the antennal mechanosensory and motor center is innervated by mechanosensory neurons from the whole antenna, comprising the flagellum, pedicle, and scape.

The terminals in the mechanosensory and motor center were found to be organized in segregated zones relating to the origin of neurons. The flagellar mechanosensory axons target anterior zones, while the pedicular and scapal axons terminate in posterior zones. This organization suggests a high degree of specificity in the processing of mechanosensory information from different parts of the antenna. The segregation of terminals from different antennal segments may allow for the integration of information from multiple sensory modalities, including olfaction, mechanosensation, and potentially other senses.

In the ventral nerve cord, the processes from the antennal sensory neurons terminate in the motor area of the thoracic ganglia, suggesting a close connection with motor neurons. This finding is consistent with the idea that sensory information from the antenna plays a crucial role in guiding insect behavior, including locomotion and flight. The termination of antennal sensory axons in the motor area of the thoracic ganglia may allow for the rapid transmission of sensory information to motor neurons, enabling the insect to respond quickly to changes in its environment.

The central projections of labial palp sensory neurons were also investigated in detail. The axons of these neurons were found to project to the labial-palp pit organ glomerulus of each antennal lobe, as well as to the gnathal ganglion and the prothoracic ganglion of the ventral nerve cord. The labial-palp pit organ glomerulus is a specialized region of the antennal lobe that is thought to be involved in the processing of olfactory information from the labial pit organ. The projection of labial palp sensory neurons to this region suggests that the labial pit organ plays a role in the detection of olfactory cues, potentially including pheromones and other volatile chemicals.

The gnathal ganglion is a region of the central nervous system that is involved in the control of feeding and other mouthpart-related behaviors. The projection of labial palp sensory neurons to the gnathal ganglion suggests that the labial pit organ may also play a role in the regulation of these behaviors. The termination of labial palp sensory axons in the prothoracic ganglion of the ventral nerve cord may allow for the integration of sensory information from the labial pit organ with information from other sensory modalities, including mechanosensation and vision.

Overall, the results of this study provide new insights into the central projections of antennal and labial palp sensory neurons in the migratory armyworm Mythimna separata. The numerous neuropils innervated by axons from both the antenna and labial palp indicate the multiple roles these sensory organs serve in insect behavior. The specific projections of antennal sensory neurons to different regions of the central nervous system, including the antennal lobe, mechanosensory and motor center, and thoracic ganglia, suggest a high degree of specificity in the processing of sensory information from different parts of the antenna. Similarly, the central projections of labial palp sensory neurons to the labial-palp pit organ glomerulus, gnathal ganglion, and prothoracic ganglion provide evidence for the importance of the labial pit organ in insect sensory perception and behavior.

In clinical trials, the ability to stop a study early, either due to demonstrated efficacy or futility, is a crucial aspect of efficient and ethical research. This is particularly important when the planning assumptions required for power calculation are based on limited evidence, which can lead to a high risk of an underpowered or overpowered study. One such scenario is when a trial includes two primary endpoints in the confirmatory analysis, where the power of the trial depends on the effects of both endpoints and their correlation. Assessing the feasibility of such a trial can be challenging, as the number of parameters that need to be correctly specified is large, and small deviations from these assumptions can have significant consequences on the trial's performance.

Group sequential designs have become a popular approach in this setting, allowing for interim analyses to be performed at predefined points during the trial. These designs enable the trial to be stopped early if the interim results show a statistically significant treatment effect, thereby saving time, resources, and exposing fewer patients to an ineffective or even harmful treatment. Additionally, group sequential designs can also be used to stop a trial early for futility, which is the case when the interim results suggest that the treatment is unlikely to show a statistically significant effect, even if the trial were to continue to its planned end.

While the choice of adequate boundaries to stop a trial early for efficacy has been extensively discussed in the literature, the selection of optimal futility boundaries has received relatively little attention. However, this aspect is crucial, as poorly chosen futility boundaries can have serious consequences on the trial's performance characteristics, such as power, type I error rate, and expected sample size. For instance, if the futility boundary is set too conservatively, the trial may continue unnecessarily, wasting resources and putting more patients at risk. On the other hand, if the futility boundary is set too liberally, the trial may be stopped prematurely, potentially missing a true treatment effect.

The problem of choosing optimal futility boundaries is further complicated when dealing with multiple primary endpoints. In this case, the trial's power depends on the effects of both endpoints and their correlation, making it even more challenging to determine the optimal futility boundaries. The intersection-union test (IUT) is a commonly used approach for testing multiple endpoints, which controls the family-wise error rate (FWER) by testing each endpoint separately and then combining the results. However, the IUT requires a high level of evidence for each endpoint, which can lead to a low power for the overall test, especially when the endpoints are correlated.

In recent years, several group sequential designs for multiple endpoints have been proposed, including the repeated significance test, the repeated confidence interval approach, and the alpha-spending function approach. However, these methods typically focus on stopping for efficacy, and the choice of futility boundaries is often not explicitly addressed. As a result, practitioners often rely on ad-hoc methods or rules of thumb to determine the futility boundaries, which can lead to suboptimal performance characteristics.

The aim of this work is to propose a general method for constructing optimal futility boundaries for group sequential designs with two primary endpoints. Our approach is based on predefined criteria, such as maximizing the probability of correctly stopping for futility while limiting the power loss and the probability of stopping the study wrongly. We will also present three different group sequential designs for two endpoints, applying these optimal futility boundaries, and illustrate our methods using a real clinical trial example and Monte-Carlo simulations. By providing a systematic approach to choosing futility boundaries, we hope to contribute to the development of more efficient and effective clinical trials, especially in situations where the planning assumptions are uncertain or based on limited evidence.

The performance of these designs will be evaluated using Monte-Carlo simulations, and the results will be illustrated using a real clinical trial example. Finally, we will discuss the implications of our findings and provide recommendations for practitioners.

The construction of optimal futility boundaries for group sequential designs with two endpoints requires a careful consideration of the trade-off between the probability of stopping the trial early in case of small or opposite effects and the potential loss of power. In this work, we propose a general method to derive such boundaries according to predefined criteria. Our approach is based on the intersection-union test principle, which is commonly used in clinical trials with multiple endpoints.

First, we define the test statistics for the two endpoints, denoted as $T_1$ and $T_2$, and their corresponding critical boundaries, $c_1$ and $c_2$. The critical boundaries are chosen such that the overall type I error rate is controlled at a predetermined level, typically 5%. The test statistics $T_1$ and $T_2$ are assumed to be normally distributed with means $\mu_1$ and $\mu_2$, and standard deviations $\sigma_1$ and $\sigma_2$, respectively. The correlation between $T_1$ and $T_2$ is denoted as $\rho$.

To construct the futility boundaries, we consider the following criteria: (1) the probability of stopping the trial early in case of small or opposite effects, denoted as $P_{stop}$, should be maximized; (2) the power loss, denoted as $P_{loss}$, should be minimized; and (3) the probability of stopping the study "wrongly", denoted as $P_{wrong}$, should be limited. The probability $P_{stop}$ is defined as the probability of stopping the trial at an interim analysis given that the true effects are small or opposite. The power loss $P_{loss}$ is defined as the difference between the power of the trial without futility stopping and the power of the trial with futility stopping. The probability $P_{wrong}$ is defined as the probability of stopping the trial at an interim analysis given that the true effects are large and in the same direction.

We propose to derive the futility boundaries by solving the following optimization problem:

$$
\max_{b_1, b_2} P_{stop}(\mu_1, \mu_2, \rho, b_1, b_2)
$$

subject to

$$
P_{loss}(\mu_1, \mu_2, \rho, b_1, b_2) \leq \alpha_1
$$

$$
P_{wrong}(\mu_1, \mu_2, \rho, b_1, b_2) \leq \alpha_2
$$

where $b_1$ and $b_2$ are the futility boundaries for the two endpoints, and $\alpha_1$ and $\alpha_2$ are predefined constants that control the power loss and the probability of stopping the study "wrongly".

To solve this optimization problem, we use a Monte-Carlo simulation approach. We simulate a large number of clinical trials with different true effects, correlations, and sample sizes. For each simulated trial, we calculate the test statistics $T_1$ and $T_2$ and determine whether the trial would be stopped at an interim analysis using the futility boundaries $b_1$ and $b_2$. We then estimate the probabilities $P_{stop}$, $P_{loss}$, and $P_{wrong}$ using the simulated data.

For each design, we derive the optimal futility boundaries using the proposed method and evaluate their performance using Monte-Carlo simulations. We also compare the performance of the optimal futility boundaries with that of commonly used futility boundaries, such as the "0.5 SD" rule, which stops the trial if the test statistic is less than 0.5 standard deviations away from zero.

Our results show that the optimal futility boundaries derived using the proposed method outperform the commonly used futility boundaries in terms of maximizing the probability of stopping the trial early in case of small or opposite effects while limiting the power loss and the probability of stopping the study "wrongly". We also demonstrate the importance of considering the correlation between the two endpoints when constructing the futility boundaries. Ignoring the correlation can lead to suboptimal futility boundaries that result in a lower probability of stopping the trial early in case of small or opposite effects and a higher power loss.

In addition to the Monte-Carlo simulations, we illustrate the application of the proposed method using a real clinical trial example. We consider a trial with two primary endpoints, where the planning assumptions are based on a low level of evidence. We derive the optimal futility boundaries using the proposed method and evaluate their performance using Monte-Carlo simulations. Our results demonstrate the benefit of using the optimal futility boundaries in this trial, which can lead to a significant reduction in the expected sample size and trial duration while maintaining the power and controlling the type I error rate.

The method takes into account the correlation between the two endpoints and the trade-off between the probability of stopping the trial early in case of small or opposite effects and the potential loss of power. The increasing anthropogenic release of reactive nitrogen (Nr) to the environment has significant implications for human and ecosystem health. The global nitrogen cycle has been substantially altered by human activities, with the production and use of fertilizers, burning of fossil fuels, and cultivation of legumes being major contributors to the increasing levels of reactive nitrogen in the environment. One of the key challenges in addressing the issue of excessive reactive nitrogen is the complexity of the nitrogen cycle. Nitrogen exists in many different forms, including nitrogen gas (N2), ammonia (NH3), nitrate (NO3-), and nitrous oxide (N2O), each with its own unique characteristics and effects on the environment. Additionally, nitrogen can be transported and transformed through various pathways, including atmospheric deposition, leaching, and runoff, making it difficult to track and manage. To better understand and manage the nitrogen cycle, it is essential to develop metrics and tools that can quantify and connect human activities with nitrogen losses.

The concept of a nitrogen footprint has emerged as a novel metric to quantify the amount of reactive nitrogen released to the environment as a result of human activities. The nitrogen footprint is a consumer-based perspective that connects lifestyle choices with nitrogen losses, providing a unique opportunity for individuals and societies to understand and manage their impact on the nitrogen cycle. The nitrogen footprint is calculated using the N-Calculator model, which takes into account the amount of nitrogen embedded in food and energy consumption, as well as other factors such as waste management and transportation. By quantifying the nitrogen footprint, individuals and societies can identify areas where they can reduce their nitrogen losses and make more informed choices about their lifestyle and consumption patterns.

To assess the nitrogen footprint of Australia, we utilized the N-Calculator model, a well-established framework for estimating anthropogenic nitrogen losses at the individual or national level. The N-Calculator is based on a bottom-up approach, where nitrogen inputs and losses are calculated from various sources, including food and energy consumption. We obtained data on Australian food consumption patterns from the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) and the Australian Health Survey (AHS), which provided information on the average consumption of different food items, including meat, dairy products, fruits, and vegetables.

This study utilized data from the 2015 National Survey of Multicultural Families, a nationwide survey conducted by the Korean Ministry of Gender Equality and Family. The survey aimed to gather information on the socioeconomic and health status of multicultural families in South Korea. A total of 15,231 married immigrants were included in the analysis. The survey employed a stratified sampling design, with sampling frames constructed from the national registry of foreign-born spouses and their families. Trained interviewers conducted face-to-face interviews using a structured questionnaire.

The dependent variables of interest were self-reported depression and self-rated health (SRH). Self-reported depression was measured using a single question that asked respondents if they had experienced depressive symptoms in the past year. The response options were "yes" or "no". SRH was assessed using a single question that asked respondents to rate their current health on a 5-point scale, ranging from "very good" to "very poor". For the purpose of this analysis, SRH was dichotomized into "poor/very poor" and "good/very good/fair".

The main independent variable of interest was household income, which was categorized into quartiles. The lowest quartile represented the poorest 25% of the sample, while the highest quartile represented the richest 25%. Other independent variables included sociodemographic characteristics such as age, sex, duration of residence in South Korea, country of origin, education level, employment status, and subjective social status. Subjective social status was measured using a 10-point ladder, where respondents were asked to place themselves on the ladder based on their perceived social status.

To measure the extent of income-related inequalities in self-reported depression and SRH, we calculated the Erreygers concentration index. The concentration index is a measure of health inequality that takes into account the distribution of health outcomes across different socioeconomic groups. It ranges from -1 to 1, where a negative value indicates a pro-poor inequality (i.e., the health outcome is more prevalent among the poor) and a positive value indicates a pro-rich inequality (i.e., the health outcome is more prevalent among the rich). A value of 0 indicates no inequality.

To decompose the income-related inequalities in self-reported depression and SRH, we used a regression-based decomposition approach. This approach involves estimating a regression model that includes the independent variables of interest and then calculating the contribution of each variable to the overall inequality. The decomposition was performed using the method proposed by Wagstaff and colleagues, which involves estimating a linear regression model of the health outcome on the independent variables and then using the coefficients from this model to calculate the contribution of each variable to the overall inequality.

All analyses were weighted to account for the complex sampling design of the survey. The weights were constructed using the survey's sampling frame and were designed to reflect the probability of selection for each respondent. Statistical analyses were performed using Stata version 15.1, with statistical significance set at p < 0.05.

Phytophthora root and stem rot of soybean, caused by the oomycete pathogen Phytophthora sojae, is a devastating disease that affects soybean production worldwide. The disease can lead to significant yield losses, and its management is a major challenge for soybean breeders and farmers. Phytophthora sojae is a hemibiotrophic pathogen that infects soybean plants through the roots, causing root rot, and can also infect the stems, leading to stem rot and plant death. The disease is favored by wet conditions, and its severity is increased by factors such as high temperatures, excessive moisture, and poor soil drainage.

Soybean is one of the most important legume crops, providing a significant source of protein and oil for human consumption and animal feed. The crop is also a valuable source of bioactive compounds, including isoflavones, which have been shown to have various health benefits. However, the susceptibility of soybean to Phytophthora root and stem rot limits its production and affects its quality. Breeding for resistance to the disease is a viable approach, but it is a complex and time-consuming process. Understanding the molecular mechanisms underlying the soybean response to P. sojae infection is essential for the development of effective strategies to control the disease.

Phenylalanine ammonia-lyase (PAL) is a key enzyme in the phenylpropanoid pathway, which plays a crucial role in plant defense against pathogens. PAL catalyzes the conversion of phenylalanine to trans-cinnamic acid, which is a precursor for the synthesis of various phenolic compounds, including lignin, flavonoids, and isoflavones. These compounds have been shown to have antimicrobial properties and play a role in plant defense against pathogens. PAL is also involved in the synthesis of salicylic acid (SA), a key phytohormone that regulates plant defense responses. The PAL gene family is composed of multiple members, which are differentially expressed in response to various biotic and abiotic stresses.

In recent years, significant progress has been made in understanding the role of PAL in plant defense against pathogens. Studies have shown that PAL is induced in response to pathogen infection and that its overexpression can enhance plant resistance to diseases. However, the molecular mechanism of PAL in soybean in response to P. sojae is not well understood. Several studies have identified PAL genes in soybean, but their functions and regulation in response to P. sojae infection are largely unknown. The identification of novel PAL genes and the characterization of their functions in soybean will provide new insights into the molecular mechanisms underlying the soybean response to P. sojae infection.

The phenylpropanoid pathway is also involved in the synthesis of glyceollins, which are a group of pterocarpan phytoalexins that have been shown to have antimicrobial properties. Glyceollins are synthesized in response to pathogen infection and have been implicated in the defense of soybean against P. sojae. The synthesis of glyceollins is regulated by the PAL gene, and its overexpression can enhance the accumulation of glyceollins in soybean. However, the regulation of glyceollin synthesis in response to P. sojae infection is complex and involves multiple genes and pathways.

Isoflavones, including daidzein and genistein, are also important compounds in soybean that have been shown to have antimicrobial properties. These compounds are synthesized through the phenylpropanoid pathway and have been implicated in the defense of soybean against P. sojae. The synthesis of isoflavones is regulated by the PAL gene, and its overexpression can enhance the accumulation of isoflavones in soybean. However, the regulation of isoflavone synthesis in response to P. sojae infection is not well understood and requires further study.

Salicylic acid (SA) is a key phytohormone that regulates plant defense responses against pathogens. SA is synthesized through the phenylpropanoid pathway and has been shown to play a crucial role in the defense of soybean against P. sojae. The synthesis of SA is regulated by the PAL gene, and its overexpression can enhance the accumulation of SA in soybean. However, the regulation of SA synthesis in response to P. sojae infection is complex and involves multiple genes and pathways.

In this study, we characterize a novel member of the soybean PAL gene family, GmPAL2.1, which is significantly induced by P. sojae. We use overexpression and RNA interference analysis to demonstrate the role of GmPAL2.1 in soybean resistance to P. sojae. Our results show that GmPAL2.1 enhances resistance to P. sojae in transgenic soybean plants and that its overexpression leads to an increase in PAL activity, glyceollin, daidzein, genistein, and SA levels. These findings suggest that GmPAL2.1 plays a crucial role in the soybean response to P. sojae infection and provide new insights into the molecular mechanisms underlying this response.

To investigate the role of GmPAL2.1 in the soybean response to Phytophthora sojae infection, we employed a combination of molecular biology, biochemical, and physiological techniques. The soybean cultivar Williams 82 was used as the wild-type control in this study. Seeds were surface-sterilized with 10% bleach for 10 minutes, rinsed with distilled water, and germinated on moistened filter paper in a growth chamber at 25°C with a 16-hour photoperiod.

For Phytophthora sojae infection assays, the P. sojae isolate PSR-6 was used. The pathogen was cultured on V8 juice agar plates at 25°C in the dark. Zoospores were harvested from 7-day-old cultures and resuspended in sterile water to a concentration of 1 × 10^4 zoospores per milliliter. For root inoculation, 7-day-old soybean seedlings were inoculated with 1 mL of the zoospore suspension, while for stem inoculation, 14-day-old soybean seedlings were inoculated with 1 mL of the zoospore suspension. Inoculated plants were maintained in a growth chamber at 25°C with a 16-hour photoperiod and high humidity.

To clone the GmPAL2.1 gene, total RNA was extracted from soybean roots 24 hours after P. sojae inoculation using the Trizol reagent (Invitrogen). First-strand cDNA synthesis was performed using the SuperScript III reverse transcriptase (Invitrogen) and an oligo(dT) primer. The GmPAL2.1 cDNA was amplified by PCR using gene-specific primers designed based on the published soybean genome sequence. The PCR product was cloned into the pMD18-T vector (Takara) and sequenced.

For overexpression and RNA interference (RNAi) analysis, the GmPAL2.1 cDNA was cloned into the pCAMBIA1301 vector (CAMBIA) under the control of the cauliflower mosaic virus 35S promoter. The resulting construct, GmPAL2.1-OX, was transformed into Agrobacterium tumefaciens strain EHA105. For RNAi, a 300-bp fragment of the GmPAL2.1 cDNA was cloned into the pCAMBIA1301 vector in the sense and antisense orientations, separated by a spacer sequence. The resulting construct, GmPAL2.1-RNAi, was also transformed into A. tumefaciens strain EHA105.

Soybean transformation was performed using the Agrobacterium-mediated cotyledonary node method. Transgenic soybean plants were selected on MS medium containing 50 mg/L hygromycin and confirmed by PCR and Southern blot analysis. T2 or T3 transgenic soybean plants were used for further analysis.

To analyze the expression of GmPAL2.1 in response to P. sojae infection, total RNA was extracted from soybean roots and stems at various time points after inoculation. First-strand cDNA synthesis and quantitative real-time PCR (qRT-PCR) were performed using the SYBR Green Master Mix (Applied Biosystems) and gene-specific primers. The soybean actin gene was used as an internal control.

PAL activity was measured using a spectrophotometric assay. Briefly, 0.5 g of soybean tissue was homogenized in 1 mL of extraction buffer (100 mM Tris-HCl, pH 8.0, 1 mM EDTA, 1 mM phenylmethylsulfonyl fluoride) and centrifuged at 12,000 × g for 10 minutes. The supernatant was desalted using a Sephadex G-25 column and used for PAL activity measurement. The reaction mixture contained 100 mM Tris-HCl (pH 8.0), 1 mM L-phenylalanine, and 100 μL of the enzyme extract. The reaction was incubated at 30°C for 30 minutes, and the absorbance at 290 nm was measured using a spectrophotometer.

To analyze the levels of daidzein, genistein, and salicylic acid (SA), soybean tissues were extracted with methanol and analyzed by high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) using a C18 column and a UV detector. The mobile phase consisted of 0.1% trifluoroacetic acid in water and acetonitrile. The levels of glyceollins were analyzed by HPLC using a C18 column and a UV detector. The mobile phase consisted of 0.1% trifluoroacetic acid in water and methanol.

Statistical analysis was performed using the SPSS software. Data were analyzed by one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) followed by the Duncan's multiple range test. Significant differences were determined at P < 0.05. All experiments were performed with at least three biological replicates, and the data are presented as the mean ± standard deviation.

To investigate the role of GmPAL2.1 in soybean response to Phytophthora sojae infection, we first examined the expression pattern of GmPAL2.1 in soybean plants after P. sojae inoculation. Quantitative real-time PCR (qRT-PCR) analysis showed that GmPAL2.1 transcripts were significantly induced by P. sojae, with a peak at 12 hours post-inoculation (hpi) (Figure 1A). This result suggests that GmPAL2.1 is involved in the early response of soybean to P. sojae infection.

To further explore the function of GmPAL2.1, we generated transgenic soybean plants overexpressing GmPAL2.1 (GmPAL2.1-OX) and RNA interference (RNAi) plants with reduced GmPAL2.1 expression (GmPAL2.1-RNAi). The expression levels of GmPAL2.1 in these transgenic plants were confirmed by qRT-PCR (Figure 1B). We then inoculated these transgenic plants with P. sojae and evaluated their resistance to the pathogen. The results showed that GmPAL2.1-OX plants exhibited enhanced resistance to P. sojae, as indicated by reduced disease severity and lesion size compared to non-transgenic plants (Figure 2A and 2B). In contrast, GmPAL2.1-RNAi plants displayed increased susceptibility to P. sojae, with more severe disease symptoms and larger lesions (Figure 2A and 2B).

We also investigated the PAL activity in these transgenic plants after P. sojae infection. The results showed that PAL activity in GmPAL2.1-OX plants was significantly higher than that in non-transgenic plants at 12, 24, and 48 hpi (Figure 3A). In contrast, PAL activity in GmPAL2.1-RNAi plants was lower than that in non-transgenic plants at these time points (Figure 3A). These results suggest that GmPAL2.1 plays a crucial role in regulating PAL activity in response to P. sojae infection.

To understand the potential mechanisms underlying the enhanced resistance of GmPAL2.1-OX plants, we analyzed the levels of several phytoalexins and signaling molecules in these plants after P. sojae infection. The results showed that the levels of daidzein, genistein, and salicylic acid (SA) were significantly increased in GmPAL2.1-OX plants compared to non-transgenic plants at 12, 24, and 48 hpi (Figure 4A, 4B, and 4C). Additionally, the relative content of glyceollins, a type of phytoalexin, was also markedly increased in GmPAL2.1-OX plants (Figure 4D). These results suggest that GmPAL2.1 may enhance resistance to P. sojae by regulating the production of these defense-related compounds.

We also examined the expression of several defense-related genes in GmPAL2.1-OX and GmPAL2.1-RNAi plants after P. sojae infection. The results showed that the expression of genes involved in the phenylpropanoid pathway, such as GmC4H and Gm4CL, was upregulated in GmPAL2.1-OX plants (Figure 5A and 5B). In contrast, the expression of these genes was downregulated in GmPAL2.1-RNAi plants (Figure 5A and 5B). These results suggest that GmPAL2.1 may regulate the expression of these defense-related genes, which in turn contributes to the enhanced resistance of GmPAL2.1-OX plants.

To further confirm the role of GmPAL2.1 in regulating the production of defense-related compounds, we analyzed the levels of daidzein, genistein, and SA in GmPAL2.1-RNAi plants after P. sojae infection. The results showed that the levels of these compounds were significantly reduced in GmPAL2.1-RNAi plants compared to non-transgenic plants (Figure 6A, 6B, and 6C). Additionally, the relative content of glyceollins was also decreased in GmPAL2.1-RNAi plants (Figure 6D). These results suggest that GmPAL2.1 is required for the production of these defense-related compounds in response to P. sojae infection.

Overall, our results suggest that GmPAL2.1 plays a crucial role in regulating the soybean response to P. sojae infection. The enhanced resistance of GmPAL2.1-OX plants and the increased susceptibility of GmPAL2.1-RNAi plants demonstrate that GmPAL2.1 functions as a positive regulator of defense against P. sojae. The increased levels of daidzein, genistein, SA, and glyceollins in GmPAL2.1-OX plants suggest that GmPAL2.1 may regulate the production of these defense-related compounds, which in turn contributes to the enhanced resistance of these plants. Further studies are needed to fully elucidate the molecular mechanisms underlying the function of GmPAL2.1 in soybean defense against P. sojae.

The change-of-base semantics presented herein provides a powerful tool for the analysis and design of modal type theories, and its potential applications in computer science and related fields are substantial [17]. As research in this area continues to unfold, our work will serve as a foundation for future explorations, guiding the development of more sophisticated and expressive models of computation [18].

Prostate cancer is one of the most common malignancies affecting men worldwide, with a significant impact on public health. The development and progression of prostate cancer involve a complex interplay of genetic, environmental, and lifestyle factors. Despite advances in early detection and treatment, prostate cancer remains a leading cause of cancer-related deaths in men. Therefore, identifying novel biomarkers and understanding the molecular mechanisms underlying the development and progression of prostate cancer are crucial for improving diagnosis, treatment, and prognosis.

The RhoA and ROCK1 genes play a critical role in the regulation of cell proliferation, migration, and invasion, which are key processes involved in cancer development and progression. The RhoA/ROCK1 pathway is a signaling cascade that regulates the actin cytoskeleton, cell adhesion, and motility. Activation of the RhoA/ROCK1 pathway has been implicated in the development and progression of various types of cancer, including prostate cancer. RhoA is a small GTPase that activates ROCK1, a serine/threonine kinase, which in turn regulates downstream effectors involved in cell migration, invasion, and proliferation. Aberrant activation of the RhoA/ROCK1 pathway has been shown to contribute to cancer cell metastasis, angiogenesis, and resistance to apoptosis.

Genetic variants in the RhoA and ROCK1 genes may affect the function and activity of the RhoA/ROCK1 pathway, potentially influencing an individual's susceptibility to prostate cancer. Genetic variants, such as single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs), can alter gene expression, protein function, and signaling pathway activity. These genetic variations can be used as biomarkers to predict disease risk, progression, and response to treatment. Several studies have investigated the association between genetic variants in other genes and prostate cancer risk, but the role of RhoA and ROCK1 genetic variants in prostate cancer has not been well studied.

Prostate cancer is a heterogeneous disease, and the clinical outcome can vary significantly among patients. Biochemical recurrence, defined as a rise in prostate-specific antigen (PSA) levels after radical prostatectomy or radiation therapy, is a common indicator of disease recurrence. Clinico-pathological characteristics, such as tumor stage, grade, and PSA levels, are traditionally used to predict disease recurrence and prognosis. However, these factors have limitations, and there is a need for novel biomarkers to improve prognostication and treatment decision-making.

The identification of genetic variants associated with prostate cancer risk and progression can provide valuable insights into the molecular mechanisms underlying the disease. These genetic variants can be used to develop novel biomarkers for early detection, prognosis, and treatment monitoring. Furthermore, understanding the genetic basis of prostate cancer can help identify potential therapeutic targets and develop personalized treatment strategies. In this study, we investigated the association between genetic variants in the RhoA and ROCK1 genes and the development, progression, and prognosis of prostate cancer. We aimed to clarify the role of these genetic variants in prostate cancer and explore their potential as novel biomarkers for clinical treatment decision-making.

The RhoA and ROCK1 genes are attractive candidates for investigation, given their critical role in regulating cell proliferation, migration, and invasion. Previous studies have shown that aberrant activation of the RhoA/ROCK1 pathway contributes to cancer development and progression. However, the specific genetic variants in the RhoA and ROCK1 genes that contribute to prostate cancer risk and progression are not well understood. In this study, we genotyped six potentially functional genetic variants in the RhoA and ROCK1 genes and investigated their association with prostate cancer risk, progression, and prognosis. Our study provides new insights into the role of genetic variants in the RhoA and ROCK1 genes in prostate cancer and highlights the potential of these variants as novel biomarkers for clinical treatment decision-making.

This case-control study was conducted to investigate the association between genetic variants in the RhoA and ROCK1 genes and the development, progression, and prognosis of prostate cancer. The study population consisted of 1699 subjects, including 849 prostate cancer patients and 850 healthy controls. The patients were recruited from the urology department of a tertiary care hospital, while the controls were selected from a pool of healthy individuals who underwent routine health check-ups at the same hospital. The inclusion criteria for the patients included a confirmed diagnosis of prostate cancer, while the controls were required to have no history of cancer. The study was approved by the institutional review board, and all participants provided written informed consent.

The patients' clinical and pathological data, including age, prostate-specific antigen (PSA) levels, Gleason score, tumor stage, and nodal status, were collected from their medical records. The biochemical recurrence (BCR) status was also determined, which was defined as two consecutive PSA measurements of 0.2 ng/mL or higher after radical prostatectomy. The follow-up period for the patients ranged from 12 to 60 months, with a median follow-up time of 36 months.

Genomic DNA was extracted from peripheral blood samples using a commercial DNA extraction kit (Qiagen, Hilden, Germany). The DNA samples were then genotyped for six potentially functional genetic variants in the RhoA and ROCK1 genes, which were selected based on their potential functional significance and minor allele frequencies. The variants included rs2410, rs2269736, rs3599, rs3902981, rs6849, and rs10848464. The genotyping was performed using a TaqMan genotyping assay (Applied Biosystems, Foster City, CA, USA) on an ABI 7900HT real-time PCR system.

The genotype and allele frequencies were calculated and compared between the cases and controls using the chi-squared test and Fisher's exact test. The odds ratios (ORs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated to determine the association between the genetic variants and the risk of prostate cancer. The genotype-phenotype correlation analysis was performed to examine the association between the genetic variants and clinico-pathological characteristics, including PSA levels, Gleason score, tumor stage, and nodal status.

To evaluate the prognostic significance of the genetic variants, the Kaplan-Meier method was used to estimate the BCR-free survival rates, and the log-rank test was used to compare the survival curves between the different genotype groups. The Cox proportional hazards regression model was used to assess the independent prognostic value of the genetic variants, with adjustment for clinico-pathological characteristics. The Bonferroni correction was applied to account for multiple testing, and a P-value of less than 0.05 was considered statistically significant.

The patients were categorized into three groups based on the number of risk alleles they carried: 0-1 risk allele, 2 risk alleles, and more than 2 risk alleles. The association between the number of risk alleles and the risk of prostate cancer was evaluated using the chi-squared test and Fisher's exact test. The ORs and 95% CIs were calculated to determine the association between the number of risk alleles and the risk of prostate cancer.

To validate the findings, we performed a series of sensitivity analyses, including the exclusion of patients with missing data and the use of different statistical models. We also examined the potential interactions between the genetic variants and clinico-pathological characteristics, including PSA levels, Gleason score, tumor stage, and nodal status. The results of these analyses were consistent with the primary findings, suggesting that the associations between the genetic variants and the risk of prostate cancer were robust and not influenced by potential confounding factors.

In conclusion, this study provides a comprehensive analysis of the association between genetic variants in the RhoA and ROCK1 genes and the development, progression, and prognosis of prostate cancer. The findings suggest that the rs2410 mutant allele and the rs2269736 wild allele are risk factors for prostate cancer, and that individuals carrying more than two risk alleles are exposed to a higher hazard of prostate cancer. The study also demonstrates that the risk of biochemical recurrence may be linked to clinico-pathological characteristics and genetic factors, although the associations between the genetic variants and clinico-pathological characteristics were not significant. The results of this study have important implications for the clinical management of prostate cancer and highlight the potential of genetic variants in the RhoA and ROCK1 genes as novel biomarkers for prostate cancer diagnosis and prognosis.

We conducted a case-control study to investigate the association between genetic variants in RhoA and ROCK1 genes and the development, progression, and prognosis of prostate cancer. The study population consisted of 1699 subjects, including 899 prostate cancer patients and 800 healthy controls. The demographic and clinico-pathological characteristics of the study population are presented in Table 1. The median age of the prostate cancer patients was 65 years (range: 45-85 years), and the median PSA level was 10.2 ng/mL (range: 0.5-100 ng/mL). The majority of the patients had a Gleason score of 7 or higher (63.2%), and 45.1% of the patients had advanced tumor stage (T3/T4).

We genotyped six potentially functional genetic variants in the RhoA and ROCK1 genes, including rs2410, rs2269736, rs10932885, rs37374, rs35996865, and rs10581669. The genotype frequencies of these variants are presented in Table 2. The genotype distribution of all variants was in accordance with the Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium in the control group. We found significant associations between two genetic variants (rs2410 and rs2269736) and the risk of prostate cancer. The rs2410 mutant allele (CT/TT) was associated with an increased risk of prostate cancer (OR = 1.43, 95% CI: 1.12-1.83, P = 0.004), whereas the rs2269736 wild allele (CC) was associated with an increased risk of prostate cancer (OR = 1.27, 95% CI: 1.01-1.59, P = 0.04). The other four variants did not show any significant associations with prostate cancer risk.

We further analyzed the combined effect of the risk alleles on prostate cancer risk. Individuals carrying more than two risk alleles had a significantly increased risk of prostate cancer compared to those carrying zero or one risk allele (OR = 2.15, 95% CI: 1.43-3.23, P < 0.001). The risk of prostate cancer increased with the increasing number of risk alleles, suggesting a dose-response relationship.

To investigate the association between the genetic variants and clinico-pathological characteristics, we compared the genotype frequencies of the variants between different subgroups of prostate cancer patients. However, we did not find any significant associations between the variants and clinico-pathological characteristics such as Gleason score, tumor stage, and PSA level. This suggests that the genetic variants may not be directly related to the aggressiveness or severity of prostate cancer.

We also examined the association between the genetic variants and biochemical recurrence in prostate cancer patients. Biochemical recurrence was defined as a PSA level of 0.2 ng/mL or higher after radical prostatectomy. The median follow-up time was 36 months (range: 12-60 months). We found that the risk of biochemical recurrence was associated with clinico-pathological characteristics such as Gleason score and tumor stage. Patients with a higher Gleason score (≥ 8) had a significantly higher risk of biochemical recurrence compared to those with a lower Gleason score (HR = 2.56, 95% CI: 1.63-4.03, P < 0.001). Similarly, patients with advanced tumor stage (T3/T4) had a significantly higher risk of biochemical recurrence compared to those with early tumor stage (T1/T2) (HR = 1.93, 95% CI: 1.23-3.02, P = 0.004).

However, we did not find any significant associations between the genetic variants and biochemical recurrence. The genotype frequencies of the variants were similar between patients with and without biochemical recurrence. In the Multivariate Cox regression analysis, none of the genetic variants were significant independent prognostic predictors for biochemical recurrence survival after Bonferroni correction. This suggests that the genetic variants may not be directly related to the risk of biochemical recurrence in prostate cancer patients.

In conclusion, our study provides evidence that genetic variants in RhoA and ROCK1 genes are associated with the development and progression of prostate cancer. The rs2410 mutant allele and rs2269736 wild allele were identified as risk factors for prostate cancer, and individuals carrying more than two risk alleles had a significantly increased risk of prostate cancer. Although the genetic variants were not directly related to clinico-pathological characteristics or biochemical recurrence, they may still be useful as novel biomarkers to facilitate clinical treatment decision-making. Further studies are needed to validate our findings and to explore the potential clinical applications of these genetic variants in prostate cancer management.

Cronobacter species are a group of gram-negative, rod-shaped bacteria that have been recognized as important food-borne opportunistic pathogens [1]. These bacteria have been implicated in the cause of severe infections, including necrotizing enterocolitis, sepsis, and meningitis, primarily in neonates and infants [2]. The most notorious species within this genus is Cronobacter sakazakii, which has been associated with outbreaks of neonatal meningitis and has a high mortality rate [3]. However, Cronobacter species are not exclusively pathogenic, and they can be found in a wide range of environments, including foodstuffs, clinical specimens, and environmental samples [4].

The genus Cronobacter was first proposed in 2007, and it currently comprises seven species: C. sakazakii, C. dublinensis, C. malonaticus, C. turicensis, C. universalis, C. condimenti, and C. helveticus [5]. These species can be differentiated based on their genetic and phenotypic characteristics, including their ability to utilize various carbon sources, their fatty acid profiles, and their susceptibility to different antibiotics [6]. The genetic diversity of Cronobacter species has been studied extensively using various molecular typing methods, including multilocus sequence typing (MLST) and pulsed-field gel electrophoresis (PFGE) [7]. These studies have revealed a high level of genetic diversity within the genus, with some species exhibiting a higher degree of diversity than others [8].

Cronobacter species have been isolated from a variety of food products, including powdered infant formula, dairy products, and spices [9]. The presence of these bacteria in food products is a concern, as they can survive in a desiccated state for extended periods and can grow rapidly in the presence of moisture [10]. The ability of Cronobacter species to form biofilms on surfaces has also been recognized as an important factor in their persistence in food processing environments [11]. Biofilms are complex communities of microorganisms that adhere to surfaces and are embedded in a matrix of extracellular polymeric substances [12]. The formation of biofilms by Cronobacter species can make them more resistant to cleaning and disinfection, and can also provide a protective environment for the bacteria to grow and survive [13].

The antimicrobial susceptibility of Cronobacter species has also been studied, and it has been shown that these bacteria can exhibit resistance to a range of antibiotics [14]. The development of antibiotic resistance in Cronobacter species is a concern, as it can limit the treatment options available for infections caused by these bacteria [15]. The use of antibiotics in food animal production has been implicated as a factor in the development of antibiotic resistance in Cronobacter species, and the overuse of antibiotics in human medicine has also been recognized as a contributing factor [16].

In recent years, there has been an increasing interest in the study of Cronobacter species in spices and cereals, as these products have been recognized as potential sources of contamination [17]. Spices and cereals are often imported from countries with limited regulatory oversight, and they can be contaminated with Cronobacter species during processing and storage [18]. The contamination of spices and cereals with Cronobacter species can have significant implications for public health, as these products are often consumed raw or are used as ingredients in a variety of food products [19].

In China, the study of Cronobacter species in spices and cereals has been limited, and there is a need for more research in this area [20]. The aim of this study was to investigate the genetic diversity, antimicrobial susceptibility, and biofilm formation of Cronobacter isolates recovered from spices and cereals in China. A total of 40 Cronobacter isolates were recovered from spices and cereals during 2014-2015, and these isolates were characterized using a range of molecular typing methods, including MLST and O-antigen serotyping [21]. The antimicrobial susceptibility of the isolates was also determined, and their ability to form biofilms was assessed [22]. The results of this study provide new insights into the genetic diversity and antimicrobial susceptibility of Cronobacter species in spices and cereals, and highlight the need for continued surveillance of these products to improve our understanding of the epidemiology of Cronobacter infections [23].

The study was conducted from 2014 to 2015, and a total of 40 Cronobacter isolates were recovered from spices and cereals in China. The samples were collected from various provinces in China, including Beijing, Shanghai, Guangdong, and Jiangsu [1]. The spices and cereals were purchased from local markets and stored at room temperature until processing. A total of 200 samples, including 100 spice samples and 100 cereal samples, were analyzed for the presence of Cronobacter species.

The isolation and identification of Cronobacter species were performed according to the protocol described by the International Organization for Standardization [2]. Briefly, 25 grams of each sample were added to 225 mL of buffered peptone water and incubated at 37°C for 24 hours. After incubation, the enriched samples were streaked onto Druggan-Forsythe-Iversen (DFI) agar plates and incubated at 37°C for 24 hours [3]. The presumptive Cronobacter colonies were then subcultured onto DFI agar plates and incubated at 37°C for 24 hours. The colonies were identified as Cronobacter species based on their morphology, biochemical reactions, and molecular analysis.

The molecular analysis was performed using the fusA sequencing method, which is a widely used method for the identification of Cronobacter species [4]. The fusA gene was amplified using the primers fusA-F (5'-GGT GGT GAT GGT GAT GGT-3') and fusA-R (5'-CTT TCA GCA CTT TGT TCG-3') [5]. The PCR products were sequenced using the BigDye Terminator v3.1 Cycle Sequencing Kit (Applied Biosystems, USA) and analyzed using the BLAST program [6]. The sequences were compared to the reference sequences in the GenBank database to determine the species of the isolates.

Multilocus sequence typing (MLST) was performed to determine the genetic diversity of the Cronobacter isolates [7]. The MLST scheme for Cronobacter species involves the sequencing of seven housekeeping genes, including atpD, fusA, glnS, gltB, gyrB, infB, and ppsA [8]. The primers used for the MLST scheme were described by Baldwin et al. [9]. The PCR products were sequenced and analyzed as described above. The sequences were compared to the reference sequences in the MLST database to determine the sequence type (ST) of each isolate.

The O-antigen serotyping was performed using the protocol described by Sun et al. [10]. The O-antigen serotyping involves the use of specific antisera to react with the O-antigen of the bacterial cell wall. The antisera were prepared using the method described by Liu et al. [11]. The isolates were reacted with the antisera, and the results were recorded as positive or negative.

The antimicrobial susceptibility testing was performed using the broth microdilution method, as described by the Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute [12]. The isolates were tested against a panel of 16 antibiotics, including ampicillin, ceftriaxone, meropenem, aztreonam, gentamicin, and ciprofloxacin. The minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) of each antibiotic was determined, and the results were interpreted according to the guidelines of the Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute [13].

The biofilm formation assay was performed using the crystal violet staining method, as described by Stepanovic et al. [14]. The isolates were grown in trypticase soy broth (TSB) at 37°C for 24 hours. The cultures were then transferred to a 96-well microtiter plate and incubated at 37°C for 24 hours. The biofilm formation was measured by staining the biofilm with crystal violet and measuring the absorbance at 595 nm using a microplate reader. The results were interpreted as follows: weak biofilm producer (OD595 < 0.1), moderate biofilm producer (0.1 < OD595 < 0.5), strong biofilm producer (OD595 > 0.5), and non-biofilm producer (OD595 = 0) [15].

The data were analyzed using the SPSS software (version 20.0, IBM, USA). The descriptive statistics, including the frequency and percentage, were used to summarize the data. The chi-square test was used to compare the differences between the groups. A p-value of less than 0.05 was considered statistically significant. The MLST data were analyzed using the eBURST software (version 3, Imperial College London, UK) to determine the clonal complexes and the population structure of the Cronobacter isolates [16].

The genetic diversity of the 40 Cronobacter isolates recovered from spices and cereals in China during 2014-2015 was investigated using fusA sequencing analysis [1]. The results showed that the majority (23/40, 57.5%) of the isolates were identified as C. sakazakii, while the remaining strains were identified as C. dublinensis (6/40, 15.0%), C. malonaticus (5/40, 12.5%), C. turicensis (4/40, 10.0%), and C. universalis (2/40, 5.0%) [2]. These findings are consistent with previous studies, which have also reported C. sakazakii as the most prevalent species among Cronobacter isolates [3, 4].

To further investigate the genetic diversity of the Cronobacter isolates, multilocus sequence typing (MLST) analysis was performed [5]. The results produced 30 sequence types (STs) among the 40 Cronobacter isolates, with 5 STs (ST4, ST13, ST50, ST129, and ST158) related to neonatal meningitis [6]. The pattern of the overall ST distribution was diverse, with no single ST dominating the population. However, it was revealed that ST148 was the predominant ST, presenting 12.5% within the whole population. This is consistent with previous studies, which have also reported ST148 as a common ST among Cronobacter isolates [7].

MLST also assigned 12 isolates to 7 different clonal complexes (CCs), including CC4, CC13, CC16, CC17, CC72, CC129, and CC143 [8]. These CCs have been previously associated with clinical isolates, suggesting that the Cronobacter isolates recovered from spices and cereals may have the potential to cause disease in humans [9]. The results of O-antigen serotyping indicated that C. sakazakii serotype O1 and O2 were the most two prevalent serotypes, accounting for 40% and 30% of the isolates, respectively [10]. These serotypes have been previously associated with clinical isolates, and their presence in spices and cereals highlights the potential risk of Cronobacter infection from these sources [11].

The antimicrobial susceptibility of the 40 Cronobacter isolates was tested using a range of antibiotics, including ampicillin, ceftriaxone, meropenem, aztreonam, and gentamicin [12]. The results showed that the isolates were susceptible to most of the antibiotics tested, except for ceftriaxone, meropenem, and aztreonam, to which they exhibited resistance [13]. This is consistent with previous studies, which have also reported resistance to these antibiotics among Cronobacter isolates [14]. The emergence of antibiotic-resistant Cronobacter isolates is a concern, as it may limit the treatment options for Cronobacter infections [15].

The ability of the Cronobacter isolates to form biofilms was also investigated [16]. The results showed that 13 (32.5%) of the isolates were assessed as weak biofilm producers, one (2.5%) was a moderate biofilm producer, and one (2.5%) was a strong biofilm producer, while the others (62.5%) were non-biofilm producers [17]. Biofilm formation is an important virulence factor, as it allows bacteria to persist in environments and evade host immune defenses [18]. The presence of biofilm-producing Cronobacter isolates in spices and cereals highlights the potential risk of Cronobacter infection from these sources [19].

The genetic diversity of the Cronobacter isolates recovered from spices and cereals was further investigated using phylogenetic analysis [20]. The results showed that the isolates were divided into several distinct clades, with some isolates forming tight clusters and others being more distantly related [21]. This suggests that the Cronobacter isolates recovered from spices and cereals are genetically diverse, and that they may have originated from different sources [22]. The presence of clinical isolates, such as the C. sakazakii ST4 neonatal meningitic pathovar, in spices and cereals highlights the potential risk of Cronobacter infection from these sources [23].

In conclusion, the results of this study demonstrate that Cronobacter isolates recovered from spices and cereals in China are genetically diverse, and that they may have the potential to cause disease in humans [24]. The presence of antibiotic-resistant and biofilm-producing isolates highlights the potential risk of Cronobacter infection from these sources [25]. Therefore, the surveillance of Cronobacter spp. in spices and cereals should be strengthened to improve epidemiological understandings of Cronobacter infections [26]. This can be achieved through regular monitoring of Cronobacter isolates in spices and cereals, as well as through the development of effective control measures to prevent the contamination of these products [27]. By taking these steps, we can reduce the risk of Cronobacter infection from spices and cereals, and protect public health [28].

The proliferation of social media has led to an unprecedented amount of user-generated content, which has, in turn, fueled the development of social media mining techniques [1]. A crucial component of these techniques is the ability to analyze and understand the sentiment and subjective nature of text data [2]. Sentiment lexicons, which are collections of words annotated with their sentiment scores, have been widely used for this purpose [3]. However, the construction of these lexicons is a challenging task, as it requires a large amount of annotated data, which can be time-consuming and expensive to obtain [4].

Recent approaches have addressed this challenge by leveraging pre-trained word embeddings, such as Word2Vec [5] and GloVe [6], which capture latent semantic properties of words [7]. These embeddings have been shown to be effective in sentiment analysis tasks, including sentiment lexicon induction [8]. However, the embeddings obtained by optimizing the performance of a given task, such as predicting contextual words, are often sub-optimal for other applications [9]. This is because the embeddings are biased towards the specific task they were trained on, and may not capture the nuances of other semantic properties [10].

To address this limitation, several studies have proposed methods for adapting pre-trained embeddings to specific tasks [11]. One approach is to use embedding sub-space projection, which involves projecting the pre-trained embeddings onto a lower-dimensional space that is specific to the task at hand [12]. This allows for the capture of task-specific representations that are more relevant to the application [13]. However, most existing methods focus on adapting embeddings for a single task, and do not consider the problem of expanding lexicons that describe multiple semantic properties [14].

The intricate relationship between the immune system and cancer has been a subject of extensive research in recent years, with a particular focus on the role of macrophages in tumor growth and progression [1]. Macrophages are a type of white blood cell that play a crucial role in the innate immune response, acting as a first line of defense against pathogens and foreign substances [2]. However, in the context of cancer, macrophages can have a dual role, either promoting or inhibiting tumor growth, depending on their polarization state [3]. In the case of brain tumors, such as gliomas, meningiomas, and medulloblastomas, the role of macrophages is particularly complex, due to the unique characteristics of the brain microenvironment [4].

### Macrophage Polarization and Brain Tumors

Macrophage polarization refers to the process by which macrophages acquire specific functional phenotypes in response to environmental cues [5]. The two main types of macrophage polarization are M1 and M2, which are characterized by distinct gene expression profiles and functional properties [6]. M1 macrophages are typically pro-inflammatory and are involved in the defense against pathogens, while M2 macrophages are anti-inflammatory and are involved in tissue repair and remodeling [7]. In the context of brain tumors, M2 macrophages have been shown to promote tumor growth and progression, by secreting factors that support angiogenesis, cell proliferation, and immune suppression [8]. For example, a study by [9] found that M2 macrophages in glioblastoma tumors expressed high levels of vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF), which is a key regulator of angiogenesis.

### Tumor-Associated Macrophages and the Tumor Microenvironment

Tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) are a type of macrophage that is found in the tumor microenvironment [10]. TAMs are derived from circulating monocytes that are recruited to the tumor site, where they are polarized towards an M2 phenotype [11]. The tumor microenvironment is characterized by hypoxia, inflammation, and immune suppression, which all contribute to the polarization of TAMs towards an M2 phenotype [12]. In brain tumors, TAMs have been shown to play a key role in promoting tumor growth and progression, by regulating the immune response, promoting angiogenesis, and supporting the invasion and metastasis of cancer cells [13]. For example, a study by [14] found that TAMs in meningioma tumors expressed high levels of matrix metalloproteinase-9 (MMP-9), which is a key regulator of tumor invasion and metastasis.

### Regulation of Neoangiogenesis by Tumor-Associated Macrophages

Neoangiogenesis, or the formation of new blood vessels, is a critical step in tumor growth and progression [15]. In brain tumors, neoangiogenesis is regulated by a complex interplay between tumor cells, endothelial cells, and TAMs [16]. TAMs have been shown to promote neoangiogenesis by secreting pro-angiogenic factors, such as VEGF and platelet-derived growth factor (PDGF) [17]. For example, a study by [18] found that TAMs in glioblastoma tumors expressed high levels of VEGF, which was associated with increased angiogenesis and tumor growth. In addition, TAMs have been shown to regulate the expression of anti-angiogenic factors, such as thrombospondin-1 (TSP-1), which can inhibit angiogenesis [19].

### Circulating Tumor Cells and the Role of Macrophages

Circulating tumor cells (CTCs) are cancer cells that have detached from the primary tumor and are circulating in the bloodstream [20]. CTCs are a key indicator of metastatic potential and are associated with poor prognosis in many types of cancer [21]. In brain tumors, CTCs are relatively rare, due to the fact that brain tumors only rarely metastasize [22]. However, the study of CTCs in brain tumors can provide valuable insights into the mechanisms of tumor growth and progression, and can potentially identify new targets for therapy [23]. Macrophages have been shown to play a key role in the entry of CTCs into the bloodstream, by promoting the invasion and intravasation of cancer cells [24]. For example, a study by [25] found that TAMs in glioblastoma tumors expressed high levels of CD163, which is a marker of M2 macrophages, and was associated with increased CTCs in the bloodstream.

### Future Directions and Therapeutic Implications

The study of macrophages in brain tumors has significant implications for the development of new therapeutic strategies [26]. By understanding the role of macrophages in tumor growth and progression, it may be possible to develop new therapies that target the tumor microenvironment and the immune response [27]. For example, therapies that promote the polarization of macrophages towards an M1 phenotype, or that inhibit the function of M2 macrophages, may be effective in inhibiting tumor growth and progression [28]. Additionally, the study of CTCs in brain tumors can provide valuable insights into the mechanisms of metastasis and can potentially identify new targets for therapy [29]. Overall, the study of macrophages in brain tumors is a rapidly evolving field that holds significant promise for the development of new therapeutic strategies.

### Cell Culture and Polarization
We isolated macrophages from the peripheral blood of healthy donors and polarized them into M1 or M2 phenotypes using established protocols [2]. M1 macrophages were induced by stimulation with lipopolysaccharide (LPS) and interferon-γ (IFN-γ), while M2 macrophages were induced by stimulation with interleukin-4 (IL-4) and interleukin-13 (IL-13). We also cultured brain tumor cells, including glioma (U87 and U251), meningioma (IOMM-Lee), and medulloblastoma (Daoy) cell lines, under standard conditions [4].

To examine the interactions between tumor cells and macrophages, we performed co-culture experiments using Transwell inserts [5]. Tumor cells were seeded in the bottom chamber, while macrophages were added to the top chamber. The co-cultures were maintained for 24-48 hours, and the conditioned medium was collected for further analysis. We measured the levels of various cytokines, including tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α), interleukin-1β (IL-1β), and vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF), using enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) kits [6].

We analyzed clinical samples of brain tumors, including gliomas, meningiomas, and medulloblastomas, using immunohistochemistry and immunofluorescence [7]. To characterize the immune cell infiltrate in brain tumors, we performed flow cytometry analysis of single-cell suspensions prepared from clinical samples [10]. We used a mouse model of glioma to study the role of macrophages in tumor growth and progression in vivo [13]. The effects of macrophage depletion or inhibition on tumor growth and progression were evaluated using histological and immunohistochemical analysis [16].

All data were analyzed using GraphPad Prism software, and statistical significance was determined using the Student's t-test or one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) [17]. A p-value of <0.05 was considered statistically significant. Ulcerative colitis (UC) is a chronic inflammatory bowel disease characterized by recurring episodes of intestinal inflammation, which can lead to severe complications such as colorectal cancer and osteoporosis. The exact pathogenesis of UC remains unclear, but it is generally accepted that a combination of genetic predisposition, environmental factors, and an abnormal immune response contributes to the development of the disease. Intestinal epithelial cells play a crucial role in maintaining the integrity of the gut barrier and regulating the immune response to luminal antigens. Disruption of this barrier function and dysregulation of the immune response can lead to the infiltration of inflammatory cells, including neutrophils, into the intestinal mucosa, which is a hallmark of UC.

Neutrophil transmigration is a critical step in the development of intestinal inflammation, as these cells can release a variety of pro-inflammatory mediators, including cytokines and chemokines, which amplify the inflammatory response. The transmigration of neutrophils across the intestinal epithelium is regulated by a complex interplay of adhesion molecules, chemokines, and cytokines. Syndecan-1 (SDC1), a transmembrane heparan sulfate proteoglycan, has been implicated in the regulation of neutrophil transmigration and the development of intestinal inflammation. SDC1 is expressed on the surface of intestinal epithelial cells and can interact with a variety of ligands, including chemokines, cytokines, and extracellular matrix components.

The role of SDC1 in the regulation of inflammatory responses is complex and multifaceted. On the one hand, SDC1 can act as a co-receptor for various growth factors and chemokines, enhancing their binding to their respective receptors and promoting cell signaling. On the other hand, SDC1 can also act as a decoy receptor, binding to pro-inflammatory mediators and preventing them from interacting with their target cells. The ectodomain of SDC1, which carries the heparan sulfate chains, can be shed from the cell surface in response to inflammatory stimuli, releasing soluble SDC1 into the extracellular environment. This shed SDC1 can then interact with other cells and matrix components, influencing the inflammatory response.

The shedding of SDC1 has been implicated in the pathogenesis of various inflammatory diseases, including UC. Elevated levels of soluble SDC1 have been detected in the serum of patients with UC, and this has been correlated with disease activity and severity. However, the exact mechanisms by which SDC1 shedding contributes to the development of intestinal inflammation are not fully understood. It is possible that the shed SDC1 acts as a pro-inflammatory mediator, promoting the recruitment of inflammatory cells to the site of inflammation. Alternatively, the loss of SDC1 from the cell surface may disrupt the normal functioning of the intestinal epithelial barrier, allowing the transmigration of neutrophils and other inflammatory cells.

The NF-κB pathway is a key regulator of inflammatory responses, and its activation is a hallmark of UC. The NF-κB pathway is normally kept in check by the inhibitor of κB (IκB) protein, which binds to the NF-κB transcription factor and prevents its translocation to the nucleus. In response to inflammatory stimuli, IκB is phosphorylated and degraded, allowing NF-κB to translocate to the nucleus and activate the transcription of pro-inflammatory genes. The activation of the NF-κB pathway leads to the production of a variety of pro-inflammatory cytokines, including tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α), interleukin-1 beta (IL-1β), and interleukin-6 (IL-6), which play critical roles in the development of intestinal inflammation.

In addition to the NF-κB pathway, other signaling pathways, including the mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) pathway, have been implicated in the regulation of inflammatory responses in UC. The MAPK pathway is activated in response to inflammatory stimuli and leads to the production of pro-inflammatory cytokines and chemokines. The interaction between the NF-κB and MAPK pathways is complex and involves the activation of various downstream kinases and transcription factors.

Given the complex interplay of molecular mechanisms involved in the development of intestinal inflammation, it is clear that a detailed understanding of the role of SDC1 in this process is essential. The aim of this study is to investigate the impact of cell surface-anchored SDC1 on intestinal inflammation and neutrophil transmigration in UC. By suppressing the shedding of SDC1 from intestinal epithelial cells, we aim to determine whether this can ameliorate the severity of intestinal inflammation and improve the outcome of UC.
