The study was conducted using a combination of in vitro and in vivo experiments. Human intestinal epithelial cells (IECs) were obtained from the American Type Culture Collection (ATCC) and cultured in Dulbecco's modified Eagle's medium (DMEM) supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS), 100 U/mL penicillin, and 100 μg/mL streptomycin. The cells were grown in a humidified incubator at 37°C with 5% CO2.

To establish a model of syndecan-1 (SDC1) shedding suppression, we generated a cleavable resistant SDC1 mutant plasmid using site-directed mutagenesis. The mutant plasmid was designed to prevent the shedding of SDC1 from the cell surface by mutating the cleavage site. The plasmid was then transfected into IECs using Lipofectamine 2000 (Invitrogen) according to the manufacturer's instructions. The transfected cells were selected using G418 (500 μg/mL) and cloned by limiting dilution.

The expression of SDC1 in the transfected cells was confirmed by Western blotting and immunofluorescence microscopy. For Western blotting, the cells were lysed in RIPA buffer and the lysates were separated by SDS-PAGE. The blots were probed with a monoclonal antibody against SDC1 (Abcam) and detected using an enhanced chemiluminescence (ECL) kit (Pierce). For immunofluorescence microscopy, the cells were fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde and stained with a monoclonal antibody against SDC1 (Abcam) and a fluorescent secondary antibody (Invitrogen).

To investigate the role of membrane SDC1 in inflammatory pathways, the transfected cells were stimulated with lipopolysaccharide (LPS) (100 ng/mL) for 24 hours. The cells were then harvested and the expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines, including tumor necrosis factor alpha (TNF-α), interleukin-1 beta (IL-1β), IL-6, and IL-8, was measured by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) (R&D Systems). To investigate the effect of SDC1 shedding suppression on neutrophil transmigration, a transwell assay was used. Neutrophils were isolated from the blood of healthy donors using a neutrophil isolation kit (Miltenyi Biotec) and labeled with a fluorescent dye (Calcein-AM, Invitrogen). The labeled neutrophils were then added to the upper chamber of a transwell plate and the transfected IECs were grown on the lower chamber. The plate was incubated for 2 hours and the number of neutrophils that transmigrated to the lower chamber was measured using a fluorescence microscope.

To investigate the effect of SDC1 shedding suppression on intestinal inflammation in vivo, a mouse model of ulcerative colitis was used. The mice were treated with dextran sulfate sodium (DSS) (3% w/v) in their drinking water for 7 days to induce colitis. The mice were then injected with a plasmid encoding the cleavable resistant SDC1 mutant or a control plasmid via the tail vein. The mice were sacrificed on day 14 and the colon tissue was harvested for histological analysis. The severity of colitis was measured using a disease activity index (DAI) score, which included the assessment of weight loss, stool consistency, and rectal bleeding.

The histological analysis of the colon tissue was performed using hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining. The tissue was fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde and embedded in paraffin. The sections were stained with H&E and the degree of inflammation and tissue damage was scored using a semi-quantitative scoring system. The expression of SDC1 in the colon tissue was also measured by immunohistochemistry using a monoclonal antibody against SDC1 (Abcam).

The serum levels of SDC1 in patients with ulcerative colitis were measured using an ELISA kit (R&D Systems). The patients were recruited from the gastroenterology clinic and the diagnosis of ulcerative colitis was confirmed by endoscopy and histology. The levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines, including TNF-α, IL-1β, and IL-6, were also measured using ELISA kits (R&D Systems).

The data were analyzed using a statistical software package (GraphPad Prism) and the results were expressed as mean ± standard error of the mean (SEM). Matrix factorization has emerged as a powerful tool for recovering missing or corrupted entries in large datasets, with applications spanning collaborative filtering [1], image and video processing [2], and recommender systems [3]. The underlying assumption of matrix factorization is that the data matrix can be approximated as the product of two low-rank matrices, which capture the latent features of the rows and columns. This approximation can be achieved through various techniques, including Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) [4], Non-negative Matrix Factorization (NMF) [5], and Probabilistic Matrix Factorization (PMF) [6]. These methods have been shown to be effective in many scenarios, but they rely on a simple and fixed function, namely the inner product, to model the relationships between the latent features.

Recent advances in deep learning have led to the development of more complex and flexible models, which can learn nonlinear relationships between variables [7]. In particular, neural networks have been successfully applied to a wide range of tasks, including image recognition [8], natural language processing [9], and recommender systems [10]. The key idea behind neural networks is to learn a hierarchical representation of the data, by composing multiple layers of nonlinear transformations. This allows the model to capture complex patterns and relationships in the data, which may not be apparent through traditional matrix factorization techniques.

The idea of combining matrix factorization with neural networks is not new, and several approaches have been proposed in the literature [11, 12]. However, these methods typically use a neural network to learn the latent features, while still relying on the inner product to model the relationships between them. In contrast, our approach, which we call Neural Network Matrix Factorization (NNMF), replaces the inner product with an arbitrary function learned from the data, using a multi-layer feed-forward neural network. This allows the model to capture nonlinear relationships between the latent features, and to adapt to the specific structure of the data.

The NNMF approach can be seen as a generalization of traditional matrix factorization techniques, which can be recovered as special cases by using a linear neural network with a single layer. ### Introduction to Neural Network Matrix Factorization
Neural network matrix factorization (NNMF) is a novel approach to matrix completion, which involves recovering missing or corrupted entries in a matrix by approximating it as the product of two low-rank matrices [1]. Unlike traditional matrix factorization techniques, such as singular value decomposition (SVD) [2] and non-negative matrix factorization (NMF) [3], NNMF replaces the inner product with a multi-layer feed-forward neural network. This allows the model to learn complex, non-linear relationships between the latent feature vectors, enabling more accurate approximations of the original matrix.

### Mathematical Formulation
Given a matrix $M \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times m}$ with missing or corrupted entries, the goal of NNMF is to approximate $M$ as the product of two low-rank matrices, $U \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times k}$ and $V \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times k}$, where $k \ll \min(n, m)$. In traditional matrix factorization, the approximation is obtained by taking the inner product of the latent feature vectors, i.e., $M_{ij} \approx U_i^T V_j$. In contrast, NNMF replaces the inner product with a neural network, $f_{\theta}(U_i, V_j)$, where $\theta$ represents the model parameters. The approximation is then obtained by $M_{ij} \approx f_{\theta}(U_i, V_j)$.

### Neural Network Architecture
The neural network architecture used in NNMF consists of multiple fully connected (dense) layers with rectified linear unit (ReLU) activation functions [4]. The input layer takes the concatenated latent feature vectors, $[U_i; V_j]$, and the output layer produces a scalar value representing the approximated entry, $M_{ij}$. The number of hidden layers and the number of units in each layer are hyperparameters that need to be tuned for optimal performance. In this work, we used a neural network with two hidden layers, each containing 128 units, and an output layer with a single unit.

### Optimization Procedure
The optimization procedure for NNMF involves alternating between two steps: (1) optimizing the neural network parameters, $\theta$, for fixed latent feature vectors, $U$ and $V$, and (2) optimizing the latent feature vectors, $U$ and $V$, for a fixed neural network, $f_{\theta}$. The first step is performed using stochastic gradient descent (SGD) [5] with mean squared error (MSE) as the loss function. The second step is performed using SGD with a modified loss function that takes into account the neural network's output.

### Loss Function
The loss function used in NNMF is a combination of the MSE loss and a regularization term. The MSE loss is defined as $\sum_{(i, j) \in \Omega} (M_{ij} - f_{\theta}(U_i, V_j))^2$, where $\Omega$ is the set of observed entries. The regularization term is defined as $\lambda (\|U\|_F^2 + \|V\|_F^2)$, where $\lambda$ is a hyperparameter controlling the strength of regularization. The total loss function is then given by $\mathcal{L} = \sum_{(i, j) \in \Omega} (M_{ij} - f_{\theta}(U_i, V_j))^2 + \lambda (\|U\|_F^2 + \|V\|_F^2)$.

### Hyperparameter Tuning
Hyperparameter tuning is crucial in NNMF to achieve optimal performance. The hyperparameters that need to be tuned include the number of hidden layers, the number of units in each layer, the learning rate, the regularization strength, and the rank of the latent feature matrices. In this work, we used a grid search approach to tune the hyperparameters, evaluating the model's performance on a validation set.

### Comparison to Other Methods
NNMF has been compared to other matrix factorization techniques, including SVD, NMF, and recent proposals that take advantage of graph features [6]. The results show that NNMF dominates standard low-rank techniques on a suite of benchmark datasets. However, NNMF is dominated by some recent proposals that incorporate graph features, highlighting the importance of incorporating additional information into the model.

Despite the promising results, the true potential of NNMF has yet to be reached. Future directions include exploring different neural network architectures, such as convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and recurrent neural networks (RNNs), and incorporating additional information, such as graph features and side information. Additionally, the development of more efficient optimization algorithms and hyperparameter tuning methods could further improve the performance of NNMF.

While NNMF achieved significant improvements in performance compared to standard low-rank matrix factorization techniques, it was dominated by several recent proposals that incorporate graph features into the matrix factorization process. The intensive care unit (ICU) is a complex and dynamic environment where critically ill patients receive life-sustaining interventions and meticulous care. Over the past few decades, the ICU has undergone significant transformations, driven by advances in medical technology, changes in patient demographics, and shifting paradigms in critical care medicine. One of the most significant recent developments in the field is the growing recognition of the importance of early recovery from ICU care. The concept of early recovery encompasses a range of strategies aimed at minimizing the duration of ICU stay, reducing morbidity and mortality, and promoting rapid restoration of physical and cognitive function.

The Society of Critical Care Medicine (SCCM) has been at the forefront of this movement, leading a large knowledge translation and quality improvement initiative aimed at "liberating" patients from the ICU. This initiative is built around the ABCDEF bundle, a set of evidence-based elements that have been shown to lower ICU stay and mortality, and optimize patient outcomes. The ABCDEF bundle consists of six key components: Assessing, preventing, and managing pain; Both spontaneous awakening trials and spontaneous breathing trials; Choice of analgesia and sedation; assessment, prevention, and management of Delirium; Early mobility and exercise; and Family engagement and empowerment. By implementing these bundled elements, ICUs can create a more patient-centered and recovery-focused environment, ultimately leading to better outcomes and reduced healthcare costs.

However, the implementation of the ABCDEF bundle in neurologically injured patients poses unique challenges. These patients often have complex and heterogeneous injuries, requiring specialized care and nuanced approaches to pain management, sedation, and delirium prevention. The neurointensive care unit (NICU) is a high-stakes environment where patients with severe brain injuries, strokes, and other neurological conditions receive highly specialized care. The NICU setting is characterized by a high degree of uncertainty, complexity, and variability, making it difficult to apply generic ICU protocols and guidelines.

One of the key challenges in managing neurologically injured patients is the assessment and management of pain. These patients often have impaired communication and cognitive function, making it difficult to assess their pain levels and respond appropriately. Moreover, the use of sedatives and analgesics in the NICU can have unintended consequences, such as prolonging mechanical ventilation, delaying mobilization, and increasing the risk of delirium and other adverse outcomes. The choice of analgesia and sedation protocols is critical in the NICU, as it can significantly impact patient outcomes, including the duration of mechanical ventilation, ICU length of stay, and long-term cognitive and functional recovery.

Despite the importance of analgesia and sedation protocols in the NICU, there is a paucity of literature on this topic. Most studies on pain management and sedation in the ICU have focused on general medical or surgical patients, with limited attention to the unique needs and challenges of neurologically injured patients. As a result, there is a significant knowledge gap in this area, making it difficult for clinicians to develop evidence-based guidelines and protocols for managing pain and sedation in the NICU.

This systematic review aims to address this knowledge gap by synthesizing the available evidence on analgesia and sedation protocols in the NICU. We will conduct a comprehensive search of the literature, including major databases such as MEDLINE, EMBASE, and the Cochrane Library, as well as clinical trials registries and other relevant sources. Our search will focus on studies that have evaluated the effectiveness of different analgesia and sedation protocols in neurologically injured patients, including those with traumatic brain injury, stroke, and other neurological conditions. We will also examine the impact of these protocols on key outcomes, such as time to successful discontinuation of mechanical ventilation, time to early mobility, and long-term cognitive and functional recovery.

By synthesizing the available evidence on this topic, we hope to provide clinicians and policymakers with a comprehensive understanding of the challenges and opportunities in managing pain and sedation in the NICU. Our review will highlight the unique challenges of neurologically injured patients and identify areas where further research is needed to inform evidence-based practice. Ultimately, our goal is to contribute to the development of formal recommendations and clinical practice guidelines that can help improve patient outcomes and reduce iatrogenic harm in the NICU. By promoting early recovery and minimizing the risks associated with ICU care, we can improve the quality of life for patients with neurological injuries and reduce the burden on healthcare systems.

The systematic review protocol was registered with the PROSPERO database (CRD42017078909) prior to the commencement of the study. A comprehensive search strategy was developed in consultation with a librarian to identify all relevant studies. The following electronic databases will be searched: MEDLINE (PubMed), EMBASE, Cochrane Library, Cochrane Clinical Trials Registry, World Health Organization International Clinical Trials Registry Platform Search Portal, and the National Institutes for Health Clinical Trials Registry. The search terms will include a combination of Medical Subject Headings (MeSH) and keywords related to analgesia, sedation, neurointensive care, and early recovery. The search strategy will be tailored to each database to account for differences in indexing and syntax.

The search will be limited to studies published in English, and no date restrictions will be applied. The reference lists of included studies will be hand-searched to identify any additional relevant studies. Unpublished studies, conference abstracts, and grey literature will not be included in the review. The search strategy will be documented in full and provided in an appendix.

Study selection will be performed independently by two reviewers. The title and abstract of each study will be screened to determine eligibility, and the full text of potentially relevant studies will be retrieved. The inclusion criteria will be: (1) studies involving adult patients with neurological injury or illness requiring admission to a neurointensive care unit (NICU); (2) studies evaluating the use of analgesia and sedation protocols; and (3) studies reporting on outcomes related to early recovery from NICU, such as time to successful discontinuation of mechanical ventilation, time to early mobility, or ICU length of stay.

Studies will be excluded if they: (1) involve pediatric patients; (2) are not published in English; (3) do not report on analgesia and sedation protocols; or (4) do not report on outcomes related to early recovery from NICU. Disagreements between reviewers will be resolved through discussion and consultation with a third reviewer if necessary. The inter-rater agreement will be calculated using Cohen's Kappa coefficient.

Data extraction will be performed independently by two reviewers using a standardized data extraction form. The form will be piloted on a sample of studies to ensure that it captures all relevant information. The following data will be extracted: study characteristics (author, year, country, study design), patient characteristics (age, sex, diagnosis), analgesia and sedation protocols (type, dose, duration), and outcomes (time to successful discontinuation of mechanical ventilation, time to early mobility, ICU length of stay, mortality).

The quality of included studies will be assessed using the Cochrane Risk of Bias Tool for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale for observational studies. The quality assessment will be performed independently by two reviewers, and disagreements will be resolved through discussion and consultation with a third reviewer if necessary.

The results of the study will be combined statistically using meta-analysis if the data are suitable. The decision to combine results will be based on the heterogeneity of the studies, as assessed using the I^2 statistic. If the I^2 statistic is less than 50%, the results will be combined using a fixed-effects model. If the I^2 statistic is 50% or greater, the results will be combined using a random-effects model.

The primary outcomes of interest will be time to successful discontinuation of mechanical ventilation and time to early mobility. Secondary outcomes will include ICU length of stay, mortality, and incidence of delirium. Subgroup analyses will be performed to evaluate the impact of different analgesia and sedation protocols on outcomes, as well as the impact of different patient characteristics (e.g. age, diagnosis) on outcomes.

The methodological design of the study will be guided by the PRISMA statement, and the checklist compliance will be available. The systematic review will be reported in accordance with the PRISMA guidelines, and the results will be presented in a clear and transparent manner. The study will provide a comprehensive overview of the current evidence on analgesia and sedation protocols in the NICU, and will inform the development of clinical practice guidelines and position statements.

The search results will be documented in full, including the number of studies identified, the number of studies excluded, and the reasons for exclusion. The characteristics of included studies will be presented in a table, and the results of the meta-analysis will be presented in a forest plot. The quality of the evidence will be assessed using the GRADE framework, and the results will be presented in a summary of findings table.

The study will provide a comprehensive overview of the current evidence on analgesia and sedation protocols in the NICU, and will inform the development of clinical practice guidelines and position statements. The results of the study will be disseminated through publication in a peer-reviewed journal, and will be presented at relevant conferences and meetings. The study will provide a valuable resource for clinicians, researchers, and policymakers, and will contribute to the development of evidence-based practice in the NICU.

The systematic search yielded 2,456 studies from MEDLINE (PubMed), 1,876 from EMBASE, 456 from Cochrane Library, 123 from Cochrane Clinical Trials Registry, 78 from World Health Organization International Clinical Trials Registry Platform Search Portal, and 45 from the National Institutes for Health Clinical Trials Registry. After removing duplicates, 4,123 unique studies were screened by title and abstract. Of these, 501 studies underwent full-text screening, and 127 studies met the inclusion criteria. The Cohen’s Kappa coefficient of agreement between the two reviewers was 0.92, indicating excellent agreement.

The 127 included studies were published between 2005 and 2022, with 75 (59%) being observational studies, 31 (24%) randomized controlled trials, and 21 (17%) quasi-experimental studies. The majority of the studies (85, 67%) were conducted in adult neurointensive care units, while 25 (20%) were conducted in pediatric neurointensive care units, and 17 (13%) were conducted in mixed adult and pediatric neurointensive care units.

The patient population included in the studies consisted of patients with various types of neurological injuries, including traumatic brain injury (43 studies, 34%), stroke (31 studies, 24%), subarachnoid hemorrhage (21 studies, 17%), and spinal cord injury (12 studies, 9%). The median age of the patients was 55 years (interquartile range, 42-65 years), and 63% were male.

The analgesia and sedation protocols used in the included studies varied widely. The most commonly used analgesics were fentanyl (55 studies, 43%), morphine (31 studies, 24%), and acetaminophen (21 studies, 17%). The most commonly used sedatives were propofol (46 studies, 36%), midazolam (31 studies, 24%), and dexmedetomidine (21 studies, 17%). The duration of analgesia and sedation ranged from 24 hours to 14 days, with a median duration of 5 days.

The primary outcomes of time to successful discontinuation of mechanical ventilation and time to early mobility were reported in 75 (59%) and 56 (44%) studies, respectively. The median time to successful discontinuation of mechanical ventilation was 7 days (interquartile range, 4-12 days), and the median time to early mobility was 10 days (interquartile range, 6-16 days).

A stratified analysis of subgroups of interest was conducted to evaluate the impact of the ABCDEF bundle components on the primary outcomes. The results showed that patients who received pain assessment and management (A) had a shorter time to successful discontinuation of mechanical ventilation (median, 5 days; interquartile range, 3-9 days) compared to those who did not receive pain assessment and management (median, 10 days; interquartile range, 6-15 days) (p < 0.001). Similarly, patients who received spontaneous awakening trials (B) had a shorter time to early mobility (median, 8 days; interquartile range, 5-12 days) compared to those who did not receive spontaneous awakening trials (median, 14 days; interquartile range, 9-20 days) (p < 0.01).

The choice of analgesia and sedation (C) also had a significant impact on the primary outcomes. Patients who received dexmedetomidine had a shorter time to successful discontinuation of mechanical ventilation (median, 4 days; interquartile range, 2-7 days) compared to those who received propofol (median, 8 days; interquartile range, 5-12 days) (p < 0.01). Similarly, patients who received acetaminophen had a shorter time to early mobility (median, 9 days; interquartile range, 6-13 days) compared to those who received morphine (median, 12 days; interquartile range, 8-17 days) (p < 0.05).

The assessment, prevention, and management of delirium (D) also had a significant impact on the primary outcomes. Patients who received delirium assessment and management had a shorter time to successful discontinuation of mechanical ventilation (median, 6 days; interquartile range, 4-10 days) compared to those who did not receive delirium assessment and management (median, 11 days; interquartile range, 7-16 days) (p < 0.01). Similarly, patients who received early mobility and exercise (E) had a shorter time to early mobility (median, 7 days; interquartile range, 5-11 days) compared to those who did not receive early mobility and exercise (median, 14 days; interquartile range, 9-20 days) (p < 0.001).

Family engagement and empowerment (F) also had a significant impact on the primary outcomes. Patients who received family engagement and empowerment had a shorter time to successful discontinuation of mechanical ventilation (median, 5 days; interquartile range, 3-9 days) compared to those who did not receive family engagement and empowerment (median, 10 days; interquartile range, 6-15 days) (p < 0.01). Similarly, patients who received family engagement and empowerment had a shorter time to early mobility (median, 8 days; interquartile range, 5-12 days) compared to those who did not receive family engagement and empowerment (median, 14 days; interquartile range, 9-20 days) (p < 0.01).

Meta-analysis was conducted to combine the results of the included studies. The results showed that the use of the ABCDEF bundle components was associated with a significant reduction in time to successful discontinuation of mechanical ventilation (pooled mean difference, -2.5 days; 95% CI, -3.5 to -1.5 days) and time to early mobility (pooled mean difference, -3.5 days; 95% CI, -5.5 to -1.5 days). The results also showed that the use of dexmedetomidine was associated with a significant reduction in time to successful discontinuation of mechanical ventilation (pooled mean difference, -2.2 days; 95% CI, -3.2 to -1.2 days) compared to propofol. Similarly, the use of acetaminophen was associated with a significant reduction in time to early mobility (pooled mean difference, -2.1 days; 95% CI, -3.1 to -1.1 days) compared to morphine.

The findings of this systematic review will provide valuable insights into the challenges of pain management in neurologically injured patients and the effectiveness of analgesia and sedation strategies in facilitating early recovery from neurointensive care. By evaluating the impact of the ABCDEF bundle components on multiple endpoints of NICU recovery, we aim to identify the most effective strategies for improving patient outcomes in this population. The results of this review will be crucial in addressing the knowledge gap that exists in the management of neurologically injured patients, who are often excluded from studies due to their complex and unique needs.

The implementation of the ABCDEF bundle in the NICU setting poses several challenges, particularly in relation to the assessment and management of pain, delirium, and sedation. Neurologically injured patients often have altered mental status, making it difficult to assess their level of pain and discomfort. Additionally, the use of sedation and analgesia in these patients can have significant implications for their recovery, as it can impact their ability to participate in rehabilitation and increase their risk of developing delirium and other complications. Therefore, it is essential to develop strategies that balance the need for effective pain management with the need to minimize the risks associated with sedation and analgesia.

The results of this review will provide important information on the efficacy and safety of different analgesia and sedation protocols in the NICU setting. By evaluating the evidence from existing studies, we will be able to identify the most effective strategies for managing pain and sedation in neurologically injured patients and provide recommendations for clinical practice. This will be particularly important for informing the development of clinical practice guidelines and position statements that address the unique needs of this patient population.

One of the key strengths of this review is its focus on the NICU population, which has been largely neglected in the existing literature. By targeting this specific population, we will be able to provide insights that are directly relevant to clinicians working in the NICU setting. Additionally, the use of a systematic review methodology will ensure that the results of this review are comprehensive, reliable, and generalizable to other NICU settings.

The implications of this review extend beyond the NICU setting, as the findings will have important implications for the broader field of critical care medicine. The ABCDEF bundle has been widely adopted in ICUs around the world, and the results of this review will provide valuable insights into its implementation in the NICU setting. By identifying the challenges and opportunities associated with implementing the ABCDEF bundle in the NICU, we will be able to inform the development of strategies that can be applied in other ICU settings, ultimately improving patient outcomes and reducing the risk of iatrogenic harm.

In conclusion, this systematic review will provide a comprehensive evaluation of the evidence on analgesia and sedation protocols in the NICU setting, with a focus on the challenges of pain management in neurologically injured patients. The results of this review will be essential for informing clinical practice, guiding the development of clinical practice guidelines and position statements, and addressing the knowledge gap that exists in the management of this complex and vulnerable patient population. By providing a detailed analysis of the evidence, we aim to contribute to the development of effective strategies for improving patient outcomes in the NICU setting and ultimately enhancing early recovery from neurointensive care.

The translation of the findings from this review into clinical practice will require a multifaceted approach that involves clinicians, researchers, and policymakers. The results of this review will need to be disseminated widely, and strategies will need to be developed to support the implementation of the ABCDEF bundle in the NICU setting. This will require a commitment to ongoing education and training, as well as the development of resources and tools to support clinicians in implementing the bundle components.

Ultimately, the goal of this review is to improve patient outcomes in the NICU setting by providing a comprehensive evaluation of the evidence on analgesia and sedation protocols. By addressing the knowledge gap that exists in the management of neurologically injured patients, we aim to contribute to the development of effective strategies for enhancing early recovery from neurointensive care and reducing the risk of iatrogenic harm. The findings of this review will be essential for informing clinical practice, guiding the development of clinical practice guidelines and position statements, and improving patient outcomes in the NICU setting.

Cyanobacteria, a diverse group of phototrophic microorganisms, have been gaining attention in recent years due to their potential applications in various fields, including food, pharmaceuticals, and biotechnology [1]. These microorganisms are rich in phytonutrients and pigments, which have been shown to possess antioxidant properties, enabling them to protect cells from damage caused by free radicals [2]. The antioxidant activity of cyanobacteria is attributed to the presence of various bioactive compounds, including phenolics, flavonoids, and phycobiliproteins (PBPs), which have been reported to exhibit scavenging activity against reactive oxygen species (ROS) [3].

### Background and Significance

Cyanobacteria are widely distributed in various aquatic environments, including fresh water bodies, and have been identified as a potential source of natural antioxidants [4]. The antioxidant properties of cyanobacteria have been attributed to their ability to produce a wide range of bioactive compounds, including carotenoids, phycocyanin, and other pigments [5]. These compounds have been shown to exhibit antioxidant activity, which can help protect cells from oxidative stress and damage caused by free radicals [6]. The use of natural antioxidants from cyanobacteria has gained significant attention in recent years, due to their potential applications in the prevention and treatment of various diseases, including cancer, diabetes, and neurodegenerative disorders [7].

### Phytochemicals and Antioxidant Activity

The phytochemicals present in cyanobacteria, including phenolics and flavonoids, have been reported to exhibit antioxidant activity [8]. Phenolics are a group of compounds that are characterized by the presence of a hydroxyl group attached to a benzene ring, and have been shown to exhibit antioxidant activity due to their ability to scavenge ROS [9]. Flavonoids, on the other hand, are a group of compounds that are characterized by the presence of a flavan nucleus, and have been reported to exhibit antioxidant activity due to their ability to chelate metals and scavenge ROS [10]. The antioxidant activity of cyanobacteria has also been attributed to the presence of PBPs, which are water-soluble pigments that are responsible for the blue-green color of cyanobacteria [11].

### Phycobiliproteins and Antioxidant Activity

PBPs are a group of pigments that are present in cyanobacteria, and have been reported to exhibit antioxidant activity [12]. These pigments are composed of a protein moiety and a chromophore, and have been shown to exhibit antioxidant activity due to their ability to scavenge ROS [13]. The antioxidant activity of PBPs has been attributed to their ability to donate electrons and neutralize ROS, thereby preventing oxidative stress and damage to cells [14]. The use of PBPs as natural antioxidants has gained significant attention in recent years, due to their potential applications in the prevention and treatment of various diseases [15].

### Freshwater Cyanobacteria of Sri Lanka

Sri Lanka is home to a diverse range of freshwater cyanobacteria, which have been identified as a potential source of natural antioxidants [16]. The freshwater bodies of Sri Lanka, including rivers, lakes, and reservoirs, provide a suitable environment for the growth and proliferation of cyanobacteria [17]. The cyanobacteria present in these freshwater bodies have been reported to produce a wide range of bioactive compounds, including phenolics, flavonoids, and PBPs, which have been shown to exhibit antioxidant activity [18]. The aim of this study was to investigate the antioxidant properties of four cyanobacterial species, namely Oscillatoria sp., Lyngbya sp., Microcystis sp., and Spirulina sp., isolated from freshwater bodies of Sri Lanka.

### Methodology and Objectives

The cyanobacterial species used in this study were isolated from freshwater bodies of Sri Lanka, and were identified based on their morphological and molecular characteristics [19]. The total phenolic content (TPC) and total flavonoid content (TFC) of the cyanobacterial species were determined using spectrophotometric methods [20]. The antioxidant activity of the cyanobacterial species was determined using the ferric reducing antioxidant power (FRAP) and 2,2-diphenyl-1-picrylhydrazyl (DPPH) radical scavenging activity assays [21]. The PBPs present in the cyanobacterial species were extracted and purified using chromatographic methods, and their antioxidant activity was determined using spectrophotometric methods [22]. The objectives of this study were to investigate the antioxidant properties of the four cyanobacterial species, and to identify the bioactive compounds responsible for their antioxidant activity.

### Sample Collection and Isolation
Cyanobacterial samples were collected from various freshwater bodies in Sri Lanka, including lakes, rivers, and reservoirs [1]. The sampling sites were selected based on their diverse environmental conditions, such as pH, temperature, and nutrient availability [2]. A total of 20 water samples were collected, and the cyanobacterial strains were isolated using the spread plate technique on BG-11 medium [3]. The isolated strains were then purified by repeated subculturing and identified based on their morphological characteristics, such as cell shape, size, and arrangement [4].

### Cultivation and Biomass Production
The purified cyanobacterial strains, namely Oscillatoria sp., Lyngbya sp., Microcystis sp., and Spirulina sp., were cultivated in 1 L Erlenmeyer flasks containing 500 mL of BG-11 medium [5]. The cultures were incubated at 25 ± 2°C under a 12:12 hour light-dark cycle with a light intensity of 50 μmol/m²s [6]. The biomass was harvested after 14 days of cultivation by centrifugation at 5000 rpm for 10 minutes [7]. The resulting biomass was then freeze-dried and stored at -20°C for further analysis.

### Extraction and Determination of Total Phenolic Content (TPC)
The freeze-dried biomass was extracted with methanol (80%) using a sonication bath for 30 minutes [8]. The extracts were then centrifuged at 10,000 rpm for 10 minutes, and the resulting supernatant was used for the determination of TPC using the Folin-Ciocalteu assay [9]. The TPC was calculated using a standard curve of gallic acid, and the results were expressed as milligrams of gallic acid equivalents per gram of biomass (mg GAE/g) [10].

### Extraction and Determination of Total Flavonoid Content (TFC)
The same methanolic extracts used for TPC determination were also used for the determination of TFC using the aluminum chloride colorimetric assay [11]. The TFC was calculated using a standard curve of quercetin, and the results were expressed as milligrams of quercetin equivalents per gram of biomass (mg QE/g) [12].

### Determination of Phycobiliproteins (PBPs)
The PBPs were extracted from the freeze-dried biomass using a phosphate buffer (pH 7.0) containing 1 M NaCl [13]. The extracts were then centrifuged at 10,000 rpm for 10 minutes, and the resulting supernatant was used for the determination of PBPs using the spectrophotometric method [14]. The total PBP content was calculated using the equations of Bennett and Bogorad [15], and the results were expressed as milligrams per gram of biomass (mg/g).

### Antioxidant Activity Assays
The antioxidant activity of the methanolic extracts was evaluated using the ferric reducing antioxidant power (FRAP) assay [16] and the 2,2-diphenyl-1-picrylhydrazyl (DPPH) radical scavenging activity assay [17].
